summary: The respondent was charged under section 7 read with section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for an offence under section 7 of the Act. The Food Inspector, P.W. 468 in the case of Food Inspector, Delhi, in his report, stated that the Food Inspector had reported that the sample was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kajus. The Food inspector, P.Ws. 468 and 468, however, did not state that the sample had been adulterated. The Food Inspectors, P.w. 468, however stated that the sample of Kajus was adulterated due by insect infestation. The Food Analyst, P. W. 468, in his opinion, stated that it was adulterated due the insect infiltated pieces of Kajuus to the extent of 21.9% and that the sample should be sent for analysis to the Public Analyst. The Food Controller, Delhi, on receipt of the report of the Public Analyst, sent the sample to the Public analyst for analysis. The Public Analyst, Delhi, after examination of the sample, sent the report to the Public Health Officer, Delhi, who, in turn, sent the same to the Public Food Analyst for analysis. On receipt of the said report, the Public Analyst sent the report, which was received by the Public Analyst on the same day. The Food Crl. A. No. 539 of 1984, Crl. A No. 539/84, Crl.A. No. 540/85, Crl. M.P. No. 468/85, and the report of Public Analyst, New Delhi, were received by the Food Inspector, on the same date. The Public analyst, Delhi, sent the samples to the Public Laboratory for analysis. After the receipt of the reports of the Public analyst, the Public analyst sent the report of analysis to the Central Food Laboratory, New Delhi. The Public Health Officer sent the report on the same evening to the Public Medical Officer, Delhi. The Food Medical Officer, New Delhi sent the report under section 16 of The Act to the Public Crl. A.. No. 539 /85. The Public Medical Officer sent the sample for analysis to Central Food Laboratory. The Public Crl.A., No. 539./85 was received by him on the same night. The Public Chemical Officer, Delhi sent the sample of the sample to Central Food Analyst, NewDelhi, for analysis. In the meanwhile, the Food Inspector sent the sample again to the Public Chemical Officer for analysis. Thereafter, the Public Health Inspector sent the report with the report that the sample sent by the Public analyst was adulterated due, and that the report was received by it on the same morning. The Public Food Inspector, New Delhi forwarded the report to Central Food Crl.A.. No. 540 of 1985, Crl. P. No. 541 of 1985, and the Public Analyst to send the report to him. The Public Prosecutor, Delhi, forwarded the report of Food Inspector to the Central Public Laboratory, NewDelhi. The Public Laboratory, Delhi, received the report of Central Food Laboratory on the same very day, and sent the report again to the Central Government, New Delhi on the same time. The Public Prosecution, on receipt thereof, filed a complaint against the accused under section 7 and 16 of the Act, before the Court of Sessions. The trial Court, after considering the evidence, convicted the accused under sections 7 and 16 read with section 17 of the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . The High Court, in appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in its inter est in its inter se judgment.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order. The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case cannot be drawn. HELD : (i) The presumption under para 3(2) could not be drawn against him. The presumption under paragraph 3(2), could not be taken into account. [901 B] (ii) The presumption in the case of a person is not drawn unless a series of transactions by him of sale are proved against him. If that be so, then he is an agriculturist and it is easy to see that the evidence which was led before the Magistrate is not concocted to set up a false defence. [902 C] (iii) The presumption is not drawn against a person. The presumption is that he is an agricultural and it is difficult to see that he is a dealer. [903 D] (iv) The presumption of innocence can not be drawn. The presumption in this case cannot be taken into consideration because the presumption is not based upon them. [904 D] (v) The presumption against the appellant under para 3 (2) could be drawn against the appellant. [905 D] (vi) The presumption that the appellant is an agriculturist is not based on the evidence. The presumption against him is not drawn.

The appellant was a monthly tenant in respect of a premises in suit. The respondent was a monthly tenants. The appellant was a tenant from month to month under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The respondent paid rent to the Receiver in the years 1925 and 1926. The appellant paid the rent to the receiver in the years 1926 and 1926. In 1926 the respondent filed a suit for ejectment of the appellant on the ground that the appellant was a permanent tenant under section 106 and that the tenancy was determined by a proper notice to quit. The trial judge held that the appellant had no permanent right in the land and that the respondent was not a tenant from the month to month. The High Court, on appeal, held that the respondent had no permanent rights in the land by prescription or otherwise and that by reason of the payment of rent to the appellant the defendant became a tenant from year to month under the provisions of section 106, Transfer of Property (Amendment) Act, 1929. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the respondent 's tenancy was one from month to months under section 106, transfer of property by payment and acceptance of rent from the defendant, and the appellant became a tenant on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease. The respondent 's lease was one from year to year under section 106 Transfer of Property. The appellant became a permanent tenant from month and to month under that section, the respondent became a tenant of the land from month to monthly under the provisions Of section 106, and the respondent became the tenant from month. The appellant could not be said to be a tenant from a month to month as he was not a permanent tenant. The respondent had no right to the land by virtue of the payment to the Receiver. The appellant had no right in the property by prescription or else. The respondent could not be deemed to be a permanent tenant in respect thereof. The respondent having been a permanent tenant, the appellant became the tenant on the expiry of the period of the lease.

The appellant assessee, a third party, filed a return of income for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards, in respect of assessment years 1964 66 onwards, and claimed that the income derived by it from the sale of certain properties was exempt from tax under section 138(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee and held that the income was exempt from income tax under section 139(1)(a) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of the exemption under section 138 (1)(b). The Appellate Tribunal, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee. The High Court, on a reference, held that since the assessee had not produced the original documents, the onus was on the assessee to prove that the income had been received by him during the assessment proceedings before an Income Tax Officer after April 1, 1964 in respect of the assessment years, and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under section 138 of the Act had no relation to the power of the court to summon the production of documents from the income tax authorities after April 1. 1964 in respect thereof. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after the repeal of section 137 of the Act by Act V of 1964, there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a court to summon production of documents in a court on being summoned by it without the approval of the Commissioner of Income Tax, and that, the finality attached thereto to the order of the Commis sioner under section 138, could not be called in question in any court of law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finality attached to the order passed by the Commissioner under section 138 is limited to the cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the section is called for by any person, other than a court of law by a judicial order. The finality attached thereto is not conclusive of the rights of the parties to the proceedings before the Income Tax Officer. [562C D] 1.2 The finality attached under section 138 to the order is, thus, restricted to the cases which are pending before the court when the court, by a judicial orders, requires the production of the record, considered relevant by it for decision of a case pending before it. [562D] 1.3 The finality attached by the order of Commissioner under section 139 of the Act is, thus restricted to the case where the information, etc. as envisaged by the section, is called for in a court.

The appellant was the father of the minor daughter of the respondent. He made a gift of his properties including immovable property to the minor. The respondent 's father died in 1947. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties. The respondent filed a suit claiming that the appellant had gifted his properties to his minor daughter and that the appellant was not entitled to any share in the properties. He also claimed that the appellant should be given the possession of the properties as the guardian of his minor daughter. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in second appeal held that the appellant could not have made a declaration of gift and taken possession on behalf of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for after the celebration of marriage a husband could receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father was living. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant 's father had taken over possession of the property as the guardian and as the gift was by a registered deed no question in this behalf can arise. HELD: (i) The appellant 's mother was living at the time of the gift in the house of his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who had no guardian of the property in existence, was capable under Muhammadan law to accept the gift and take possession on behalf the minor. [550 E] (ii) The appellant was not a guardian of the minor and the gift was made by a registered document. The gift was by the registered deed no doubt created a gift and it was not a gift by a registered instrument. [550 F] (iii) The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's mother when the gift is from the husband to his minor wife and when the minor 's father and father are not alive and there is no executor of the one or the other. [550 G] (iv) The question is whether possession can he given to the husband 's mother if the gift is by a registered Deed. [550 A] (v) The question of title cannot arise because possession was not delivered to the wife. The question is one of fact. The question of possession is one of law. The question whether the possession can be taken by the wife 'S ' mother when the gifted is from the wife to his minor son and when the father is living. [550 C] (vi) The question as to whether possession can only be given to a minor is one of facts. The question as regards the title to the property can arise only if the minor 'S ' is living at the date of the gift. [550 D] (vii) The question regarding the title to property can arise when possession is not delivered to a minor. If the father is alive, without delivery of possession to the father, the gift would have been complete under Muhammadan Law and it seems impossible to hold that by handing over the deed to his wife, the gift will have been complete. [550 H] (viii) The question that the appellant has to establish that the appellant is the mother of the minor is one and the same. [550 B] (ix) The question about the title to a minor and the completion of the gift for his benefit is the sole consideration. The intention to make the gift was clear and manifest because it was made by the deed which was registered and handed over by Mammotty to his mother in Law and accepted by her on behalf of minor. There can be no question that there was a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammotties and to transfer the property to the donee. [550G H] (x) The question for determination is whether possession could be given to wife 's father when the gift was from the husband 'S ' to his minor child.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, was enacted to provide for better administration of Hindu Religious and Charitable Institutions and endowments in the State of Madras. Section 76(1) provides that the Commissioner shall determine the fee for the audit of the accounts of every religious institution, the annual income of which is to be determined, and the amount to be paid to the Commissioner annually. Section 76 (2) provides that every religious institution shall from the income derived by it, pay to the Commissioner quarterly such contribution not exceeding five per centum of its income as may be prescribed. The Commissioner has to determine the fee payable by the religious institution. The Commissioner is to determine the fees for the benefit of the services rendered by the religious institutions. The Commissioner may, in his discretion, determine the fee. The Commissioner, however, may not under section 76(2) impose a flat rate of audit fee on the religious institutions governed by the provisions of the Act. The Commissioner 's power to determine the amount of contribution is not circumscribed by the provisions contained in the Act. Section 76 of the Act provides that the Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, fix the fee payable in respect of any religious institution. Section 76 provides that the amount of the contribution shall be paid to Commissioner annually by the Commissioner annually for meeting the cost of audit of the institution. The High Court has not investigated the question whether there is a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services are to be rendered. The High court has not investigated whether there is any reasonable relation between expenditure incurred by Government for providing service and the amounts proposed to be collected by the Commissioner. The High Courts have not investigated the questions whether there is reasonable relation between these expenditure and the expenditure. The High courts have not investigated whether the audit fee demanded is in truth for meeting the expenses of auditing the accounts of the religious institutions, and the High Court has failed to determine whether the audit fees demanded are in truth or not. The High. Court has not determined whether the audit Fees demanded are in reality for meeting the expenditure incurred for audit of the religious institution, and the question whether the audit is in truth or in substance for meeting the costs of auditing the account of the religious endowment is a decision on one of the material questions arising in that case.

The appellant, a contemner, filed a suit against the respondent for committing contempt of the High Court. The respondent contended that the notice was not a notice as no appeal lies to this Court under section 19 of the Act from an order rejecting the prayer of the appellant for the issuance of notice as no such appeal lies to the Supreme Court under section 20 of the Act. The High Court held that the notice issued by the appellant was not a valid notice as no notice was issued to the appellant as no appeal lay to this Court. The High court, however, held that the proceeding was not barred by section 20 of Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal as a matter of right from the order rejecting the request of the appellant to drop the proceeding. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High court is set aside. The proceeding is initiated under section 17 by issuance of a notice. The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Court affecting the right of the party aggrieved. [512C] 2. The order passed by the High Court will be without jurisdiction if it is in violation of section 20. If the alleged contemner in response to the notice appears before the High court and asked it to drop the proceedings on the ground of its being barred under section 20, the mere initiation of the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appeal against as a matter Of right under section 19. [513D E] 3. The order dated 2nd April, 1975 is set aside and the proceeding is directed to be proceeded with. [514E] 4. The appeal is disposed of as not maintainable.

The appellant was prosecuted for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The appellant contended that section 6(1 A) of the Act was repealed by the 1952 Act and that the repeal of the 1952 Act did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the 1952. The High Court held that the repeal was not retrospective and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the amended section 6( 1 A) of Act XVII of 1933. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the amending Act of 1949 was repealed by section 4 of the 1952, and the repeal of section 6(l A) was not retrospective. The amending Act of 1948 was repealed by Act XLVIII of 1952, and therefore, the repeal of it was not retrospective, and the appellant was entitled to the benefits of the amended sections 6(1A) and 6(1 B) of the 1952. Held, further, that the amendment of the 1952 Acts was not retrospective in operation and the repeal did not affect any continuance of the amending Act. The amending Acts were not retrospective in nature and were not retrospective. Held, also, that the amendments made by the amending Act were retrospective in operation. The amending provisions were not retrospective and the repeal was in operation only when the amending Act was repealed. The amending sections 6(lA) and 7 of the 1952 were not retrospective, but were retrospective in nature. The amending section was not retrospective but was retrospective in operation, and the amending Act continued to be on the statute book even after the amending Act, and therefore the repeal did affect the continuance or the continuance of any of the amending Acts.

The appellant was the owner of certain properties in the State of West Bengal. The properties were sold and the appellant was the purchaser of the properties. The appellant filed a suit for the reopening of the decrees and for restoration of possession of the properties to the deities of the deity. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant was a mere benamidar for her husband Aghore in respect of the purchase of Ga Schedule properties in court sale, and that the sale was a fictitious transaction. HELD : (i) The sale was not a benami transaction. The sale was a benami transaction and the sale was not void. The sale in favour of Oramba Sundari was not annulled, and in case of default in payment of any one of the instalments, the properties were returned to the decreeholder purchaser purchaser. The sale itself was not annulled. [991 B] (ii) The sale itself is not annulled, but in case of a sale, the property is returned to the judgment debtor purchaser. The property is returned by the decree holder purchaser. The decree holder is not a mere benamidars for another person in respect of a decree. The sale is not void. [992 C] (iii) The sale is a benami transaction, and the sale is not annulled. The sale proceeds are not the sale proceeds of the property. The sale does not amount to a benami transaction; it is only a benami transaction which is void. [995 C] (iv) The sale proceeds of a benami transaction are not the property purchased by the decreeholder and there is no proof of the decree holder being in possession of the property when the decree is reopened. [995 D] (v) The sale of the property is not a benami sale. The sale of property is not void, and the property is sold only for the purpose and so far as it is necessary to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act, namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Act. [995 E] (vi) The sale in the instant case was not a fictitious transaction and the High Courts were not justified in interfering with the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below. [995 F] (vii) The sale did not amount to benami transaction. [995 G] (viii) The sale deed was not a genuine transaction. The High Court was right in holding that the sale did not constitute a benami transaction but was a benami transactions. [995 B] (ix) The sale by the appellant was not a sham transaction. The appellant was not the purchaser of any of the instalments. The sale did therefore not amount to the benami transaction.

The appellant was the owner of a property in which the respondent was the owner. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract of sale of the property. The appellant contended that the respondent was not a transferee of the decree and that the respondent had no right to apply for leave under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and held that the respondent could not be said to be transferees of the decree by an assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, Rule 16 of the Civil Procedure Code. The High court held that the appellant was not a 'transferee ' within the meaning Of Order XXI, r. 16 of the C.P.C. and that the appellant could not claim to be transferees. The High. Court also held that the transfer in writing of a property which is the subject matter of a suit without in terms transferring the decree passed or to be passed in the suit in relation to that property does not entitle the transferee to apply for the leave under Order 21, rule 16. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the respondent should be permitted under Order XXI Rule 16 of C.P.,C. to execute the decree passed in future. The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that the language of Order XXI Rule 17(1) of the C..P.C., does not exclude the application of Order XXI rule 16. The words 'decree holder ' must be construed in the light of the context in which they occur and the context in the context in Which they occur. The words of Order XXI are not intended to be construed in a narrow sense and are not intended as meaning a decree holder. The words in Order XXI, Rules 16 and 16 are intended to be interpreted in the light and context of the context. The words are intended to convey the meaning of the words in the context of the particular case. The words used in the context are intended to indicate the intention of the legislature and the context of each case. The context in which the words are used is the same as the context in question in the context.

The respondent was a manufacturer of steel doors, windows, sashes and other goods. The respondent submitted a tender for providing and fixing the windows and the windows in a specified building. The respondent accepted the tender and the contract was for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount of Rs. 1,00,000. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. The High court held that the respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling window and door leaves and sashes etc. and entered into a contract for "sale of windows" and to promote sale of its manufactured goods undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that services. The High. Court held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted: one for providing doors and windows and another for the labour charges in fixing the windows. The contract was for "fixing" certain articles made by a manufacturer and the contract for the sale of its finished products was one of work and labour. The High 'Court held that the contracts were not "sale of doors and windows" and that the contract did not fall within the definition of "sale of goods". The High Court further held that the appellant was not entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the "invoice" for payment made out by the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The contract was a works contract and not a contract for sale of windows and for rendering service in connection with the installation of the windows. [505 H] (2) The contract is a contract whose main object is the transfer of the property in and the delivery of the possession of a chattel as a chattel to the buyer. The contract may be for work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials used in the execution thereof. The contract is not a contract of sale of property but a combination of two distinct and separate contracts. The contract of sale is a contract of work and not a sale of service. [507 H] (3) The contract may also be for work and labour and the contract is not rendered under a separate contract or is the service shown to be rendered customarily or generally as incidental to the execution of the contract of sale. [508 H] (4) The question whether the contract is one for work and Labour or one for the sale or the sale of goods for consideration, is a mixed question of fact and law. The test in each case is whether the object of the party sought to be taxed is that the chattel as chattel passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection with installation are under a separate contracts or are incidental to the completion of the work of sale. In the present case, the specifications of the windows were set out in the contract. The primary undertaking of the respondent was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows. It was not the service shown in the contract that the windows were rendered customarily and generally as incidental. [509 H] (5) The question of the contract was whether the contract was a sale of windows or not. If the windows were not properly "fixed" the contract would not be complete, and the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [510 H] (6) The question as to whether the contract in question was one of works contract or not was a mixed question.

The appellant was charged with the offence of cheating under section 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellant was an agent of the foreign company and had entered into a contract with the foreign company for sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The appellant was charged under section 420 read with section 511 Indian Penal Code for cheating and for cheating. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court, however, acquitted the appellant on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had committed the offence of criminal conspiracy. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The report of the police was lodged with the police against the appellant. It was lodged by Ram Avtar with the police. The part which was attributed to Raj Kumar Agarwalla was that he was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought the said goods. The part was attributed to him because it was the case of the prosecution itself that he was an agent. The part attributed to Raj Kr. Agarwalla was the case that he was not present along with Shankar Lal when the former brought the goods. The fact that the appellant did not want to be present at the time of the commission of the offence of the offence was not a material fact. [279E F] The report of Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agarwal. The part of which was attributed by the prosecution was that he had been present along with the Shanker Lal when he brought the said article. The part that was attributed to the appellant because it was his case that he had not been present at the place of the commission. The part ascribed to Raj Kumar is that he was also present along with him. The part assigned to Raj Kumar was that he did not appear at the place. The part entrusted to Raj Kumar, Agarwalla was also that he was the same person who was present along alongwith Shanker Lal when his earlier brought the article. The parts attributed to Raj Kishore were that he was himself present along with his brother Shankar Lal when he took the article.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of Kerala, was a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Bihar and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways. He was a commuters of the Indian Railway. He was allotted a railway quarter in the State. He was served with a notice dated 6.6.1981 under section 6 of the Railway Act, 1950, calling upon him to show cause why he should not be punished for contempt of court. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country were owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties was not available. The petitioner denied the allegation and stated that no accident had taken place on account for defective bridges and had pointed out that the accident of June 6, 1981 on a river bridge in the Bihar State was attributable to this factor only. The petitioner further stated that the accident had taken out of the railway premises and that the accident was attributable to the traffic on the road. The petitioner also denied the allegation that no accident has taken place on the ground that the accident took place on account of defective bridges and has pointed out that it was a case of defective bridges. The petitioner, however, denied the allegation. The petitioner filed a counter affidavit and denied the allegation of the allegation. In the counter affidavit the respondents denied the allegation in the counter affidavit and stated that the petitioner had not been able to perform the constitutional obligations by the railways. The petitioner stated that the Railways had no authority to do so. The petitioner contended that the Railways were not entitled to maintain an action like this. The petitioner relied on the decision of this Court in Shaw vs Director, Public Prosecution, and urged that the petitioner was not entitled to the relief claimed. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner has maintained that he has been denied the allegation, and that the Railways have denied the allegation made in the counter affidavits. [331E] 2. The petitioner had maintained that he had been negligent in the discharge of his duties and that he had pointed out the accident of the road and that the accidents took place on the road and the accident took out of the railways premises. The petitioner was not able to perform his duties as Judges. The petitioner could not be said to have been negligent in discharge of his duty as Judges. [332F] 3. The petitioner 's case is rather that this Court has worked out the improvements referred to in the counteraffidavit and in the decision. The respondents have denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to the stand taken in the writ petition. [334F] 4. The petitioner is entitled to demand that the State shall provide adequate facilities and create and maintain an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. [335G] 5. The petitioner cannot be said to be negligent in discharge his duty as the Judges of the Court and the Administration would rise to the necessity of the occasion and take it as a challenge to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. [337H] 6. The quality of the service should improve. [338H] 7. The quality and the capacity of the service must improve. [330H] 8. The quality is of the nature of the service. The quality has to be maintained. The quality cannot be maintained. [330A] 8. It is only in a country of that order that the common man will have his voice heard. [330B] 9. The quality in the service should be maintained. It is not necessary that the common person should be a citizen of this country. [330C] 10. The quality should improve. The quality may be of the quality of the services.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. The lands were acquired by the State of Bombay for the purpose of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958. The appellants filed applications for restoration of the lands to the State of Maharashtra. The applications were dismissed by the Tribunal. The appellants then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal. In the High Court the appellants contended that the applications for restoration were barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits and to record its decision even though there was default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal. The Tribunal had not power to dismiss the appeal for non prosecuting the appeal. [143 G] (ii) The Tribunal was right in taking the view that the applications were barred by time. The Tribunal was not right in dismissing the applications. [143 C] (iii) The Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the application of the appellants. The Tribunal committed no error of law. [143 E] (iv) The Tribunal has no power to reject an appeal for failure to comply with the provisions of Regulation 21. The Tribunal has power to dismiss it for non prosecution. The Tribunal is not bound to decide the appeals on merits. [143 F] (v) The Tribunal is bound to decide an appeal on merits even though there is default on the side of the appellant. [143 A] (vi) The Tribunal 's order dismissing the appeals was not correct. [143 D] (vii) The Tribunal acted in an erroneous way and did not have the power to dismiss appeals. The Tribunal 'has no power to do so. [143 B] (viii) The Tribunal, in the instant case, committed an error in dismissing the appeals. [143 H] (ix) The Tribunal failed to exercise its jurisdiction under Regulation 21.

The appellant 's father was the Mahant of a temple in the village of Telibandha. The Mahant was appointed as the manager of the temple by the Collector of Telipatnam. The appellant 's case was that the temple was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandraji as early as 1857 by the Collector. The appellant claimed that the temple belonged to the temple and was given possession of it as the manager. The appellant contended that the temple had been dedicated to the deity in the temple by a Patha in 1857 and that the temple could not be used for the temple. The trial court held that the dedication was proper and that the appellant was entitled to succeed. The High Court held that the appellant 's claim was not established. The High court also held that the temple did not belong to the temple. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the appellant had not been given any proprietary interest in the village. The fact that the appellant used to credit the income from Telibandha to the Gharu Khata which was maintained for the general expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication. The fact, therefore, that the appellant did not have any proprietary interest therein was not relevant. The fact therefore that the appellant continued to be the manager of a temple was not relevant for the purpose of the suit. The fact however, that the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 was made by the Collector in 1857 as alleged in the plaint had not been established.

The appellant was a tenant of a premises in which the respondent was a tenant. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of nonpayment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the respondent had waived his right to sub let the premises. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court affirmed the decree. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The respondent 's suit was brought under section 13(i)(e) which provides that the protection of the Act is available to a tenant who has been in occupation of the premises for a period of not less than one year. The respondent was not a tenant of the appellant and the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 13 (1)(e). [227 D E] (ii) The respondent ' s right of the appellant to sue for ejectment on a ground of subletting being a personal right for his benefit, the landlord must be taken to have waived it as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant to sub let and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 13 (i)(e).

The respondent Board was constituted under the Maharashtra State Electricity Board Act, 1956. The Board was constituted in the year 1976. The Board made regulations for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of the Act. The regulations were made in exercise of the powers conferred by the Act. In the year 1976 the Board made regulations to conduct examinations and to conduct the examinations. The regulations made by the Board were published in the official gazette on January 1, 1977. The regulations provided for the conduct of examinations and the procedure to be followed by the Board. The regulations also provided for the procedure to conduct examinations. The Regulations were made in the year 1977. The Board issued a notice to the respondent Board to show cause why the regulations should not be made applicable to the respondent. The respondent Board filed its objections. The Board filed its reply. The Board did not apply its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The Board, however, did not apply their mind to the fact that the Board was acting in conducting the examinations and dealing with the use of unfair means at the final examination. The Board also did not apply the mind to the factual position. The Board then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the regulations. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The Board preferred a Letters Patent Appeal. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed it. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Board that the regulations were not applicable to the facts of the case since the Act, Regulations and the Resolutions empowered the Divisional Board and its Standing Committee to deal with the use and conduct of unfair means in the examination. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Regulations and the resolutions empowered the Divisional Boards and the Standing Committee to make regulations for the conduct and conduct of examinations. The Board had the power to make regulations to conduct the examination and to deal with any of the matters in which the Board or the Divisional Board may deal. The Regulations and Resolutions empowered the Zonal Board and its standing committee to deal with use of unfair methods at final examinations including fabrication of documents issued by the Board as an integral part of the power of the Divisional Board. The Regulations, and the resolutions were made in accordance with the provisions of law. [799E F] 1.2 The Regulations and resolutions were made after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State Board at Bombay and before the moderators ' mark sheets were taken out to Pune to feed the computer. It was not open to the High Court under article 226 to itself evaluate the evidence and to interfere with the finding and to quash the impugned notification. [798F G] 1.3 The Regulations and Resolution were made after scrutiny by the authorities in the office and the moderators ' marks were taken out from the record. The Board 's report was accepted by the Board and the Board was directed to take action against the erring examinees to maintain the educational standard. [797F G] 2.1 The Board was not justified in taking the view that the Board, parents or guardians were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication was done at the instance of either the examinees or their parents or guardians. [795G] 2.2 The Board was also not justified in considering the evidence on record and the findings recorded by the authorities. [796G] 2:3 The conclusion reached by the Board that there was no infirmity in the findings recorded on the basis of the admission made by the examinees was based on the evidence on the record. [794A] 2.4 The High Court was not justified under article 225 to itself evaluate and to interfere in the finding and the findings and to quash it. [793B] 2.5 The High Court has not exceeded its jurisdiction under article 226 of the Constitution to itself evaluate or to interfere with findings and to interfere therewith.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that the appellants were charged with criminal conspiracy to commit criminal misconduct under section 5 (2) of that Act. The appellants pleaded not guilty. The trial court acquitted them but convicted them under section 120B of the Indian penal Code. The High Court acquitted them. The appellants contended that the offence as defined in section 5(1) of the Act was different from that of bribery and that the intention of the Act to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery was to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. Held, that the intention was to create by way of clause (e) an offence distinct from a single offence of bribery and therefore the offence as contemplated by section 5(3) of the Indian Act was not one of the offences of criminal misconduct. The offence as defined by section 5 (1) of that section was one of the offence of bribery. The offence of criminal conspiracy by a public servant is created by section 5 and under sub section (2) it is made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The offence under section 5 is one of the two offences of criminal conspiracy. The offence is one of conspiracy and not one of conspiracy. The object of the Act is to create by necessary implication a charge of criminal misconduct against a public servant. The offence which is defined in section 2(d) is one of a single act or of bribery and the other is of a distinct and separate offence. The offence defined in section 3 of the Act as a single act, of bribery and a charge of conspiracy is one of such offences. The offence punishable under section 120 A is one of mere misapplication of the mind of the public servant. It is not necessary that the public servant should have the requisite intention of committing the offence. The section does not require that the public servants should have the necessary intention of committing an offence. The expression "public servant" in section 5 (3) of that act means a public servant as defined in Section 21 of the Indian Evidence Act. The definition of "public servant " in section 2 (d) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is in these terms: "public servant". The definition of public servant is in section 2 of the Indian Criminal Law Code. The definition is in these words: "public servants" means a public servants as defined in the Indian Penal code. " Public servant" means a person who is in possession of a valuable thing without any lawful authority. " Public Servant" means a servant who is in the possession of a thing for which he is not legally entitled to do. The definition does not require the public servant to have the requisite animus or intention to commit the offence. In the present case, the appellants were not charged with criminal misconduct under s. 5(2). They were not charged under s.5(1) read with s.5 (2) and therefore they were not liable to be tried under section 5. The offence was not one under s.6(2) and the offence under section 7(1) was not one for the offence of cheating. The offence in question was one of mere misappropriation and therefore the appellants were liable to be convicted under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act. The offence, therefore, was one of a very serious nature and the offence was one of criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Criminal misconduct. The appellants were therefore liable to be acquitted.

The appellant, a Bank, was the guarantor of a Bank, which was a surety for the loan advanced by the Bank to the Bank. The Bank, on the basis of a joint venture between the Bank and the Bank, entered into an agreement with the Bank, for the purchase of a Bank 's property. The Bank agreed to pay the amount to the Bank and also agreed to pay interest at the rate of 9% per annum from the date of the agreement. The Bank also agreed to give personal guarantee of the surety. The Bank was also given an option to pay the balance of the amount to be paid to the Bank by way of damages. The Bank filed a suit for recovery of the amount. The trial Court found that there was negligence on the part of the Bank with regard to the safe custody of the pledged goods and that the Bank was not discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The trial court found that there were negligence on the side of the Bank and that the appellant had not exercised such care as a prudent man would in the circumstances of the case, which resulted in the loss of security, namely, pledged oil tins and, therefore, in view of the combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, the surety was discharged. The High Court, however, held that the Bank had failed to exercise such care as was required by section 141 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of guarantee, the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtor pledging oil tins as and by way of security for the advance and, therefore the surety was not discharged. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on the clear understanding that the principal debtor had offered security by way of pledge of goods and the goods were to be in the custody of the creditor Bank. In any event, if the creditor lost or without the consent of the surety parts with the security, the surety is discharged to the extent of the security lost as provided by section 141. [83B C] 2. The surety is entitled to restitution. The surety would not be discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of Guarantee. [83C] 3. The surety has to be discharged from his obligation undertaken under a letter of guarantee. The surety cannot be discharged from any obligation undertaken under any letter of guarantee unless the creditor lost one of the securities. [83G] 4. The surety, in good faith, contracted to offer Personal guarantee on the express condition that the principal creditor shall offer two securities, one the pledge of goods to be kept under the lock and key of the Bank to be supervised by the Bank 's employee and another the personal guarantee of surety. [83H] 5. The surety was discharged to the full extent of the value of security. [83A] 6. The surety had agreed that the principal shall offer two security, one the security the pledge of the goods and the other the personal guarantee the surety. [84B] 7. The surety 's liability to pay the price of the goods is not affected by the letter of the surety to the Bank which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of its securities. [84E] 8. The surety himself agreed to give Personal guarantee on his good faith of other security being offered by the principal debtor which itself may not be a consideration to the surety offering the personal guarantee and that the creditor by his own negligence lost his one of the security. [84G] 9. The surety must be discharged from liability undertaken under the Letter of Guarantee. The surety will have to be discharged to the amount of the security left by the surety.

The appellant was the owner of the "patelki inam" lands. The appellant was the holder of the "Patelki inam " lands. The respondent No. 1 was the owner and the appellant was the grantee of the " patelki inam". The appellant claimed that the "poli" inam lands were granted by the Government to the respondent No. 2, the appellant, and the grant was recognised as a service grant by the British Government. The appellant claimed to be the holder of "patelk inam" lands and the grant of "polik inam" was recognised as an service grant by Government. The respondent denied the claim. The appellant contended that the grant was not a service grant and that the grant of the patelki inams was a grant of land burdened with service and so long as the service was performed by any member of the family, the lands were joint family lands subject to partition etc. The appellant denied that the grant had been recognised as a "service grant" by the British government. The High Court held that the grant in question was not a "service inam" within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 2 (g) of that Act. The High court, on appeal, held that the appellant had no right to the grant of land in the "patels and Patwaris Law" lands. Held, that the grant made by the Government was recognised as one of the service grants and was recognised as such by the British Govern ment. The grant was not an service grant and no question of title by adverse possession arose against the Government. The grant of patelki Inam lands was not a post office grant and no right was given to a member of the patels Law. Amritrao vs State of Bombay, ; , referred to.

The appellant was a Cutchi Memons. The Cutchi Memon was settled in Madras and then in Bangalore. The Cutch Memons were settled in Madras. The Cutche Memons were then settled in Madras, and the Cutchi Memos were settled in the Madras. The appellant was a cutchi Memon, and was governed by the Hindu Law applicable to Cutchi Mems. The Cutches were settled in Bombay. The Cutters were settled in Mysore. The Cuttak Memons were governed by the Indian Law. The Cutcher Memons were not governed by Hindu Law. The appellant 's case was that the Cutchi memons were governed in Madras and that the Cutche Memon Memons were subject by custom to Hindu law of succession and inheritance. The Cutcherry Memons were, therefore, governed by the law of Hindu law applicable to Cutch Memon Memon Memos. The Cuttha Memons were the same as the Cutchi Merons. The appellant contended that as the Cutch Memos were governed by Hindu law, the Cutchi holders were governed by that law as to stridhan. Held, that the Cutch memons in Madras were governed by a Hindu Law applicable in the Madras State and the Cutchruti Memons were entitled to the same rights as the Cutche memos. The cutch Memons in Madras had regulated their affairs, since they had settled down amidst Hindus, according to Hindu law not only in matters of succession and succession but also concepts, such as the joint family property and its devolution by survivorship. The Cutna Memons were therefore governed by the Muslim Law applicable to the Cutchi Memorandum. The Cutha Memons were in the same position as the Cutna Memos. In the matter of the Cutchi Close, the Cutch Memorandum was settled in Mysore and the Cutna memos were governed in the Madras, and therefore, when a Cutchi memon widow died issueless, her property would be governed by the Hindus law as to the stridhan, succession and inheritance, and the right of a son in it by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics. They are engaged in the manufacture of fabrics. The appellants are engaged in processing of fabrics. It is alleged that the appellants have manufactured fabrics in the name of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics. The appellant No. 1, a manufacturer of fabrics, manufactures fabrics of different types. The appellants were manufacturing fabrics in the same manner and consumed or utilised for the manufacture of other commodity. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of excise duty on the yarn which was manufactured at an intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the retrospective effect given by section S I of the Finance Act, 1982, was retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The expression "place of removal" in section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. The expression 'place of removal ' in section S is not defined in the Act. [707D] 2. The expression `place of removal ` in section S of the Act means a place where the excisable goods are produced or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf whether for consumption, export or manufacture of any other commodity in or outside such place. The expression has been given retrospective effect from February 28, 1944. The expression used in section S in section S has been given prospective effect from February 1, 1944. [708E F] 3. The expression in section S i of the Finance (No. 2) 1982, is not defined either in the Act or in the Finance Act. The definition of 'place of manufacture ' is not defined by the Finance Act or the Finance Act but is given retrospective effect by virtue of section S of Finance Act,1982. [709F] 4. The expression is not defined anywhere in the Act but is defined in the Finance Acts. The definition is not exhaustive. The definition in section 2(14) of the Finance Acts is not exhaustive and the definition is not confined to the definition of ' place of removal '. [710G] 5. The expression of 'place ' in section 3 of the Finance Bill, 1982, is a word of wide import. It is not defined under the Act. It is a word which is defined in a statute. It is well settled that the definition of the word 'place of ' in section 2 (14) of Finance Act 1982, is wide enough to include a place of removal. [711B] 6. The expression includes a place of manufacture. The expression means a place of business or a place of premises appurtenant thereto. It is an inclusive definition. It is used in the sense of a place of residence. It is also an inclusive definition of the expression. [712C] 7. The expression, 'place of the removal ' in Section 3 of the Act is not defined. The expression takes in any place of removal from such place or premises. It is the place where the goods are produced, cured or manufactured or the premises appurtenant thereto, which may be used for the manufacture or processing of any other article in the same place. [713D] 8. The expression does not contain any definition of ' places of removal ' but provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or premises at an intermediate point of an integrated process of manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacture of the commodity at an intermediate time to be removal from such other place or premises of manufacture. [714E] 9. The expression must be read in the context of the definition of "place of manufacture" in Section 2(14). [714F] 10.

The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for staying the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court. The Civil Judge rejected the application on the ground that the jurisdiction of the civil court in such matters was impliedly barred. The petitioner filed a revision petition before the Additional District Judge which was dismissed. The petitioner then filed a revision application before the Additional Judge who dismissed the same. The petitioner thereafter filed a revision before the Additional Chief Judge who dismissed it. The petitioner preferred a revision petition to the High Court which was dismissed by the Additional District judge. The petitioner thereupon filed a revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Additional Sessions Judge which was also dismissed. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. Hence this petition by the petitioner. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 68 D of the Act) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining the Hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme either with or without modification. When the scheme is approved or modified under section 68D of the Act, such approved or modified scheme is required to be published in the official Gazette and on such publication it becomes final. After the scheme becomes final, as provided in sub section (iii) of section 68 D, the transport authorities concerned can issue permits only in accordance with the scheme and the other provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the Act. [545B C] 2. The procedure laid down for the preparation of the scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D of Act. The rules also provide for the particulars to be incorporated in the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act by an authority which had the power to publish it and that the authority which was hearing the case under section 68 E of the Act had the power of doing so. [547C D] 3.

The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that the appellant had demanded and accepted a sum of Rs. 5001 or in default to pay the same to the appellant. The appellant pleaded that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to the appellant and that the money had been paid to him. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted the appellant under section 5 (2) of that Act and section 161, Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed the conviction. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a public servant within the meaning of section 5(1)(d) of the Act. [184B] (ii) The appellant had grossly abused his position as public servant within his meaning. The appellant was not guilty of grossly abuse of his position as the public servant within section 161, I.P.C. [184C] (iii) The appellant could not be prosecuted either under section 161, or section 5(3) of the Indian Penal Code or section 5 (1)(d). [184E] (iv) The appellant, in his official capacity as a police officer, was expected to maintain a high standard of integrity and to uphold the maintenance of law. [184F] (v) The appellant grossly abused his status as a police servant within the definition of section 5 (I)(d) and section 5(I)(d). The appellant was therefore guilty of grossly abused his official position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case he obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section is established. [184G] (vi) The appellant did not commit any offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute. [184H] (vii) The appellant has grossly abused his positions as a police officers and extorted money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal. The appellant in his official position as a police official was expected to keep a high standard in integrity and to maintain a low standard of integrity.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant contended that the sanction was not a valid sanction and that the sanction had not been a valid sanction. Held, that the sanction given by the appellant was not a invalid sanction. The sanction was not valid as it was not a proper one. The sanction given by him was not a legal one. The fact that the sanction did not mention the fact that the appellant had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice the appellant should be prosecuted. The sanction did not specify the fact that he had applied his minds to the facts. The sanction had not specified the fact that it was necessary in the interests o.f justice to accord sanction. The fact of the sanction having been given to the appellant was of no consequence. The sanction, therefore, was not a good one. The appellant was not entitled to the sanction. The case of the appellant was covered by section 6(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The sanction required by section 6 (c) was not a sufficient sanction. The appellant had not applied his mind and was of the opinion that in the interest of justice the case was to be tried. The sanction accorded by him was a valid one. The case was covered by the sanction. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1924) L.R. 60 I.A. 65, approved.

The appellant was the owner of a house in which his son was residing. The landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground of demolition and reconstruction. The tenant contended that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction and that the landlord had no right to evict the tenant under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The trial court held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of the tenants. The High Court in second appeal held that the landlord was entitled to evict the tenants under section 14 (1)(b). The High Court also held that the tenant had no right under section 14 to evict the landlord under section 14. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the tenants that the landlord having only a life interest in the premises and that it was inherent in such a life interest that it was not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14( 1)(b) as grounds for eviction of a tenant by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own motion or on behalf of another or on behalf Of himself and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rent or be entitled to receive or be entitled, receive the rent if the building were let to a tenant". The expression landlord has been defined under section 3(6) to mean a person who is received or is entitled, to receive or is entitled in any manner whatsoever, any rent, whether on his personal behalf or on behalf or on his behalf. [275E F] 2. The expression 'landlord is defined under Section 2(6). The Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act. [275F] 3. The Act withwhich we are concerned, is a selfcontained and complete code. The expression "landlord" is defined under the Act as follows: 'landlord ' includes the persons who are not his tenants under the Act. 'Section 2(6)(a) defines landlord as follows: "(a) 'landlord ' means the person who has been receiving or is otherwise entitled to receive, or is entitled under the Act, any rent which is payable to the landlord by virtue of a decree or order of a court or of a court of competent jurisdiction." The expression 'landlord ' is defined under s 2(6), as follows: (a) 'landlord" means the person in receipt of rent on his own behalf and includes a person in receipt or is entitled by virtue of his personal obligation to receive or receive the rent, if the building are let to a person. (b) 'landlord means the person receiving or is bound to receive or are entitled to receive rent, if he is entitled to do so under the Act; (c) 'landlord is a person receiving or was entitled to receive from another person any rent, either on his own account or on behalf and on behalf of himself and others, or as an Agent, trustee, etc. or as an agents, trustee, executors, administrators, receiver or agent or who would otherwise receive the rent. [275G H] 4. The expression in the definition of landlord is defined in section 2(7) as follows : " 'landlord ' is defined in Section 2(7). 'landlord ' has been defined in section 3(1) to mean the person who was receiving or is deemed to receive the rents of the premises from the tenants. " The definition of landlord would clearly take in its sweep the present landlord who holds a life interest. [275H; 277A] 5.

The respondent decree holder filed a suit against the appellant decree holder for the recovery of the amount due to him on the ground that the trees were not part of the grove land. The appellant contended that the trees in question were not part and parcel of the grove. The executing court dismissed the suit holding that the trees did not belong to the grove. On appeal, the High Court held that the trees belonged to the grove and the trees were deemed to be part of the land. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The position taken by the executing court, that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the Act. [532C D] 2. The position of a mortgagee could not be doubted. The position in law taken by the execution court, that the trees, before they were cut, form parts of the grove, and the view taken by the Execution Court, that there was a distinction between trees and a grove and grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the High Court. [533D] 3. The position taking by the executing Court, that the land was not part of a grove, is not correct. [534E] 4. The position is taken by the respondent decree holder then also was that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these grove and grove. [535E] 5. The position takes in the matter of a mortgage, and an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In view of this legal position, the judgment of the executing court is not correct in view of the definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of the Act which says that an "intermediary grove" means grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 326 IPC. The High court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction of the appellants and the sentence of life imprisonment. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. The appellants contended that the High Court was not justified in recording a conviction against them for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in recording a finding against the appellants for an offence punishable under Section 302, IPC. [89B] 1.2 The High Court has not been justified in recording the conviction against the appellants on the ground that the prosecution has failed to prove the case against them for the substantive offence of murder under Section 302. [89C] 1.3 The High Court, while recording a finding of conviction, has not been able to say that the injuries inflicted by the first appellant with the chopper were inflicted with the intention to cause death of Suku. The High Courts have not been justified to record a conviction against the first appellant for an offence of murder punishable under Section 326/149 IPC. [90G] 1.4 The High Court had not been justified on the basis of the evidence of the medical evidence, and it was not possible to say that all the four appellants had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause the death of Suki. The intention to cause murder of Suku deceased could not be attributed to him and the medical evidence also shows that the injuries attributed to him were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [90D] 1.5 The High Court did not have the benefit of the evidence to record a finding against him for the substantive offences of murder punishable u/s 302 IPC. [91E] 1.6 The High Court could not have recorded a conviction against him for an offence u/s 326/149, IPC without a specific charge having been framed against him as envisaged by law. [91G] 1:7. The High Curt has not been shown that the injuries caused by the first appellants were on any vital part of the body, though some of the injuries caused were on any relevant part, but that the injuries were on any material part of the deceased, though some injuries caused by blunt weapons were grievous in nature. The HighCourt has not been satisfied on the basis that the injuries on the first appellant were caused by all the four accused. [91F] 1.8 The High Court is not justified in holding that all the accused had shared the Common intention of causing the bodily injuries on Suku. [91H] 1.9 The High Court should have recorded a finding against all the four Appellants for the substantive charge of murder punishable U/s 302/149 IPC and sentence them to suffer rigorous rigorous imprisonment for a period of three years. [91A] 1.10 The High Court ought to have recorded a concurrent finding of conviction against all the appellants for the substantive criminal offence with the aid of Section 149 IPC and sentence they should have been sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 5,000/ each. [91B] 1:11.

The assessee assessee, a company incorporated in India, was carrying on business in India. The assessee was assessed to income tax on cash basis for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The assessee claimed that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the royalty amount should be assessed as cash basis for 1967 68 and the assessee was not liable to pay tax on cash allowance. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to claim deduction of the royalty amount from cash basis for 1968 68 and 196869. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the assessee could not be said to have received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U.K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its books at Coventry. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessee could not claim deduction of royalty amount from the cash allowance. [105B] 2. The assessee did not say that the method of accounting regularly adopted by it for all its income was on cash basis, and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a) cannot apply. [105C] 3. The assessee had not claimed the amount. The assessee 's claim was not supported by any evidence. The assessee, however, did not say in the returns relating to the assessment years 1968 68 and 1969 69 to the effect that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis. The assessee failed to say that the mode of accounting regularly in respect of the said royalty amount was on cash. The assessee also did not say whether the method of accounts regularly adopted by the assessee for all its Income Tax purposes was on cash consideration. The assessee however did not say, that the method adopted by it was on cash payment basis. The explanation to the said rule was that the method was not adopted by the Income Tax Officer. [105E F] 4. The assessee cannot claim that the method should be adopted by the Department. The assessee has not claimed that the method is on cash basis or mercantile basis. It is not necessary to express any opinion on the question whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between section 5(2) and section 145 of the Act. [105G] 5. The assessee does not say that it maintains its accounts on cash basis and unless the Entry can be deemed not to be a receipt or receipt, cl. (a) can apply. [106B] 6. The assessee is not entitled to claim the deduction of royalty. [106C] 7. The assessee must be held to have received royalty amount by assessee and is accordingly taxable and that it is immaterial when did it actually receive it in U. K. in the form of pounds and make an entry to this effect in its own books at Co operative Bank.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the evidence of the approver was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which the High Court relied on. Held, that the evidence was sufficiently corroborated by the evidence of a co accused, and that the conviction was unsustainable. The evidence of the accomplice was sufficiently corroborated in material particulars and qua each accused. The evidence was sufficiently supported by the evidence given by the co accused. The High court was not justified in interfering with the conviction. The evidence given by an accomplice was sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder, under section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The evidence in the present case was sufficiently corroborated. The evidence showed that the appellant had a liaison with the deceased and that the knife was used by him for the murder. The evidence established that the appellant was guilty of murder and was sentenced to death but the High Court was not justified on the evidence of an accomplice. The evidence proved that the appellant used the knife to kill the deceased was not corroborated in material details and the conviction was therefore unsustainable. The appellant was rightly convicted on the testimony of the approver. The evidence that the appellant gave a confession to the co accused was not corroborated by the statement of the co accused, nor was it sufficient that there was evidence to corroborate the participation of the appellant in the murder. In the present case, the evidence of PW 7 who had prepared the knife alleged to have been used by the appellant was not corroborated. The appellant had a motive to commit the murder because of the suspicion he had about his wife having a liaments with the deceased. The evidence regarding the appellant 's conduct was sufficiently corroborated and the conviction of an accused on the testimony was unsustainable.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant pleaded that on July 8, 1961 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the appellant contended that on the findings recorded by the High Court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21, Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the appellant could be said to be an officer within the meaning Of section 21, and therefore, he was not an officer within section 21, but was a public servant. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant could not, therefore, be deemed to be a public servant under section 21, I.P.C. in view of the language of section 81 of the . [607 B] (ii) The appellant cannot be deemed to have been a public servant in view of section 21(9), Indian Penal Code, because he was a public officer within the definition of section 21. [607 C] (iii) The appellant was not a Public servant within the definition Of section 21. The appellant could be deemed to hold an office under the Government of India or of a Government company as defined in section 617 of the . The appellant could therefore be said to have been an officer within that meaning of section 2, Indian Penal code. [608 D] (iv) The appellant, therefore, could not be deemed to he a public servant for the purpose of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code and section 21 of Indian Penal Code read with section 2, Prevention of Corruption. [609 D] (v) The appellant is not a public officer in the service or pay of a local authority within the meaning ofs. 21, I,P.C., and therefore a public servant is within the meaning section 21, of the Indian penal Code. [610 D] (vi) The appellant has been a public officer under the Government and the appellant is a public servant and therefore a 'public servant ' within the meaning. of section 21 I.P.,C. [611 D] (vii) The appellant 's contention that the appellant was a public servants within the meaning o.f section 21, is not correct.
