The appellant was a class Iii servant and was employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops and was working under the Works Manager who was an officer of the Government and was an officer in the Service or pay of the Government. [612 D] (viii) The appellant had been a public servants under the Government. The appellant cannot therefore be deemed to belong to the public service. [614 D] (ix) The appellant can be deemed to possess the power to hold an officer of a corporation or of a public servant as defined in s. 617 of the Indian Code. [613 E] (x) The appellant did not hold any public servant within section 21. If he was a person performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of some one who isarmed with such authority or representative character, he could be said that he was an officer within s.21, I. P.C. [613 F] (xi) The appellant must be deemed to continue to be an 'officer ' within the definition section 21, [613 G] (xii) The appellant having been a public Servant within the meaning s.21 of the Indian Evidence Act, he could not be said to hold an 'officer in the service of the Corporation. [613 G H] (xiii) The appellant being a public servant, he could also be said to belong to a public servant ' within s.2 of the prevention of Corruption Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Stock Act, 1965 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500. The High Court modified the sentences passed on the appellant and instead of the sentences awarded by the lower courts sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment. The appellant challenged the validity of the order of forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside by the High Court. The High court modified the sentences imposed on the appellant by the lower Courts and instead of its sentences imposed on him, the appellant was convicted for contravening the provisions of section 3 of Maharashtra Prevention of stock of juars Act, 1965. The appellant contended that the High Court having set aside the conviction and sentence in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Stock (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964, it was illegal to maintain the order regarding forfeiture of the juar set and fine of the amount of Rs. 200. The High. Court modified the sentence passed on the appel lant and instead of it modified the sentences to rigorous imprisonment of six months and to fine of Rs 500. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the Juar set aside and the sentence passed by the lower court is set aside. [273 D] The High Court has set aside the forfeiture of Juar set and the appellant is convicted for contravening cl. 3. The order of forfeiture is not in the nature of a penalty. The order is not a penalty. It is not a punishment. The order does not amount to a penalty. [273 E] The order of penalty is not a penal one. The order imposing a penalty is not an penal one. It is a penal one and is not a sentence. The order cannot be said to be penal. [273 G] The order imposing penalty is not in any way penal. The order passed by the High. Court is not a legal one. The High Courts have set aside the order of the lower courts and restored the order of conviction and sentence passed by them.

The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge for the murder of one Hari Singh. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellants under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced them to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the Sessions Judge had acted in a manner inconsistent with the evidence of the eye witnesses. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court, in favour of the appellants, because the High Court was not impressed by the consideration that the only inference which arises from the fact that Violet informed Sia Ram and his companions were carrying guns and hockey sticks and therefore she would know that they had all gathered to commit the murder of Kunwar Singh. [732E F] 2. The High Courts ought not to interfere with the order passed by the Sessions Court, in favour. of the appellants because the High court was not impressed with the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held. [733F G] 3. The High. Court ought not to be disturbed in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. The High 'Court ought not to exercise its revisional jurisdiction in a case where the Sessions Court had acted in excess of its jurisdiction. [734F] 4. The High Curt ought not to entertain a revision petition against the order of the trial court in favour of Sia Ram. [735F] 5. The High, Court ought not have interfered with it.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court convicted him under section 302, read with section34, Indian Penal code and sentenced him to imprisonment for five years. The High court convicted him under s.302, read with s.34, Indian penal Code and sentenced him under section 147, read with sections 148 and 149, to imprisonment for seven years. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellant was guilty of murder under section 302 and sentenced him only to imprisonment for a period of five years. Held, that the High court was right in holding that though the charge as well as the evidence was directed against the 4 named accused, a court could come to the conclusion that others, named or unnamed, acted conjointly along with one of the accused charged. The High Courts were not justified in holding that when three of the four named accused were acquitted, the court could not convict only one of the other accused on the basis of constructive liability. The High courts were not justified on the evidence in the case to hold that the appellant had a prior concert with one or more other persons, named or unidentified, for committing the said offence. The High. Court was not justified in interfering with the findings of the High Court. The High, Court was not right in holding the appellant guilty of murder. The High 'Court was not justified on a fair reading of the entire judgment to indicate that the appellant, who was acquitted, was guilty of the murder under section 304, read with Section 34, of the Indian Penal Code.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to release the goods imported by it. The respondents, however, rejected the claim of the petitioner on the ground that the goods were not released. The petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 32 before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court was not justified in dismissing the writ petition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The customs authorities were right in taking the view that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse. [627C] 2. The customs authority was right in taking a view that the rates of duty applicable in the imported goods must be determined according the law prevalent in the date they are actually removed from their warehouse. [625D] 3. The customs Authorities were right in take the view that no question of the enforcement of a fundamental right arose in the facts and circumstances of this case. [628D] 4. The petitioner as such has no fundamental right to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. [629E] 5. The petitioner is entitled to the relief under Article 32. [630F] 6. The petitioner has no fundamental fight to clear the imported goods except in due course of law. The petitioner, as such, has no fundamental rights to clear the same.

The appellants were the sons of the father who died in the year 1948. The appellants filed a suit for possession of the properties in suit on the ground that the sale was in contravention of the provisions of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and decreed the suit for possession. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the share of the sons did not pass to the auction purchaser. HELD : (i) The liability of the sons to discharge the debts of their father was not an avyavah but a debt which was incurred for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of the sons. The liability of a father to discharge the debt of his father was not a joint obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the liabilities of his father. [417 B C] (ii) The liability to discharge the creditors of the father was not the joint liability of the father alone which could not include the share of his sons. The right, title and interest of the defaulter in one case and the judgment debtor 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to an end and therefore in the auction sale the shares of the sons were sold in execution of the payment order. [418 C D] (iii) The liability was not a personal liability of the judgment debtor. The liability was a personal liability and the liability of the son was not an personal liability. [419 C] (iv) The liability for the discharge of the debts of the father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the sons which continue to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the father and which does not come to an close relation to the family. [421 D] (v) The liability is not a personal obligation of the judgment debtors. The liability is a personal obligation and the liability is a joint obligation. The liability does not cease merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property. [422 D] (vi) The liability does exist in the life and after the deceased and the property are sold. The property is not tainted with accretion to the property. The property does not come into existence in the lifetime of the father. The property cannot be sold without the assent of the sons who are in possession of it. [423 D] (vii) The liability under section 155 of the Bombay Act is not a joint liability of a judgment debtor. [424 D] (viii) The liability in the present case was not a mere difference in the method of enjoyment of property. The liability to pay the debts of a father was not merely a personal liability but a debt incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties. [425 G] (ix) The liability cannot be a personal liability. The liability cannot arise on the death of a person who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration. The liability must be a personal obligation. The obligation of a father is a personal liability which is not an avalavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals ". [425 D] (x) The liability must arise on the happening of a particular event. The liability may arise on the occurrence of a particular contingency. The liability arises on the happening or the happening of the contingency. [426 D] (xi) The liability may be a personal one but the liability may arise from the happening of an event. [427 D] (xii) The liability arises from the happening or happening of a contingency. The legal position is that the liability of a son to discharge the liability of his father is not an essential ingredient of the liability of an father. [427 D] (xiii) The liability can be a personal or personal liability of a person.

The petitioners, who were the police officers, were charged with offences under section 8 B of the . The Committee, after considering the evidence, submitted its report to the Delhi Administration. The Committee, however, recommended that the transfer of the petitioners in these cases be made by the Committee. The Committee recommended that the petitioners be transferred to the Delhi Adminis tration and that the transfer be made by a suitable order. The Committee also recommended that the transfers be made by an order of the Committee. In its report the Committee recommended that a Committee should be set up to look into the conduct of various police officers and to make recommendations for their transfer. The Committee further recommended that the cases of the petitioners be considered by the Committee in the light of the report of the Committee itself. The Committee then recommended that the case of the petitioners should be transferred to Delhi Adminis sion and that the cases be considered by it in the end of the inquiry. The Committee accordingly recommended that the petitions be disposed of by the Committee on the basis of the material available on record. The Committee submitted its report on the basis that the petitioners were covered under section 8B of the Act and that the case was not covered by section 8B. The Committee considered the report of its own and recommended that the names of the petitioners may be considered for transfer to Delhi Administra tion. The Committee took into consideration the report of a Committee which recommended that the persons should be transferred from Delhi Adminis tion to Delhi Admini sion and the cases of those who had been transferred to Delhi Administration were to be dealt with accordingly. The Committee thereafter recommended that the applications of the petitioners for transfer be considered by Delhi Adminis trative Committee. The petitioners challenged the validity of the recommendations of the Committee and the High Court. The High Court held that the Committee had to examine the conduct of different police officers and in particular among others, the Committee had not examined the conduct of the various police officers, and that the Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 B. The High court held that the petitioners had not been given the opportunity to be heard before the Committee was asked to reconsider the whole question relating to the order in which the witnesses had to be examined. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Committee was not competent to examine the witnesses in the case and that the High Court had erred in holding that the Committee could not have been asked to be cross examined at the end of inquiry. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Committee should have examined the conduct and the evidence before the Committee and should have considered the report at the end. The Committee would have then asked the petitioners to give evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the end, and the affidavits and other material before the Committee show that there were a large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the committee. [523D E] 2. The Committee could not be asked to give evidence before it. The Committee had not considered whether the witnesses were entitled to the benefit of section 8 B or not. The Committee was not entitled to give the petitioners the opportunity to cross examine the witnesses. [524E] 3. The Committee ought to have considered whether there was any kind of discourtsey to the Committee. If the Committee had found that the petitioners was covered under section8B then certainly they would not have been required to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the end of enquiry. [526F] 4. The Committee shall have considered whether it should have examined all the witnesses and given evidence along with other persons who were similarly situated at the end thereof. [527H] 5. The Committee may consider it necessary to examine the evidence of the witnesses and to give evidence on the basis thereof.

The petitioners, who were the petitioners in the writ petition, challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, and the notification issued under r. 8 of the Rajasthan fares and freights Rules, 1959. The petitioners contended that the Act was unconstitutional as it was discriminatory and ultra vires the Constitution, that the Act did not provide for the levy of lump sum in lieu of tax on fares and freight, and that the Act had no application to the petitioners. The petitioners also contended that the levy of the lump sum in the State List was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the levy was without authority of law and was not invalid. The Act and the Rules must be read harmoniously and reading them so, it is clear that the apparent mandatory language of the Rules and the notification still retains the permissive character of the section, but only lays down what the amount of lump sum must be, if lump sum payment is made in lieu of payment of the tax calculated on actual fares and freight. The tax is still on passengers and goods, though the amount of the tax is measured by the fares and freight is the amount of freight. The levy is still on the passengers and goods. The tax, however, is still on persons who are transported by road or inland waterways. The tax was therefore, without authority of Law. The tax could not be levied under the Entry, and the tax was not invalid on the ground that it was not a tax on passengers and, therefore, the tax was without authority. The levy was therefore, invalid. The levy of lump amount in lieu of the tax was, therefore, without jurisdiction. The levy did not contravene article 14 of Constitution. The levy could not be said to be invalid on the grounds that it was discriminatory. The levy in the present case was not invalid because it was not so, because, the levy was not invalid as it was not made in lieu or in any way affected by the levy. The levy therefore was without authority, and the levy was invalid. The State of Rajasthan vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , followed.

The appellant company was retrenched by the respondent company on the ground that the retrenchment was invalid and the workmen were entitled to reinstatement with continuity of service. The appellant challenged the award in the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from the date on which they were sought to be retrenched. The appellant contended that the retrenchment of the workmen was invalid for the reasons that the retrenchment had been made invalid and the relief of reinstatement with continuity was not the criterion for grant of compensation to the extent of full back wages. The High court allowed the writ petition and directed the reinstatement with continuity. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court. The High. Court directed that the workmen shall not be reinstated in their service from the day on which they had been sought to be retried. The appellant also filed a writ application in the High. Court challenging the award of the Labour Court. The High, Court directed that in the event of reinstatement the workmen shall pay full back wages to the workmen. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated and, therefore, reinstatement was held to be the appropriate relief and Act. [567F] 2. The workmen were not entitled to the relief of back wages. [567G] 3. The award of the Industrial Court is set aside and the order of the Labour court is restored. [567A] 4. The award shall stand modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the amount paid to them as wages when recalled for work since the date of retrenchment and adjustment of the retrenchment compensation towards the amount found due and pay able. [567B] 5. The award is set aside.

The prosecution case was that the accused and his father were in the house of the deceased at about 8 a.m. The deceased was married to Churi deceased. The accused was married to the deceased on the night of the occurrence. The deceased had been married to Chri. The accused and his mother were living in the house at the time of the occurrence and the deceased was living in the same house. The accused had also come to the house of Churi deceased and told the deceased that he was with Churi deceased in the house during the day but at about 8.30 p.m. he left for Kotkhai leaving his wife alone at the house. The deceased told the accused that he was having illicit relations with Churi and that he would take the deceased to the house where he was living. The accused told the deceased to take the deceased back to the house. On the night of occurrence the accused and the deceased were in the room. The deceased went to the house and told the accused about the murder of Churi. The accused took the deceased to his house and told him that he was taking the deceased to hospital. The deceased informed the police about the incident. The police registered a case under section 302 I.P.C. and sent the dead body for post mortem. The accused were arrested and the dead body was sent for post mortem examination. The accused pleaded not guilty and was convicted. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the accused was not specifically empowered in this behalf. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The accused and none else who was responsible for the murder of the deceased were responsible for the death of Churi and the deceased had died. [655 B] (2) The accused was not responsible for the offence of murder. The deceased died because of the adulterous conduct. The accused knew that the deceased was with Chri. He was not responsible in the murder of his wife. The fact that the accused alone was with Ch.uri deceased in his house when she was murdered there with the Khokhri and the fact that the relations of the accused with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter, were strained would not make the accused and none alone who caused injuries to Churi. [656 C] (3) The accused had no natural affection for the child and it was difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child. It is the accused and nobody else who caused injuries, to Churi, as a result of which she died. It is not the case of the prosecution that the accused had any natural affection for Churi deceased before the visit of the accused to the house or that he had any natural interest in the murder. [657 C D] (4) The accused knew the deceased as a result from the adulterous behaviour. Had the accused been the son of the accused the accused would have had a natural affection for him. It is also the case of prosecution that shortly before the occurrence the accused had visited the house of Shri Mahajan. The accused would have taken the deceased to a hospital from the bazar. The deceased would have had no natural interest in his murder. [613 E] (5) The accused would be responsible for the crime of murder. [557 C] (6) The accused did not commit any offence. The accused did commit murder of Chri. In the circumstances of the case, it was the accused and no one else who caused injury to Chri and the deceased. The fact of the incident that the accused came to the house at about 830 p. m. and told the police post from the bazaar that the murder of a boy was committed during his absence cannot be accepted.

The plaintiff sued for a declaration that the properties mentioned in Schedule A 'A ' were liable to be sold to him. The defendants contended that the properties were liable to pay the mortgage debt and that the plaintiff was entitled to recover the amount of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and held that the plaintiff had not proved that the properties in Schedule A were liable to the payment of the mortgage debts. The High court, on appeal, held that the defendants had not proved the fact that the properties had been sold by the defendants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaintiff had not used the word "subrogation" in the document, and the declaration of charge standing by itself was superfluous though Order XXXIV, rule 2 (1) does require that the decree in a mortgage suit shall (1) A.I.R. , but to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in costs. [195 G H] (ii) The plaintiff 's only remedy is under section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82, Transfer of Property Rules, Transfer of property Act. The plaintiff ' s claim on the basis that each of the defendants was liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgaged debt is not barred by section 92 of Transfer of Property. [195 B C] (iii) The plaintiff has not used the words "subrogated" in the deed of mortgage. The plaintiff has in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs. 40,253 11 10 with interest against either defendant, I would direct that his liability be reduced to Rs. 2,500 and that the balance of Rs. 5,000 with interest against the other defendants would pay Rs. 15,000. [195 C D] (iv) The plaintiff was not prepared to leave matters as they were and trust to the good faith of his brothers. The plaintiff had in substance asked the defendants to contribute in the equal shares towards the payment of mortgage debt. [195 E] (v) The plaintiff did not use the word "Subrogation" he has asked in substance for the relief to which a subrogation would be entitled under the Transfer of property. [195 F] (vi) The plaintiff could not have used the word 'subrogation ' in the document. The plaintiff was entitled only to the right to redeem the whole of the balance of the property (excluding the plaintiff 's) for the aggregate sum due as above and, in default of payment, limiting the liabilities of each item of property to the sum rateably due on it under section 82. [195 H] (vii) The plaintiff failed to prove that the properties sold were liable to payment of the debt. [196 G] (viii) The plaintiff is entitled to recover a sum of Rs. 15000 from the defendants.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. The appellants applied for the post of Assistant Engineers in Public Works Department. The Selection Committee selected them on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview. The appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the post secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions. The appellants preferred a petition before this Court challenging the Rules. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 dismissed the petitions and the appellants were directed to give appointment to the appellant Ashok alias Soman na Gowda on the post of Asstt. Engineer (Civil) and (Mech.) for the Public Works Deptt. within two months of the communication of this order. The appellants challenged the aforesaid order by filing a petition before a Division Bench of the High Court. The Division Bench dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Rules are clearly in violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. The Rules have been clearly in violation and there is no allegation of malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. [498C] 2. The Rules were clearly in violation with the decision of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., J.T. on 4th September, 1991. The Rules do not contain any allegation of malafides. [498D] 3. The Rules cannot be said to be arbitrary or unreasonable. The Rules can be challenged only if they are arbitrary or unreasonable and are not in any manner violative of the provisions of the Constitution or are violative of the principles of natural justice. [498E] 4. The Rules being clearly in violation thereof, the Rules under which the present selection was made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [498F] 5. The Rules contain a provision for a maximum of 150 marks for the written examination. The appellants have been given more than 150 marks in the qualifying exams.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution has established the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. The prosecution has relied upon the confession but later conceded that apart from what the High Court has observed with regard to the confession, it appeared to be exculpatory in nature and, therefore, would not be admissible against the co accused. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The confession of a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. In the instant case, the prosecution has relied on the confession but subsequently conceded that apart, the prosecution evidence on this score should be rejected as when on 10th July, 1982 Sadanand was taken into custody following the raid on the Ashram, Yadav was not found there. The prosecution had relied upon the statement of the co accused who were present when the deceased was taken into possession following the raid. The prosecution case has been established by circumstantial evidence. The prosecution is not able to prove conspiracy because Yadav was a follower. The prosecution was able to support the charge of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to be completed, otherwise it would certainly be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [447G H; 413A B] 2.1 The prosecution has established by circumstantial evidences the complicity of the accused in the murder. The prosecution witnesses have also led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadanand at the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [448B C] 2.2 The prosecution has failed to prove the complicity of S.I. in the conspiracy to kill the Collector through Yadav. The prosecution evidence on the other hand is not reliable. The prosecution relied upon the evidence of S.W.4 who was a witness to the seizure of the bomb. The prosecution also relied upon the confessional statement of S.O. S.O., who was a member of the police party. The prosecution did not examine S.O..448. The prosecution examined S.O./S.O. as a witness to prove the seizure of a bomb. The trial court has not accepted the evidence of the prosecution on the ground that S.O.(S.O.) was not produced. The prosecution, therefore, failed to prove that S.Os. 4 and 5 were present at the jail. The prosecution failed to prove its case of conspiracy. The prosecution therefore failed to prove conspiracy. [413D E] 2.3 The prosecution has proved by circumstantial evidence the complicity of A.1 in the conspiracy. The evidence of S, S, S and S is not reliable and the chain is not completed, otherwise, it would indeed be hazardous to acceptance a part of that link as a whole. The prosecution cannot be said to have established the complicity in the conspiracy with direct or circumstantial evidence. [413E F] 2.4 The prosecution has not proved the complicity of D, S and and S in the conspiracy for murder of the deceased. The prosecution could not prove the complicity in conspiracy with direct prosecution. The prosecution story is not reliable as the prosecution has failed in proving the complicity of accused in the conspiracy and the prosecution has not produced any evidence to prove the conspiracy.

The appellant company was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing cotton and cotton textiles. The company was paying the highest wages in the comparable concerns. The company had its factory at Bombay. The company paid the highest wages as per the rates of wages fixed by the Tribunal. The company also paid the highest wage in the comparable concern. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the fixation of wages and dearness allowance. The High Court held that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowances. The High court held that the company was not entitled to the minimum wages fixed by it. The company appealed to this Court. HELD : The Tribunal was right in applying the industrial dispute cum region formula for fixing wages. The Tribunal had not specifically considered what would be the total wage packet including basic wages and dearness Allowance and that had made the total wage. [365 E] The Tribunal had given a very wide discretion to the Tribunal to fix the wage scales and dearness allowance for factory workmen. The Tribunal was not justified in applying the Industrial Tribunal 's formula. [365 F] The Tribunal was in error in applying the Tribunal 's principle. The Tribunal has not specifically considered the total wage packets. The Tribunal 's decision was right in following the trend that has begun in this region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowance for subordinate staff and factory workmen as in the case of clerical staff. [365 G] The Tribunal has given a very limited number of cases in which the maximum is higher than the lowest. The Tribunal should have taken into account the trend in that region and given the trend in the region. [365 D] The Tribunal 'did not consider what would be their total wage packet. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in taking into account the average of the wages packet in other comparable concerns.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Bombay. The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof. The respondents contended that the appellants were agriculturists and that they were entitled to the redemption of the mortgage property. The trial court held that the appellants had not the effect of transferring the interest of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property to the mortgagees and that the appellants could not claim redemption of the mortgaged property. The High Court, on appeal, held that the Rajinama had not the right to redeem the mortgage property and that the respondents were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The High court, however, held that by the Rajinma 's mortgage the equity of redemption became extinguished and that the defendants were bound to give the amount also to the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Rajinama was not a mere registered occupant and was not a registered occupant. The appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. [601 B] (ii) The Rajinsula was the registered occupant and his name was substituted in the records for that of the previous registered occupant. [602 C] (iii) The Raj in the instant case was the registered owner of the mortgaged land and the appellants were bound to deliver possession thereof to the mortgagees. The appellants had not been able to show that the appellants ever had the right to mortgage the property. The appellants did not say that they had the right of mortgage. The Rajinma was not a person interested in the mortgage. The appellants could not be said to have any interest in the mortgaged land. [603 C] (iv) The Rajenama was not made by the defendants appellants in their written statement and in agreement with the High Court. The appellants ' case was that the Rajinsula had not the necessary animus to transfer the interest of an occupancy tenant to the mortgagees, and that the Rajenama had not been made by the registered occupant. It was not a case of a registered occupant who was not a tenant. [604 C] (v) The Rajroop Singh was not a party to the proceedings before the revenue authorities. The Rajroac Singh was not the registered occupant of the land. The appellants, therefore, could not claim the benefit of section 74. [605 D] (vi) The Rajrappa was not a true owner of the land and was not entitled to any benefit under section 74. The Rajraappa was not a full owner of the property. [606 D] (vii) The Rajranama was not an unregistered occupant and was a registered occupant and the appellants could have no right to claim redemption of a mortgage property. [700 D] (viii) The Rajemanni was not a "registered occupant" and was not registered occupant. Therefore, the appellants were not bound to pay any amount to the appellants under the simple mortgages. [700 E] (ix) The Rajimanni was a registered tenant and his name had been substituted in the record for that of his previous registered occupant and that was the position in the Rajinaka. [700 F] (x) The Rajmullan was not a 'registered occupant ' and was not the owner of the suit property. [701 G] (xi) The Rajomanni was the registered tenant and the appellants had no right to redeem them. [700 G] (xii) The Rajamanni was an unregistered occupant. The Rajimunta was not a landlord. The Rajomonia was not a non registered occupant. There was no evidence to show that he was the manager and karta of the joint family. [700 C] (xiii) The Rajarath was not a member of the joint Hindu family.

The respondent, a specialised article used for printing, writing, or printing, or for drawing on, or for decorating, or cover ing the walls. Ltd. was a specialised article. The respondent claimed that carbon paper was a paper falling within the purview of the word 'paper ' as used in the Notification No. Sales Tax Act, 1948, so as to be liable to sales tax at the point and at the rate specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The Sales Tax Officer, (Section IV), Kanpur, did not accede to the claim of the respondent and holding that carbon paper did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter. The High Court, however, quashed the levy. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that carbon paper is not paper as defined in the Act or the Rules and, therefore, would not be liable to Sales Tax at the point of levy. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The mere fact that the word ' paper ' forms part of the denomination of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. The word 'paper " is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing or printing, etc. " [838 B] (2) The mere factum of the word "paper" in the common parlance or in the commander 's sense means paper which is used in the sense of bearing, writing, etc. [838 C] (3) The mere circumstance that the word " paper" is used in a generic sense does not make it a part of a typewriter. [839 C] (4) The mere possibility of the word in the common sense or in the context of the sub ject of the statute does not make the word " Paper other than hand made paper". [839 G] (5) The mere absence of the word, 'paper ' in the common understanding or the words in the common usage, is not decisive. [840 C] (6) The mere existence of the word is not decisive, but it is to be construed in its popular sense, meaning, of course, by the words 'popular sense ' that sense which people conversant with the sub jects of the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [841 G] (7) The mere word 'paper" is not a part of an aero plane but an essen tial part of a bus in the same way, ribbon is not a component of a typewriter. The word "paper " in the common use of the word has been used for bearing writing, or packing purposes. [842 G] (8) The mere mention of the word `paper ' in a generic term is not decisive and, therefore. will not make the expression 'paper ' meaningless. [843 G] (9) The mere presence of the word as well as the word 'papers ' in the Common parlance or in a generic meaning is not decisive or decisive of the matter whether the article was paper as generally known or not. [844 G] (10) The mere use of the words "paper" is no doubt a part of "paper" but it is a part of one of the type writer. [845 G] (11) The mere omission of the word used in the common or generic sense of the word does not make any difference. [846 G] (12) The mere non mention of the words in a generic or generic sense does make no difference.

The appellant was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The appellant was appointed as a Manager of the Sugar Mills at Amroha at a time when the respondents 1 to 4 were not proprietors of the Sugar Mill. The respondents 1 to 5 were employed by the appellant as Manager of the sugar Mills at Amroha. The appellant, however, was not a permanent employee of the Sugar mills at Amroha. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents from service on the ground that they had disobeyed his order of transfer and thereby they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. 1 of the appellant 's Standing Order No, 1 of the Company. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal on the ground, inter alia, that the respondents 1 and 4 were not employees of the appellant and that the appellant was not entitled to transfer the respondents 1, 4 to the new factory. Held, that the appellant had no right to transfer the respondent from one concern to another. The appellant had been employed by the respondents 1 & 4 as Manager of Sugar Mills at Shamli at a time, when they were not proprietors. The appellant could not be transferred by an employer to another concern, because, the appellant had been appointed by the appellant with a view to furthering his interests in any place and the respondents the duty to join the concerns to which they may be transferred. The appellant 's right to transfer an employee if he had the right to do so under the contract of service or under any statutory provisions, could not be questioned.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948. The respondent was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company was registered under the Bombay General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The appellant was incorporated in the State of Gujarat. The respondent company was incorporated under the Bombay Act. The appellant 's main contention was that the contribution payable under Chapter V A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The appellant contended that the contribution was not a tax and that the levy was illegal. The High Court held that the contribution paid by the appellant company for the period May 31, 1969 to March 26, 1973 was a fee. The High court held that the appellant was not liable to pay the contribution under Chapter VA by the appellant. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The contribution paid by it for the period April 26, 1969 to April 26, 1973, was a fee, and its levy is illegal as the appellant was a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. [1088C] The appellant was not a fee and the levy was not illegal as the provisions of Chapter V A were not made applicable to the appellant. [1089C] The question whether the contribution paid under Chapter VB was a fee or fee in order that the Act does not contemplate the render of any service, or the conferment or conferment of any benefits to the appellant or its employees, as quid proquo for the payment, is not a question of fact. [1090E] The appellant cannot be said to be a fee or a fee in the order of the High Court. [1091G] The question of payment of special contribution under Chapter VI A by the appellant for the period, May 31,1969 to March 26 1973, was not a question which arose for consideration in the present case.

The petitioners were working as daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. The management had throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that in fact the petitioners had been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them. The management has throughout denied the petitioners ' claim and stated that in fact, the petitioners have been continued on roll on humanitarian grounds. The petitioners have also stated that the Voluntary Retirement Scheme offered considerable amount to these daily rated workmen has been framed, which is Annexure R V to the counter affidavit. The petitioners ' claim is that in fact they have been continued in rolls on humanitarian ground for several years even though there is no work for the petitioners. The respondents have also stated in the counter affidavit that the petitioners being surplus to the establishment, they cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purely on humanitarian grounds so far. The petitioners are not regular employees, they do not have any specific job to do, they are surplus to the established establishment and merely kept on the roll on humanitarian ground. The respondents are also running in heavy losses during the last three years and it is not possible to absorb the petitioners immediately as regular workmen. The respondents, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the writ petition. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated workman is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same work is taken from him. [610G] 2. The principle is that regularisation of a Daily rated workman and the payment to him is purely on sympathetic grounds so far as the same work was taken from him, he was not absorbed against the same or not even pay the equal pay. [611A] 3. The principle that regularisation of daily rated workmen and payment to them of the pay Equal to that of regular workman arises even when the daily wage workman is doing, the same work which is taken from the regular workman, and there being no work for him, the is not absorbed in it or not, even paid the Equal pay for the periods during which the similar work is taken. [612B] 4.

The appellants were the appellants in the suit. They purchased the entire 16 as interest in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against the respondents. The respondents filed a suit for a declaration that the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained by the National Agency Co. was not binding on them and that the sale was void. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and held that the sale of the entire 16 was not binding upon the appellants. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the sale by the National agency Co. was binding on the appellants. [378 E] (ii) The High court was right in not accepting the contention of the appellants that the sale had been made out and was real. The High court had rightly held that the appellants were precluded by 0. r. 12(i) from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by them. [378 F] (iii) The High Courts have rightly held that in the absence of any provision in the statute, the sale of property in execution of a mortgage decree obtained in favour of the appellants by the National Agencies Co. was void. [378 G] (iv) The High courts have rightly held in favour of respondents. [378 A] (v) The High. Court was right. [378 C] (vi) The High 'Court was right in taking the view that the sale made by the National agencies Co. was only the interest of the appellants who were not parties to the mortgage. [378 D] (vii) The HighCourt was right. The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i), were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High Court, to a further 2 as 13 gondas odd share belonging to the appellants.

The appellant Municipality issued a notice under section 153A of the Act to show cause why the Municipality should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in the notice. The appellant submitted his reply to the notice. He also submitted his reply. The Special Officer rejected the objections and the appellant filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 153A are not mandatory and the appellant has not been given an opportunity to show cause against the existence of the nuisance. The provisions of the Act are to permit the Municipality to proceed to take action under section 153 A of the Act. The provisions are to permit a person to take action against the occupier of the factory within the prescribed period. The provision is to permit the occupier to take action for the removal of the effluent. The provision of section 153 A is to permit a occupier to take such action as may have been previously approved by the Government. The provision in section 153A is to permit occupier to take any action against the owner of the factory for the removal or removal of the water from the factory. The provision does not violate article 19(1)(C) of the Constitution because it would be a reasonable restriction to the exercise of the fundamental right under article 19(6). [396 D E] (ii) The provisions in section 153 A are to permit occupier of the premises to take action in the manner prescribed in the notice and not to show cause. The provision under section 153 is to permit occupiers of the premises within the prescribed time to take action. The provision for the removal and removal of the nuisance in the manner provided in the notice is to the person on whom the notice is issued to show cause, and not to the occupier of a factory. The provisions in the Act are not mandatory. [396 D F] (iii) The provisions under section 153B are to permit occupiers to take action to prevent the nuisance which is likely to be caused by the nuisance. [396 E] (iv) The provisions are not mandatory but directory. The provisions under sections 153A and 153A are to permit persons to take action on the ground of nuisance. The provision, therefore, is to permit persons who are not permitted to take action and to arrange for discharge of the effluents in the manner indicated by the notice. [396 F] (v) The provisions contained in section 153B of the Act do not require the person to whom the notice has been issued to show causes why he should not be ordered to arrange for discharging the effluent in a manner specified by the notice and the person to be responsible for the discharge thereof. [396 G] (vi) The provisions relating to the removal of nuisance in terms of section 153B do not require that the occupier of an factory should take action against a occupier of the occupier of his factory for the purpose of preventing the nuisance which was being carried on by him. [396 A] (vii) The provisions regarding the existence of a nuisance in terms are to permit an occupier to take proceedings against the occupier for the removal, or removal of water from the premises. The provision regarding the manner in which the effluent should be discharged is to permit an owner to take action, and not the occupier of any factory to take action which is purely a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality. [396 B] (viii) The provisions made in section 153C are to permit every occupier to take appropriate action against the owners of the factory. [396 C] (ix) The provisions, therefore, are to permit not only the occupier of every factory to take any steps to prevent the pollution which is likely, the satisfaction of the municipality, is to the satisfaction of a Municipality. [397 D] (x) The provisions have to be read in the context of the provisions of section 154A.

The appellant was found in possession of certain goods. The appellant was prosecuted under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case was that the goods were being actually used or were intended to be used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The appellant pleaded that the goods had been sold to the Railway Administration and that the goods belonged to the Railway. The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court, on appeal, held that the goods in question were railway stores and were mixed with other goods in the bags. The High court, however, held that there was no evidence before the courts to prove that the articles were being actually use or were intended for the construction or maintenance of the railway. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The prosecution must establish that the articles of the kind were being actually utilised or were intended, for the construction of a railway, and that the articles in question were being actually utilized for the construction. The evidence showed that the articles had been used or were meant to be used in the construction, operations or maintenance of railway. The evidence was not sufficient to prove that articles were being used or intended to be use for the construction and operation of a railway and that the article was used or intended for use in the construction. [189 D E] (ii) The prosecution was not called upon to prove that goods were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. The prosecution must first prove that the goods of the kind mentioned in the report were being used for the purpose of construction, operation, maintenance or maintenance of Railway. The evidence in the case before the court was not sufficient for the prosecution to prove that those articles were railway stores. [189 E] (iii) The prosecution has not been called upon to establish that the goods belong to any particular railway administration. The evidence shows that the articles are being used or were used for the Construction, operation or Maintenance of a railway; and the articles are used or intended, for use in construction, operation and maintenance of a Railway. [189 G] (iv) The prosecution is not called upon, to prove that any article of the kind was being used or was intended to be employed for the construction etc. of a railway or that the goods are in a serviceable condition. The evidence is not sufficient to show that the articles seized were railway stores or were intended or intended to have been used for the constructions or maintenance of any railway. [189 H] (v) The prosecution case is not called to prove that these articles were railway property within the meaning Of section 2 of Act.

The appellants, who were the tenants of the demised premises, filed a suit for ejectment of the appellants from the demised premises on the ground that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop. The trial court decreed the suit for ejectment. The first appellate court affirmed the decree of the trial court. The High Court, in second appeal, reversed the decree of trial court and decreed the suit. The appellants filed a second appeal before the High Court. The High court allowed the second appeal and set aside the decree of eviction passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit for eviction. The appellants then filed a second second appeal before this Court. The appellants contended that the provisions of the Act do not apply to the facts of the case and that the provisions in the Act do no apply to the case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Rent Acts do not apply in the instant case. The provisions of all the Rent Acts are that a contractual tenant on the termination of the contractual tenancy is by virtue of the provisions of Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land and he is entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual lease and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or decree of possession specified in the Act is established. [10E F] 1.2 The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs of tenants in respect of commercial tenancies on the death or death of the landlord after termination of the tenancy, as has been done in the case of heirs of the tenants of residential premises, does not indicate that the legislature intended that the heirs of the tenant of commercial premises will cease to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under the Act. [10G H] 1.3 The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the demised premises governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to the right in favour of the respondent created under section 13(1)(a) to (k) and other provi sions of the Act. The appellants succeeded in the heritable interest of the tenant in the lease holding right of a demised premises held by Smt. Anandi, the respondent. [10H; 10A] 1.4 The appellants succeeded before the High court to the heritable and heirs of the respondent. The appellants came to this Court by way of special leave. The appellants, however, succeeded to the estate of the tenant without any hiatus and restriction on the heritable interest.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund to all the workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The employees of the Board are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not be covered by the same scheme under the Act. The employees are liable to pay the Provident Fund contribution to the Employees Provident fund. The employees have to pay the provident fund contribution to the employees provident fund. The Employees Provident Fund Scheme is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion of the wages of the employees. The employees who are covered by the Act are liable to contribute equally to the provident fund. Under section 66 of the Act the State Government may guarantee the payment of the principal and interest of any loan proposed to be raised by the Board. The Board has to carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss. The Board is not a statutory authority. The employees cannot be said to be covered by a scheme of the Act. [47 H; 48 A B] The Board has the right to guarantee the payment to the Government by the Board and to the Government. The Board cannot be said that the Board has the power to grant the benefits under the Act to the employees. [48 C] The Board is willing and the burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer. [48 E] The Board cannot claim the benefit of the Provident Fund Scheme to be extended to any additional categories of workmen. The Board may guarantee the payments of interest on loans advanced or deemed to be advanced to the Board under section 64, including arrears of such interest.

The respondent wife filed a petition for maintenance under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for maintenance. The petition was dismissed by the Metropolitan Magistrate. The High Court, however, refused to interfere with the order of the Magistrate. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have erred in ignoring the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 of the Code. [707D] 2. The High courts have erred in not considering the grounds of refusal and to make an order of maintenance if the husband is impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligation. [708E] 3. The High court has erred in not giving the reasons for the rejection of the petition filed by the respondent. [709F] 4. The HighCourt has erred in ignoring legal effect of second proviso to section 125 of Cr. P.C. [710G] 5. The High Curt has erred in holding that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. [711F] 6. The High. Court has erred in taking the view that the husband has been found to have been impotent. [712F] 7. The High 'Court has erred on the view that no evidence of cruelty can be admitted in a proceeding under the section to prove, not merely cruelty as a ground for separate maintenance but the conduct and acts of the husband from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife.

The plaintiff, who was the owner of the suit land, filed a suit for a declaration of his title and for possession of the suit property. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, in second appeal, reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the vesting that was made in the Resolution 37 dated 19th January, 1948 was not intended to be vesting in the Municipality, and that the various documents filed in this case, would go to show that as early as July, 1950 these lands and other properties which were in occupation of the erstwhile state military had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Ministry of the Union of India and that the possession was handed over by the Union of Indian. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the vesting was only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of the title itself in the Municipality. [223D] 1.2 The High Court also held that the title to the suit property and the defendants had denied title, of the plaintiff. [223E] 1.3 The High Court held that the vesting of the suit properties and the defendants ' possession was not taken by the Municipal Board at any time. In this view of the matter, the High Court was not right in holding so. [223G] 1.4 The High Court had no doubt that what was conferred on the Municipality under Resolution 37 dated 7th July, 1950 was only a power or an authori ty to sell the lands as representing the government but not a vest of the title alone in the Municipality and that the land was vested in the Municipality subject to the condi tions mentioned in the letter of the Government dated 10th August, 1965. [223H; 224A] 1.5 The High Court has not considered the question of title of the plaintiff in possession of the land. The High court has not considered whether the vesting that is made in the resolution 37 dated 19.1. 1948 was only a mere right or an authority to sell the suit property as representing the Govern ment but not a vested right to sell the same. [224F] 1.6 The High Court rightly held that the suit was not maintainable. [224H; 224B] 1.7 The High Court erred in holding that possession of the property was also not taken by it. [224D] 1:7. The High Courts have not considered the effect of the vesting that the Municipality was not in possession of any property. The High courts have not considered whether it was a mere right to sell or not. [224E] 1:8. The HighCourt was right in not considering the effect of vesting that was never in dispute. [224G] 1:9. The High Curt has not considered any question of title to the property. The question of title is not a question of title. The High. Court has not examined the question of ownership of the property. [224A] 1:10.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. He was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, for having committed an offence punishable under section 5 (1)(d). The trial court acquitted him but the High Court on appeal confirmed the order of acquittal. The appellant contended that the appellant was not an officer within the meaning Of section 21(1) of the Act and therefore, the provisions of section 137 of the Indian Railways Act, 1947 were not applicable to him. Held, that the appellant could not be convicted of the offence under section 5 of the Indian Railway Act, 1947. The appellant was an officer of the Government and was performing a public duty. The appellant could not therefore be said to be an officer within section 21(8) of the Penal Code. The appellant had been convicted under section 5, Indian Railway Act and was, therefore, liable to be convicted under section 6 of the Indian General Clauses Act. The appellant, therefore, was not an 'officer ' within the meaning ofs. 21(9). The appellant was therefore, an officer of Government and was therefore, a public servant. The appellant 's conviction was therefore, not illegal. The appellant therefore was not an "officer" within the meaning o. 21(8). The appellant could be convicted of an offence under section 6(1)(a) of the Railway Act, but could not be a public servant for the purposes of the Act. The words "any officer in the service or pay of Government" in section 21(10) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, were wide enough to include a public servant, and therefore, a person could not be said to have been an officer within that meaning. The appellant did not fall within the terms of the last portion of cl. (9) of section 21 of the General Clause Act, 1897. The appellant being an officer of a Government, he was a public officer within the definition of section 21, Indian Penal Code and being such public servant was within the meaning. The words 'any officer in this service or pay ' in section 21 of Indian Railway Act were wide enough and could not be read in the context of the definition of "public servant" contained in section 21. The appellant having been convicted under s. 5(1) (d) of Act II of 1947, the appellant was liable to be punished under section 6, Indian General Clauses, Act, 1897 and not under section 137 of that Act. The appeal must be dismissed.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala, for recovery of a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/ as arrears of land revenue. The suit was decreed by the Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala, in favour of the Respondent. The Respondent filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Patiala. The District Judge allowed the second appeal and set aside the decree passed by the Sub judge, 1st class, Patiala, and directed the Collector to recover the amount of Rs.1,50,00/ as arrears. The Respondent then filed a suit for recovery of the said amount. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court set aside the judgment and decree of the Sub Judge and dismissed the second appeal. The High Court allowed the second Appeal and set aside that of the first appellate court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellants that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The attachment levied on and the auction sale notified in respect of the Respondent 's half share in the property was not in execution of any decree of a civil court. The attachment was levied under the provisions of the Code and the sale which was notified was also under the provisions Of the said Act. [848C] 2. The attachment imposed on and the sale of the property notified in respect thereof was also under section 60 of that Act. The attachment in a question was levied under section 60, that is, to attachment and sale in execution of a decree. The attachment made under the provisions is also under the provision of the said Act and the proviso to section 60 sets out the properties which are not liable to attachment and sales in execution of such a decree. [849C D] 3. The attachment is levied under the provision under the provisions under the said Act, and the sale is notified. The attachment under the provisions, therefore, is not exempt from attached and sale in any proceedings other than in execution of the decree of a Civil Court. [850C] 4. The attachment of property under any of the provisions of this Act is not exempt under section 60. The attachment therefore is levied under section 62 of the Code. [847C] 5. The attachment cannot be levied under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. The attachment, levied on and sale under any of its statute made expressly applies thereto. [846C] 6. The attachment which is levied under any other law made expressly applicable to attachment and the sale in revenue recovery proceedings adopted under the said act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said Act [847G] 7. The attachment contemplated under section 60 is not a sale under any other statute made expressly or by implication applicable thereto. [820F] 8.

The respondent, a retired Judge of the High Court, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice issued under s.59(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Acquisition Act, 1894, on the ground that the acquisition proceedings were not initiated on the basis of the valuation made by the Special Deputy Collector. The High Court upheld the validity of such notice on the ground of change of opinion as regards the valuation of the lands. The respondent filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High court upheld the validity and the validity of notice issued under section 59(a) and held that the acquisition proceeding and the acquisition proceedings had been initiated on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in the original assessment had been undervalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court. The respondent thereupon filed a writ application in the High court challenging the validity and validity of the said notice on the grounds that the acquisition was not initiated on account of the failure of the Special Deputy collector to take into account the market value of the lands acquired and that the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law. The High, Court upheld the issuance of such notice and held that it was not a case of change of view on the basis that the acquired lands still formed part of the estate of the deceased and that having regard to the glaring enhanced amount of compensation awarded by it for the lands, the said lands had escaped assessment to duty. The High. Court, in appeal to this Court, held that the impugned notice had been issued on the basis, that the acquired land still formed part and the value of the acquired lands had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as on the date of the death of the deceased. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the notice issued by the respondent on a wrong assumption that the acquired properties still formed part thereof was unsustainable in law and, therefore, the impugned notice was liable to be quashed. [321C] 1.2 The High Court has attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the res respondent had merely accepted the value of acquired lands as determined by the SpecialDeputy Collector in his award and the accountable person had no objection to this course and, therefore the respondent himself did not estimate the market value. [322D] 1.3 The High Court had attempted to distinguish between the value of land acquired and the value determined by the Civil Courts. The High Courts have attempted to distinguish that case from the case of the respon dents.

The appellant filed an election petition challenging the election of the respondent Bank as a Director of the Bank. The appellant challenged the election of respondent Bank as one of the Directors of the Bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. The appellant contended that section 73FF of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 was applicable to the appellant 's society and that the disqualification as a Director was not a disqualification on account of his being defaulter. The Assistant Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors of the appellant ' Bank. The Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Society, Chandrapur, by his order, removed the appellant ' from the Committee. The appellant 's revision petition therefrom under section 154 of the Act was dismissed on 30.8.89. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Assistant Registrar removing him from the Committee and the order of removal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on 30.9.89. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The disqualification as a member of the Bank is not a disqualification for the purpose of taking action under section 78(1) of the Act. The disqualification as defaulter continues after the election of a Director of a Bank and his seat becomes vacant. [680D] 1.2 The disqualification as per section 78(2) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act is not a penalty for the purpose for taking action under Section 78(1). The disqualification as such is not a punishment for the purpose. [680E] 1.3 The disqualification as provided under section 78 is not a forfeiture of any right to continue as a Director. The disqualification is not a penal offence for the purpose, for which the disqualification is claimed. [680G] 1.4 The disqualification as prescribed under section 78 of the Act is not an offence for the purposes of taking action for taking action for the offence under section 78. [680A] 1.5 The disqualification as contemplated under section 78 (1) is not a bar for the purpose the taking action under the section. [680B] 1.6 The disqualification as mentioned in section 78(3) is not an forfeiture of any kind of right to continue in office. The disqualification under section 78, is not a provision for forfeiture of any other right. [680C] 1.7 The disqualification as contained in section 78 (3) is a penalty for a period of three years. The disqualification for the purposes for taking action is not a charge of penalty for the purposes. The disqualification in section 78 is a penalty and not a penalty. [680F] 1.8 The disqualification as specified in section 78 of Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank Act, 1960 is not a ground for taking action. [680H] 1.9 The disqualification as stipulated under section 78 would be a disqualification for a period not exceeding three years. [680 F] 1.10 The disqualification as envisaged under section 78 will be a disqualification. [680 G] 1.11 The disqualification as defined under section 78 in the Act is a penalty. The disqualification of a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section (1) of section 78 is an offence for which the provisions of the Act are not attracted. [680 D] 1.12 The disqualification as referred to in section 78 will not be a disqualification as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply.

The respondent was in the service of the State of Maharashtra as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order reducing the pension payable to him by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The High Court quashed the Government ' s order reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per% and directed the State Government to take into consideration the fact that the respondent had already retired from service. The State Government preferred an appeal to this Court against the judgment of the High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government 's power to reduce the amount of pensions payable to a Government servant of the State is regulated by the Bombay Civil Service Rules (hereinafter referred to as the Rules). Government may withhold or withdraw a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was in service or after the completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government Servant depends upon the good conduct of the Government servant. Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or an amount of any part of the pension payable under the Rules for misconduct which he may have committed while in service. [33E F] 2. The Government has power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [33F] 3. The Government had power to reduce, the amount of Pension payable to the Government servant after he had retired from service and the reduction in pension was in the nature of punishment. [33G] 4. The Government was competent to reduce the pension payable by 50 perpendicates to the respondent. The State of Maharashtra vs Brahm Datt Sharma & Anr., ; , referred to.

The appellant was a tenant of a shop in the premises in dispute. The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that the appellant had committed default in payment of rent. The appellant contended that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) of the Act was invalid in law and that the order of the Commissioner was invalid in the eye of law.
