The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the permission was invalid in view of the provisions of section 3(4) read with section 16 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that the permission had been properly or validly granted or refused by the Commissioner. [563 E] (ii) The High court was in error when it held that the appellant 's suit was incompetent. [563 D] (iii) The High Courts were not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3(2) of the U.P. Act. [563 G] (iv) The High. Court was in wrong in coming to its conclusion that the appellant was not entitled to raise the question of jurisdiction in a civil court having regard to the bar created by sections 3(4), 16 of the U P. Act. The High.Court was in error. [563 A] (v) The High 'Court was in wrong, in coming to a finding that the permission given by the Commissioner in exercise of the powers conferred on him by section 3 (3) was invalid in Law. [563 C] (vi) The HighCourt was in a wrong view of the fact that the question as to whether permission had been validly granted or not was not raised in a civil Court. [563 B] (vii) The High Curt was in error, in coming the conclusion that permission granted by Commissioner in exercise Of the powers conferred by section 3 was invalid in fact. [563 F] (viii) The High, Court was in a error in coming the finding that the appellant could move the Commissioner under s. 3 (3).

The appellant was a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission. He was appointed as a member of Punjab Public Service commission. He was promoted as a member in the Punjab Public Services Commission. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of his promotion. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that before making the reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from the High Court on the question of the alleged misbehaviour of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have been invested with the power to make a reference to this Court under Article 317(1) of the Constitution. [645C] 2. The power of the President to make a refer to this Court is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission can only be removed from his office on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court on a reference made to it by the President reports that the Chairman and such member ought to be removed on any such ground. [646C D] 3. The power to make reference to this court under Article 317 (1) is not subject, to the condition that he must have the facts considered by some other person or authority. [647C] 4. The power conferred by Article 317(2) is not in the nature of a power to make the reference to this Bench. [648C] 5. The power under Article 317 is not subject only to the condition laid down in Article 317(3). [648D] 6. The power is subject to the conditions precedent that he should first have the fact examined by some person or authority and then only then he should have the power to examine the evidence. [649E] 7. The power given to the President to pass a reference to the Supreme Court under Article 318(1) is subject to condition precedent that the President or any other person ought to be examined or cross examined as a witness, except with the leave of the Supreme Court. [650F] 8. The power in Article 317 (2) is subject only to a condition precedent that it must first have been examined by some another body or authority and that it must be exercised in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 145(1). [649F] 9. The power has to be exercised in a manner prescribed by the rules made under Article 145. [652F] 10. The power cannot be exercised in the limited sense of that expression. The power can be exercised only by a person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court. [613H] 11. The power must be exercised within the limits of the authority conferred on the President under Article 317. [654H] 12. The power vested in the President under article 317(1), is subject to conditions precedent that the Chairman of the Public Service Commission is guilty of misconduct and is liable to be removed from office on that ground.

The appellants were the trustees of a temple. The temple was dedicated for the worship of a family idol. The temple is a public trust. The temple has no right to worship in the temple. The appellants claimed that the temple was a public trust and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having no right to perform the public. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the temple is a private one and the deity is installed in the Temple and the deity was installed in the said temple and the deity has no right in the temple to worship in it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The temple being a public trust, it is a private and not a public trust within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowment Act, 1939. [833C] 2. The temple in question is a public temple. The question as to whether the temple is of a private nature or of a public nature has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is not necessary to decide the question as to the nature of the endowment. [834D] 3. The question whether the temple was of a private character or of a private endowment, is a question of fact which may in some cases conclusively establish that the endowment was of a public character. [835E] 4. The finding of the High Court that the endowment is of a public kind is not a conclusive proof of the intention to dedicate the temple to public and not to the members of the family. [836F] 5. The finding that the temple has been installed in the public temple is not a finding of fact. The finding is not a final finding of fact and the High Court has not given any finding on the question of the nature of endowment. [820F] 6. The finding recorded by the High Court is a finding of facts and the High court has not given a finding on the questions of fact. [820G] 7. The finding on the facts of each case whether an endowment is of public nature or of public nature is an important element to indicate the private nature of the endowments. [820A] 8. The finding has to be based on the facts proved and it is open to the High Court to interfere with the findings of the High court.

The appellant Bank was a contractor to the military and other authorities. The appellant Bank was to pay the amounts due under the bills of the appellant. The appellant was also authorised to sue for recovery of the amounts due in connection with the contracts with the approval of MaLhotra. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur, against the appellant Bank, for recovery of certain amounts due under a bill. The appellant contended that the appellant was an assignee of the bill and that the appellant had no right to attach it. The Trial Court held that the appellant 's suit was not maintainable. The High Court held that there was no transfer of the decree or of the claim which was the subject matter of the pending appeal as the borrower continued to be the owner and the lender was merely authorised to act as his agent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power of attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill and amounted to an equitable assignment of the funds by way of security. [707 D] (ii) The power to attorney coupled with endorsement on the bills dated July 19. 1948 was a specific engagement by Malhotra and the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. [708 D] (iii) The power conferred on attorney coupled with an endorsement on the Bill dated July 19., 1948 was a valid equitable assignment of money. [709 D] (iv) The power under attorney coupled with endorsements on the bill of 1948 was a necessary and proper equitable assignment of a specific fund in favour of the appellant and endorsed on it. [710 E] (v) The power is discretionary and is discretionary. [711 F] (vi) The power given to attorney coupledwith the endorsement on bill dated July, 19, 1948 is a clear engagement of an equitable assignment. [712 G] (vii) The power in the present case coupled with the endorsements on the bills of 1948 was not a clear engagement. [713 G] (viii) The power was expressed to be irrevocable.

The appellant was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The respondent was the manager and the appellant was the Manager of the Tea Estate under managing agency of the M/s Gillanders. The appellant was the managing agent of M/S Gillanders of M/ s. Gillands Arbuth not. The respondent paid the amount of Rs. 27,948/ to the appellant. The Income tax Officer assessed the amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the receipt in question was exempt from tax. The Appellate Tribunal held that the receipts in question being profits in lieu of salary, the same was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The High Court, on reference, held that there was no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the receipt was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and the same having not been assessed as his salary, the assessment order relating to that item of receipt was not legal. HELD: (i) The receipt of Rs.27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17(3) (ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to calling into aid any other rule of construction as it is sought to be made by the High court. [439B] (ii) The receipt by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from the payment of tax. [440C] (iii) The receipt in question is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on the securities. income from house property or profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. it has to be considered as "income from other sources" and brought to tax under section 56. [445C] (iv) The receipt is not salary but is a receipt. The receipt of a sum of Rs. 28,948/ is undoubtedly an income. [446C] (v) The receipt must be considered as income. But then the question is what is meant by "profits in lieu of income". [446E] (vi) The receipt cannot be considered to be salary though undoubtedly, an income. The receipt cannot therefore be considered as a salary though undoubtedly an income, but the same cannot he said to be one for salary. [447E] (vii) The receipt does not amount to salary. The receipt is therefore not salary. [441F] (viii) The receipt was not salary and was therefore not assessable to income tax.

The Madhya Pradesh Act, in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of cows and calves, of cows and buffaloes, is valid. The Act, however, does not prohibit the slaughter of the cows of all age and calves in the State of Bombay. The Act is not unconstitutional as it is not in consonance with the directive principles laid down in article 48 of the Constitution. The Act does not prohibit slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle. The Act has been enacted with a view to prevent the slaughter of animals of all ages, calves, and other milches. The Act provides for the imposition of a total ban on the slaughter of a cows of all years. The Act also provides for the levy of a total prohibition on the slaughter by the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Act was amended by the Bihar Act, which came into force on April 1, 1956. The Act provided for the imposition and collection of a total restriction on the slaughter and the imposition of the maximum limit of the maximum permissible limit on the slaughter. The Act further provided for the levy and collection of the maximum amount of tax on the slaughter, of cows, animals, calves of cow, calves or buffalo, and the slaughter of buffaloes, male and female, and the use of the same for the purpose of slaughter. The petitioners, who were the petitioners in the writ petitions, challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act violated the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1)(g) and (g) of the Constitution and was, therefore, void. Held, that the Act was not unconstitutional as the Act violated article 48 of Constitution. The impugned Act was not invalid as it was not in consonance of the directive principles of State policy laid down in Article 48 of the constitution. The Act did not prohibit the use of cows of the animals of all age or calves of animals, male and male, and the animals of calves of buffaloes, female and female, were not useful for the purpose. The Act in so far it prohibited the slaughter of bulls and bullocks, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) was valid. The impugned Acts were not unconstitutional as they infringed the fundamental rights of the petitioners under article 19(i)(g) of Constitution.

The respondent was a public limited company which was a public company. The company was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The respondent was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The company had its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh. In the year 1956, the company was incorporated under the Indian Company Act, 1913, and its registered office was situated at Nagpur. The company, however, was not registered under the Act. The company filed a petition under section 30 of the Act for a declaration that the Standing Orders applied to it and that the Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Order No.(e) of the Standing Orders No. (f) of the Company was applicable to it. The respondent contended that the Standing orders applied to him and that the respondent was not an 'employee ' within the meaning of the Act. Held, that the Standing order No. (g) of the company was applicable to the respondent and his service had been terminated in accordance with Standing Order No (e) and (f) and that the Company had committed a breach of the statutory provision in section 30 of that Act. The Standing Orders in question were not applicable to the company and the respondent was therefore not an ' employee ' within the definition of the expression for the purpose of the Standing Order. The Standing Order No, (e) was applicable to a company which was registered under the Companies Act, 1956, and the respondent had no ticket. The Standing order No (e), therefore, was applicable to him. The Standing orders in question being confined to those employees to whom tickets had been issued, the respondent who had no ticket was outside his purview and the result was that the Company was committed a breach Of the statutory provision.

The appellant company was a company incorporated in the year 1961 and it was constituted under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent company was incorporated in the State of West Bengal. The appellant company was incorporated on April 1, 1961. The respondent was incorporated in 1956. The appellant was incorporated in 1957. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Alloy Steel Project. The High Court held that the Alloy steel Project was a separate establishment and could not be treated as a separate establishment for purposes of section 16 of the Act. The High court held that the alloy steel Project could not be held to be a separate establishment because, under the Act, a company is itself an establishment, so that all units of a company like Hindustan Steel Ltd. will constitute one establishment. The High. Court also held that the appellant was not a separate establishment. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was against the decision of the High Court. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that merely because Alloy Steel project is owned, controlled and managed by Hindustan Steel Ltd., it has to be treated as part of the establishment for computation of bonus under the Act. [637C] The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that only because Alloy steel project is owned by Hindustan Steel Limited, it has to he treated as a part of the parent establishment for computation.

The appellant State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution Act, 1974, was constituted under the Act. The Act was amended by the Punjab Act No. 36 of 1977. The Act came into force on 1.4.1977. The appellant State Board was constituted under section 3 of the Act. Section 3 of the said Act provided for the levy of cess on the basis of water consumed by a person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis thereof as the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette specify. The appellant was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of rayon grade pulp a base material for manu facturing of synthetics or manmade fabrics. The appellant Company was registered under the Act as a 'processing vegetable products industry '. The appellant 's factory was established under the Factories Act, 1948. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of the cess on the ground that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable product industry". The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of the cess. The High Court held that the sugar industry would come within the Entry 15 as 'processing Vegetable products industry ' and that the sugar factories would come within entry 15 as " processing vegetable products industries". The High court also held that the cess was payable by the appellant company on the basis that the sugar factory was an industry as defined in the Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sugar manufacture industries would come under Entry 15 as the process of manufacture of rayson grade paste a base material was to be used for the table. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The sugar manufacturing industry does not come within Entry No. 15 of Schedule I. The sugar manufacture is not an industry within the meaning of Entry 15 and a fortio ri the manufacture of alcohol from molasses could not be considered to be an industry within Entry 15 of Schedule 1. [526C] 2. The sugar factories do not, therefore, come within Entry 14 of Schedule I of the Cess Act. [527C] 3. The sugar factory does not, therefore. come within Entry 17 of Schedule I and a fortification of the cess is to be done only by the predominant purpose and process and not by any ancillary or incidental process carried on by a particular industry in running its business. [528D] 4. The sugar industry does not, however, come within the ambit of Entry 15 of the Schedule I. [529E] 5. The sugar producing industry does not fall within Entry 15. [530F] State of West Bengal vs Delhi Cloth and General Mills, AIR 1963 SC 79; State of West Punjab vs Delhi Cloth & General Mills, ; ; State of West Nath & Ors. vs Delhi Cloth Mills, AIR 1964 SC 969; State of Bihar vs Delhi Cloth Mill, AIR 1964 Patna 969; and State of Bihar & Ors. etc. vs Delhi cloth Mills, AIR 1965 SC 969, referred to.

The respondent, an Advocate, filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant, on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application. The High Court, in revision, held that the practice of the profession was 'business ' within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. The High court, however, held that it did not fall within the meaning ofs.10(3)(b)(iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of the tenant on the ground of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the practice was 'business of an Advocate ' within the definition of Section 10 (3)(a) (iii) and that the practice in the present case was 'business'. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression 'business ' in Section 10(1) (a)(iii), is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice of a profession. The word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the context or other statutes or in a manner alien to the context of other statutes or the in a manner extraneous to the context. [14 E] 2. The word 'business ' is used in the context in which it occurred and not in any context of other statute or in a way alien to the statute concerned. [14 F] 3. The word "business" is used in Section 10 (1) (b) of the Act, the same meaning that the word may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. The word is used in another statutory provision. The word may have, when it occurs, in other statutory provision. [14 G] 4. The word should be interpreted in a context of the Statute in which it occur and not in a manner alienated to the context or in other statutes or even in a manner alienation of conduct amounting to nuisance to the occupiers of the other portions in the same building, securing of alternative accommodation by the tenant and denial of the title of the landlord. [14 H] 5. The word business occurring in Section 10 of the Andhra Act, 1908, is used in A wide sense so that the word 'business' has when it occurs.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of Rs. 4,00,000 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that the respondent was a debtor to the respondent for the approximate sum of Rs.4,00,00, and that the respondent would be entitled to withdraw the deposit on demand. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the appellant was a debtor and that the suit was barred by time. The High court also held that the respondent had a right to withdraw the amount of Rs. 1,00,0000 from the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had a right in the sum of Rs 4,00.000 to the respondent. [577 F] (ii) The High court was right in not accepting the contention that there was a demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 because the appellant had to be put on a footing of financial stability by giving the appellant the use of the sum. The respondent was not a party giving loan to the appellant for a approximate sum of money. The appellant was not a creditor to the respondent who was then unable to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills. [577 C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of time. [577 D] (iv) The High courts were right in not considering the question whether it was a case where money was deposited under an agreement and that the appellant could not be said to be a case of deposit of the sum of money by the respondent with the appellant under an agreement that the same would be paid on demand. [577 E] (v) The High. Court was right. [577 G] (vi) The High 'Court was right in taking the view that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can star in case of demand for return of the amount deposited. [577 A] (vii) The HighCourt was right. The High.Court was right, in not accepting that the appellant 's demand for a portion of the amount was not effective because there were common partners in the firms of the respondent and the appellant.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986 under section 3(1) of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The petitioner challenged the order of detention on the ground that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of his detention was necessary for put ting him back in jail. The petitioner contended that the order was passed in a routine manner and that the order could not be sustained because it was not a case of that nature and that the detaining authority had not been informed of the grounds of detention. The High Court dismissed the petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive Detention could only be sustained against a person who is in jail. [845C] 2. The fact that the detenu is in jail for at the most one day, does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive custody. [846C] 3. The fact of the detenu being in jail for the last more than one day, is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining authori ty was aware of the fact that the petitioner was already in custody and yet he was sub ject to be detained. [847D] 4. The fact, that the detenu was already in jail, does not taken away the jurisdiction or the order of the detention. [848F] 5. The fact remains that the detenu has been in jail for a period of at least one day. The relevant facts in connection with the making of the order may differ and that may make a difference in the application of the principle that a detention order can be passed against a person while he is in detention or in jail. But the relevant facts in the present case are not of a case of the petitioner in detention. [820F] 6. The fact is that the detenu in jail is in jail, for at the best one day. [849F] 7. The fact whether the detenu is already in jail or has been acquitted, the appeal is pending and in re spect of which he may be granted bail may not in all circumstances entitle an authority to direct preventive detention and the principle enunciated by the aforesaid decision must apply. [850F] 8.

The petitioners are working as casual labourers in the Telecom Department of the Telecom Department. The petitioners are working in the Telecom. Department of the Government of India. The petitioners were working as casual labour in the Telecom department of the Telecom. The petitioners filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the . The High Court held that the petitioners were not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees were enjoying. The High Court also held that the provisions of section 3(1) of the . were not applicable to the casual labourers. The petitioners have filed these petitions challenging the constitutional validity of the Act. The petitioners contended that the provisions are not applicable to casual labourers and that the provisions were not applicable in the case of the casual labourers and the petitioners were entitled to the benefits of the Act, and that the Act was not applicable to them. Dismissing the petitions, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Act are not applicable in cases of casual labourers. [609G] 1.2 The provisions of section 2(1) are not applicable. The provisions of Section 3(1)(a) are not attracted to the casual labour. The provisions are not attracted in the case. [610G] 1:3. The provisions in the Act are applicable to the semi skilled/skilled labour who have not completed 720/1200 days of service over a period of three years or more. The provisions do not apply to casual labourers. They are not being regularly employed. They are being regularly employed for more than six months. [611A] 1.4. The provisions relating to the provisions of Section 2(1)(b) are not relevant to the case. The provisions relate to casual labourers who have been continuously working for more than one year in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The provisions contained in the Act do not apply in cases of the casual labour who have been in continuous service for more than two years. [612B] 1.5. The provisions regarding the provisions of Sections 2(1), 2(1A) and 3(1B) are not available to the casual labourer. The provisions have not been made applicable to casual labour. [613C] 1.6.

The assessee, who was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 47, filed a return under section 22(3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on January 5, 1950, showing a non taxable income of Rs. 1,00,000. The Income tax Officer, on January 6, 1950, issued a notice under section 22 (2) of the Act to the assessee under section 22 of the Act, calling upon him to furnish a return of his income for the assessment years 1950 47 and 1950 48. The assessee filed a return on January 5. 1950, showing an income below the taxable limit. The Income Tax Officer, on February 5, 1950 issued a notice to the assessee to show cause why the return should not be rejected. The assessee did not file a return under s. 22(2) of that Act. The assessee then filed a return showing an income above the taxable limit and the Income tax Officer issued a notice on January 5 to the assessee on January 5 and directed him to furnish the return. The assessee thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the notice was not a valid notice under section 24(2) and that the notice under section 23(2) was not a notice under s. 24(2). The High Court, on appeal, held that the Department ought to have issued a notice in the present case and that the assessee was entitled under section 22 to make a return. The High court, on appeal to this Court, held that section 22(1) of the Income tax Act required a return of income and not a return of the income, which shows a loss or is below the taxable limits. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the notice issued under section 22 was not a proper notice under section 34(1) and that it was not necessary to issue a notice under that section. The notice under section 29(1) was issued to the assessee after the assessment was made and the assessee was not entitled to make a statement under section 24 (2). The notice under s 24(2), therefore, was not a good return under section 24. The notice was issued under section 29 (1) and the assessee had no right to make a claim under section 22. The notice issued under s. 29(1), was a valid notice and the assessee could not be allowed to make a fresh notice under section 31(2).

The Central Government issued a notification dated 23.8.1982 under section 9 of the , declaring the employees of the respondent Union to be the employees of a corresponding new bank. The respondent Union filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court held that the notification dated 23 8 1982 was ultra vires the Act and the Scheme was not even more defective. The High court held that the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of the Board of Directors and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Government. The HighCourt held that the scheme would not be even more defective if it was to receive the same construction as sub clause (b) so as to restrict the choice of appointment to the three persons specified on the panel furnished by the representative Union. The High Curt held that the impugned notification was ultra vires and that the scheme was not even a defective one. The High. Court held that it was not open to the Central Govern ment to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, and that the Scheme would not be available to the Central government. The High, Court held that there was no violation of the provisions of the Act and that the Act was not only ultra vires the Central Government but also beyond the scope of the Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that the Act contemplates only election or nomination of members and not election of members of a Board of Directors. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme of the Act is not only a part of the bank as the management is. It is open to the central government to amend the scheme so as to include representatives of the employees and other speci fied categories. [561C] 1.2 The scheme of election or nomination must, therefore, be such as would be conducive or conducive or conducive to the proper conduct of an election. [561D] 1.3 The scheme of appointment or nomination must be such as will be conducive or subserve the main purpose of the Act, namely, to enable the Central Government to continue the practice of an appropriate Election. [561E] 1.4 The scheme of appointing or nomination must necessarily be such as to give the best form of repre sentation to every category of persons mentioned in the Act. The scheme must be such that the Central Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, constitute the Board of a nationalised bank. [561F] 1.5 The scheme of selection or nomination must satisfy the test of election or nominations. The Central Government may also prescribe the manner in which the nomination or nomination must he made. The Central Govern ment may, by a notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Board of a nationalized bank. [560F] 1:6. The scheme of nomination or nomination, as the case may be, is not a mere formality.

The appellant was assessed to sales tax for the year 1962 63. The appellant filed a return of his income for the assessment year 1962 63 and claimed that the amount of tax due from him was not liable to be recovered from him. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of assessment. The High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery of the tax and the collection of the tax. The High court held that the appellant had the power of stay and that the Tribunal was not justified in staying the recovery proceedings. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the Tribunal has the power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. [69F] The High Court had the power under section 255(5) of the Act to stay the collection of tax or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in the disposal of appeals by the Appellate Tribunals. [69G] The High Courts have the power to pass orders staying recovery of tax or penalty due from an assessee. [69H] The power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal has been given to the Income tax officer only when an appeal has already been presented under section 246. The power of the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter or course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue.

The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police at the time of the departmental trial. He was charged with committing cognizable offences and was charged with misappropriation of Government money. The trial was conducted by the Superintendent of Police and the respondent was charged with misappropriating Government money. He was convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 500 and a fine of rupees 500. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the respondent was not a police officer senior in rank to a Superintendent and that the order of his dismissal was invalid. HELD : (i) The respondent was not charged with committing a cognizable offence and therefore he was not liable to be tried under section 7 of the Police Act. [655 B] (ii) The respondent had no power to dismiss him, because he was officiating as Sub Inspector of police at the time when the departmental trial was held. The order of dismissal was invalid because it was not passed under the statutory power conferred upon the Superintendent of police. [656 C] (iii) The order of the High Court was not a mere administrative order and was not passed in exercise of the statutory power. The order was not passed by the Superintendent. The order did not amount to a judicial order. The order passed by the High Court did not amount either to a judicial or quasi judicial order. [657 D] (iv) The order was passed by the Deputy Superintendent of Police in exercise of his pleasure. The order could not be made by a police officer junior in rank to the respondent. The order had to be passed by a police officers senior in rank. The order made by the Superintendent was not a judicial order and was therefore not a judicial or administrative order. [683 D] (v) The order passed in the present case was not a quasi judicial order and could not be challenged under article 226. [683 E] (vi) The order dated August 5, 1954, was not a purely administrative order and could only be made by the police officer senior. The order dated September 12, 1953, was not passed on the basis of a judicial order but was passed by a Magistrate who was competent to pass the order. [685 E] (vii) The order did no more than indicate that the respondent had been appointed as Sub Inspector. The order merely stated that he had been appointed to the post of Sub Inspector of the Police. The order also stated that the respondent 's general reputation for integrity was not good. [685 G] (viii) The order could only be passed by the police officers senior to the respondent and not by the Superintendent or the Sub Inspector. [685 D] (ix) The order made in the present cases was not a simple administrative order and therefore could not be said to be a judicial order within the meaning of article 226 of Constitution. [685 F] (x) The order in the present appeals was not passed as required by the said sub paragraph. The order in question was not passed either under the statutory powers conferred upon the superintendent or the Superintendent of the Police in accordance with the following rules: "A police officer may be departmentally tried under section7 of the Police act. " [685 G H] (xi) The order under the said sub para. was not passed within the express terms of para. 486 of the Police Regulations. The order therefore did not amount any judicial order. It was therefore not passed under any statutory power. [685 C] (xii) The respondent 's conduct was not a criminal or quasi judicial one. The order is not a quasi administrative order and is not passed under section 7.

The appellant was appointed as a Director of Health Services in January, 1971. He was promoted as a Director in February, 1971. The post of Director was converted into a specified post in super time grade II. The post was converted into an unspecified Specialists ' grade. The appellant was promoted as Director in February 1971. The appellant challenged the promotion of the appellant in the High Court. The High Court allowed the petition. The appellant contended that the post was not in the same cadre as that of Director in February 1970 and that the post of Director in March 1971 was not a cadre post in the same service. The High court held that the post in question was not a post in the cadre of Director in the year 1971 and that the appellant was not eligible for promotion to supertime grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' grade in the year 1973. The High. Court held that the appellant could not be promoted to supertime Grade II because he was not eligible to be promoted to the supertime grade I because he had been promoted to super time grade I in February 1971 and that he was not qualified for promotion to the super time grade. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is a senior and is not unqualified for the post of director in February 1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for promotion. [53E] 2. The post in question is a post in a cadre of Director. The post is a selection post and the post can be filled in by promotion. The post can be a selection post. The post cannot be filled in either by promotion or by promotion. [54F] 3. The post has to be filled in accordance with the relevant rules. The post may be filled in according to the relevant rules but it cannot be filled by promotion. It is a selection grade post and the promotion is to be made on the basis of seniority. [54H] 4. The post carries a fixed salary of Rs. 100 per month. The post carrying a fixed salary is a selection scale post. The pay scale of Rs. 200 is a selection pay post. The appellant has not put in any service in the post of the Director in February 1972. He is not qualified for the post. [54G] 5. The post which was originally converted into a definite post was unspecified Specialist 's post. The promotion of the said post was made on the assumption that the appellant had not put the said post in the category in the category. The post vacated by him which was created was unspecified specialists ' post. The posts were filled in by direct recruitment. The post held by him was unspecified post. The appointment of the appellant was made in February 1971, and he was promoted to the post of Deputy Director in February 1973. The post remained at that stage and there was no justification for giving a direction that the appellant should be considered for the post which was deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on the invalidation of promotion of Dr. P.R. Gupta.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) was enacted to provide for the acquisition of certain lands of the State of Punjab. Section 19B of the Act provides that the provisions of the Act shall not apply to any land acquired by the State Government under any law for the time being in force or by an heir by inheritance or bequest or gift from any person. Section 19 B provides that the excess land of such person shall be at the disposal of the State Government for utilization under section 10 A. Section 19 C provides that the surplus area shall be at disposal of the Government for utilization. Section 19 D provides that the State Government may, by notification direct that the excess area shall be deemed to have been acquired by the Government. Section 19 E provides that the amount of compensation shall be paid to the person entitled to receive the compensation. Section 19 F provides that the compensation shall be payable to the person who has acquired any land by inheritance or devise or gift from a person who is an heir by succession. Section 19 A provides that the Collector shall, after the commencement of the Act, determine the surplus area of any person under this section. Section 19 G provides that the land acquired by a State Government under section 19 A shall be deemed, for the purposes of the Act to have been transferred to the State Government. Section 20 B provides that if after the commencement, any person acquires any land by succession or bequest or gifts from any person, he may acquire any such land by gift or gift from the person to whom he is an heir. Section 19 H provides that the owner who acquires any land shall, by succession or testamentary transfer, be entitled to hold the land in excess of the permissible area. Section 19 K provides that the Government may, after the publication of the notification, direct that the surplus land shall be deemed for the purposes for the resettlement of tenants ejected or to be ejected under clause (a) of section 10 A or section 9 A. Section 20 A provides that if the land of such a person is situated in more than one patwar circle, he shall, by inheritance or testamentary transfer or gift from such person, be entitled, subject to the provisions of section 10A, to be determined by the Collector for utilization as surplus. Section 19 L provides that the area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 was not hit by the ceiling set up by the Punjab Security of land Tenures Act, 1954. The State Government issued a notification under section 19 B of the Act on April 15, 1954, declaring that the surplus pool will be deemed to be surplus for the resettlement. The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State of Haryana had no power to acquire any land by gift, gift or gift and that the State had no power under section 19B to acquire any surplus area for the resettlement and rehabilitation of tenants ejected, or to retain the surplus area. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of the Act was to see that no one held in excess of his permissible area and since by the gift to the son or wife the latter had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [632B] 2. The scheme was to see, that no one holding in excess of permissible area and no surplus area was to be allowed. The scheme is to see that the surplus surplus pool will not be affected by the interdict of section 10 B. [633C] 3. The scheme has to see that there is no surplus area. The scheme does not provide for the vesting of surplus area in the State Government, but only provides for the vesting in the State. The scheme provides that the entire surplus pool will vest in the State for utilization as a surplus.

The plaintiffs claimed the Zamindari of Amarshah under the will of Amarshi. The plaintiffs claimed that the Zamindari was granted to the first defendant by the State of Madhya Pradesh on December 3, 1950, and that on the death of Amarsh, the first plaintiff became entitled to the Zamindari. The plaintiffs contended that the suit was barred by the decision of the Compensation Officer. The Compensation Officer held that the claim was barred by section 14 of the Act. The plaintiffs appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the suit had not been filed within two months from the date of the notification under section 3 of the Act, and that the plaintiffs were entitled to the claim for compensation. The High court held that the plaintiffs had not filed the suit within two months of the notification and the plaintiffs were not entitled to claim the compensation paid or payable in respect of the Malguzars. The High. Court held that section 14 of Act 1 of 1951 did not invest the Compensation Officer with jurisdiction to determine competing claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3 of Act 1 Of 1951. The High 'Court held that the decision of this Court in the case of Amarshad was binding on the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the decision was instituted within two months. The High, Court held that in any event the decision of that Court declaring the claim of the plaintiffs to the lands vesting in the State by the operation Of section 3 of that Act had become final and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date. The High C.A. No. 24 of 1959 filed by the plaintiffs was allowed by the High Court and the plaintiffs ' suit with regard to Malguzart lands was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awardable to the plaintiffs. [334 B] (ii) The High Courts were in error in interfering with the decision of a court of competent jurisdiction. [335 B] (iii) The High court was in error when it held that the decisions of the Compensation officer were binding on the appellants. [337 C] (iv) The High Curt was in error. [338 C] (v) The High.Court was in error, in not reducing or setting aside the decision of an Compensation Officer. [339 C] (vi) The HighCourt was in wrong in not reducing any amount of mesne profit awardable to a decree passed more than six months after the notification under s.3 of the Act was issued. [340 C] (vii) The High ' Court was in wrong, in not interfering with the findings of the Compensation Officers.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that the respondent landlord had failed to pay the standard rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and held that the provisions contained in section 12(3) (a) of the Act apply to the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 12(2) (a), (b) and (c) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, do not apply to the case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The provisions contained in sections 12(3)(a) and (b) of the Gujarat Act are as follows: "12(3)(b) Where the rent is payable by the month and there is no dispute regarding the amount of standard rent of permitted increases recoverable under this Act, the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if, before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2), he makes an application to the Court under sub section (3) of section 11 and thereafter pays or tenders the amount of rent or permitted increases specified in the order made by the Court. The provisions contained therein are as follows; "12(1) Where the amount of the standard rent or permitted increase recoverable under this section is in arrears for a period of six months or more and the tenant neglects to make payment thereof until the expiration of the period for one month after the notice referred to under section 12(1) the Court shall pass a decree for eviction in any such suit for recovery. " The Bombay High Court in Ambalal 's case (supra) held that the dispute as to standard rent was to be raised within one month from the date of service of notice under section 12 (2) of the Rent Act and that the suit was governed by the provisions contained therein. The Gujarat High Court also held that the suit is governed by the Bombay Rent Act and the Bombay High Court held that the question as to standard Rent was to be decided by the Court of Small Causes. The Gujarat State Legislature passed the Bombay Rents Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act 1947, which came into force on April 1, 1947. The Bombay Act was passed on April 1. 1947. The Gujarat Act was passed with a view to give protection to the tenants from the operation of section 12 (3) (b) (i) of the said Act. The Bombay High Courts held that the Act was applicable to the suit and the suit was not governed by the Act. The Gujarat Legislature passed the Gujarat Act on April 1 of 1947. The Act was passed in the year 1947. The High Courts held the Act applicable to the suits. The Gujarat legislature passed the Gujarat Amendment Act, 1976. The Gujarat Amendment Act was passed by the Gujarat Legislature on April 1 and the Bombay Act was made applicable to the Bombay area. The Bombay Rent Act was passed to give protection of the tenants from eviction. The Bombay Legislature passed the Maharashtra Act on April 2, 1947. In the Bombay Act, the Bombay Act came into force. The Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House rates Control Act, 1946 was passed on May 1, 1947, and the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1949 came into force from April 1, 1948. The Bombay Amending Act, 1976 was passed on June 1, 1976. In the Gujarat Act, the Gujarat Act was amended by the Bombay Act No. 1 of 1976. The Bombay Amendment Act, 1977 was passed on July 1, 1977. The Bombay Ordinance No. 1/77 was passed on August 1, 1977, and the Gujarat Act No. 2/77 was made applicable on August 1/77. The Bombay amendment Act, 1976 came into force with effect from April 1/77, and the Act was made effective from April 1 /77.

The respondent company was incorporated in the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, as a limited company. The respondent company was a limited company and its directors were appointed to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. The respondent was a director of the Aluminium Company. The respondent filed a petition under section 21 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, read with section 66(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 for the assessment of the excess profits tax for the assessment year 1943 to 1943. The Income tax Officer rejected the petition and the High Court answered the question in the affirmative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the directors of the respondent company did not themselves hold the majority of the shares which were registered in the name of the Aluminium company and the respondent company was not liable to be assessed to income tax. [193 H] The question whether the directors of a company were holding the majority of shares as trustees or as a representative of the Aluminium Limited or as a director of a company could not be said to have a controlling interest in the company when they hold the majority. The directors of a limited company are the shareholders, and as such, have "a controlling interest" in the company. [193 B C] The respondent company is a limited company, and its directors are the shareholders. The directors are the directors and the right to vote is vested in them, though as between them and their beneficiaries the beneficial interest is vested in the latter. The directors, therefore, are the shareholders and as such have "a control" in the respondent company. [194 C] The question of law referred to the High Court should be in the negative. [194 D] The question referred to the high Court should be answered in the affirmative, and the High court should not be bound to answer it in the negative, because, the question of law is not a matter of application to the present case.

The respondent was promoted as Accounts Superintendent on the basis of seniority cum merit on his having passed the S.A.S. examination while promotion was denied to him. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of the respondent as Accounts Superintendent. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent was exempted from passing the S. A.S. Examination before qualifying for the promotion. The High court allowed the writ appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that the Board was exempted from the passing of the S.As. The High Courts were not justified in construing the provisions of the regulations and the Resolutions. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High courts cannot be justified in construing a Regulation which was passed by the Board in exercise of the powers conferred by the statute. The Board itself considered the ques tion in all its aspects and resolved that passing of the Resolution by the Board cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which is passed by the board in the exercise of the power conferred by the Statute. [512C D] 2. The Board by a subsequent Resolution had resolved on insisting on the passing of examination. Examination for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents as before be in sisted" the court found that it wouldmean that where the passing of S.AS. examination was insisted prior to that Resolution in the same shall continue to be insisted in future also, and if passing of the s.A. S. Examination was not insisted prior to the Resolution in the case of allot tees for promotion to cadre of Accounts Superintendent, the inference that the allottees were exempt from passing the Departmental Examination was not justified. [513C D] 3. The HighCourt was in error when it allowed the writ petitions. [514D] 4. The High Curt was in error. [515E] 5. The High. Court cannot be justified on the ground of equity.

The petitioner, a retired employee of the respondent No.6, filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for a declaration that the action of the State for payment of compensation to the petitioner was illegal and unconstitutional. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the State had no right to claim compensation in a proceeding under Article 32 or 226 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution, which enable the award of monetary compensation in appropriate cases, where that is the only practicable mode of redress available. [608C D] 1.2 The relief of monetary compensation as exemplary damages in proceedings under Article 32 by this Court or under Article 226 of the constitution is a remedy available in public law and is based on the strict liability for contravention of the guaranteed basic and indefeasible rights of the citizen. [609D] 1.3 The relief of compensation in proceedings under article 32 or 226 by this Court under Article 226 is a remedy provided in public law by way of penalising the wrongdoer and fixing the liability for the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental rights of the citizens. [610E] 1.4 The relief of damages in exercise of the power under Article 32 is a remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. [611F] 1.5 The relief of compensating the victims for deprivation of their fundamental rights in proceedings through petitions under Article 32 and 226 of the Supreme Court under Article 32, is a remedy under Article 32. [612F] 1:6. The relief of payment of compensation in such cases is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the public law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty of not protecting the fundamental rights under the private statute. [613F] 1 6. The compensation is in the nature ofoluble compensation ' awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public law duty and is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the private Law in an action based on tort. This Court and the High Courts are, therefore, not helpless and are not helpless and, therefore, no other form of appropriate redressal by the Court in the facts and circumstances of the case is possible. [614G H] 1:7. The relief in exercise of power under Article 226 or 226 of this Court or Under Article 226 by the High Court or under Articles 226 or 226 by the Court or Courts or conse quently invoked by the aggrieved party is a remedy which is available in public Law and is based upon the strict liability of the State which is possible. The relief is in the form of punitive damages. [615H] 1:8. The relief to the victims for loss of their fundamental right in proceedings through petition under Article 226 and/or 226 of the Court or under article 226 of the Consti tution is a remedy not available in public interest. [616B] 1:9. The relief for compensation in exercise of its power under Article 142 or 226 would be granted only once it is established that there has been an infringement of the fundamental rights. [617C] 1:10.

The petitioner, a prisoner, was sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by him to the President of India for commutation of the sentence were rejected by the President. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the death sentence. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right to means of information through the medium of an interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to death. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President of the India rejected the petitions filed against him. The petitioner is not the right of the Press, to have an unrestricted access to means of Information. [1187E] 2. The petitioner was asked for permission to interviewed the prisoners right from the time of the death of the petitioner. The petitioner had been asked for permission from the Superintendent of Jail to interview the prisoner. The petitioner did not ask for permission to be interviewed. The petitioner, therefore, was not entitled to express any specific view or opinion. [1188F] 3. The petitioner 's right to express his views or opinion is not an absolute right. [1189F] 4. The petitioner should be allowed to interview the two convicts, namely, Billa and Ranga. [1190G] 5. The petitioner must be allowed to interviewed the two convicts as he is willing to be interviewed and, indeed, if it were to appear that the prisoners themselves do not desire to be interviewed, it would have been impossible for him to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be permitted to interview them. [1191G] 6. The petitioner cannot be allowed to appear at the examination of the two convicts who are sentenced for life. [1192H] 7. The petitioner can be allowed to meet the petitioner in the main writ petition.

The respondent was the Receiver of a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but the respondent 's application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22, 1956 filed by the Receiver against the appellant was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner. The appellant 's application was dismissed for non compliance with the terms of the bond. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a revision petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. The appellant contended that the respondent was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. The High court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant was not answerable to the loss caused by fire and the respondent was liable for the loss suffered by the tea garden due to the fire. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The surety bond was executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District Judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond. stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. [360 F] The surety bond had, undoubtedly to be construed strictly but it was impossible to accept the contention that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in relation to the tea gardens. The surety bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the District Judge because "successor in office" would mean successor of the District judge in the post or office of the District Court. But the Subordinate Judge was, for the purposes Of the present proceedings, a successor of the district judge who was seized of the suit and who transferred it to the Subordinate Judge under the Tripura (Courts) order of 1950. The surety bonds were executed in and the possession of the tea garden in his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea garden was managed by the Receiver economically and efficiently. The surety Bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the Court.

The appellant was a dealer in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller, Lucknow. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellant. The appellant challenged the validity of the tax on the ground that the goods supplied were not sold by them to the Controller. The Sales tax Officer levied tax on the aggregate value of wheat by treating it as a sale. The appellant contended that the goods were supplied pursuant to the directions of the Controller and that the sales tax was not liable to be paid on the sales made to the Controller, that the goods had been sold by the appellant to the Controller within the meaning of the U. P. Sales Tax (Levy) Order, 1959. The Salestax Officer levied tax at the controlled prices. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of tax. The High Court held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning Of the U.p. Sales Tax. The High court held that the sales made by the appellant were not sales within the meaning ofs. 2(h) of the U P. Sales tax Act and that the appellant was liable to pay sales tax on the sales effected by it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The sales made by a dealer to the State pursuant to directions issued under cl. 5 of the Levy Order are not liable to tax. [534 E] (2) The tax payer is under the control of the State and he has to pay the tax on his own account. The tax payer has to pay tax on the sale of goods. The tax is payable by the dealer to the Government. The tax recipient is not under the control and supervision of the State. The tax payee is under the supervision of the Sales Tax Officer. The tax holder is under the management of the State Government. The State Government is under the Control Order. The taxer is under the superintendence of the State, and the tax payer is not under any contract. [535 H] (3) The tax recipient has to pay to the State Government 50% of the price. The tax provider is under the direct control of the Government. [536 A] (4) The tax payee has to pay his own money in the shape of a fixed deposit. The money is paid by the dealer in the shape or by the deposit. The deposit is made by the dealer himself. The money has to be paid by the purchaser to the State. [537 B] (5) The tax is not liable to pay on the sale made to the State by the dealer. The tax collecting agent is not under a contract of sale. The tax collected is not in any contract. The tax collection is not a sale. [538 C] (6) The tax collecting agency is a statutory authority. The tax collect agent is under the general control of the Sales tax. The tax receives the agent from the State Government and the State Government is the agent of the State in the matter of the sale of the goods. The State is under the exclusive control of the taxing authorities. The tax has to be collected by the State Government by way of tax. [546 E] (7) The tax collected by the appellant is not in the nature of a sale. It is not a tax on the goods. It is a tax on goods. The appellant is under the administrative control of the authorities. The State has the power to levy tax on the transactions of supply of goods. [546 F] (8) The tax collection of the tax is a tax. The State can levy tax on goods only if the goods are supplied by the dealer at the commencement of the Act. The tax Collection is not a 'sale ' within the meaning section 2(h). The tax payer must pay the tax in the shape and by the deposit of the amount.

The appellant was in jail for a period of three months. He was released on June 23, 1986. He was again released on June 24, 1986. The appellant was released on July 23, 1986, on the ground that he had been detained under the provisions of the Act. The appellant challenged the order of detention by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of article 22(4) of the Constitution were not complied with and that the Advisory Board constituted under the Act had not been constituted. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The report of the Advisory Board was more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order of the detention, though it was within three months from the date of the second order of detention. The fact that the report of the advisory Board was not made within three months of the date of detention, would not make the detention of the person beyond the date on which its report or beyond the period of three month after the date of order of detention was made. [206E G] 2. The report submitted by the Advisory Board is more than three months after the detention of a person. The report is more than two months after the date on the date of his detention. [206F] 3. The report must be obtained within three months. If the report of such an Advisory Board is not made within 3 months of the first order of detention, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three months after it is made. [207H; 207A] 4. The report cannot be said to be made within three weeks of the date on account of the fact that the Advisory board has not been constituted to which a reference could be made under the Act and whose report could be obtained as required by the Constitution. [207B] 5. The report, if not made within the three months, was made before the hearing of the case. If the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it is not answer to say that the representation, though not made within a three months, is disposed of before the hearing. If the Advisory Board has reported within three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for the detention of that person, the detention is illegal notwithstanding that the report is within three month from the date on whose report the report could be made. [208C D] 6. The report which is not made in the present case within three months, must be made within 3 weeks of the receipt of the report. If the Board is not satisfied with the report, the detention would be illegal notwithstanding that no report of the Board has been made within three month after its receipt. [208D] 7.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ . The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 2,00,00,0.5. The respondent filed a written statement and contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court rejected the objections and dismissed the suit. The High Court dismissed the civil revision application. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the notice under section 17 of the Act was not served on the respondent and the respondent had agreed to such entrustment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to arbitration of the named arbitrator. In that view of the matter, the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. [539C] 2. The conduct and the conduct of the respondent that there was no arbitration agreement and the respondent was dead at the time the suit was instituted or decree was passed or any such other ground which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matter of the suit or over the parties to it. [540C] 3. The conduct is of the parties who have agreed to refer their disputes in writing to the arbitration of the said arbitrator. The award was signed by both the parties, about which there is no factual dispute. The conduct was of the parties and by signing it, it could be stated that the parties have agreed to reference the dispute in writing to arbitration of their named arbitrator. [545D] 4.

The appellants were the mortgagees of a mortgage debt in respect of certain properties. The mortgage was executed in the year 1941. The mortgage deed provided that the mortgage debt was to be paid in the manner provided in the mortgage deed. The mortgage debt was not paid in the year 1943. The mortgage amount was paid in 1943. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and held that the mortgage was not a mortgage and that the mortgage amount was not a debt in the year 1944. The High court in appeal held that the decree was not a decree in a suit to which the Act applied and that the suit was not one for recovery of a loan advanced before or after the commencement of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words and that he had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of section 28 make it clear that an assignee of a mortgage decree is within the sub section, since section 28 sub section (1) is concerned only with assignment of debts. [118 D] (ii) The words "all the rights of the mortgagee" used in section 2 (22) of the Act make it clear, that an assignee is within the subsection, since section 29 sub section (I) is concerned with assignment of debt. [118 E] (iii) The words 'all the rights ' used in section 28(5) are wide enough to include the rights of a mortgagee in the original mortgage. [118 G] (iv) The words of section 28(1) are wide and include the rights in the original mortgagor. The words "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after the 1st day of January, 1939, or pending on that date and includes a proceeding in execution for (among other things) the recovery of a debt advanced before or during that period. [118 H] (v) The words in section 28 (1) are not wide enough to cover a case where a decree is passed in a suit for which the Act applies. The words and the words "all such rights of the mortgagor" used in the section make it clear. that an assignee or a mortgagee is within the section, since the mortgage was in the form of an English mortgage, and that the interest taken by the mortgagee was not an absolute interest. [118 F] (vi) The words, "all the right of the mortgagee", in section 28, sub section (i) is concerned merely with assignment of assets. The words 'any suit or proceedings instituted or filed ' in section 28 do not take in the present case. The words are not wide and include a proceeding in executing a decree. [118 B] (vii) The words are wide enough and include the right of a mortgagee to recover the debt from the original mortgagor and of the mortgagee 's right to recover the amount from the original mortgagee. [118 C] (viii) The words used in section 29(1) (a) are wide. The words used are "all the interest of the mortgagor". The words "other things" are wide enough. The words in the section are wide enough, and the words are wide. [118 A B] (ix) The words do not take within their sweep the rights of an assignee of the mortgage decree. The words do. not take within the sweep of the words "any suits or proceedings instituted on or after that date and include a suit or proceeding filed on that date.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided into two equal shares. The properties belonged to the joint family. The appellant and his four brothers were joint owners of the properties. The properties in dispute were divided into three equal shares. In 1947 the appellant and his three sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant and the other two persons for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 15, 1946, were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court confirmed the decree in O.S No. 12/54. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfers were made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the appellant in view of past illicit cohabitation. The appellant contended that the transfers in question were made by the joint family consisting only of himself and their four sons and that the transactions were invalid. HELD: (i) The transfers were not hit by section 6(h) of the Act. The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts. The gifts were not hit under section 6(j) of the . [46 B] (ii) The transfers are not hit by the provisions of section 6(g) of the , by reason of the fact that they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubine for her past services. [46 C] (iii) The transfers under Exs. A 1 and A 2 were not hit. The transfers under Ex. 186 were without consideration by way of gift and as such were invalid. [46 E] (iv) The transfers in question are not hit under sec. 6(h). The transfers were made without consideration by the appellant and were by means of gifts. [46 G] (v) The transfers made by the appellant were without consideration. The transfers are without consideration and are by way of Gift. [46 F] (vi) The transfers did not amount to gift. The gifts under Exs. 186 and 186 were not hit either by section 6 or section 6(k) of the and were invalid. The transfers in the present case were not hit on section 6(l) of the. [46 H] (vii) The transfers could not be said to be invalid. The gifts in question were not hit as they were motivated. The gifts are not hit. [47 C] (viii) The transfers, were not hit, by section 6 (h) of Act No. 12 Of 1954. [48 C] (ix) The transfers had not been hit by section 3(h) and were invalid as they were made in consideration of past cohabitation. [48 D] (x) The transfers must be held to be invalid and the subsequent transfers must be declared invalid. [48 E] (x)(x) The transfer was without consideration and was therefore invalid. [49 C] (xi) The transfers have been made without consideration and they were by way or gift. The transfers have not been hit. [49 E] (xii) The transfers cannot be said to have been made in consideration by way or in lieu of the transfer. The transfers must therefore be held to have been invalid. [50 F] (xiii) The transfers being in the nature of gifts, the transfers were invalid. They were not hit in the absence of any consideration. [50 G] (xiv) The transfers which were made without any consideration by way Of gifts were invalid. There was no ground for interfering with the decrees passed by the High Court. [51 F] (xv) The transfers of the properties under Exs. 187 and 186 were invalid. After the disruption of the joint family, Venkatacharyaiah was free to make a gift of his own property to his concubine. The transfers could be made by way of testamentary disposition.
