The appellant, a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, was incorporated in the year 1948. The company was incorporated in 1948. The appellant was incorporated in 1950. The company had been incorporated in 1948 and the company was incorporated on April 1, 1948. The Company was incorporated in 1947. The company, in the year 1949, was incorporated with effect from April 1, 1949. The company made an application to the Income Tax Officer for the issue of a certificate of fitness under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, for the purpose of making the requisite statement on oath under section 226 of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Income Tax Officer issued a notice under section 226 to the appellant on May 5, 1977, to show cause why the company should not be directed to pay interest for the period after the date of maturity of the insur ance. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the company was not making the payment to the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question of revoca tion of the notice under section226(3) is a question of fact and the High Court has rightly held that the question of revo ry of the notice was a question of law. [114F] 2.1 The question of re spondent 's revoca tions of the notice is a question which is a question arising for decision in the present case. [114G] 2.2 The question of res judicata is a question relating to the liability of the appellant to pay interest on the amount of interest. The question whether the appellant was entitled to interest for the said period after the expiry of the period of maturity of insur ances is a question to be decided in the present appeal. [114A] 2.3 The question of the revoca tement of the notice issued under section 226 (3) of Income Tax Act 1961 by the I.T.O. is, therefore, clearly justified. [114B] 2.4 The question of reco ry of interest under section 244(3) does not arise in the present cases. The question is whether the appellant is entitled to interest on the amounts of interest. [114C] 2.5 The question of retu ments of interest under the Income Tax Law, 1961, arises in the present appeals. The question as to whether the appellant should be directed to make the payment of interest to the respondent is a question that arose in the present proceedings only after the L.I.C. made the requisite statement. [114D] 2.6 The question of refund of interest to a party is a question on which the Court can decide. The question, therefore, is whether the claim of the appellant is barred by limitation. [114E] 2.7 The question of limitation is a question regarding the liability of a person to pay interest. The appellant has not been able to prove that the notice issued by the IIC.C. was not in accordance with the provisions of section 226(2) of the Act. [114H] 2.8 The question of jurisdiction of the I.I.T. is a question involving a question of jurisdiction. The question regarding the jurisdiction of the L. I.C. is a matter of fact and it is not possible for the assignee of the policies to obtain revocation of the notice by the ICI. [114 E] 2.9 The question of validity of the notice of the IICC is a question as to the liability to pay interest to the assessee in the manner prescribed in clause (vi) thereof. The question has to be decided by the L.l.C.

The appellant was the owner of certain lands in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the lands in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appeal should be deemed to be one under the Code of Civil Procedure in which case it would fall under article 156 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act. HELD: (i) The Act provides a period of limitation different from that prescribed therefor by the First Schedule. The first limb of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act is concerned only with proceedings under special or local law for which a period of time is prescribed in that Schedule. The second limb of section 30(2) is concerned only to proceedings under special and local law for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local laws. [143 E F] (ii) The first limb is concerned only in the case of proceedings under special law for which no period of limitation is prescribed in the First Schedule, and for the purpose Of determining any period Of limitation prescribed for such an appeal. [143 G] (iii) The first part of section 29, sub section (2) of section 29 is not attracted. The first part is concerned only of proceedings of this kind. The first is concerned only where the special law prescribes for any suit appeal or application a period of Limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by first schedule. [143 A] (iv) The first and the second limb of sub section (1) of section 30 are concerned only with proceeding under special orlocal law for which the period of limitation are prescribed. [143 B] (v) The first clause of section 29 (2) is not attracted because the second part of section 30 (2) does not apply to a case where the First Schedule is not prescribed for such a special or local Law. [143 C] (vi) The first proviso to section 29(1) is not applicable because it is enough if the special law provides for such an application a period which is different from any period prescribed therefor. [143 D] (vii) The first sub section (3) will apply even to a case when the First Schedule prescribes for an appeal or application for a particular period. [143 F] (viii) The first portion of section 29 of the Limitation (Amendment) Act, 1951, is not attracted to an appeal under the Act even though it does not fall under article 154 of the First schedule. [144 G] (ix) The first paragraph of section 29 does not apply because it is not of a type for which a prescribed period of limitation has been prescribed in the first schedule. The first paragraph is concerned only for proceedings of this type, that is, proceedings under special, or local law. [143 H] (x) The first para of section 29 will apply only to proceedings of this nature and not of the type prescribed therefor by second paragraph.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He challenged the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate, Mathura on the ground that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a bus stand under section 76 of the Act. The High Court held that section 76 of The Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate to fix the places for the bus stand and the power to issue a notification fixing the places for bus stand was implied in section 68(2)(r) of the Act and that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses was only a halting place and hence the order made under section 76 was unassailable. The appellant challenged the validity and validity of the said order passed by him. The High court held that section 77 of the Act conferred wide power on the District Mags trate to fix the place for the bus stands and the power of issuing a notification fixing a bus stand was implicit in section 68 of the Act, and that the power to fix a bus stand could be exercised only by the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the District Magistrate. The High, Court, however, held that section 78 of the Act had nothing to do with the fixation or alteration of a bus stand and that the order made thereunder was not a valid one. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the District Magistrate had no power under section 76 to appoint any Area as a bus stands and that the area where the appellant was asked to stop his buses was only one halting place and therefore the order made by the District Magistra trate was unassailable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The District Magis lrate had been authorised by the State Government under section 76(2)( r) of the , to pass an order fixing the Municipal Bus Stand as a bus Stand for purposes of the Act; and therefore, rules could be framed by the State Govern ment as a bus scheme. [717C] 1.2 The District Magistri trate had been authorized by the State Govt. to pass an impugned order. The District Magi trate cannot be equated with the Regional Transport Author ity constituted under the Act. [718C] 1:3. The District Magistrate had the power to pass an o r order fixing the Regional Bus Stand as the bus stand. The power to issue the notification fixing a Bus stand was implied from section 68(1) of the . [718D] 1.4. The High Courts have erred in holding that the District Magistrates had the power under section 77 of The Act to pass an exer cise order fixing the limits of the bus stand, and the power under Section 68(2) of the is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional transport authority as held by this Court in T.B. It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by the Regional TRANSCO to determine the area in question as a bus bus stand and hence the impugned order passed by District Magistrate is not a valid order. [719E F] T.B., it is not disputed, that in the case of no order has already been passed by any authority, the Regional Transport Commis sioner has the power to make an order fixing a bus stands. [720F] T. B. it is not a case of a person providing any transport service in a District. The District Magistrates cannot be equated to the Regional Transport Officer constituted under the . Act.

The appellant was charged with the offence of attempt to commit theft of paddy. The prosecution case was that on October 19, 1961, the appellant was driving the truck which was loaded with 75 bags of paddy. On October 19,1961, the appellant came driving the truck as a cleaner of that truck. The truck was intercepted at the spot and the truck was intercepted. The appellant was found to be carrying 75 bags of rice. The appellant 's name was not mentioned in the FIR. The appellant contended that there was an attempt on the part of the appellant to transport paddy from Delhi to Delhi and so there was an attempted attempt on the side of the appellant and that the truck was not carrying any quantity of rice. Held, that the appellant was not guilty of the offence of export within the meaning of Para 2(a) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. The fact that the appellant had given a letter to the consignee Sawan Ram and Chiranji Lal were partners of the firm and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to commit it. The sufficiency of the actus reus is a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt to commit the offence. The sufficiency is a question which had led the difficulty because of necessity of distinguishing a person from acts which are mere preparatory to the crime.

The appellant was the Managing Agent of the respondent company. The Managing Agent of respondent company was appointed as the Managing Agent on the terms of the Managing Agency Agreement. The Managing Agency Agreement provided that the Managing Agent shall be responsible for the payment of the entire remuneration and not any part of the commission actually earned by him or which had accrued to him under the terms of his Managing Agency Agreements. The Managing Agents were to be paid the remuneration in the manner prescribed by the Managing Agency Agreements and the remuneration was to be paid in the manner provided by the Managing Agent Agreement. The respondent company was to receive the Managing Agent 's commission from the Managing Agents. The Managing agent was to receive commission from the Company on the remuneration of the Managing Agent. The Managing agents were to receive commission on the remuneration and not on the remuneration. The Managing agency agreement provided that the remuneration was payable to the Managing Agents on the remuneration paid to them. The Managing Agencies were to receive the commission from the company on the remuneration received by them. The respondent was to receive remuneration in the same manner as the remuneration paid by the Managing Agents to the Managing Agent but the remuneration was not paid to the Managing Agency. The Managing remuneration was to become a part of the remuneration paid and the remuneration paid was to be treated as remuneration for the purpose of convenience. The Managing agencies were to receive remuneration from the company in the manner laid down in the Managing Agency agreement. The Managing Company was to receive a commission from the appellant on the remuneration payable to the employees. The Managing Director of the respondent was to be responsible for payment of the commission to the employees and was to be entitled to the remuneration paid in the same way as the remuneration of other employees. The respondent paid the commission to its employees on the remuneration agreed to be paid to them on the remuneration so paid. The Managing Partner of the respondent paid the remuneration to the employees on the commission paid to them and the remuneration so received was the remuneration paid for the entire year. The Managing partner was to receive from the company the commission paid by him on the remuneration given to the employees in the year of assignment. The Managing Firm was to receive payment in the manner specified in the Managing Agent Agreements. The respondent received commission from the appellants on the remuneration which was paid to the employees as remuneration. The respondent contended that the Managing Agency was not liable to pay any commission to the appellants and that the Managing Agents were not liable to tax in respect of the same. Held, that the Managing agent was not liable for the payment to the appellants. The Managing Business of the respondent is a business and the remuneration to be income by way of commission is not by itself sufficient to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to the remuneration of his year of assignment since the assignment is an indivisible contract for a whole year 's remuneration on the completion of a whole year. The remuneration paid to the appellants on their remuneration was not by itself enough to vest in them a beneficial right in the remuneration of their year of assignment because the Managing Agent was to be held to be the person entitled to the amount by way of remuneration not as per this agreement. The respondent had no right to receive the entire remuneration. The remuneration was not a part of his remuneration and was not liable under the agreement to pay the same. The Managing Committed was not liable as the Managing Agents had not been paid the remuneration for the entire period of the assignment. The respondent could not be said to have been a person entitled to receive the remuneration not as a matter of right but as a matter which was not liable. The Managing Crew of the respondent had been appointed as the Agent on the basis of the Managing Agents Agreement. The remuneration for the whole year was the income of the respondent and the remuneration in that year was the remuneration of a commission paid by the appellants to the employees, and was the profits and gains of the business carried on by the respondent.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be. a confession under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. HELD : (i) The evidence of the two witnesses is not reliable. The evidence of P.W.s 11, 13 and 15 is not reliable and the evidence of P,W.s 1, 2 and 3 is not reliable, and the evidence is not reliable in the case of an oral statement. [808 D] (ii) The evidence in the case is circumstantial. The circumstances found by the High Court are found to be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved. [809 D] (iii) The circumstances found proved should be consistent only in the hypothesis of guilt of the appellant and the circumstances must be of a definite nature and tendency and that they should not be such as are likely to drive the accused to commit the offence. [810 D] (iv) The circumstances proved should be such that they should reasonably be consistent only if they are consistent only with hypothesis of the crime of which they are charged. [811 D] (v) The circumstances should be such which would exclude other hypothesies but the one intended to be proved should be of such a nature that it should be consistent with the hypothesis that of the guilt Of the accused and that of the accused. [812 E] (vi) The circumstances so established should be consistent either with the hypothesis or with the hypothesis, of the guilt. [813 F] (vii) The circumstances must be such as would reasonably be consistent with hypothesis of guilt. [912 G] (viii) The circumstances show that the accused had committed the murder. The circumstances show the guilt of all the accused. The circumstances should not be so consistent as to exclude others from the crime of the crime. [913 G] (ix) The circumstances relied upon by the High court are not such as to justify the conviction of the accused under section 302. [914 G] (x) The circumstances established by the High Courts are not such that they are consistent with the innocence of the accused, and the circumstances are such that they must be of such conclusive nature and character that they should have been such as to make the sole ground of conviction. [915 G] (xi) The circumstances of the case are not such which would justify the conviction.

The appellant was appointed as a temporary employee in the respondent Corporation. He was confirmed in the post of temporary employee in December, 1973. The respondent was appointed as temporary employee in January, 1973. He was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the respondent corporation on probation. He was also confirmed in the service of the respondent Corporation on the same terms and conditions. The respondent Corporation terminated his services on the ground that he had been found guilty of misconduct. The appellant 's service was terminated by the respondent Corporation in terms of the provisions of the Orissa Insurance Corporation Act, 1962. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a Letters Patent Appeal before the Division Bench. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent Corporation was empowered to terminate the services of the appellant under the Act and Scheme, 1976, which came into force on May 1, 1976, and the scheme called the General Insurance (Rationalisation of Pay Scales and other Conditions of Service of Development Step) Scheme, 1976 which came into effect on May 1. 1976, was not applicable to the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent corporation was empowered to cancel the service of a temporary employee by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. If the provisions of law or the rule are construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. [224F G] 2. The expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee 's service whether permanent or temporary which shall be decided by the Board" is susceptible of two interpretations. The one interpretation put up by Sri Ramamurty is that the Board may unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there is no need for the services of a particular employee, in given facts and circumstances, though the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving one months ' notice or pay, in lieu thereof, pay one month ' s salary including allowances upto the period of termination. [224H; 224A B] 3. The expression 'in the event the Society not being having any further requirement of the employee 's services whether permanent or Temporary which shall be decide by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days ' notice or payment in lieu thereof and also a direction to pay all the allowances upto that date including the period of his suspension. [224C D] 4. The expression `in the event, of the Societynot having any further needs of the employee, in giving facts and circumstances the employee ' s service whether permanent, or temporary which may be decided by Board, is susceptible of both the interpretations. [224D] 5. The expression used in law or the rules is capable of two interpretations, namely, that the Board of Management may form an objective opinion on the basis of the material, that the post which is the employee is occupied no longer is in need. Thereby, the post would be abolished. [224E] 6. The expression, 'in the case of the Society ' is capable of that interpretation. But from the facts, it is clear that the Board did not abolish the post but put an end to the service of appellant. [224G] 7. The expression has been interpreted in the context of the constitution and the law.

The appellant was a licensee of a shop in Orissa. The appellant was the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his name was entered in the bid register and the entry was signed by the Collector of Mayurbhanj. The Collector of Mayompet issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 under the provisions of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915, cancelling the licence of the appellant. The appellant challenged the order of cancellation of the licence by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court quashed the order of the Collector on the ground that the appellant was not a fee or tax, as the primary purpose of the Act was to restrict the manufacture and sale of country liquor. The High court held that the appellant had the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor and that the appellant could not be said to be a fee or a tax, as it was not a tax. The High. Court also held that the Collector had no authority to issue a notice under section 22(1) of the Act and the Collector had not been concerned and did not in fact issue any public notice for purposes of sub section (1) of section 22. The High 'Court further held that the case was completely covered by its decision dated January 3, 1974 in O.J.C. Govind Das on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector was not for the grant of an exclusive privilege under section 22 of the Act. The State Government issued a fresh notification dated August 19. 1970 under the Act for fresh settlement of the shops and the appellant was entitled to the grant of the exclusive privilege under Section 22 by virtue of section 6(a) of the Amending Act irrespective of the validity of rule 103(1) and Rule 103(1). The High Court held that the sale of country Liquor was not a sale of liquor within the meaning of section 2 of the Amending Ordinance. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have the exclusive right to manufacture and sell liquor and the appellant has the exclusive right of manufacturing and sale of liquor. The appellant has the right to sell liquor and sell liquor. The State has the exclusive privilege of manufacturing, selling and selling liquor. The power of the State to issue a notification under the Act is not a legislative power. The power to issue a Notification under the Act cannot be delegated to the Board of Revenue. The power is not a judicial power. The High courts have the exclusive power to issue the notification. [814 B C] 2. The HighCourt has the exclusive power of the Government to issue a fresh notification under the provisions contained in the Act. [815 C] 3. The High Curt has the exclusive jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus to the State to disregard the decision in Ajodhya Prasad 's case that the amount realised by auction was illegal and that section 6 was therefore ultra vires the powers of the Legislature. [816 D] 4.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court reduced the sentence of the appellant to one of life imprisonment. The appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant was altered and the sentence of death was altered and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of doubt. The High court accepted the evidence of the tailor and convicted the appellant under section 302, read with section34, I.P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The High, Court also held that there was corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar in material particulars in regard to the connection of the accused with the crime and in regard to conspiracy as well as the common intention. The High. Court also held the appellant guilty of the offence under section 201 read with section 120B I.P.,C. and convicted him of an offence of murder under section 302 I.P,C. The High 'Court also held that the appellant had not been convicted of the offence of murder. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that there was sufficient corroboration of the prosecution evidence. [601 B] (2) The High court rightly came to a conclusion that there is corroboration of the testimony of Dinkar. The High C.J. had rightly come to the conclusion, that there was no corroboration of the eye witnesses. [602 C] (3) The High.Court rightly came to that conclusion. [603 D] (4) The High Curt rightly came to its conclusion that there were sufficient corroboration of evidence of Dinakar in material particulars. [604 D] (5) The High ' Court rightly came the conclusion that the appellant has not been convicted under section 302. [605 D] (6) The High Courts rightly came to this conclusion that there had been sufficient corroboration of prosecution evidence. The High Courts were, therefore, right in holding that there was enough corroboration of the case of Dinkar and the appellant was not guilty of the offences. [606 D] (7) The High,Court rightly came the finding that there was evidence to connect accused No. 3 with murder. [607 D] (8) The HighCourt rightly came that there was a corroboration of the medical evidence.

The appellant 's land was acquired by the Town Planning Officer under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1948. The appellant 's application for a declaration under section 6 of the Act was rejected by the Town planning Officer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order. The High Court held that the Town Planning officer was not competent to determine the amount of compensation in the appellant 's case. The High court held that the appellant ' s land was not acquired by the appellant and that the Town planning officer was not entitled to determine the compensation in the present case. The appellant appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Town Planning Officer is required to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner of any property or right injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions of section 69. [876C] 2. The Town planning officer under section 32 (1) (iii) has to find out the market value of each plot of the original plots and the value of the plots included in the final scheme. The market value of the plot is determined on the basis of the market value. [877D] 3. The Town Plan Officer under section 32(1)(iii) has a duty under clause (viii) to calculate the increment to accrue in respect of each plot included in the preliminary scheme. The principle for determining the compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not. The principle is that the owner of an original plot who is not provided with a plot in the final Scheme gets his right to compensation from section 71 of the Act which says that the net amount of loss shall be payable to him by the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. The principle of compensation is the principle of compensation which is the basis of compensation. [878E F] 4.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama. The appellant was the second son of Seethama. The first son of Seethamami was the eldest son of Seethirama. The second son of the appellant was the eldest daughter of Seetharams. The first respondent was the eldest of the children of Seetharaman. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the gift was invalid. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the gift of the appellant 's property was invalid for uncertainty and that the appellant was entitled to a declaration that it was invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not entitled to a decree for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89 of the Indian Evidence Act. The words "he shall give to the female children" in section 89 of that Act are not intended to be exhaustive. The words used in the will are "he shall deliver possession of the remaining properties to the children as and when they become major". The words "his shall give to female children" are not intended by the legislature. The words are not intended for the purpose of construing a will. The words in the will must be read as intending that the daughters should get the lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The words 'he shall give the female children ' in section 89 are not intended as a guide to the interpretation of a will. [882 C D] (ii) The words "she shall give to a female children" used in section 89 must be read in the context of the words used in that section and the words "he may give to the male children" used therein. The words of the will are not intended in the context. The words must be read with the words " he shall give to each son and shall give to every female children". The words 'his shall give the male children ' in the will have to be read as if they were not married. The words do not mean that the testator intended that the daughters would get their lands after taking them into account the bad and bad quality. The words were not intended to have the intention of the testator to give one kani out of one kani and three quarters of land to the daughters. The words did not mean that they intended that the daughter should get the land devised to them taking into account their good and bad Quality of the land and that the land was to come, the area of nanja and punja lands to be taken by each daughter was fixed.

The plaintiff appellant, a co sharer, filed a suit for partition of the plots in dispute, being co bhumidars, alleging that the defendants were in joint possession of the plots, being co sharers, because after the abolition of the zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the plaintiff became the owner of the plots and the defendants were not in joint possession thereof. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court, however, held that the defendants had not been in joint possession, and that the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. The first Appellate Court also held that the plaintiff 's name was never informed about any proceedings by the defendants and was assured by the defendants that they would take proper care of their share in any proceedings that may be instituted. The first appeal was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the defendants being in joint possession were in joint occupation of the plots of the plaintiff and the plaintiff had no concern with the defendants. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The possession of the defendants, apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of the plaintiff. The fact remains that the District Judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. [867G H] 2. The possession is not a joint possession. The possession must be in the nature or joint possession of a joint owner. The possession in the instant case, apart from the mere possession of the respondents, would be the possession of a co sharers. The fact remained that the District judge has come to the clear finding of facts after consideration of evidence that a specific finding was recorded by the District Judge after consideration of all the documentary evidence. [868C D] 3. The High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the defendants assured the plaintiff that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. [869F G] 4. The High court erred in law.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Haryana. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as Deputy Prime Minister in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioner has filed this writ petition challenging the appointment of the Respondent No.1 as Deputy Prime Minis ters. The petitioner also challenged the appointment as Deputy Prime Ministers of India. Dismissing the writ petition, the Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner himself does not press the writ petition challenging his appointment as Deputy Chief Minister. [1033C] 2. The petitioner is not a Minister of the Union and there is no separate form even for the Prime Minister. The petitioner does not press it. [1034D] 3. The petitioner was not a Minister at the time of his appointment as a Deputy Prime Mini cation of India. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Secretary is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is nothing else in the nomination paper. [1035E] 4. The oath Register is by the incumbents of the Council of Ministers. He has also been described as Deputy Prime Ministry. He has been described as Prime Minister. He has not 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minister. [1135E] 5. The petitioner, himself does not Press the Constitution, and he does not press this.

The appellant was a public utility industry. The management of the appellant 's factory was directed to close the factory on the night of 1st November, 1948. The management was directed to take steps to close the appellant ' s factory on the following day. The appellant was directed to report to the management immediately after the closure. The management did not report the closure to the management. The management took steps to close down the appellant 'S 's factory on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the directions of the management. On the question whether the appellant was entitled to holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act, the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the continuity of service of the workers was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that the appellant was not entitled to annual holidays with pay. Held, that the appellant 'was entitled to the benefit of holidays under section 49B (1) (a) of the Act. The appellant had no right to the benefit under the Act. It was not open to the management to terminate the services of the workmen on the ground of strike without giving them an opportunity to show cause. The appellant 's right to the benefits under section 49(B) (1) was not affected by the strike. The management had no right under the Act to terminate the service of the workmen. The appellant could not be said to have been deprived of the holidays under section 48 B (1)(a) of Factories Act. The management could not be held to be entitled to the benefits of holidays under the Act because the appellant had not been given an opportunity to explain the circumstances in which the strike was held. The appellant having failed to give the opportunity to explain his conduct, the management was entitled to the relief under section 49. The appellant did not have the right to claim the benefit of the holidays. The appellant, therefore, could not be allowed to raise the plea of the workmen that the stoppage of work on 1st November 1948 amounted to a strike. The appellant should have given the workmen an opportunity to make a representation to the management before the management could take a decision that the continuity in service of the appellant was broken by it. The appellant cannot be said to be entitled under the Act, because, the appellant had no opportunity to explain its conduct. The appellant has no right to claim any benefit under the provisions of the Act because, the management had no power to terminate the employment of the workmen by giving them an option to pay them. The appellant is entitled to the protection of the provisions of section 49 B(1)(a).

The appellant was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the , the public exhibition, circulation or distribution or the production of the film, even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence, section 292 I P.C. notwithstanding. the absence of such certification, may constitute an offence under section 292, I.P.,C. notwithstanding, the film has been certified by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious or any material to quash the proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The trial court when itars the case, is unsustainable because, the trial court has not considered the certificate issued under section 5A(1A) of the Act. [5A B] 2. The High Courts in exercise of their appellate jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, have jurisdiction to entertain the petition under section 482 of the Code. [5B] 3. The High court has jurisdiction to entertain a petition under section 561A of the Code, and it is an inherent power of the High Court to entertain a writ petition. [5C] 4. The High courts have jurisdiction to try the petition under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, and the High Court has jurisdiction to exercise it. [5D] 5. The High Censors are not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 79 of the Penal Code. [506D] 6. The High. Court has jurisdiction under section 482 to entertain a complaint. [506E] 7.

The petitioner, a retired High Court Chief Justice, was appointed as a Judge of the Patna High Court in a writ petition filed by him. He was appointed as an Additional Judge of the High Court in the Patna High court. He was also appointed as a member of the High court. The petitioner was appointed as the Judge of the Bihar High Court in July, 1973. The petitioner challenged the appointment of the Judge of Patna High Court by a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High court held that the petitioner was not a legal representative of the Government Pleader and that his client 's claim as the sole representative of the State Pleader was not a legally cover for seeking lucrative conduct of the cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf. The petitioner 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court. The petitioner then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The main contention of the petitioner was that his client was the Government Pleader for the Patna District, and that his clients were not his members. The High Courts held that the Government Pleader was only an agent of the Government pleader and that his duties were only to the Government who were his principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a Public office. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner is a retired High court Chief Justice and, in a sense, every member of the legal profession, has a higher dedication to the people. The office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [775C D] 2. The petitioner has a number of other duties to discharge. He owes no duty either to the public or to the public. He has a number. He owes a duty to the Public at all times. [776D] 3. The duty of the Government Advocate is to the Government Pleader, Madras. [778E] 4. The duty to appoint a number of Pleaders as the Judge is a dignified renunciation of office, not a chase for the lost briefs through the 'writ ' route. The Government Pleader is only an agent. [779F] 5. The Government Advocate is only an Agent of the Government. [780F] 6. The Government pleader is only an agency of the Government, that his duties are only to the government who are his principles and he owes no responsibility to the public, at all and he owes a duty of responsibility to the Public. [782F] 7. The Government advocate is only an officer of the legal department. He is only an employee of the Government and he owes nothing to the public in the land of Gandhi is a dignified user to the people, and he owes the duty of the public at every time.

The Mills purchased 5,000 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Bank. The shares were to be distributed among the shareholders of this company in the proportion of 1,666 shares offered by the Bank of Indian Ltd. The shares of the bank of India were to be Rs. 100 per share. The shares in question were to be sold by the Bank to the shareholders of that company in the ratio of 1:1. The shares to be sold were to be valued at Rs. 100. The shares had to be valued by the Bank at Rs. 200. The shares sold were to the extent of Rs. 100 and the shares were to the value of Rs. 200 for acquiring the shares. The shares purchased by the Bank were to be divided between the shareholders of each company in the proportions of 1,667 shares offered by each of the shareholders. The shares so purchased were to be allotted to the shareholders at the rate of Rs. 150 per share. On the question whether the distribution of the right to apply for the shares amounted to a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, the High Court answered the question in the affirmative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the distribution of a right to apply was a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning Of section 2(06A) of that Act. [570 G] (ii) The High court was right in not taking into account both the normal and extended meaning of that expression. The High Court had not taken into account both these normal and extended sense of that expression and even if the distribution of right to apply could not be regarded as dividend within the extended meaning of section2(6A), it was still dividend within the ordinary meaning of that term. [570 D] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding, that the distribution was of a capital nature and not an exhaustive definition. [570 E] (iv) The High. Court was right, in holding that it was open to the Mills to sell the right to the shares of the company in the market, and to distribute the proceeds among the shareholders. [570 F] (v) The High 'Court was right in the view that the distribution must be made by the company to the shareholders. It was open to it to sell the shares of that company to the shareholder of the Mills. The High.Court was right, on the facts and circumstances of the case, in holding, the distribution of, the right to applied for the shares had a market value of Rs, 100. [570 A B] (vi) The High, Court was right. [570 C] (vii) The High C.I.T. Bombay vs The Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, ; , referred to.

The appellant was the returned candidate. The election petitioner filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant. The High Court refused to examine the returned candidate and dismissed the election petition. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High court allowed the appeal and set aside the election of respondent No. 1. The High Curt held that the election petitioner was not entitled to examine the respondent No. 2 as the name of the witnesses was not mentioned in the list filed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI. The High, Court also held that the appellant was not entitled for examining the respondent No 2 as the witnesses were not mentioned in sub rule (2) of Rule I of Order XVI and that the appellant had failed to produce the witnesses in the list. The High. Court also held the appellant to be entitled to examine respondent No. 3 as the witnesses. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant could not examine the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 as the witness was not mentioned as a witness in the list and that the High Curt had erred in holding that respondent No.2 was not a witness in his list. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule 1 of Rule 1 is in respect of witnesses to procure their presence and the Court may, if it is satisfied that the party has sufficient cause for the omission to mention the name of such witness in the List filed under sub Rule (1) or (2) and make an application as provided by sub rule (3) to procure the presence of the witness and the Court shall, if it so desires, allow the witness to examine those witnesses and to produce documents through the witnesses who are called to produce documents under Rule 1A. [532B C] 2. The obligation of the appellant to supply the lists of witnesses within time prescribed under Rule 1 of order XVI is in respect to witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the Court is t necessary. If the party wants the assistance of a Court to procure presence of a witness on being summoned through the Court, it is obligatory on the party to file the list with the gist of evidence of witness in the Court as directed by sub rule 1. [533C D] 3. The obligation under sub rule(3) of Rule l of Order XVI is in regard to witnesses to obtain the assistance of Court and the Court has no jurisdiction to refuse to examine the witness who is present in the Court on the short ground that the name of witness is not mentioned in his list filed under Rule 1. [546D] 4. The only jurisdiction the Court has to decline to examine the witnesses produced by the party and kept present when the evidence of the party is being recorded and is not closed, and the Court had no jurisdiction to refusal to examine the party who is present. [546E] 5. The Court has no power to refuse to answer the witness produced by the parties and kept present on the date fixed for recording the evidence on the sole ground that the names of witnesses are mentioned in the List prepared under sub rule 2 of Rule 1. The Court may refuse to examine witnesses on the ground that the party is not in a position to produce the witness in the party on the short point that the name is not mentioned therein.

The appellant was appointed Principal of the College in the year 1981. He was appointed as Principal of the college in the year 1982. He was confirmed in the post of Principal in the year 1983. He was promoted as Principal of a college in the years 1981 and 1983. He continued to be Principal till the year 1983 when he was appointed as the Principal. He was also confirmed in the same post. In the year 1983, the appellant was appointed as a Principal of the institution. He was not given any opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The appellant challenged the order of his appointment by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Principal was not competent to make the appointment and therefore the Committee of Management had no power to make the selection on April 27, 1981. The High court held that the Selection Committee had no power on April 27 to make the Selection Committee and that the Committee of management had no power under the Act to make the appointments. The High. Court held that there was no power to appoint the appellant as Principal of an institution in contravention of the provisions of the Act. The High, Court held that since the Principal had no power of appointment, the Committee of the Management had no authority to make the appoint ment. The High 'Court held that the Committee had no authority or power to make appointment and therefore, the Committee had the power to make an appointment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment was made in contravention of section 9 of the Act and the Committee of its Management had no right to make the order. [975C] 2. The appointment of the appellant was therefore valid. [976D] 3. The Committee of Management was not competent under the Act or the Committee of any Management or the Institution. [977E] 4. The Committee was not competent for making the appointment. The Committee had no right of appointment to make appointment. [978F] 5. The Committee did not have any power to make appointments. The Committee could not make appointment. The appellant was not given the opportunity to show that the Committee was not authorised to make the Appointment. [979F] 6. The Committee has no power to frame the appointment. If the power to appoint is not suspended, it would not be open to the Selection Committee to make and select appellant or the Committee. [982F] 7. The Committee is not competent to appoint the Principal of an Institution in contravention of sections 9 and 9 of the . [982G] 8.

The Delhi Cloth Mills (Control) Act, 1941, was passed by the Central Government in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the Act. Section 3 of the said Act provides that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the Act and for regulating the procedure and the procedure of the authorities of the Central Government. Section 3(1) of the Act provides that all rules made under the Act shall be deemed to have been made under the provisions of the Act, and shall be deemed always to have been in force on the date on which they are made. Section 3 provides that the provisions of this Act shall apply to every person who is a citizen of India and who is not a citizen of any country. Section 3 (2) provides that the State Government may, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, by notification, make rules to carry out the purposes and objects of the Act with respect to the matters enumerated in the Schedule. Section 3 empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purpose of the Act in the manner provided therein. Section 3, however, provides that the rules made under section 3 shall be deemed, for the purpose, to have been validly made. Section 4 provides that the Rules made under the , shall be deemed not to have been duly made. Section 5 provides that the Government may, after consultation with the State Government, make rules, for the purposes of carrying out any of the provisions of that Act. Section 6 provides that the Act shall come into force on such date as the Central Government deems fit. Section 7 provides that the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall apply to all proceedings under the Act. The petitioners in the writ petition challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not applicable to them. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Act did not apply to them as the Act was a piece of legislation and that the Act had been enacted in the interest of the general public. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act was not a piece of law. It was enacted in the interests of the general good. It was not intended to be a piece of Legislation. It was intended to be an Act to be a law in the interest and for the benefit of the general community. It was, therefore, not possible to find fault with the view of the High Court that there was no error apparent on the face of the record and that the taxing authorities should be left to determine whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption. [503C D] 2. The Act is a piece of social legislation and is intended to be used in a welfare state. It is a social legislation and not a piece or piece of legislation. It is not possible to see that the legislature intended to be so used. [504D] 3. The Act does not require the attention of the authorities to the circumstances of the case. The Act has been enacted in exercise of powers conferred by the Act. [505E] 4. The Act cannot be said to be a legislation in the interest or for the benefit and welfare of the general people. It is the stage reached by this product, in the process of manufacture of fabrication of a "textile" which should decide the question. [501E] 5. The Act, therefore, does not apply to the Act. It does not, therefore, appear to be a case of a mere book entry.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied and incidental work. The appellant company was also a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. The appellant was a Senior Supervisor. The appellant 's establishment was situated in Dhanbad. The respondent was a Senior supervisor in the company. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the transfer of the case to Labour Court, Patna. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workman and transferring the case from the Labour Court, Dhanbad to Labour Court Patna should have given an opportunity to the management to transfer the case to the Labour Court Patna. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government was misled by the representation of the workman. The Government had not denied the documents annexed to the Special Leave Petition. The Government in support of the order of transfer had relied on the letter dated September 8, 1988 written by the Assistant Electrical Engineer in proof of the electricity supplied to the respondent. The letter dated September, 8, 1988 was not a genuine letter. The Government could not have refused to give an opportunity to transfer the matter to the Labour court. [295B C] 2. The Government is not justified in refusing to give an oppor tunity of representing his views when any order to the prejudice of the normal procedure laid down in section 64(1) and (2) of the Act is sought to be made against him, be it a transfer from one Income Tax Officer within the State to an Income Tax Officer without it, except of course where the very object of the transfer would be frustrated if notice was given to the party affected and he is afforded a reasonable opportunity of representing his view on the question and the reasons of the order are reduced accordingly. [295C D] 3. The Government has been misled by the representations of the workman, and the order of transferring the case is quashed for not communi cating reasons to the assessee. [295D] 4. The Government should record reasons in making the order of transferred after affording a reasonable opportunity to the assessee in the matter. The order of transfer in that case was quashed for not commu nicating reasons to be recorded. [295E] 5.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. The company was incorporated on October 7, 1955. The company had its registered office in Delhi. The company, its employees and workmen were employed in the hotel. The company made an application under section 12(4) of the , for a reference of the dispute to a tribunal. The tribunal held that the reference was incompetent and the reference was vague. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the reference. The High Court held that the dispute was incompetent and two grounds had been urged in support of it. The High court held that the company was not made a party to the reference and that the reference did not mention any officer of the trade union, but mentions the union itself. The High. Court held that there was a dispute between the management and its workmen as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi. Held, that the reference which was otherwise valid did not become incompetent merely because it was mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the dispute. The fact that in the order of reference the quoted words were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent. The fact remains that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer and its workmen which were mentioned as its workmen. The fact therefore that in the orders of reference the words " as represented by Hotel Workers ' Association, Katra Shahalshahi,Chandni Chowk,Delhi " have been added for the purpose of the case.

The appellant imported a consignment of rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it. The Customs authorities assessed the goods under Heading No. 84.06. The appellant filed a refund claim for the duty paid on the goods. The Assistant Collector of Customs rejected the claim on the ground that the goods were not parts of the engines. The appellant preferred an appeal before the Customs Excise and Gold Control Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that the goods are parts of the engine, and that the goods in question are parts of such engines. The Tribunal held that the goods imported were parts of the machinery and not parts of internal combustion piston engines. The Revenue filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Notification grants exemption in part from payment of the Customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and, therefore, is not readily understandable. When the Notification grants exemption to the parts of the Engine or engines, the intention of the Notification is clear enough to provide that the parts of their engines, mentioned under Heading No 84.06, will get the benefit of exemption as provided by the Notification, irrespective of the fact that they or any of them have already been included under Heading No, 84.06 or under any other Heading. 84.6. 84.2006 will not get the benefit as provided in the Notification. [228C D] 2. The Notification is applicable to parts of the vehicles mentioned under Heading 84.06 only. The parts of the vehicle or engine in question and not the parts thereof. [228D] 3. The Notification does not, however, contain or refer to the parts thereof, but only refers to parts of such vehicles. [228F] 4. The Notification will apply to parts of a engines mentioned under Heading Nos. 84.07, 84.6, and falling under Heading No., 84.06 and not to parts of other parts thereof. The Notification would apply to parts only of the engines mentioned under heading 84.06 which is to say, parts of such engine or engines in question. [228G] 5. The Notification cannot be said to be in any way inconsistent with the Notification. The Notification has to be read in the light of the Notification. It is not possible to accept the contention of the respondents that the parts are parts of a particular engines or engines. [228H; 228A] 6. The Notification, therefore, will apply to the parts only of engines mentioned under the heading 84.6 and not to the parts mentioned in the Notification, and not to those parts of the motor vehicles mentioned under heading No. 84,06.06. [228B] 7. The Notification applies to parts of engines mentioned in Heading No.84.06. In the instant case, there is no material or evidence nor is there any finding of the Appellate Tribunal or the Customs authorities that the bushes, which have been imported by the appellant, are parts of internal fire piston engine, as mentioned under Heading 8.06. It is also not possible to hold that the parts in respect of which the exemption is claimed, are parts thereof. In the circumstances, it is necessary that the Customs authorities should embark upon the question and decide whether the bushes, imported by the appellants, are really parts of such machinery.
