The appellant was a tenant of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy the quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The respondent 's application for house rent allowance was rejected by the Authority. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Authority. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rules in terms contemplated the grant of house rent allowance to every employee of a particular category but the rules did not make the grant in such absolute terms. Held, that the rules which were included in the terms of the contract between the parties included the rule in question in the terms contemplated by section 2(vi) of the Act. The rules in terms envisaged the grant of a house allowance to every person of a particular type but the rules do not make the grants in such absolute term. The rules which were not included in the contract between parties could not be said to be inconsistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Act and therefore the rules in the terms excluded the rule in terms of section 2(vii) of the ,. The rules did not create any absolute right in the appellant to claim the house rent allowance and the rules did no affect the rights of the appellant to the house rent allowances. The rules were not included within the definition of "wages" contained in the Act. It was not necessary to decide whether the rules in question were applicable to the case. The rules of the appellant did not make any provision for the grant of the house rent Allowance to every employee. The rules made under the Act did not make a grant in such an absolute terms. The rules could not be considered as part of the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplated by section 3(i) of the . The rules did no validity in the present case.

The detenu was detained under section 3(1) of the (3) of the . The grounds of detention were served on him on March 25, 1980. The grounds of the detention were served upon him on March 31, 1980. On March 31,1980, the detenu was served with a copy of the grounds of detention. The grounds were served on the detenu on March 31. 1980. The detenu was served a copy of a letter dated March 31, 1981, addressed to the first respondent, requesting him to furnish copies of certain statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of the order of detention. On March 25, 1981, the detenu received a letter from the State Government requesting him to supply the copies of certain documents. On March 26, 1981, he received a letter, dated March 31. 1981, from the State of Maharashtra, requesting him for supply of copies of certain records. On March 29, 1981, a letter was addressed to the detenu that the copies of the statements and documents were supplied to him. On March 30, 1981, an order of detention was served on the first respondent. The detenu filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the detention on the ground that the order of the detention was vitiated because the concerned Minister of the State Government never passed any such order and under the rules of business framed by the Governor under Article 166 of the Constitution, the detaining authority could not pass the order of his detention. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the detenu that (1) the order of preventive detention was vitiated by the non supply of the copies of statements and documents referred to in the grounds and (2) the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies of which were asked for by the detenus, and that the grounds of order of detention were not supplied to the detenu. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The delay of more than three weeks in supplying the copies of all the statements and the documents to the detenus has vitiated the detention. [352B] 2. The delay in supplying the documents to detenus has vitiated their detention. [351C] 3. The delay is of a very long duration. The delay has to be explained satisfactorily. The delay cannot be explained satisfactorily unless it is satisfactorily explained. [351D] 4. The delay, if any, in supplying the statements and other documents to the detenu has vitiated the order of their detention. The delay does not affect the validity of the detention. The detaining authority has to explain the delay in the light of the facts and circumstances of each case. [351E] 5. The delay caused in supplying the material to the detenus is not fatal to the detention. It is only when the detenu is supplied with the material that the detaining authority can make an order under clause (6) of Article 22 of the Constitution withholding the supply of those portions of statements after satisfying itself that their disclosure would be against the public interest. [351F] 6. The delay on the part of the detaining authority in supplying the relevant documents to the petitioners has vitiated the impugned detention. [353F] 7. The delay which has been caused in supplying copies of the basic materials and documents to the appellants has vitiated the continued detention. [354G] 8. The delay was of a very short duration. The supply of the documents to detenu was not in the interest of the security of the State. The delay could not, by any reckoning, expose the persons to any alarm or danger at the hands of the agents or partisans of the detenus. [354A] 9. The delay between the date of the documents and the date of detention cannot be explained at the earliest. [354B] 10. The delay must be explained satisfactorily and the delay must be satisfactorily explained.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by the sections and particularly by section 419 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against the common order acquitting several accused persons. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that a joint appeal was maintainable in law. [447B] (2) The High court was wrong in not considering the scheme of the Code. [448C] (3) The High Courts were wrong in holding the joint appeal not to be maintainable. [449C] (4) The High courts were wrong in not giving the benefit of section 419 of Cr. P.C. to the accused persons. [445C] (5) The High. Court was wrong. [446D] (6) The High 'Court was wrong in upholding the maintainability of the joint appeal by a State against several accused persons convicted at one trial. [455E] (7) The High, Court was wrong, in holding the common appeal not to the appellant. [456E] (8) The High Curt was wrong in directing the State to hear the appeal on merits. [457F] (8). The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the joint appeal.

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in foreign territory. The assessee was a partner in the firm. The assessee filed an income tax return for the assessment year 1962 1962. The Income tax Officer held that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the assessee had not claimed relief under section 26(3) and therefore the assessee was entitled to relief. The Appellate Tribunal held that the foreign business of the assessee was charged under the 1918 Act within the meaning of section 25(1) of the Act and therefore the foreign business was not liable to tax under the 1918. The High Court held that the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 was applicable to the assessee and the foreign business had been charged under the Act within the definition of section 25. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The assessee was entitled under the 1918 law to relief under the 1922 Act with regard to the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. [912 B] (2) The assessee is entitled to relief in respect of interest on securities as well as on foreign business. [913 C] (3) The assessee 's income was not liable for tax under the 1922 law. [914 D] (4) The assessee had not been able to claim relief under section 24(3) in respect of the rental income. [915 D] (5) The assessee could not claim relief under the 1961 Act on the ground that the foreign income was not chargeable under the 1918 Acts. [916 D] (6) The assessee, therefore, was entitled to claim relief in respect to the rental of the house properties owned and owned by the Indian firm which was discontinuance in the year. [917 E] (7) The assessee cannot claim relief under Section 25(3). [917 F] (8) The assessee has not been able in the present case to claim relief. [918 G] (9) The assessee must be taken to have claimed relief under Section 24(3). The assessee was not able to claim that relief under section 23(3) was not available to him. [919 G] (10) The assessee would be entitled to relief only under the 1922 Acts. [936 G] (11) The assessee should be given relief under the 1918 laws. [936 D] (12) The assessee did not claim relief in the present cases.

The respondent company entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for the manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said Department for the construction of the Capital Project, mahalhinagar. The respondent company supplied the bricks to the Public Works department for the construction. The appellant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The respondent received payment for this payment for the said period. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contract in question was a works contract and not a works contract. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The contract in this case was a contract of sale and not a work contract. The contract in that case was a works contracts. The contract was a contract for sale and not an agreement for sale. The contract of sale was a contract to supply and supply of bricks to the contractor. The contract did not contain any provision for the supply of bricks. The contract also did not contain a provision for the payment of the price of the materials. The contract itself was a contract in fact cast in a different mould and it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special features and characteristics of the contract with which we are concerned that the decision of the High Court was not correct. [163E F] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, who was a member of the Lok Sabha, was elected to the Lok Sabha in the year 1971. He was declared elected to the Rajya Sabha on the ground that he had been elected to the Legislative Assembly in the year 1972. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency dated 25th June, 1975 issued by the President of India on the ground of the duration of the House of the People during the extended period of the House. The petitioner contended that the duration of his House of the President was not in operation on the date of the meeting of the Lok Council of Parliament and that the Proclamation of emergency was not in force on the date on which the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 was passed by Parliament. The President of India rejected the contention of the petitioner and held that the Proclamation was invalid. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of his Proclamation of Emergency. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Proclamation dated 25th6 1975 had ceased to be in operation on 3rd December, 1971 because the resolutions passed by the two Houses of Parliament approving the Proclamation dated the 3rd December 1971 had ceased to exist on 3rd February, 1972 and the Proclamation of the Emergency dated 25.6. 1975 had ceased not to be in force on 3rd January, 1972. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3rd of December, 1971 had ceased not in operation. The Proclamation was issued by the Vice President acting as President of India in the year 1977. The Proclamation had been duly issued in the official Gazette. The period of five years (being the period for which the House was constituted) had not been published in the official gazette. The period during which the Proclamation was in operation was in operation. [439B C] 2. The Proclamation dated 25.06. 1975 had been issued by the State Government in the year 1978. The period for which it was issued was in operation on 4th February, 1976. The period was in operation when the House of Parliament was in operation and therefore Parliament was entitled to extend the period of the house of the People for a period not exceeding one year at a time. [440C D] 3. The Proclamation issued by the Governor acting as President acting as the President of the State (Extension of duration) Act, 1977 was not in existence on the date when the House was enacted in the year 1976. The Proclamation could not be challenged on the ground, that the two Proclamations of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions passed in the Houses of Parliament until they were duly revoked by the two Pro cemeations which were issued by the Chief Minister acting as President.

The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the premises No. 29 South Masi Street, Madurai, which was originally constructed by the respondents, was a private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The Trial Court held that the premises were private property and set aside the decision of the Trial Court. The High Court, however, held that the property was a private one and set aside that decision. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the property in question was a public temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. [156 B] (ii) The appellant 's case was that the property belonged to the Thoguluva family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf of the family. The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 1 of 1950, being OWP No. 650 of 1882, and the appellant 's ancestor, for a declaration of his title to the property. The suit was therefore not one for a public temple. [156 C D] (iii) The appellant was entitled to contend at the time of the leave application that the property belongs to and was an alienable private property of the family and that the property had been inalienable and was a public Temple. [156 D] (iv) The High court was right in proceeding on the aforesaid assumption. [156 E] (v) The High Courts were wrong in proceeding on a assumption that whether the property was private or a public temple, it was incapable of valuation. The High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere on the assumption that the property is a private or a private temple. [157 D] (vi) The High courts were wrong in holding that property was a public trust.

The appellant, a company, was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, and its employees were paid wages in lieu of the tiffin arrangements made by the appellant. The company was not paid any cash allowance for the tiffs. The appellant, however, claimed that the company should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffin arrangement at present made by the company. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiffin. The Tribunal also held that the company was not entitled to the cash allowance in the nature of tiffs and directed that the clerical staff should be paid as per the provisions of the Factories Act. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant ' s claim was not maintainable under the Industrial Disputes Act. The Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance for lndin arrangements made in respect of tiffins. The Tribunal was wrong in making an order in respect of cash allowance for thiffin arrangements. [572 D] (ii) The Tribunal had overlooked the fact that the appellant had throughout been making provision for tiffs in respect of its employees and in fact when after the award was pronounced in the proceedings of 1956 and this question was taken up for direct negotiations between the parties. The Tribunal has overlooked the fact. that the appellant has throughout been making provisions for tiffins which are always superior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the appellant by the award. [572 E F] (iii) The Tribunal has erred in law. The appellant has throughout worked out the policy adopted by the appellant in re employing the retired persons. The Tribunal, therefore, erred in law on the ground that the impugned decision is erroneous in law. [572 F] (iv) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant is under an obligation not to provide any further facility to the employees by way of giving them a cash allowance for ness. [572 G] (v) The Tribunal erred in law by holding that the Tribunal has overlooked that the appellant 's claim for cash allowance in respect of lndin arrangement was either improper or unjustified. The Tribunal erred on the ground, that the appellant could not, therefore, be blamed on that account.

The respondent, a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund, was a subscriber to a State Railway Provident fund. He was a subscriber of the State Railway. He was the subscriber to the Provident Fund. The respondent was a subscriber thereto. The respondent applied to the 3rd respondent for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law. The 3rd respondent applied to be made a party to the proceedings. The 3 rd respondent applied to this Court for relief. The 3th respondent contended that the money was not immune from attachment. The 3RD respondent contended that by sending the two cheques to the Reserve Bank of India in performance of the obligation under section 3 of the , the debt was discharged and the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber. Held, that the money in the hands of the Reserve Bank was exempt from attachment. A person who had received the money on his behalf, cannot be said to be a person who had no authority to receive it. The Bank was in respect of the provident fund money in the position of a trustee for Browne and it had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into sterling and to remit it to Browne. The Bank had been in respect of provident fund money. The Bank could not be said to have been in respect to the provident fund. The Bank did not have any interest in the provident fund in the position as a trustee for Whitee and it was liable to be attached. The Bank, therefore, was not entitled to recover any amount from the respondent.

The appellant was a contractor. The respondent was appointed as a contractor. He was paid a monthly salary of Rs. 500 per month. The appellant was paid a month 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing Orders. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his services. The High Court held that the appellant had merit on his side and that the appellant was not a 'workman ' within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act. The High court held that the respondent was not a workman within the meaning Of section 2(s) of the Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The respondent was not an 'workman ' under the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act. The Tribunal was not justified in interfering with the finding of fact recorded by the trial court on this point. [505C] (ii) The respondent 's contention that the appellant has merit on his part judged by the social conscience and judicial interpretation of the law in this branch of discharge simpliciter, is not correct. [508C] (iii) The respondent had not even filed a counter affidavit and the counsel for the Union and the workman agreed that the order of termination was not a camouflage to cover up what really was an order (1) of dismissal. The appellant had not even file a counter affidavit. The counsel for the respondent agreed that the appellant 's termination was not an camouflage. [509D] (iv) The respondent did not even file any counter affidavit and, therefore, the order of dismissal was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good. [510E] (v) The respondent could not be said to be a camouflage. The appellant 's contention was that the respondent had lost confidence in the employee and that the ground given was a mere camouflage. The respondent ' s case was not a mere camouflage and the finding of the trial court was not a sham one. [512E] (vi) The respondent has not even filed any counter affidavit. [513F] (vii) The respondent is not an 'employee ' under the Act. [514F] (viii) The respondent cannot be said to have lost confidence in him. The appellant has not even file an counter affidavit and no counter affidavit has been filed. [515F] (ix) The respondent, in the instant case, did not even filed an counter affidavit. It was not a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice. [516F] (x) The respondent having not filed a counteraffidavit and the counsel representing the Union and workman agreed that he was not a clean and honest person, the High Court was not justified. [517F] (xi) The respondent should have filed a counter affidavits and the counsel of the Union and workmen agreed that the respondent should be a clean and efficient person. [518F] (xii) The respondent would be free, if it had sufficient material and if so advised, to proceed against the workman for misconducts or on other ,grounds valid in law. [519G] (xiii) The respondent must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. [520A] (xiv) The respondent does not have any locus standi to file the counter affidavit and it is not a mere device to deny the allegations made by the appellant. [521B] (xv) The respondent will be free, when it has sufficient material and, if so advised. to proceed against him for misconducts, or on other, grounds valid in Law. [522C] (xvi) The respondent may have sufficient material and the appellant ' s case may be tested properly.

The petitioners, who were the beneficiaries of the Victims ' Scheme, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the V exoneration of the victims of the Veti tions, and the validity of the scheme. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Victi tions were not amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Victims of Victims are not amenable to writ jurisdiction. They are not amenable either to the writ of mandamus or writ of mandamus. They are amenable to the jurisdiction of the Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. [245C] 2. The Veti tors are not amenable, under Article 32, to the writ. They are entitled to the same as those who have been subjected to the same treatment under any of the existing schemes now in force in the State. [245D] 3. The Vatimes of Victi ties are not amenable for writ of mandamus, but are amenable to writ of mandamus and mandamus. [245E] 4. The Ventilators of Victimes are not amenable under Article 32 to the writ, and they are not amenable. [245F] 5. The Viro ties of Victima ties are amenable to public interest. They are also amenable to public law. [245G] 6. The Vishamma ties of the Vatimes are not subject to public law, but are subject to public order. [245H] 7. The Vitrams of Vatimes, which are not subject matter of any public law, are not amenable in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. [245A] 8. The Vitimes of Vatims of Veti ties are subject to the provisions of any of the new schemes now in existence in the State, their cases shall be considered for such benefit. [245B] 9. The Vitama ties, which are subject matter of the present writ, are not subject of any public interest, but would look into the proceedings as an adverso ry exploration for relief. [245J] 10. The Virama ties cannot be amenable to the public interest. [245K] 11. The Vibhusha ties of a Victims, are not covered by any of the old schemes now in the State of Uttar Pradesh. [245M] 12. The Vizi lies of Vatizas are not subject matters of public interest. The Viva ties of these Victims have been subjected by the Victimes of Vetims of Viro thalmic Surgeons registered with Medical Council of India or any State Medical Council. [245N] 13. The Vibhu ties ofVictims of the Vitrams are not subject t o public law, and are not subject lo public law, nor are subject to any public law. They are subject to private law. [246D] 14. The Vithi lies are not subject in any adverso ry action but would be subject to public interest, and, accordingly, the State would take up this issue and process the claims of the victims for such other bene fits under any of these schemes providing for aid to the aged, the disabled, and the destitute, sub ject to the condi tions that the victims otherwise satisfy the conditions of those schemes.

The Assam Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over management and Control) Act, 1984 was enacted by the Legislative Assembly of Assam. The Act was enacted to provide for temporary transfer of management and control of the affairs of the Samiti. Section 3 of the Act provides that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asom Rashtrabisha Prachar Sabha had its jurisdiction immediately before the commencement of the Ordinance by a Notification No. S.O. 15/34/75 dated 1.10.84. The Act provided for temporary transfer and the management of the affairs and the rights of the members of the Samiti under Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution. The Act also provided for temporary transfers and the management and control thereof. The Act and the noti fication issued under this Act taking over the management of a Rashtrabhat Samiti. The Act, however, provided for temporary and temporary transfer of the management and the management. The Act further provided for temporary or temporary transfer of all the properties of the Samiti and the rights and liabilities of the members. The Act did not provide for temporary or permanent transfer of management of the Rashtrabhadika Sabha and the Karyapalika Sabha. The Act came into force on 1.10 84. The Act received the assent of the Governor of Assam and published in the Assam Gazette on 1.11.84. Section 3(ii) of the Act provided that the Ordinance would extend to all the areas over which a Asom R Jaipur is a public body constituted by its members having elected by the State Government and all the functions, properties and affairs of the Parishad were taken over by the State Govern ment. The Act empowered the State Government to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act. The State Government issued a notification dated 1.11 84 under section 3(ii). The State Government passed an order under section 3 of the Assam Rashtra bhasha Pra char Samiti (Taking Over Management and Control) Ordinance, 1984. The Act as its title disclosed was a temporary measure. The Act had been amended by the Act of 1984. The State Legislature passed the Assam Rationalisation (Amendment) Act, 1985. The Act of 1984 was amended by the Amendment Act of 1984 and the Act of 1985 was amended by Act of 1984 with retrospective effect from 1.1084. The State of Assam was also added as a party to the writ petition. The State filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The State preferred a Letters Patent Appeal before the High court. The High court dismissed the appeal and the appeal was also dismissed. The State appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Act is a piece of legislation enacted by the Legislature of the State of Assam. It is a piece o f legislation enacted by Parliament of the State. The Act does not provide for any temporary or temporary or permanent or temporary transfer. The Act has been enacted with the object of providing for temporary transfer. [176B] 2. The Act provides for temporary transfer, and the management thereof is taken over by State Government. The State has no desire to restore the Society back to its elected authorities and office bearers, despite the fact that the State is intending to restore it back to the Society. The Act cannot be said to be in accordance with the Constitution. [176C] 3. The Act which is a piece or legislation enacted by a legislature of the State is not a law enacted by the legislature of the Legislature of a State. The Legislature of the Legislature is the Legislature of that State. The State is the legislature of that State and the authorities, officers and servants of the State Government are the authorities, Officers and servants of that State Government. [176D] 4.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, made a gift of four houses at Asansol in favour of the respondents. The gift was made in favour of her daughter as her share on partition. The gift in question was made in the presence of the appellant and the respondents. On the question whether the gift was valid, HELD : (i) The gift in Churaman Sahu 's case was made at the time of the marriage of the daughter of a Hindu widow and the gift was made some two years after the marriage ceremony. The gift made by the appellant was made some three years after the death of the daughter. The gift, therefore, was not valid. [457 C] (ii) The gift was not made in fulfilment of the moral obligation flowing from the ante nuptial agreement made by the pre husband of the appellant. The gift is made in the absence of any consideration. The gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband, the gift in Chuman Sahu ' s case was not valid in Hindu law. [456 C] (iii) The gift being made some two year after the marriage, the gift was not valid at the time when the marriage was solemnized. [455 C] (iv) The gift made long after the marriage was not valid and the gift made long before the marriage was valid in Hindu Law. [454 D] (v) The gift is not a reasonable one. The gift must be made in accordance with the law. [557 D] (vi) The gift must have been made in fulfilment the moral obligation arising from the ante luptial agreement. The gift may be made afterwards in fulfilment of a promise. [558 E] (vii) The gift, in Churamen Sahu 's Case, was made at a time when the daughter was not competent to make the gift. The gift could not be supported upon the ground that the gift when made fulfils the moral obligation. [559 F] (viii) The gift of four house at Asansom was made some time after the marriage. The gift of the four houses was made some more time after the death ceremony. The gifts were made long after marriage. The gifts in Churaian Sahu 's cases were made only after the marriage of a daughter. The gifts made long after, the marriage were not valid. The gift by the appellant father in Churam Sahu 's favour was not valid as the gift was in fulfilment of an obligation arising from a custom. [560 F G] (ix) The gift by Churaman was made long after a marriage ceremony.

The High Court dismissed the election petition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The allegations of corrupt practice alleged by the respondent have been clearly proved. The allegations of the corrupt practices alleged are not proved. The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. The appellant is entitled to succeed on the ground of corrupt practices. [417C D] 1.2 The allegation of corrupt practices is not proved beyond reasonable doubts. The appellant had proved beyond reasonable probability that Tej Singh was actually paid for a posters. The evidence of the appellant shows that a few ( numer before Tej Singh) had withdrawn his candidature and any vote was given to him. The appellant was not shown to have indulged in any corrupt practice. The appellant, therefore, has proved beyond doubt that Tej singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of posters by Tej Singh had been clearly admitted by him. [418C D] 2.1 The appellant has not proved beyond any reasonable doubt that the corrupt practices indulged in by Tej Singh have been clearly established. The appellant cannot be said to have indulged into corrupt practices in the present case. [419D] 2.2 The appellant has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt the allegation of corrupt practice indulged in by the respondent. [421E] 2.3 The appellant has also failed to prove that the posters in question were printed at the instance of Tej Singh. The appellant also failed to establish that the posters had been printed at his behest and that the vouchers were appended by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign. [422F] 2.4 The appellant has been proved beyond reasonable suspicion that Tej Singh has actually paid for posters which were printing at his instance, and Rup Lal had no connection with the same. The appellant could not be said to be guilty of corrupt practices under section 123(2) of the Act having been proved beyond any doubt. [423G] 2.5 The appellant has established beyond reasonable doubt and therefore, the appellant has proved corrupt practices. The appellant can be said to commit corrupt practices only if he proves that he had actually paid the posters. [424H] 2.6 The appellant has pleaded guilty of corrupt practice under section 123 (2) of Act. The appellant pleaded guilty of the corrupt practice under Section 123(2). The appellant has alleged that the posters, which were printed on the basis of the posters, were printed at their instance and Rup lal was not collected from the printing of poster. The appellant further pleaded guilty of criminal misconduct under section 123 of the Act. The High court has held that the appellant has not established corrupt practice. [425H; 418A] 2.7 The appellant has produced a large number of posters, which are printed at his own instance and Ruplal had no connection therewith. The appellant 's case is that the posters are printed at the behest of Tej Singh and Ruplal had no connection to the same. The appellant was the Chief Minister of the State. He was the Chief Secretary of the State in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. The Chief Minister of State was the Chief Ministers of the State and the Chief Minister was the Chief Justice of the State of Punjab. The Chief Secretary of State was also the Chief Minister. The Chief Ministers of State were also the Chief Ministers. The Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court, on the basis of the report of the Chief Minister, held that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. The High Court, however, held that the Chief Minister had no jurisdiction to punish for contempt. The appellant filed an application under section 19(1) of the Act for contempt of the Court. The High court dismissed the application. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. The appellant thereupon filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court exercises its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have jurisdiction to punish a person for contempt of itself. The High courts have jurisdiction to impose punishment for contempt of themselves. [893C] 2. The HighCourt exercises its jurisdiction under Article 215 of Constitution when it does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor. The High 'Court has no power or power to punish for Contempt of itself. [894F] 3. The High. Court exercises its power or power as a Court of record and is not competent to punish for the contempt of itself.[894F G] 4. The High, Court exercises its powers under Article 215 and is not empowered to punish for any contempt. [895G] 5. The High is not competent under Article 215 to punish for a contempt of itself, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without remedy. [896H] 6.

The appellant was the owner of certain lands in the State of Bombay. The rent note was executed by the appellant in favour of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that the appellant had failed to pay rent. The appellant contended that the notice was necessary before the lease could be terminated. The trial court held that the notice had been served on the appellant and the respondent was not entitled to the relief against forfeiture. The High Court held that the provisions of the rent note that on non payment of rent the rights of the tenant would come to an end was a clause of nullity and not merely a clause of forfeiture and that the lease was determined under section 111 (b) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. Held, that the provisions in section 111 (g) of the Act were not applicable to the case. The provisions of section 111 (a) and (b) were not applicable in the present case. The notice was not necessary for terminating the lease in suit. The notice must be given or tendered to the lessor at the hearing of the suit. The provisions in section 112(g) of that Act were not intended to apply to leases made prior to the coming into force of the Act. The provisions contained in section 111(g) were not intended for the purpose of determining the lease. The provisions relating to notice in writing as a preliminary to a suit for eviction based on forfeiture of a lease are not intended to be applied to leases made after 1st April, 1930, but are intended to apply only to leases made before 1st April. The provisions regarding notice in writing and the provisions of section 112(b) are not intended for determining the lease in a suit for possession. The provisions as to notice in the notice are not intended only to apply to lease made before 1.4. 1930, but also to leases made during the pendency of the suit and the provisions relating to the notice in writing are intended to be applicable to leases made between the parties.

The appellant was appointed as a driver in the respondent 's factory in the year 1965. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been found guilty of misconduct by the Enquiry Officer. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the dismissal order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the punishment of dismissal in respect of a workman who had been dismissed from service. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court has rightly held that the Labour Court had no power to interfere with punishment in the instant case having to the facts and circumstances he was not justified in setting aside the dismissal of Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan. [366C] 2. The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the Labour Courts should not interfere with the punishments awarded to a workman in respect of his misconduct unless the management gives an opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment before inflicting on him the punishment of dismissing or removing him. [366D] 3. The High courts have consistently taken a view that the first part of the Standing Order deals with several punishments and requires finding of guilt in respect of each one of them and this procedure is different from that which has been contemplated in the last part of the standing order and that last part deals only with the punishment for dismissal and for that punishment alone makes a special provision that no order awarding that punishment will be passed unless the Manager gives an opportunity of being offered to show cause. [366E F] 4.

The appellant was in occupation of a land in the State of Kerala. The land was in the occupation of a tenant. The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground of bona fide requirement of the land. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the interpretation of section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended by Act 35 of 1969 was not correct. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The interpretation of section 6D of the Act is not correct. The interpretation is not correct and the interpretation is correct. [112A] 2. The interpretation given by the High Court is correct. The construction of section 7 D is not correct, and the interpretation given by it is correct. It is not correct to say that the interpretation given is correct. If the interpretation given in the High Court was correct, it would be a case where the interpretation given was correct. [113B] 3. The interpretation placed by the High Courts on section 7D is correct. There is no merit in the contention that the interpretation placed by it is incorrect. [113C] 4. The interpretation put by the High courts on section 7 D of the Kerala Act is correct. Section 7D is not correct in view of the fact that the interpretation put by it is not correct [113E] 5. The interpretation that the interpretation is given to section 7D by the High court is correct. In the instant case, the interpretation put in by the High. Court is correct and the construction put in by it is wrong. [113F] 6. The interpretation which the High Court has placed on section 7E is correct. This is not correct as the interpretation put is correct.

The appellant was prosecuted under Section 135(a) of the . The goods were seized on 21 4 1967. The appellant was convicted under Section 135 (a) and (b) of the Act. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods in question were actually smuggled and that the goods were not smuggled goods. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant had not produced evidence to show that the goods had been legally brought into India. He had not produced any evidence to show whether the goods were legally brought into the country without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory. [501C D] 2. The appellant has not produced evidence showing that the goods are legally brought into Indian territory without payment of duty at a date when payment of duty had become imperative. [502C] 3. The appellant did not produce evidence to show the place from where the goods came to be seized. The appellant could not be said to have been in possession of the goods at all. [503D] 4. The appellant having not produced evidence, the burden of proving that the goods must have been known to be smuggled or imported into India was on the person from whose possession the goods were seized. [505E] 5. The appellant failed to produce evidence to prove that the goods which were in possession of him were illegally imported or imported into the country from another country of their assumed origin after a time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. [507E] 6. The appellant knew that the goods should have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. [508F] 7. The appellant, had not produced the evidence to show how the goods were smuggled or imported or smuggled. He had failed to produce any evidence to prove the place from which they came. He had also failed to produce the evidence to prove his possession at all. If he could have succeeded in explaining satisfactorily how he was an innocent receiver of such goods without knowing that they were illegally imported, he may have had a chance of getting the benefit of doubt. [509G] 8. The appellant must have produced evidence to prove whether the goods in respect of which the appellant was prosecuted were smuggled or brought into India without payment of custom duty at a later date when payment was made. [510H] 9. The appellant should have produced evidence showing the place from whom they came to be imported or who was imported, were questioned. The appellant would have been able to prove that he knew that the said goods were illegally imported and smuggled.

The appellants were partners of a firm which was dissolved in February 1948. The firm was dissolved in March 1948. The appellants filed a suit for accounts of the profits made on the sale of the Gwalior cloth and the profits on the sale thereof. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the suit was not maintainable by reason of the provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and the appeal filed by the plaintiffs must be dismissed. The appellants contended that the suit as framed was not maintainable because the suit was barred by the provisions of the Act. Held, that the suit must fail. The suit was not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts of an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant time. The suit must fail because the suit must be one for accounts which the law declares to be illegal. The suit is not one for accounting of a dissolved partnership which is in existence at that time. The provisions of section 69(3)(a) of the Act are not applicable to the proceedings under the Act. The suit before the trial court was not one of accounts of a dissolution of the firm but for accounting purposes. The suit for accounts must fail because of the illegality in the contract of partnership. The suit in the present case was not one under section 69(1)(a) for the purpose of the Act, and the suit was therefore not one for account of a dissolved Firm. The suit of the plaintiffs was not one in respect of accounts of the dissolved firm, but for accounts and transactions. The suit could not be said to be one for account which the courts could not adjudicate in respect of contracts which the law declared to be illegal (Senaji Kapurchand vs Pannaji Devichand, (1876) L.R. 58 I.A. 65, referred to.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 9(1) read with section 9(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that on 8.6.1986 at 2.0.1986 at 3.0. P.M. they along with two others were found in possession of a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ and a sum of money was found in possession. The respondents were charged under section 9 (1) readwith section 9(3) of the Act for having committed an offence under section 9 of the Prevention Act. The trial court found that the respondents were guilty of the offences under section 8(1) and 9(2). The High Court, however, acquitted the respondents. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the respondents had not been charged with the offence under section 8 (1) and section 9(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The ingredients of an offence under the Penal Code are: (i) that the accused person is a public servant; (ii) that he has committed an offence punishable under the Indian Penal Code; (iii) that he had committed an offence which is punishable under the Penal code; (iv) that he was a public servant within the meaning of section 2(3) and (4) of that Act. [463C] 1.2 The test is that taking the allegations and the complaint as they are, without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High Court will be justified in quashing the proceedings in exercise of its powers under section 482 of the Code. [463D] 1.3 The test is whether taking the allegations or the complaint as it are, without addition or subtracture, is an offence under any other law. [463E] 1.4 The test is: whether taking the allegation and the complaint are, without added or subtrasing anything, if the allegations are, without add or subtreasing anything, whether the allegations are not, in law constitute or spell out any offence and that resort to criminal proceedings would, in the circumstances, amount to an abuse of the process of the court or not. [463F] 1.5 The test is, whether taking the accusations and the complaint, as they are. without adding orsubtracting anything. if no offence was made out then, the High Court would be justified in quash the proceedings in exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Criminal Code. [464F] 1:6. The test is the test of whether taking the charges and the complaint is in law a result of an abuse of power of the court. [464G] 1.7. The test, is that taking a allegations and the complainant as they are; without adding or Subtracting anything the allegations, if any, are made out then it is guided by the allegations, whether those allegations are, in law, constitute or spellout any offence and whether those allegations, set out in the complaint or the charge sheet do not in law constitute an offence. [464H] 1.8. The test of whether the allegations, set forth in the complaint, are, prima facie, 'the same offence '. [464B] 1.9. The test has been that taking the allegation or the complaint, prima facie constitute an offence under Section 9(1), read with Section 50(1) of the Indian Penal code. [464D] 1:10. The test in the instant case is whether taking of the allegations and, the complaint as set forth in that section, concerns the specific act of murder of an elephant, ald that such an offence at all events, falls within the overlapping areas between the two. [464E] 1:11.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was not justified in rejecting the appellant 's prayer for bail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have not correctly appreciated the evidence and have proceeded on the assumption that release on bail included release on the accused 's own bond. [343C] 2. The law is brought out in the Report: "the evil of bail system is that either the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties for providing bail or suffer pre trial detention. " [343D] 3. The law does not permit the court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State. [343E] 4. The law requires that the accused should ordinarily be released on bail, or on his own recognizance, unless it is shown that there is substantial risk it is appearance or there are circumstances justifying imposition of conditions on release. [343F] 5. The law has been brought out in several cases of socialist republic, and the accused should normally be released on his own bond without bail, i.e., surety, cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place. [343G] 6. The law in its majestic manner requires that the person released on his personal bond should not be released on the same day. [343H] 7. The law provides that the accused must ordinarily be released by the court to further the ends of justice and nothing in Sec. 389(1) which reads: 389 (1) Where the court decides to grant bail, it shall, in the first instance, grant bail to the accused without bail or suffer from any kind of hardship to the accused. [343A B] 8. The law makes it clear that the accused shall ordinarily be released from the custody of the court to the further custody of the accused. The law also makes it clear, that the accused 'shall ordinarily be released, on his own bonds, without bail, unless it be shown that there was substantial risk it was appearance or there were circumstances justifying imposition or non compliance with the conditions on release, [343E F] 9. The law, therefore, requires that the court must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the Criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deter mination against the release. [344F] 10. The law cannot be said to be unreasonable or arbitrary. The law must be read in the Report.

The assessee, a registered firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 52, on the ground that its business was a branch of the assessee. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle Amritsar, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground of non inclusion of the income of 'Castle ' in the assessment of the assessee, but the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, in appeal, held that the assessee was a branch and not a separate entity. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that in the assessment for the year 1951 52 the income from 'Castles ' had not been computed and included in the assessment. The High Court, in reference, held that there was no question of law arising out of the order of the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax Officer in the assessment in question of the income. [431 D] The High Court had the power to call upon the Tribunal to state a case and to refer it, if the Appellate Tribunal had refused to state the case on the ground, that no question of Law arises out of the orders of the Tribunal, and also if the Tribunal had misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding. [432 D] The Tribunal had, therefore, erred in refusing to state a particular case. [433 G] The High Courts have erred in holding that there was a double infirmity in the order of reference. [434 G] The Tribunal has erred in refusing the reference. [427 G] The decision of the High Court in the present case was not a question of law. The decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs C.I.T., Bombay, , relied on.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was appointed as a Secretary to the Government of Punjab in the year 1974. He was also directed to file his affidavit. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 confirming the earlier seniority list. The Minister in charge made a speaking Order on February 18. 1975 confirming the previous seniority list. On February 18,1975 the Minister concerned passed an order fixing the seniority of the engineers n the Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. The Minister then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the earlier order fixing the inter se seniority of the Engineers n the Irrigation department of the Punjab. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Minister concerned was not a necessary or proper party and as such the High Court was in error in directing that the Minister be impleaded as a party in the writ petition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Minister was not a proper party. The Minister could not have been impleaded as a respondent in the writ peti tion. The High court was in error on the ground that allegation had been made against the Minister that he had deviated from the normal procedure while passing the impugned order dated February 18, 1976. [972C] 2. The Minister is a necessary or appropriate party. The High Courts are in error in direct ing that the Minister is a proper party and the High Court is in error in ordering that the Minister should be impleaded as an 'party '. [973C] 3. The Minister, in charge of the Irrigation Department, was directed to file an affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister concerned to decide in the light of the allegations made in the petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit, and that the Minister was not an appropriate party. [974D] 4. The Minister who was directed to be impleaded as the party in the petition, as in the view of the Court allegation had been making allegations against the Minister, was not a party.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. He was a tenant under the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of section 259 of the Act could be utilised for realisation of arrears of land rent on land and buildings provided such rent is claimable by a Board under the Act or the rules framed thereunder. HELD: The provisions of section 258 of the Act can be utilised for recovery of rent due to the appellant in the manner provided for in the section. The provisions of the Act are not applicable to the case. The provisions in the Act are applicable to the proceedings before the Magistrate. The provisions are not applicable in the case of rent of land or buildings under the management of the Board. [347 C] The provisions of sections 259 and 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, are applicable to proceedings before the magistrate. The provisions relating to recovery of arrears and other dues are not applicable. [347 D] The provisions in section 259 of Punjab Municipal Act are applicable only to cases where rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estates Officer under the Act. The provisions regarding recovery of arrears are not applicable because the provisions of the Punjab Act are applicable. [348 E] The provisions relating thereto are not applicable as the provisions of sections 258 and 259 of Punjab Act are not attracted. [348 F] The provisions regarding the recovery of arrears in the present case are not applicable, because the provisions in the Punjab Municipal Rules, 1937, are applicable only in respect of rent of lands and buildings. [348 G] The provisions contained in section 259 are not applicable when the Act or Rules in terms make the rent on land or buildings claimable by the Board. The provisions contained therein are not applicable where the Act or rules in terms make a rent on land & buildings claimable under any express provision of the Act. [348 C] The Punjab Municipal Act is applicable to the present case. The Act does not make the rent as a rent or fee which could be recovered under summary provisions of that Act.

The appellant was in the service of the respondent company as a Section Salesman. He was terminated from service on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. The respondent company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of the appellant from service on the ground of his being on unauthorised absence since 14th January, 1974 and shall be entitled to the benefits of the Industrial Disputes Act. The High Court held that the appellant was not a workman and that the reference was incompetent. The appellant filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the respondent company was not a 'workman ' and that the provisions of the Industrial Dispute Act were not applicable to him and that the respondent was not a "workman" and that the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the reference. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Labour Court has given findings in favour of the appellant on the question whether the appellant was a "workman". The finding of the Tribunal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour Court. [474G] 2. The Labour court considered the merits in detail and ultimately held that the termination of appellant from service was illegal. [474H] 3. The finding of fact is a finding of fact and the Labour Court considered the merits of the case and came to the conclusion that the termination was illegal. The finding is also borne in mind by the document. [474A] 4. The finding that the appellant is not a workman is a finding in the instant case and it is not applicable to the termination in the instant. [474B] 5. The Labour Appellate Court has given a finding that the termination is illegal. The Labour Courts have given a finding in favour of appellant on the nature and character of the work. The finding has been given by the Tribunal as an admitted case of both the parties. [474C] 6. The finding on the nature or character of the Work is a finding upon a question of law and it is further borne out by document produced before Labour Court. The finding in the present case is a finding that there is no evidence to show that the appellant had been employed for sales promotion. The finding was not based on any question of fact. It is also borneout by the document that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [474D E] 7. The Labour Tribunal considered the merits and ultimately held the termination of service was illegal but dismissed the application only on the ground, that the was not applicable to he termination in the facts and circumstances of the case which was long prior to the enactment of the Act. [474F] 8. The Labour 'Court considered the merits, and held that the is not applicable.

The Company was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The Company was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Company had been running a tea estate in the State. The Company, in its application for eviction of the Company, made an application under section 182(2)(i) of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (Act No 66 of 1950) for eviction of its employees. The Company contended that the Company was not a Government lessee within the meaning of section 181 of the MP Land Revenue and Land Revenue Act, Samwat 2007 (Act 66 of 1950). The Company contended before the Additional Collector that the Company had not been a Government lessee under section 185 of the MPS Act, Samvanta, and was therefore not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. The Additional Collector held that the Company did not enjoy the status of a Gair Maurusi tenant and that it had not become a 'pakka ' tenant under section 54(vii) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and tenancy Act, Samvar 2007 (Act 67 of 1950) and that the Company could not be evicted by the summary proceeding provided for under that section. The Company appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the company was not a 'phakka ' tenant and that the company could not be ejected by the summary proceedings provided for under section 182. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Company that the Company 's application for eviction was not maintainable because the Company was a Government lessee and was not a "pakka" tenant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Company 's claim for eviction of a Government lessee is not a "public lessee" within the meaning Of section 181 of M.P Land Revenue & Tenancy Act,Samvat 2007 ( Act 67 of 1950). [180B] 2. The Company has been successful in showing that the land in question was held by the State Government under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. [180C] 3. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [180D] 4. The finding that the Company has been holding the land in terms of the original lease or under the newly stipulated terms of the lease, the Company has not been able to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the lease. [180E] 5. The finding is, in the circumstances, totally unjustified and contrary to law. The impugned Order of the High court dated 20.9.1980 in Misc. Case No. 84 of 1980 in Misc. Application No. 84/79 is set aside. [180F] 6. The finding in the earlier proceeding that the Company failed to pay the stipulated rents and thus violated the conditions of lease, proceedings were initiated by the Additional Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977 in Case No. Appeal No. 1 of 1961. The finding was, in the earlier proceedings that the Company remained in possession of the land under the newly determined terms agreed upon between the Company and the successor State, namely, the Madhya Pradesh State. The finding on the contrary was, in our view, totally unjustified. [180G] 7.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1950, was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of the power conferred by section 1(3) of the Act. By section 1(2) of the Principal Act, the State Government was empowered to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The State Government issued a notification under section 1(1) of the principal Act, which provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part, on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the principal Acts. The State Legislature passed the Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964, which came into force on July 1, 1964. The State of Orissa amended the Act by a notification dated July 1, 1965, and the Act was amended by a notification issued on July 1. 1965. The State amended the Act and brought into force on August 1, 1965. The appellants challenged the validity of the Act by way of a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the amendment was inconsistent with or takes away or abridge or takes away the rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. The High court held that the amended Act was inconsistent with the provisions of article 31 A of the Constitution and that the amendment did not violate or take away or abridge the rights conferred under Part III of that Constitution. The appellants contended that the amendment of the Act was inconsistent and inconsistent with or take away the rights of the appellants under Part III. The High. Court held that section 1(4) of the Amendment Act was not applicable to the appellants. The High 'Court held that the Amendment Act did not violate article 31 A. The High, Court held that it was inconsistent with article 31 A and was not competent to amend the Act. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The amendment of the Principal and the Act of 1965 was not inconsistent with or taking away or abridge any of the fundamental rights conferred by part III of the constitution. The amendment of article 31A was not inconsistent or takes away any of the rights conferred on the appellants under any law for the time being in force. [337 B] (ii) The amendment was not inconsistent and did not affect the rights conferred upon the appellants under the Principal Act. The amendment was therefore not inconsistent with the fundamental rights. [338 C] (iii) The amendment did not affect or affect the rights of any person under Part III or any other law for the lime being in force in any State. The amendment did affect or affect or affect any rights conferred by any law for time being in operation.

The widow of her husband 's estate was in the hands of her husband. The widow 's estate devolved on her husband '. The widow was in possession of the estate. The widow filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that the widow had no interest left in her, and the widow had not acquired any interest in the estate. She was not entitled to any interest in her estate. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The widow ' s right to challenge the right of a prior alienee from the widow was not affected by the transfer of the estate by the widow. The widow had no right to challenge it. The widow could not claim any interest in it. The right of a subsequent alienee from her husband 'S ' was not affected. The widow, therefore, could not claim the right of her subsequent alienee. [355 D] (ii) The widow had a right to challenge her right of recovery of possession of the properties during the widow 's lifetime on grounds of equity, justice and good conscience. [355 E] (iii) The widow was not entitled under the Hindu law to recover possession of the lands during the widow "s lifetime" on grounds of equitable considerations. [355 F] (iv) The widow herself was in capable of disputing the title of the alienee or of the person who had acquired interest by adverse possession against her. [355 G] (v) The widow, her self may be incapable of derogating from her own grant and disputing the alienation which she had herself made. But as the widow herself was not entitled, she could not have obtained the properties but for the surrender made by the widow, she could have obtained the property but for the surrendering made by the husband. [355 H] (vi) The widow her self may have been incapable of derogation from her own grants and disputing the alienations which she had made. But the widow ' s claim to have the properties in her possession on the ground of equity, fairness and good conscience in proper cases, was not justified. [355 A] (vii) The widow and her self may not have any right to recover possession from the widow. [355 B] (viii) The widow has no right to recover the property during the widow's lifetime on grounds other than those of her husband, and if the title of such person has been completed already, it could not be defeated by a surrender made by her. [356 F] (ix) The widow is entitled to challenge the alienation of the property during her lifetime on grounds only of equity, equity, justice, good conscience and good conscience and the widow is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. [356 G] (x) The widow's self may be capable of disputing her title of recovering possession of the land during the widow"s lifetime on the ground 'of equity, justice or good conscience in appropriate cases, and the right created by the widow in her favour is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow the surrender must take effect from the inheritance. [356 A B] (xi) The widow cannot claim any interest on the estate during the widow life. [356 B] (xii) The widow must have a right to recover from the widow the property during she 's lifetime. [356 E] (xiii) The widow could claim the right to recover her possession of the house during her lifetime. [355 C] (xiv) The widow did not derive her title from her, and she was under no legal and moral obligation to transfer her estate. She could not have acquired any interest by adverse title against her.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Cotton Mills Company was incorporated in 1950. The Cotton Mill Company was incorporated on April 1, 1956. The Cotton mills were registered under the U.P. Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1948. The Cotton Textile Company was incorporated under the U P Agricultural Produce Marketing Act, 1948, with effect from April 1, 1957. The Cotton Textiles Company was incorporated with effect from May 1, 1957, and the Cotton Mills Company continued to be the member of the Cotton Mills company. The Cotton Cotton Mills Company had been formed on May 1, 1958, and the cotton Mills Company was formed on May 2, 1958. The Cotton Spinning Company was formed in 1958. The cotton Mills Company had a share capital of Rs. 10 lakhs. The Cotton Yarn Company was formed with effect from January 1, 1958. On May 1, 1959, the Cotton Mills Co. was formed. The Cotton Ginning Company was formed sometime in 1958. On the same day the Cotton Mills Ltd. was formed and the Cotton Yarn Co. was constituted on May 1. 1959. The Cotton Cloth Mills Company was constituted on April 1. 1959, and the appellant company was formed on April 1 1, 1959. The cotton mills were formed on May 3, 1959, and were formed on April 2, 1959. On May 2, 1959, a new Cotton Mills Company came into existence. The Cotton yarn Company was formed and was formed on August 1, 1960. The Cotton Fabric Company was formed after the Cotton Mills had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the Polytex Company. The Cotton cloth Company was formed by the Cotton Mills Limited on May 1 1, 1958 and the Cotton Mill Company ceased to be the members of the Poly Mills Company. The appellant company was dissolved on May 1 2, 1958, by the Collector of Kanpur in exercise of the powers conferred by section 169 of the Land Revenue Act, 1901. The appellant Company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Collector dated May 2, 1960, and the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton Mills did not have the right to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under section 169 of Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the collector dated May 2. 1985 was an order in the nature of a charging order. The order passed by the Collector being an order in a nature of a charge, the order passed by this Court on February 1, 1985 shall remain in force. [875C] 2. The order dated May 2 1, 1985 passed by the collector was an order of a charging officer. The order was an order passed by him in the nature o the charging officer. [876C] 3. The order under section 169(1)(a) of the Act was an order under section 18AA(1)(b) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 taking over six industrial units of the Cotton Mill company. The order made by the Collector was an order within the meaning of section 169(2) of the said Act. [877D] 4. The order in question was an order by the Collector in the nature. of a charging section.

The petitioners filed a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in possession of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur, had no sort of right in the suit land and that the suit land had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with their possession. The trial court dismissed the suit. The petitioners filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the jurisdiction of the civil court had not been taken away by virtue of Section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act. [833C] 2. The Gram Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. The Gram panchayat in question had been impleaded as defendant. The plaintiff in that case had not claimed that the suit property belonged to it as shamlat deh. The Gram Panchayats in question had failed to seek a declaration that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The Gram Panchay, in question had neither been impleaded as the defendant nor was the defendant. The plaintiffs had, therefore, not been impleaded. [834C D] 3. The Gram Panch had not been joined as a defendant in the suit. [835E] 4. The Gram Sabha in question had no right or title in the suit property. The Gram Panchas had not been arrayed as a defendant and the Gram Panchayat had not been added as a defendant, and the Gram Panch had been impleaded. The Gram Sarpanch had not been impleading the defendant. [836F] 5. The Gram Pradhan had not been implead as a defendant because he had not claimed a declaration that he was not the owner of the suit property and that it did not belong to the Gram Panchayat. The Gram Gram Panchayat in the instant case had not been impleadment as a defendant nor was he impleaded as a party. The Gram PANCH Panchayat in question has not been impleaded in the suit as a defendant since the Gram Panchayat in issue had not been made a defendant. [820F G] 6. The Gram Parchay, in the instant suit had not been filed by the Gram Panchayat as a defendant but only a defendant. It is no doubt true that the plaintiffs who claimed to be the owners along with some other persons of the suit lands had avoided to seek a relief of declaration that the land in question belonged to them as shamlat land. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamlat deh or not and whether it belonged to the Panchayat or not. The Gram Phal Kalan, in question has been impleaded as one of the defendant. It will be open in the suit to the Collector only under section 11 of the Act and not by the Civil Court.

The appellant Board was constituted under the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply Act, 1978. The Board was constituted by the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. The Board had been constituted under the Act. The Board, however, was not functioning. The Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The Board preferred a Letters Patent Appeal. The Division Bench of the High court dismissed the writ appeal. The Board appealed to this Court. The Board contended that the Board was not entitled to the benefit of the Act as it did not contain any norm of guideline with regard to framing of terms and conditions for the supply of electricity by the Board as it had direct bearing on the operations of the Board which were to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumer in trust with the Board to secure the Board against default in payment of interest. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on operations of the board which are to be conducted by the Board to ensure a Surplus. The condition is a condition of supply.
