The condition in the instant case is a condition which is liable to be appropriated for the satisfaction of any amount liable to be paid by the consumer to the Board for violation of any conditions of supply in the context of wide scale theft of energy. [578F H] 2. The condition regarding supply requiring a consumed security deposit has been made by the consumer with the Board. The condition has a direct impact on the operation of the Board. [578G] 3. The condition for supply requiring a Consumption security deposit has no direct bearing on operation of the board. [578H] 4. The condition relating to supply requiring a minimum consumption security deposit is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. No. [578A] 5. The condition that the Board shall not pay interest at the rate of 12% would be admissible. [578B] 6. The condition to pay interest is not so harsh as to shock it. [578C] 7. The condition as to supply requiring the consumption security deposit had a direct bearing to the operation of Parliament which are to he conducted in such an event as to ensure that the intentions of Parliament shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates somewhat harshly on a small section of the public, taken in conjunction with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19 (1) (f) and (g) as imposing an unreasonable restraint.

The petitioners were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre in the Telecommuni cation Research Centre under the Ministry of Communications, Government of India. The Recruitment Rules were framed by the President under the provisions of the Recruitment Rules. The Recruitment Rule provided for the method of recruitment to the various cadres in the Tele Communication Research Centre. The Recruitment rules were framed by a notification dated 1.1.1973 under the Recruitment Rules, 1962. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Recruitment Rule on the ground that the said rules were violative of Article 14 and Article 16 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the said Rules were violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the petitioners. The petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court. The petitioners also contended that the impugned Rules were violative Article 14 and 16. The petitioners further contended that the Tribunal had wrongly rejected the contention that the impugned rules were violative Article 16 of Constitution. The Tribunal dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners have filed this petition challenging the validity of Rule 2(a) of the Recruitment and Recruitment Rules, 1963. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal had completely ignored the fact that the Recruitment Rules were not violative of Article 16 of The Constitution. The Rules were not arbitrary and violative of Article 15 of the Constitution by not granting them the same special pay which was granted to the trans ferred officers who were posts and Telegraphs departmental promotees belonging to the Telegraph Engineering Service, Group A. [105B C] 2. The Tribunal has completely ignored the important aspect of the matter. The Tribunal was wrong in not granting them special pay. The Tribunal should have given them special pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same as the scale of pay of direct recruits because the transferred officials had to perform in the Tele communication Research Centre duties which are not in their general line. [105E F] 3. The Tribunal committed an error in not granting the special pay at the same rates to the direct recruits working in the Tele Communications Research Centre. [105F] 4. The Tribunal erred in not granting special pay at all to the direct recruit officers working in the Telephone Communication Centre. [106F] 5. The Tribunal ought to have given them Special Pay at the same rate at which it is paid to the transferred officers working in that centre with effect from the date from which the transferred officers have been drawing the Special Pay.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the appellant 's factory in the State of Bombay. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had failed to comply with the provisions of section 42(4) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending that the third respondent had failed to make an application under section 42(1) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed that the order of the Labour Court should be set aside on that ground alone. The Labour Court rejected the appellant ' s contention that the third Respondent had failed to furnish the necessary particulars of the appellant 'as required by section 42(2) of the said Act. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the third and fourth respondent had failed in complying with the provisions contained in section 42(3) of the aforesaid Act and that the third, fourth and fourth respondent were not entitled to make an order of dismissal under section 42 (4) of that Act. HELD: (i) The provisions of section 78(1) are not mandatory and the appellant has not been able to comply with them. The provisions of the Act are mandatory and the provisions of the Bombay Act are mandatory. [707 D] (ii) The provisions in section 78(2) are mandatory and not directory. The provisions in the Act are directory and not mandatory. [807 D] The provisions of sections 42(4), 42(5) and 42(6) are mandatory. The provisions are mandatory and are directory. [708 D] (iii) The provisions are directory and the provisions are mandatory. If the provisions are directory, the provisions are not mandatory. The provision is mandatory. [908 D] The provision is directory and not directory and the provision is mandatory and the provision does not require that the provisions should be directory. [909 D] (iv) The provisions contained in sections 42(1), 42(2), 42(6), 42(7) and 42 (7) are mandatory in character and are directory and are directory in nature. [910 D] (v) The provisions under section 42 are mandatory and they are directory. The provision in section 42 is mandatory and not mandatory and it is mandatory. The scheme of section 7 8 (1) seems to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Labour Court. [911 D] (vi) The provisions relating to the procedure of the Act do not require that a person should be able, to side step, to bring about any agreement and an application to the labour court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at. [912 D] (vii) The provisions have to be read in the light of the provisions of sections 7 8 (2) and 42 of the Act. [913 D] (viii) The provisions do not require the application of section 42 (1) to the Labour court.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground of bona fide requirement of the premises. The respondents filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif, Ranchi for evicting the appellants. The Munsif allowed the application and directed the appellants to vacate the premises. In the appeal to the High Court, the respondents contended that the appellants ' application under section 13 of the Act before the Munsif was not maintainable before the Munsif and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The High Court held that in absence of a month 's notice under section 12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable. The High court held that the appellants were not entitled to file a suit and the suit was not maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the case. In the present appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the appellants had not filed a suit under section 12 and that the suit was barred by section 12 of Act No. 1 of 1947. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the Court by an application under Section 12 of the Act is not a question of substantive right of the parties as the controversy was concluded by the first appellate court in favour of the appellants. [775C] 1.2 The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an application under s 12 should be treated as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. The question does not affect the substantive right of parties as the dispute was concluded by a first appellate court. [776D] 1.3 The question does arise only when the matter is covered by section 12, and as the respondents, by their notice, did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. [778F] 1.4 The question doesnot affect the substantive rights of the parties. The question is one of fact. The question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact. The Court has to decide the question as to whether a landlord has a right to move the court by an application for eviction under section 12. [779F] 1:5. The question whether the petition is maintainable in the instant case is a question of fact. If it is assumed that an application under the section is not maintainable in a court, the proceeding has to be treated as one under section 47, and the order passed by the court would have the effect of a final order under section 47 which would be appealable as a decree and against which no revision would lie. If it was assumed that an order under section 12 was not maintainable, the proceeding had to be treated to be a suit and, therefore, the judgment of the trial court as a decree therein. [780G H] 1.6. The question, therefore, does not affect substantive right of a party as the controversy is concluded by the second appellate court in the favour of the appellant. [781B] 1:7. The question in the present case is whether the application which was filed under section 12 should be considered as a plaint. The question did not affect the main right of the respondents as the controversy in the present appeal was concluded by first appellate court, in favour of appellants. The question was whether the petition filed by the respondents was a plaint and whether the suit was maintainable in the peculiar facts of the present case. [782F] 1.:8. The question that the appellants have not filed a civil suit under section 11 or section 12 of a Act at all, does not arise in the facts of the case, and the suit is a very appropriate one for exercise of such power.

The appellant, a registered Society, filed a suit for declaration that the respondent No. 1, the Secretary of the Society, was elected as the Secretary. The appellant Society contested the suit on the ground that the respondent had been duly elected as the secretary of the Society. The trial court after holding that the appellant 's application filed under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Proce dure, was not maintainable, proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of the society, entitled to prosecute or withdraw the suit and accepted the case of Hari Narain Swami. The trial Court, after holding that there was no valid election, allowed the suit and dismissed the suit. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed by a single Judge. The appellant filed a petition under section 1 15 1 of Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal which was also dismissed by a Division Bench. The appellant then filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in dismissing the appellant ' s petition as not maintainable. [237B] 2. The High court was in error when it held that the application under section 15 I of the Code was not maintainable. The High Courts were, therefore, right in dismissing the appeal. [237C] 3. The High Curt was in error, in dismissing the petition as not entertainable, and the High Court should have inter vened in its revisional power on the ground, that the trial court had failed to exercise its inherent power. [237D] 4. The HighCourt was in error. The High. Court was in wrong in dismissing the petitioner 's application as not maintainable, and the impugned order was passed as a result of the court being misled. [237E] 5. The High 'Court was right in dismissing a petition as not tenable, and the order was passed in a petition under Section 1 15 1. The order was passed by the trial court as a result whereof the appellant 'S 's application was rejected. [237F] 6.

The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant contended that the Ordinance was not applicable to the case as soon as the declaration that the emergency was at an end was made on April 1, 1946, and the Ordinance in question was not applicable. Held, that the Ordinance having been repealed by the Indian Penal code, the period of emergency was to continue in force until it was repealed. The Ordinance having been passed on April 1. 1946, the Ordinance having continued in operation even after April 1, 1947, the Ordinance had to continue in operation until it was superseded. The Ordinance had the like force of law as an Act passed by the Indian Legislature without any limitation on its duration. The Ordinance was not a law passed by the British Legislature without any limit on its duration and the Ordinance having the like force was to continue to operate until it was repeal. The Ordinance, having continued in force, could not be repealed by the Ordinance. The Ordinance being a law passed in the exercise of the emergency power conferred upon the Governor General under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Ordinance in substance was not a legislation passed by the Government of the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Ordinance in question had been passed on May 1, 1946 and the Ordinance had the same force of law. The Ordinance could not be said to have been repealed by section 72 during the period specified in section 3 of that Act, viz., June 27, 1940, to April 1,1946. The Ordinance did not affect the continuance of the Ordinance in force until April 1, 1945, when the Ordinance was promulgated. The Ordinance continued in operation until April 1. 1947, and the period of the duration of the Ordinance had not to be determined having regard to the provisions of section 72 as they stood with the omission of the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation " therefrom during the period of six months specified in section3 of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, and the Ordinances in question were therefore not limited to the space of six months from April 1, 1944.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the death sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the death sentence should be awarded or not. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The death sentence should not be awarded or even not should be awarded. [1066C] 2. The death penalty should be awarded only in the rarest of the rare cases. The High Courts should not interfere with the death sentence unless the death sentence is shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of the offence. [1067E] 3. The High court was justified in confirming the death sentence passed under section 302 I.P.(C) and the decision cannot, therefore, be construed as laying down a ratio decidendi. [1065E] 4. The High courts were justified in confirming death sentence. [1068F] 5. The HighCourt was justified in upholding the death sentence imposed on the appellants. [1069F] 5(a) The High Court was justified in affirming the death sentence under section 302, I.P.,C. [1070G] 5(b) The High Courts were justified in affirming death sentence. The High Curt was justified in interfering with the death sentences passed under section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. [1071A] 5(c) The High court had no sympathy for these trigger happy gentlemen and the sentence imposed on them is well merited. [1072B] 5(d) The High Cour tial Court was justified on the facts and circumstances of the case and the law applicable. [1073C] 5(e) The High courts had rightly confirmed the death sentences imposed on the two appellants. [ 1073C] 6. The High Cou rt was justified in confirmed the death penalty imposed on the three appellants. [1173G] 5.1 The High Court had rightly confirmed death sentence. There is no justification for the contention that the award of death sentence to any of the two appellants was not proper or uncalled for. [1074H] 5(f) The HighCourt had rightly confirmed that death sentence. It would therefore be manifest that it is neither feasible nor desirable to define or legally permissible for this Court to limit or circumscribe the connotation of the expression 'special reasons ' occurring in section 354(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 so as to bring about a virtual abolition of the death sentence, and that the High Court was not justified in confirming that death sentence to the two appellants, is well merri tial and the guideline given is that the 'special reasons must relate ' not to the crime as such but to the criminal ' for which there is no warrant in section 354 (3) of Code of Criminal procedure, 1973.

The appellant was a public servant. He was charged with misconduct in the discharge of his duties under the Indian Railway Establishment Code, and was charged with an offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Indian Railway Code. The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct. The appellant pleaded that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by the Chief Vigilance Officer into some of the matters mentioned in the charges and that the appellant had been exonerated of the charges. The Chief Vigilance Officer, after considering the evidence, held that the appellant was guilty of the offence of misconduct. The Chief vigilance Officer, after holding that the appellant 's case was proved, held that he was guilty of misconduct and imposed a penalty of dismissal. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Chief Vigilance officer. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Chief Vigilance Inspector had been appointed by the Commissioner of Income tax as the Inquiring Officer and that the Chief vigilance officer had looked into the case upto its final stages, that the appellant having been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries, the order of dismissal was void and inoperative. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the Chief Enquiry Officer had gone into the case beyond the stage of the enquiry. [583 E] (2) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to produce nine witnesses in defence, all that was suggested was that these witnesses could only state what opinions they had formed about the work, efficiency, integrity and integrity of the appellant. [583 F] (3) The High court did not deal with a number of submissions made by the appellant which could have had that effect upon the departmental proceedings. [583 A] (4) The High Courts have not considered the point on which special leave was granted. [583 B] (5) The High courts have not considered whether the departmental proceedings were null and void. The High Courts were not concerned with the question whether the departmental proceeding was null and void or inoperative. [583 C] (6) The High. Court did not deal in a number of issues which could be raised before it. [583 D] (7) The High 'Court did not deal specifically with the question of the question of law which should be, first raised before it and then decide the question of fact. [583 G] (8) The question of law raised by the appellant was not a matter of law. [583 H] (9) The question as to the scope of the enquiry in the present case was not raised before the Division Bench. [583A] (10) The question was not raised in the High Courts. [583D] (11) The question regarding the scope of enquiry in the departmental proceedings was not raised at the time when the first appeal was heard by the High Court. [583E] (12) The question about the scope of inquiry in the departmental proceeding is not a matter which can be raised in the appeal. [583F] (13) The question is not whether the departmental inquiry was null and invalid. The question whether it was null and non invalid arises only when the order of punishment is challenged in the appeal or not. [583G] (14) The question that the appellant has been subjected to a trial on allegations in the discharge or dismissal of his duties that he was given the lesser punishment of demotion and not that he dismissed or removed from service. [583H] (15) The question which could be asked for a certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to this court must have been before this Court. [584F] (16) The question raised by the respondent was not a question of law. The High court was in error.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The sales were effected by the appellants in the State of Hyderabad. The sales of manganese ore were effected by them in the State. The sales effected by the appellant were inter alia to the State Trading Corporation for short the State Trading. The sales made by the appellants were inter alia, inter alia to their foreign buyers. The sales in question were inter alia inter alia to them by the appellants. The sales by the appellants to the State of Mysore were inter alia in the course of export by the appellants from the State Trading, and the sales were inter alia effected by the export of the goods. The sales to the appellants were effected by their foreign buyers in the State Trading and the sales to the State. In the special leave petition, the appellants contended that the contracts between the appellants and the M.M.T.C. were similar. The contracts between the appellant and the M/s. T.C.C. and their foreign buyers were different contracts and it was the S.T.O. which entered into independent contracts with their foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis. The contracts were inter alia not inter alia, the last purchaser within the State, but the M.C.T.P. was the exporter of goods. The appellants contended that they were not the last purchasers but the M/S. T.P.C. was the last purchaser. The High Court held that the contracts were inter se between the appellants, and the M./S. Tr.P.T. and their Indian buyers. The High court held that the contract between the appellants was inter se between them and the M /S. TT.C., and that the contract of sale was inter se, between the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the contracts of sale were inter se, inter se between M/S Tr. P.T. C. and their Foreign buyers, and that the contracts in question were not inter se between these two parties. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contracts of sale entered into by the appellants with the foreign buyers were inter se. The sales between the appellants to M/S P.T.,C. and its foreign buyers were distinct contracts. The sales entered into by them were inter se and the sales between the appellant to the State trading Corporation were inter se to the appellants. [445B] 2. The contracts in question between the appellants were different contracts. The contracts entered into by both the appellants were separate contracts and it is the S. T.O.P. which entered in independent contracts with the foreign buyer to the latter will not make the two contracts either inte rated or the contract between them. [446C] 3. The contracts are inter se between two parties. The contracts have to be inter se between both the parties. The contract of sale is inter se between a foreign buyer and the foreign buyer. The contract is inter se. between the appellant, and the S.C.O. and theirforeign buyers are different. If they are different contracts, as they are in the present case, the last purchase in the State is the M.S.T.T. The sales are inter se, the last purchasers within the State is also the M.T.B. contract. [447E F] 4. The High Courts have to examine whether the contracts between both the appellants and M/S S.T.,P.T., and their foreign buyer are inter se. [448F] 5. The High courts have to examine the facts and circumstances of each case. [449F] 6. The HighCourt has to examine whether there is any evidence to show that the contracts are inter inter se between parties. [450G] 7.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. He was terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October,1974. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his service. The High Court held that the termination of service of the appellant was invalid. The High court held that the appellant was not a temporary employee and that his services were not liable to be terminated without notice. The appellant filed a writ application in the High court challenging the termination order. The HighCourt held that the respondent was not a permanent employee and that the termination was invalid. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The termination of service is ab initio void and inoperative and the declaration made by the appellant that he continued to be in service with all consequential benefits is not valid. [532B] 2. The termination is not termination of service but a termination of service. The termination does not amount to retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act. The termination was not termination of the service of the respondent. [533C] 3. The termination order was not a termination of the services of the appellant. The termination did not amount to termination of service within the meaning Of section 2(o) of the Industrial Disputes Act. [534D] 4. The termination in the instant case was not termination simpliciter but a termination simpliciter. The termination could not be said to be a retrenchment within the definition of section 2 (oo) of that Act. [506F] 5. The termination must be in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. [535E] 5. In the instant case, the termination was not in accordance with section 25B of the Act, and therefore, his case fell within section 25B(2)(a) and he shall be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of Chapter VA. [537F] 6. The termination cannot be said to have been made in accordance with law. [538G] 7. The termination can be made only in accordance with rules made under the Act and not otherwise. [539B] 8. The termination has to be in accordance, with the provisions contained in the Act and rules made thereunder and not otherwise and the termination is not illegal. [540C] 9. The termination, therefore, is ab initio invalid and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in the service with all ancillary benefits.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Officer, Bhatinda that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and bad demanded Rs. 30/ as illegal reward from one Darba Singh. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet. The Settlement Officer held that the appellant had received Rs, 150/ as unlawful gratification from the Darbara Singh. The Settlement officer held that the charges were proved. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the order of termination of employment was in the nature of an order of punishment and an order discharging a probationer following upon an enquiry to ascertain whether he should be confirmed, was not of that nature. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The order of termination was not the order of punishment. The appellant was given no opportunity to make his defence and it appears that witnesses in support of the charge and in defence were examined before the Settlement Officer. By virtue of article 311 of the Constitution the appellant was not liable to be dismissed or removed from service until he had been given reasonable opportunity against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. [732 B C] (ii) The appellant was not given an opportunity to make a representation against the order of his dismissal. The appellant had been given an opportunity of making his defence and the Settlement Officer had not acted in exercise of the authority conferred upon him. [832 C] (iii) The appellant had not been given an enquiry in the matter of ascertaining whether he should he confirmed, but the enquiry was made with the object of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for unsatisfactory work and conduct. [733 G] (iv) The appellant 's conduct was proved. The enquiry made by the Settlement Officer was made with a view to ascertaining whether disciplinary proceedings should be taken and not to an enquiry whether a probationer should be confirmed. [734 C] (v) The appellant could not be dismissed from service until the enquiry was held. [735 G] (vi) The appellant is given an opportunity and it appears to the Settlement Officer that witnesses in the defence were examined. The Settlement Commissioner was not a party to the proceedings. The Settlement Commission was not a court of law. The appellant could have been given an effective opportunity to make the defence and it was not necessary that the Settlement Commission should have acted in accordance with the terms of employment. [736 C] (vii) The appellant has been given an ample opportunity to make representation against the action taken against him. The Settlement Commis sioner was not a person who was a temporary employee. The Settlement Committee was not a Court of law. [737 D] (viii) The appellant, was given an opportunity by the Settlement Commission to make his representation and it was clearly an enquiry for the purpose of taking (1) (1958) S.C.R.828. (2) (1958). conduct of public servants for ascertaining whether they should be confirmed or not. [738 G] (ix) The Settlement Officer was not a public servant. The Settlement Report was made with an object of ascertaining the whether disciplinary action could be taken against him for unsatisfactory work. The Settlement report was made with object of ascertaining that disciplinary action should not be taken against a probationer.

The appellant was appointed as Professor in the Medical College of Jammu and Kashmir. The Commission was consulted by the Commission and the State Government at first framed rules on November 15, 1968, for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. The Commission submitted its report on April 1, 1969, and the State Govt. approved the recommendations of the Commission. The State Government, however, by its letter dated November 28, 1968, directed the Commission to submit its report to the State Government. The State Govt. by its letter of November 28, 1969, informed the Commission that the selections were not made in accordance with the rules. The State of Jammu and Kahnd Kashmir, however, submitted its report to it on April 1. 1969. The State government, however, did not agree with the report of the Commission and, therefore, the State Government issued a notification on November 28, 1970, under section 133(2)(b) of the Constitution of Jammu andKahnd Kashmir. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification on the grounds, inter alia, that the State Government had not consulted the Commission before the notification was issued and that the State Govt had not consulted it before the notification. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Commission was consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making the promotions to the posts of Professors, and the Commission was not consulted in regard thereto, and that the Commission had not consulted any of the candidates, and that it was not necessary to consult the Commission before it was issued. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Commission was not required to consult the State Government before it was made. The State Govern ment had in fact placed on record the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969, which make it quite clear that the State had referred the selections to the Commission, a Committee was appointed by the Commission for that purpose, the Committee was appointed on the basis of a resolution of the State Government, and the report of that Committee was formally submitted to the Commission under the Chairman 's note dated June 2, 1969, but the State Government did not agree to the recommendations of that Committee. [875 C D] (2) The High Court erred in holding that the Commission did not consult the Commission when the Commission was constituted. The State had not consulted either in regard to principles to be applied in making the promotion to the posts, or on the suitability of selected candidates for the promotions. The State was consulted on the suitability and the Commission had in fact referred to the recommendations made by the Commission. [876 D E] (3) The State Government had in fact produced the minutes of its Commission dated July 23, 1969, to ascertain whether the other requirements of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 of the Constitution had been complied with. The State did not agree that the Commission should consult the Commission in regard to these principles.

The petitioner was elected to the Bihar Assembly from the Bihar Assembly constituency. He was elected to that Assembly. The petitioner challenged the validity of the provisions of the Bihar Assembly Members (Disqualifications for Election) Act, 1951, on the ground that the said Act was violative of article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Act was not violative of article 194(3) of the constitution and that the Act contravened article 19(2) of the Act. The petitioner appealed to this Court. Held, that the Act violated article 19(3) and the Act was therefore void. The Act was not void as it contravened article 19 (1) (a) of that article. The Act did not violate article 19(4) of the Consti tution. The Act contravened article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore void as it violated article 19 (4) of that Constitution. The Act violated article 14 of Constitution. The petitioner was not alleged to have done so. The Act infringed article 19(5) of theConstitution. The Act, therefore, contravened article 19 of the Constitution, and was therefore, void. The petitioner, therefore, was entitled to succeed. The Act had been passed in the interests of public order and public safety and the provisions of article 19 (5) of that Article were not made subject to the provisions of that Article. The Act is not void as the Act violated the fundamental right under article 19 (6) of the Indian Constitution. The Constitution did not provide for the procedure to be followed by the House of Commons in the matter of freedom of speech and expression. The Act does not violate article 14 of any of the Constitution as it violated the fundamental rights under article 19(6) of that Act. The Act contravenes article 19(i)(a) and (b) of the present Constitution. The provisions of article 194 (3) are not made subject of article 19 of Constitution.

The appellant was appointed as Reader in the College in the year 1971. He was promoted as Reader on 4 9 1969 and was drawing a salary of Rs.600/ . The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on March 9, 1971. The appellant was promoted as a Reader on 4 10 1969 and was getting Rs.600/- per month as salary. The appellant challenged the order of the Government in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the Government to take into account the experience, experience, experience in the Government service, and to consider the case of the appellant for appointment as Readers. The High court held that the appellant was not eligible for appointment as Reader and that he was not suitable for selection for appointment as Professors. The High. Court also held that the Government was not justified in directing the Government to consider the appellant 's suitability for appointment as Professor. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court. The High, Court held that the State Government was not bound to consider the claim of the appellant. The High 'Court held that the High Court erred in directing the State Government to take the view that the appellant ' s work was not suitable. The High Curt also held that since the appellant had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Reader, the Government was bound to take into consideration the experience, the service of the Respondents while they were in the private college since they were in a private college. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have been consistently in interfering with the Government 's order of the State Government. [794F] 2. The Government has to take into considera tion the experience, if any, in Government service, for consideration for appointment as a Reader. [795G] 3. The Government is not bound to take note of the experience, but it is bound to take notice of the fact that the appellant has all the requisite qualification for the appointment. [796A] 4. The Government should take into account, as a matter of course, the experience, in Government Service, for consideration of appointment as Reader. [774A] 5. The Government cannot take into account experience, experience or experience in Government service for consideration for appointments as Reader. The Government can take into account such experience, experience and experience in Government Service. [775B] 6. The Government may take into account any other factor, if it considers it necessary to do so. [776C] 7. The Government must take into account all the requisite educational qualifications, experience, etc. make a person eligible for appointment to the post. [771D] 7. In the instant case, the Government has taken recognition of the service in the private College in the case of two (1) [1975] 1 S.C.R. 871. two (1). The Government has taken note of the distinction between eligibility and suitability. Eight years teaching experience in a college and the fulfilment of other ' requisite qualifica tion make a person ineligible for appointment as an Reader, but whether he is suitable for selection as Reader, but Whether he is suitable or not, on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government services, for consideration. [772C D] 8. The Government was not in dispute that the appellant had throughout the service. He was in a private College. He was drawing a lesser pay. He was getting Rs,600/ . . The Government has not taken note of this distinction. [773D] 9. The Government had to take into consid eration the experience, whether he is a suitable for selection or not. [777E] 10. The Government 's decision taken in the year 1963 was not challenged by complete ertion of the past teaching experience in the private colleges. [778F] 11.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 A) for plying the passenger vehicles on the route in question. The State Transport Authority granted temporary permits to the appellants. The appellants applied for the temporary permits under the section for plying the vehicle on the route. The State Government granted temporary permits under s.68 F(1 C) for plying a passenger vehicles on a route. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the grant of temporary permits. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that in respect of the route a scheme has been prepared and published under section 68C of the Act and published under s. 68C of Chapter IV A of the Act, the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others, is entitled to apply for temporary permits and if such application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled to obtain a temporary permit, the State Transport Authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be, in exercise of power conferred specifically upon it by section 68F(1 A). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The permits will have to be temporary permits because the scheme has been published in respect of a route under section 68 C. The State Road Transport Authority has power under sub section (1 C) to grant temporary permits to any person in respect of that area or route or portion thereof specified in the scheme. If the Corporation is willing to operate vehicles to the maximum strength undoubtedly the State Transport authority will have to grant permit to any one else if the Corporation has applied for all the permits. But if the Corporation is unable to provide service by obtaining all requisite temporary permits, the remaining permits will have TO be granted to any other person willing Jo obtain temporary permit and ply vehicle because in respect of such strength there would be no application by the Corporation. [985F G] 2. The State transport Authority has power to grant temporary permit to any person, in respect of any area or route, or portion thereof, specified in the Scheme. If the corporation is willing to run vehicles to the extent of strength, the State transport authority will have the power to grant such temporary permits to persons other than the Corporation to operate vehicles on the routes for which the scheme is published till modified or approved scheme is published. [986G H] 3. The State Motor Service Authority has power, under sub section(1 C), to grant temporary temporary permits to certain persons in respect of area or route specified in the schemes. If the State Government is willing to grant temporary Permit, it may grant temporary permits in respect of areas or route or part thereof specified in a scheme. If, the Corporation is unwilling to grant temporary permission, it may refuse to grant temporary stage permit to any other applicant. But if it does not apply for all the permit but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permit and section 68 F (1 C ) would be squarely attracted. But if, the Corporation does not apply, the State Road Transport Authorities will have to examine the application for temporary permits made by persons other than those who are not the Corporation and if they are found to be competent, eligible and qualified they may have to be granted permits for the benefit of the large travelling public. [987H; 987A B] 4. The State Corporation has power under section 68F to grant temporary licences to any person. The State has power under subsection (1 C), (1 C D) to grant Temporary permits to any one, but only for certain specified temporary permits. If the respondent is willing to comply with the conditions of the permit, he may have to comply with it. [988B C] 5. The State Regional Transport Authority has powers under sub section 3 to grant temporary contract carriage permits to any persons in respect thereof.

The appellant was the son of the respondent. He was the son in law of the respondent and was the son. The respondent 's father died in 1947. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the property in dispute. The respondent contended that the property inherited by him from his maternal grandfather was not ancestral property and that the appellant had no right to bring the suit. The trial court held that the property was ancestral property and the appellant was entitled to bring the present suit. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to bring a suit under article 2 of the Act. The High court held that it was not open to the appellant to bring the case under article 2. The High. Court held that it had no jurisdiction to decide the question of the title of the appellant to the property. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the High Court was in error in not following the earlier Full Bench decision of the Punjab High Court in Narotam Chand 's case (1) and that the decision of the High Court in the present case was wholly unsustainable. The High Courts were in error in holding that the property in suit was ancestral property. The High courts had no jurisdiction in the matter of the question of title to the property in question. The High, Court was in wrong in not following that decision. The High 'Court was in error when it held that the question of ownership was not a question of title. The HighCourt was in wrong, in not following this decision. The decision of the first Full Bench was wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of the relevant custom. The decision in Narotham Chand 's Case (1) was not a decision on any question of law. The decision was not a judgment on any question relating to custom. The High Curt had no jurisdiction under article 2 to decide the questions of title.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, for offences under section 449 and section 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellants came to the house of the deceased and when the deceased was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, they came there and while one of them was sleeping, the appellants attacked him with a dagger on his neck with a dagger. The appellants were convicted under section 449 read with section 307 and section 307 of the Indian penal Code. The High Court acquitted the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The conviction of the appellants under section 449 of the Indian Code is not sustainable in law. The conviction of appellants under section 450 read with section 302 of the Indian is not sustainable. [81 E] (ii) The words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 of that Code but in the two succeeding sections 450, 451 and again in section 454 and section 457 of the Indian Criminal Procedure Code. [81 F] (iii) The words 'in order to ' have been used in section 449 ' in the two preceding sections, therefore, must be read in the context of section 449 of Indian Penal Code and the words 'in the order to ' in the latter succeeding sections of the Code must be read as if the act had been done by himself alone. [81 G H] (iv) The words used in section 34 of Indian Penal code are quite clear and are not intended to be used in the sense of the words used by the Legislature not only in Section 449 of the Code but in two succeeding sections. The words " in order to" in section 449 are used in the two subsequent sections of the Criminal Procedure Code and they are not intended for the purpose of the section. [81 H] (v) The words in section 34 are not intended merely to mean "in order that the committing of any offence punishable with death, the house trespass is punishable under section 449. [81 A] (vi) The words are not intended only to mean " in order that the commission of any offence may be punishable with imprisonment. But, once it is decided that the act is so done by a number of persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act. [81 C] (vii) The words of section 34 are used in two different senses and they are used in different senses. The words used are "in order" and so, where the act is done by a person, jointly it can have no application. But once it is resolved that the act was so done by the number of persons, jointly it cannot have application. [81 D] (viii) The words, "in order for" in section 34, are quite clear. The words ' in order to ' are used in section 450 of the Indian Evidence Act. The words are used in a sense different from the words used in the section. The words in the section are used in connection with the commission of an offence punishable with imprisonment for life. [81 B] (ix) The words have been used to mean " In order to" mean "in the order of committing an offence punishable under section 450 of that Act". The words "In order to" are used in both the succeeding sections of this Code and the word "in the latter succeeding Sections of the Code" in the two previous sections. The word "in order " in the two earlier sections of the Indian Act has to be read as meaning "in order ' to" in the latter preceding sections of the Act. [81F H] (x) The words should be read as "in order of committing any offence punishable under the Act punishable with imprisonment".

The appellant was the son of one of the sons of the last male holder of the properties in suit. The respondent contested the suit on the ground that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial, but was a son of Gurdial. The appellant contended that the respondent was not a minor at all, and that the appellant had not been a collateral of the last female holder. Held, that the appellant could not succeed to the suit on a plea of a collateral of a person who was not a major. The appellant was not entitled to succeed to the property of the father who was the last male owner. The respondent was not entitled as a collateral of his father to succeed to his father 's ancestral property of his father. The appellant had not produced any evidence to show that the collaterals of one of his sons were in fact ancestral. The appellant could not be allowed to rely on the evidence of the respondent to prove that the collateral was ancestral. The respondent had not produced the Riwaj i am of the Gurdaspur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway in 1913 and the statements in a Riwaj were not admissible in evidence. The appellant 's case was that the respondent had not been in possession of the property in dispute in the suit. The appellant did not produce any evidence to prove that he was in possession of any property in dispute. The respondent did not produce the Riwraj i am of Punjab and the appellant had produced the Rwaj i am. The appellant therefore failed to discharge the onus that was thrown on him by the respondent by producing in evidence the Riwj i am of 1913 and the appellant was therefore not entitled to any relief.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company which was carrying on the business of selling and selling goods. The Managing Director of the company was the Managing Agent of the company. The Managing Agent of a company was the managing agent of the company and the Managing Agent was the Managing agent of the Company. The Managing Agents of the company were acting as Managing Agents of a company. The respondent was the managing Agent of the Company and was the Managing Agents of another company. The company was the sole proprietor of the company, and the Managing Agents were the Managing Agents. The Managing Agency was the Managing Agency of the company which was the Managing agents of the company but the Managing Agent did not act as Managing Agent. The Managing agent was the Managing Partner of the company who was the Managing partner of the company in the capacity of the Managing Agent. In the present case the Managing Agent had been acting as Managing Agent of another company and the respondent was the sole Managing Agent. Held, that the instrument in question was a power of attorney and was not a contract of sale. The instrument in question did not comprise distinct matters and thus requiring to be stamped with the aggregate amount of the duties with which separate instruments were executed. The instrument was not a single power of attorney but was a combination of several of them. The instrument did not comprise separate matters but consisted of one matter only and that matter was the execution of a general power of attorney by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the donees his attorneys to act for him in all the capacities which he enjoys. The instrument could not be split up into separate instruments each comprising or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities of the donor were concerned. The instrument does not comprise distinct matter but consists of one matter and that matter is the execution of the general power of Attorney by the donor. The instrument is not a single instrument of attorney but consists of several matters and thus requires to be stamped. The instrument must be construed as a single instrument. The word "distinct" in section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act means "to be a distinct matter". The word "transfer" in section 6 of the Indian Registration Act means "transfer of property". The word 'transfer ' in section 5 means "to transfer or to transfer or otherwise transfer or otherwise to transfer or to take effect or to take away or dispose of property". In the present ease the instrument in the present case did not comprise a distinct matter but consisted of two matters. The instrument, in question, did not comprise different matters and thus required to be stamped as a single document. The instrument had to be stamped in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The instrument of transfer did not comprise the distinct matters but consisted only of one matter. The instrument which was executed by one person was the Managing agency of the company to act for the company in all the capacity which he enjoys and cannot be split up. The instrument cannot be splitup into separate instruments. The instrument itself did not contain separate matters but consists of two matters, namely, (1) the Managing Agent, (2) the Managing Agents, (3) the Managing agent, and (4) the Managing Agency. The instrument also did not contain distinct matters. The document did not contain a separate matter but consisted only with one matter only. The instrument therefore did not comprise independent matters. The instruments in question cannot be split into separate instruments and the instrument in each case cannot be split out into separate instruments, and the instrument must be read as a single one.

The assessee, a firm carrying on business in cotton, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the assessee had not paid the tax on the profits of the firm. The Income tax Officer, in computing the written down value, deducted depreciation which would have been allowed if the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 was in force. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income tax Appellate Tribunal, however, took the view that the depreciation which would be allowed if the assessee had been in existence in the past, should be deducted in computing the taxable income. The High Court, on reference, held that the depreciation was allowable under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The words "or which would have be allowed" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order, must be read as "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating to tax on profits of business". The words "any law relating to income of business" in paragraph 1 of the Removal Of Difficulties Order must be read in the context of the words "any laws relating to tax" in paragraph 3 of the Removal Order. [230 D E] The words "and any law relating thereto" in paragraph 4 of the Removal order must be read with the words "or any law relating" in paragraph 5 of the Removal. Order. [231 E] The word "or" in paragraph 6 of the Removal, Order must be construed in the context in which it is used. [231 G] The words used in the last part of section 13(5) (b) of the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949, must be construed as "any law pertaining to tax on income of business".

The petitioner, a contractor, was awarded a contract by the Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd. for the supply of electrical energy to the respondent Corporation. The contract was to be executed within a period of three months from the date of the contract. The petitioner, however, did not comply with the terms of the contract and the contract was terminated by the respondent Corporation on the ground that the contract was not executed within the stipulated period. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of the contract by the respondent. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the contract had been terminated by the Corporation without giving any notice to the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contract was not a contract in the sense that it was a contract in which the contract was to operate. The contract in question was not a single contract in the nature of a contract in itself. The contract had been entered into in the year 1960 and the contract had not been terminated by a notice to the respondent. [236B] 1.2 The contract was a contract for supply of electrical equipment and not for supply of electricity. The contract itself was a contract of supply of electrical equipments and not for sale of electrical equipment. The contract of supply was a contract to operate within the meaning of the Act. The contract did not contain any stipulation that the contract would be completed within a period not exceeding six months. The contract also did not contain a stipulation that the contractor would be entitled to claim the supply of electricity from the Corporation. The clause in the contract was only for information and was not intended to verify the fulfillment of the three conditions set out in the other paras. [236C D] 1.3 The mere fact that the contract did not mention the pre conditions set out therein would not make the contract a contract of sale. [236D] 1.4 The mere fact of the contract did, by itself, not make it a contract of purchase. The mere fact, if not all, of the contract, would not make it the contract of sale of goods. [236E] 1.5 The mere fact whether the contract did or did not contain certain pre conditions, would not by itself make the contract of purchase a contract of transfer of property. [236F] 1.6 The mere fact in the instant case, the contract did contain a stipulation for supply of energy to the intending purchaser. The contract, therefore, did not contain the pre conditions of eligibility to the contract. [236G] 1.7 The mere fact the contract did contained a stipulation that only three prequalifying conditions were prescribed in the N.I.T. and other details called for vide para 5(c) of the N. I.T. was only for assessing the value of the certificates furnished in this regard and if the K.P.C. considered them sufficient to warrant the issue of a tender form to the applicant, the Court will decline relief. [236H; 236A] 1.8 The question whether there was any difference between the requirements in para I and para I(c) was not a question of fact. The question whether the contract was executed within six months of the contract or not was a question of law. [236A] 1:9. The question of law referred to the High Court was not a matter of law. The High Courts should not interfere with the decision of the High Court. [236K] 1:10. The High court was not justified in interfering with the decision. [236J] 1.10. The question as to whether there was a difference between the requirement in para I(a) and para I (c) was a question which could be decided only by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. [236M] 1:11.

The appellant was a displaced person. He was allotted certain lands in the State of Punjab. The Custodian of Evacuee Property, by an order dated the 20th March, 1952, directed that the appellant should be given an opportunity to show cause why he should not be evicted from the lands. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Custodian. The High Court held that the order of confirmation was not subject to appeal or revision and that the order was not subject of appeal or revision. The appellant contended that the order under appeal was not subject only to appeal or Revision but was subject to revision. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled to the confirmation. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The order of confirmation passed by the Additional Custodian in 1952 was not subject either to appeal or review. The order of the Additional Custodian was not subject by appeal or revision but became final and conclusive. [1139 C] (ii) The order under appeal is not subject to any appeal or revision, but became final. The order under section 27 of the Act is not subject only by way of appeal or review but became final, and conclusive. The order passed by the Custodian in 1952 would clearly be subject to the revisional power of the Custodian General under section 27. [1140 C] (iii) The order passed in 1952 would be subject to revision and it is not open to appeal or writ to revision. [1141 C] (iv) The order in 1952 would not be subject to appeal, or revision but would be subject only to revision. It is not open either to the Custodian or the Additional Custodian to revise the order passed in 1953. [1142 C] (v) The order made by the Additional custodian in 1952 would have to be dealt with and disposed of under section 27, and the order of confirmatory order passed in 1954 would clearly be open to appeal and revision.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of workmen employed in the establishment of the respondent company. The respondent company was a company registered under the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The respondent was a registered union of workmen. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal made a short shrift of the workmen 's plea in the said reference. The Tribunal held that the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishment before 1965 was not such a matter as had to be adjudicated and it also did not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. The Tribunal also held that the claim pertaining to the said practice was not a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees. The Tribunal further held that the appellant was entitled to bonus for the relevant years. The appellant company appealed to this Court. The question for consideration was whether the demand pertaining the practice or customs prevailing in the establishments before 1965 was a matter of statutory interpretation of the Act. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that the demand relating to the practice of custom prevailing in these establishments before 1965 is not such a question as has to be adjudicated. [608 D] The Tribunal was, therefore, right in holding the demand pertaining only to the practice and custom prevailing in this establishment. [609 D] The question of profit may or may not arise at all and such customary or traditional bonus will depend on the content and terms of that custom or the practice on which the claim for bonus is made. [610 D] The fact that the bonus Act is a complete Code and is exhaustive of the subject, does not detract from the claim of customary bonus. [607 D] The definition of "employee" in section 2(g) of the Act includes a person employed in any industry. The definition of the employee in section 2 (g) includes a person who is employed in any industrial undertaking. The definition is wide enough to include a person employed as a workman in any industry, and the definition is wide and comprehensive. [605 D] The Bonus Act is a comprehensive code and is exhaustive and is exhaustive. The definition does not exclude those employees from claiming bonus under the or such other Act. [606 D] The dispute relating to the bonus is a matter of fact and the Tribunal has to go into a different claim. The Tribunal has to look into the whole claim and decide whether it and the Tribunal is right in holding it and directing it to do so. [604 D] The claim pertaining to customary bonus is not a matter which has to be decided by the Tribunal. [603 D] The matter is not one of adjudication. The Bonus Act does not bar claims to customary bonus or those based on conditions of service. [602 D] The Act does not exclude the employees from claiming Bonus. [601 E] The Bonus (Amendment) Act, 1965 does not bar claim to customary bonus. The Bonus (Amending Act) does not bar the claim of the workmen to customary bonus by way of industrial adjudication for those who are either excluded or exempted from the Act.

The petitioners were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana and were promoted to the Superior judicial Service of Haryana. The petitioners were promoted to that service on the basis of the dates of their confirmation. The petitioners challenged the validity of the seniority list prepared by the High Court. The High Court held that the rules governing seniority were not applicable to the petitioners. The High court held that the Rules governing seniority were applicable to the service of the petitioners and that the rules of seniority were not governed by the rules of the Superior Judicial Services. The High, Court held that there was no direct decision on the question whether the Governor, in the exercise of power conferred by the proviso to Article 309, had the power to frame rules regulating the seniority of judicial officers of the State. The High. Court held that in the absence of any direct decision on any question of law, the rules of Seniority were not applicable. The High 'Court held that the rule of rotation was not applicable to a case where the Governor had the power of framing rules regulating the recruitment and service conditions of judicial officers. The HighCourt held that in view of the decision of this Court in Punjab and Haryana vs State of Haryana, the quota rule prescribed by rule 8 of the Superior judicial service Rules of Punjab and the Haryana Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 was not applicable. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Court was not justified in applying the rule of allocation at the time of confirmation of the members of the Superior judiciary, that the rules in question were not applicable in the case of the petitioners. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in considering the question whether, on a true interpretation of rules 8 and 12 of the Superior Judiciary Rules of Punjab, the quota rules prescribed by rule 12 could be applied to the service. [1038C] 2. The High courts were not justified on the question of the rules of rotation at the time when the confirmation of the Judicial officers of the cadre was made. [1039C] 3. The High Curt was not justified on a true construction of rules 8 & 12 of the Subordinate Judicial Service Rules of Punjab & Haryana. [1040C] 4. The High T Court was not right in applying the rules of allocation at that time. [1041C] 5.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G.A. Kumara Swami, were appointed as Junior Assistants in the Andhra Pradesh State Civil Service in the year 1962. The respondents Nos. 1 to 5 were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra State Civil Service. The respondents No. 6 to 9 were appointed as Assistants in the State Civil Service on the basis of a seniority list prepared by the State Government. The respondents were appointed as Senior Assistants in the year 1963. The respondents nos. 4 & 6 were appointed as temporary Assistant Engineers in 1963. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification dated 13.12.1963 appointing the respondents Nos. 6 to 8 as Assistant Engineers. The respondents no. 6 to 10 were appointed as officiating Assistant Engineers in 1966. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notification dated 13th December, 1963 appointing the respondents nos. 6 to eight as Assistant Engineers and the respondents nos 6 to 8 to 8 as temporary Assistant Engineer. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondents nos 4 & 5 were appointed on the basis that they were appointed as ad hoc Assistant Engineers in 1967 and that the respondents no.6 to 8 were appointed as Temporary Assistant Engineers in 1968 and that the appointment of the respondents nos., 6 to 8 was illegal, contrary to the order issued in G.O.Ms. No. 1 dated 13.2.1963. The High court held that the respondents Nos 4 & 5 are appointed as Assistant Engineer in 1968 and they were appointed on temporary basis in 1967 and therefore, they were not entitled to be appointed as Assistant Executive Engineers. The High Curt held that the appointment was illegal, and directed the respondents nos, 4 & 5 to appoint the respondents nos 1 to 5 as Assistant Engineers on the basis thereof. The respondents challenged the High Court 's order in the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants for different parts of the State in the manner therein provided. No.

The appellant was the auction purchaser in execution of a mortgage decree in respect of certain lands in the district of Hazaribagh. The respondents contended that the appellant was the lessee in possession of the lands in question and that the Patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage was binding on the mortgagee. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decree and held that the appellant could not grant the permanent lease of the mortgaged property in favour of the respondents. The High court held that the question whether the appellant was a subrogated to the position of the Bank was a questionable one and was not competent to grant a lease unusual terms or authorise the use of land in a manner or for a purpose different from the mode in which he himself had used it before he granted the mortgage. Held, that the appellant had no right to grant the permanent leases in possession. The mere fact that the appellant did not possess the land in the usual course of management would not make the lease a lease for a term. The mere circumstance that the appellant acquired a right to the property in the usual way did not make the lessee a lessee. The mere existence of a right in the property does not make the lessor a lessee. In the present case the appellant had not the right to grant a permanent lease in possession. It was only said that a mortgagor was not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as anything took place, to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for the term. The appellant had no power to grant the temporary lease in possession of his property. The appellant was not restricted by the consideration that the mortgagee dealt with the property in his usual course of administration. The appellant could not, therefore, in the usual manner be deemed to have granted the permanent lease in his possession. Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumar, I.L.R. , approved. Madan Mohan vs Raj Kishore Kumari, I. L. R.

The petitioner, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for the supply of electrical energy to the respondent for a period of 9 months. The respondent supplied the electrical energy to him for a period from July 12, 1979 to December 31, 1979. The petitioner sent notice on November 28, 1989 to the respondent to the respondent, for reference to arbitration. The respondent filed a petition under section 8 of the Act for appointment of an arbitrator and issued notice to the respondent. The petitioner filed a petition for appointment of arbitrator and issued a notice to the respond ent on November 28. The respondent challenged the appointment of the arbitrator by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. The petitioner appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. The Court should exercise the power sparingly, cautiously and with circumspection to permit a party to the contract of a arbitration voluntarily entered into to relieve the party from the arbitration agreement. [366C D] 2. The Court must exercise the power cautiously and with caution to permit a contracting party, as a defence. [366D] 3. The Court is not bound to grant leave unless the parties have expressly or by necessary implication waived the right of action or right to require that an arbitration takes place upon the dispute concerned. The Court cannot exercise its discretionary power under sections 5 and 12(2)(b) to permit the respondent to rescind the arbitration agreement and declare that the arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference or dispute. [366E] 4. The Court shall exercise the power judiciously and with circumspection, to permit a contract of a contract of the kind of disputes to be referred to arbitration. [366F] 5. The Court will exercise the power ordinarily within the meaning of section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908, by consent. [366G] 6. The Court would not exercise its discretionary powers under sections 5 & 12(2) (b) to allow the respondent to withdraw the petition.

The appellant, a tenant of a land in the State of Bihar, filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the arrears of rent due from him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was not entitled to proceed against the properties of the appellant. The first appellate court, however, reversed the decree and held that the decree was not barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The High Court, in appeal, reversed the judgment of the first appellate court and held that it was not open to the appellant to contend that the decree in question was barred by the principles of res judicata and further that the bar of section 4(a) of the Act was not applicable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The provisions contained in section 4(1) of the Land Reforms Act are not applicable to the proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against those lands. [916 B] (2) The provisions of section 4 (d) are not applicable in the present case. The provisions contained therein are not applicable. [917 C] (3) The provisions in section 4 (a) are not attracted to the proceedings under the Act. [918 C] (4) The provisions relating to the scaling down of the debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under section 3. Therefore, in construing section 4(b) it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the Act do not fall within the protection of the Act. The provisions of Chapter IV have to be followed in order that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officer and the decision of the claims officer or the Board has been made final by the Act. But in construing section 3 of the Act it would not, therefore, be right to hold that the interests in the properties mortgaged are affected by the sections of the Act, and therefore, the provisions of section 3(d) only to execution proceedings in which, the decree holder sought to proceed against, the estate of the debtor.

The appellants were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ' and who were permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to so appear, were allocated to I.P S.S. and Central Services Group. The appellants were allocated as Assistant Engineers in the I.D.S. in the year 1979. The appellants joined the I.S.S. as Assistant Engineers on the basis of the results of the previous Civil Services Examination. The appellants, who were allocated to a service on the basis that they were not eligible to appear in the preliminary C.S.E. Examination, were not eligible for the post of Assistant Engineers. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the C.S.(E.S. & Central Services Group A and the second proviso thereto. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellants were not eligible as they had been allocated to the Indian Administrative Service Group 'A and that they were within the permissible age limit and have succeeded. Hence this appeal by the appellants. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second proviso to the Rule is not applicable to the facts of the case. The appellants who have been allocated to a Service on the basis on the basis the previous Civil Service Examination have been allocated the same year (the year in which the previous Civil services Examination was held). The appellants who had been allocated in the year 1980 to the IP S.C. or any Central Services, Group 'A, and who had appeared in Civil Services Main Examination of a subsequent year under the interim orders of the Tribunal for the Civil Services Examination in 1988 or 1989 and have succeeded are to be given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the CSR. [512C D] 1.2 The Tribunal has used their expression "may be allowed to sit at the next Civil Service Examination but it did not restrict it only with regard to the preliminary examination as now contended by the appellants according to whom those candidates are not eligible to sit for the main examination since the Tribunal has upheld the validity of second proviso to rule 4 of the said C.S., C.S.. and Central Services, group 'A '. [513C D] 2.1 The Tribunal has given the expression "may also be allowed to appear in Civil Services Exami nation Examination for the services indicated in Rule 17 of C.S.'
