[513D] 2.2 The appellants who were allocated as Assistants to the I P S or the Central Services Group B and who were allowed to abstain from probationary training in the order of their allocation to the I S or any Central Service, Group 'B ' and who had participated in Civil Services Preami nation Examination of a later year under the Interim orders of the tribunal for the Civil Service Examination in 1988 and 1989 and have been permitted to abstain on the basis only for those appointments. The appellants have been allocated as Assistant Engineer in the I P.S. / Central Services Group C and who have appeared in Civil Service Main Examination of the subsequent year under interim orders of this Tribunal for Civil Services Examination, in 1988 or1989 and have succeeded in their success. [514E F] 2.3 The Tribunal has allowed the candidates who have been allotted to the I A.S.C. / Central Service Group 'B and who have participated in Civil Service Preami nation examination of a subsequent years under the interim order of the Tribunal. [515F] 2.4 The Tribunal has not restricted it only with regards to the preliminary Examination as now contended. The Tribunal has also used their expression 'may be allowed ' in the final order of the tribunal. The Tribunal had used their expression in the expression 'may also be permitted to sit at that stage. [516F] 2 5.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by an order dated 25th November, 1986. The Advisory Board after considering the representation of the appellant, rejected the detenu 's request for assistance of a friend. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court and that application was dismissed. The appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The detenu has no right to be represented by a lawyer before the Advisory Board. [792B] 1.2 The Advisory Board has given its finding in rejecting the detenu ' s request for assistance. The order of detention is not vitiated by any error of law or fact. [793C] 1.3 The Advisory Board is not bound to consider the representation of a friend of the detenu. The Advisory board has to be careful in permitting assistance of a lawyer. [794F] 1.4 The Advisory Board had given its finding that the detenu was not a friend of his detenu. The order was passed on the basis of the report of the Advisory Board and the request was turned down. [795G] 1.5 The Advisory Board, after considering the detenu 'S 's request, had rejected the detenu's request for the assistance of a retired Assistant Collector of Central Excise. The order passed by the Advisory Board was not vitiated by the non consideration of the representation of appellant. [796F] 1:6. The Advisory Boards have, of course, to be careful and careful in permitting help of a friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer. The Advisory Advisory Board has, of course to be careful, in permitting assistance by a friend in the order of the Advisory board the detenu must be allowed the facility of appearing before the Board through a legal practitioner. [797G H] 1.7. The Advisory Committee has, ofcourse, to be cautious in permitting assistance to the detenu when it allowed the State to be represented through an array of lawyers. [799H; 799A] 1.8. The Advisory Chairman is not bound by a lawyer 's request. [798B] 1:9. The Advisory ' Board has, in the instant case, to be vigilant in permitting assistance from a friend in Order to ensure due compliance of the policy.

The appellants were the owners of certain goods. The goods were requisitioned and acquired by the Government of India under the provisions of the , and the appellants were the owner of the goods. The appellants filed a suit for possession of the goods and for damages. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court in appeal held that the appellants were not the owners of the goods but were the owners. The High court held that the notice of acquisition was not properly served and that the appellants had not been informed of the orders of requisition on September 30, 1946. The appellants appealed to this Court. Held, that the notice was not properly serving and the appellants had been informed of their orders of requisition and notices of acquisition. The notice of acquisition did not specify the date on which the goods were requisitioned. The notice was served on the appellants as required by r. 75 A (2) of the Rules. The appellants were not served on the owners of goods. The notice did not specify that the goods were to be delivered by the owners. Held, further, that the appellants could not be said to have been served on the owner of goods. Held, also, that the notices of acquisition were not properly served. The notice must be read as a whole and the appellants must be deemed to have been duly served on the persons who were not served. The appellants had been served on them as the owners of their property. The notice could not be served on the managing agents of the mills as they were not served with the notices of requisition on the owners.

The assessee company was a private limited company. The assessment year concerned was 1963 64. The assessee claimed that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal, on reference, held that the said amount was a reserve. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the said sums were to be included in the computation of capital of the assessee company under Rule 1. of the Second Schedule of the : the Income Tax Act, 1922. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the provision made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23A) was indeed a provision and not a reserve. [113E] The High Court had rightly held that the provision was a provision and did not call it a reserve. It was not a reserve and was set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. [113G] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869, followed. Metal Box Company Of India Limited vs The Workmen, [1964] 3 S.C R. 869 and Metal Box Company, of India Limited, vs Their Workmen , referred to. The High Courts were right in holding it to be a provision and cannot be treated as reserve. [114A B] Metal Box company of India Limited. vs Their Workmen [1963] 3 S C R. 871, followed.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were appointed as Engineers on the basis of the results of competitive examinations held by the Railway Board. The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers on the same date. The petitioners challenged the classification of personnel into those that were recruited on the basis that they were appointed on the basis on the basis thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the classification of the personnel into those who were recruited on a later date was not discriminatory and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification of temporary Assistant Engineers is neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles14 and 16 of Constitution. The classification of the temporary Assistant Engineers in the instant case is well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case claiming the same relief and this time by the Temporary Assistant Officers through a body styled as the Federation of Directly Appointed Officers (Suppressed) of Indian Railways and a few others, in a representative capacity. The High Courts have taken into account the long wait involved in the process but all the same approved of the measures of the Railway Board in lessening the Iona wait by giving them weightage of half of the length of service as temporary Assistant Officers subject to a maximum of five years.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, for offences under the Indian Penal Code and section 3(1) read with section 5(2) of the Act. The appellant contended that section 5(i) of the said Act was ultra vires the State Legislature and was void. Held, that the notification issued under section 5 of the Act was not invalid. The notification issued under that section was different from the notification issued by the State of Saurashtra in that the West Bengal Act was not in force. The notification was different from that issued by the Government of Saurashtra in the West Bengal Gazette. The notification under section 5 was different from an order issued under section 3(2) read with the second Schedule to the Act. It was not open to the State Government to direct any one or more of these categories to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the Act. Section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance, which was in force in the State of Bombay, was not in existence at the time when the notification was issued. The notification did not contravene article 14 of the Constitution. The notification dated the 8th February, 1950, was different from a notification issued under the West Bengal Ordinance, which provided that "the Special Court shall try such offences or classes of cases or classes of offences or classes thereof as the Government of the United State of Saurashtra may, by general or special order in writing direct". The notification issued by it under section 5 (1) of that Act was different from one issued under section 6 of the West Act. The notification made by the State Government under section 5, therefore, was different than the notification issued in the West Act, and the notification issued thereunder was different from its notification issued under s.5(1) and therefore were void.

The appellants were convicted under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellants of the charge under section 396, I.P.,C. and convicted them under section 396 and sentenced them to death. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not justified in rejecting the evidence of P.Ws. 1, 2, 7 and 8 of the deceased and that the evidence of the deceased was corroborated by the evidence of other witnesses and that the High court was wrong in rejecting the prosecution evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in rejecting the testimony of P.W. 2 who undoubtedly was in the eastern kotha where the main part of the occurrence had taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify, with the help of the lantern which was burning the appellants who were previously known to her and not strangers and she had received as many as 19 injuries during the course of the occurrence which had gone on for about 15 20 minutes. The evidence of P,Ws. 1 and 7 in so far as it goes to prove the presence of the appellants and that their evidence could not be relied upon because he has intentionally made improvements in his version about the occurrence. [934 H; 935 A B] 2. The High Courts have not relied on the evidence of a witness who was not present at the time of the occurrence and had not mentioned the name of any of the accused to other villagers who entered the house of the deceased soon after the culprits left the place. The evidence is not convincing. [935 B C] 3. The reasons given by the High Court for rejecting the evidence are not convincing. The reasons are not convincing and the High Court has not relied on them. [936 C] 4. The reasons for rejecting the testimony are not convincing, and the High court has not relied upon them. The reasons have not been given by the Sessions Judge. [937 C] 5. The reasons of the High Court are not convincing because they are not convincing as to how the evidence of these witnesses is corroborated by the medical evidence. [938 C] 6. The reasons stated by the High court for rejecting the prosecution witnesses are not convincing; the reasons given by them are not convincing or acceptable. [939 C] 7. The reasons mentioned by the High Courts for rejecting the witnesses are not reliable. [940 C] 8. The reasons recorded by the High courts for rejecting the witness 's evidence are not reliable and the High Courts have relied on them for rejecting the same. [941 C] 9. The reasons which weighed with the High Court in rejecting the witness are not convincing but are cogent.

The appellant Corporation terminated the services of the respondent workman on the ground of unsuitability. The respondent challenged the order of termination on the ground that the services of a workman were terminated on the ground, inter alia, that the services were terminated on account of unsuitability and it was not a case of retrenchment. The Labour Court upheld the order of the Labour Court and dismissed the writ petition. The High Court held that the termination of the services of an employee was bad and that the termination was bad. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the termination in question was bad, as it was not of a termination of service of any workman for any reason whatsoever, but was in the nature of punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman, retirement of the respondent on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The termination of the service of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment '. The effect of the definition of the expression 'retrenchment ' in section 2(oo) and as used in section 25F of the , was that the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatever is not expressly included in section 25 F or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the Act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF. [794F] 1.2 The termination of service by the employer of the service is treated by Parliament, as 'deemed termination '. The expression 'ret retrenchment ' must include every termination of the employment of a workman by an act of the employer. [795G] 1.3 The expression 'termination of service for any reason BHASIAS ' is not defined in the Act. The expression "termination of service" is defined in section 2 (oo) and the expression "termination" is defined to mean the discharge of a surplus labour or of staff by the employers for any reason. [796A B] 1.4 The expression 'remuneration ' in section 25FF of the Act means the discharge of the surplus labour or the staff by the contractor for any reason, whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by the employer. The expression does not include any termination of the work done by the employer on the ground on which the termination is based. [797B C] 1.5 The expression 'terminate ' in section 3(oo) of the Act is not restricted to the discharge of any surplus labour or service by an act or order of the employer but is confined to those who have been employed by the employer in any manner whatsoever. [798C D] 1.6 The expression 'quantified termination ' in section 26F of the Act does not include termination of the contract of service by an employer for any reasons whatsoever. [789D] 1.7 The expression 'resignation ' in section 27F of the is not restricted only to the discharge or retrenchment of surplus labour but also to termination of the same. [789E] 1.8 The expression ' termination ' in Section 2(oo), means the discharge or termination of the workman by the employer, for any reason or otherwise howsoever, than as a penalty inflicted by way disciplinary action, voluntarily retirement of the workmen, retirement of any workman on reaching the appropriate age of superannuation, if the contract is terminated by the employer or termination of service, of a probationer, on the ground or as a punishment imposed by the employer under the contract of appointment. [789G H] 1.9 The expression 'retirement ' in section 24F of the does not include voluntary retirement of a workman. The expression has to be read in the context of the context in which it is used.

The assessee, South Eastern Railway, disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying in the factory of the assessee. The assessee applied for registration as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax Officer examined the case and found that the disposal of the scrap was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee then proceeded in revision to the Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes. The Board of Revenue rejected the application on the ground that the disposal was a regular event of the assessee and that therefore, the assessee fell under the scope of section 56 of the Act, and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. The Board held that the disposal could not be treated as a regular feature. The assessee thereupon filed revision before the Board of Revenue. The Board rejected the revision application on the view that the disposal would be a regular feature and that the assessee fell outside the scope of that Act. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the disposal in the present case was a regular affair of the assessee, and that the disposal had not indicated that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The disposal of the goods did not indicate that the Railway was carrying on any business as carrier of the goods. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier or for the purpose of its business as carriers of goods. It seems to South Eastern Railway that the activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It seems that South Eastern Railway was a "dealer" for the purposes of the Bengal Finance Act, 1941, and therefore, the sale of goods took place. [781E F] 2. The disposal was not incidental or ancillary. It was an activity which might be regarded as incidental or ancillary or ancillary to the business as carrier and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity was regarded as necessarily ancillary or ancillary. [781G H] 3. The activity of so disposed of the goods, did not indicate, that the Railway concern was carrying on the business as a carrier of the good. It was not an activity which could be regarded as merely incidental or ancillary, to its business. It was a "business" which may be described as incidental or incidental to its business, and it was an activity incidental or ancillary which could be described as carrier of goods. [781A B] 4. The activity was not necessarily incidental or incidental. The activity carried on by so disposing of goods was adjac tionally incidental to its commercial activity as carrier of good goods. It was therefore an activity which was regarded as incidental to its trading activity as carrier or as carrier of a goods. [778C D] 5. The activity in question was not necessarily ancillary or incidental to the business of carriage of goods. The activity did not indicate any incidental or ancillary activity of the carrying on of the business as carriers. It was merely an activity which is regarded as incidental and ancillary to its commercial activities as carrier of that goods. It does not amount to incidental or ancillary thereto. [781D E] 6. The activity is not necessarily incidental to its carrying on the activity as carrier. It is a "business". It is an act which may be termed as incidental or subsidiary to its business and it is an activity incidental to its activity as carrier and it is a "dealer". [781E] 7. The activity must be incidental or ancillary and it is not an activity incidental and ancillary. It is not an act which is regarded by the carrier as incidental or auxiliary to its business or for the purposes for which it is constituted. [781F] 8.

The appellant was a Director of a company which was incorporated in the United States of America. The appellant was a director of the company. The company was incorporated in India in the year 1948. The appellant and the other directors of the company were directors of the Indian company. The appellant made a statement of the affairs of the company in the books of the company that the company was in the hands of the appellant and that the money was paid to the Union Agencies through the agents of the company and that the funds were not available for the payment of money to the Union agencies. The appellant also made a statement that the money had been paid to the Central Government and that the Union Agencies had no knowledge of the transactions. The appellant denied that the money paid to the respondent was not in the hands oof the Union Agencies. The appellant contended that the money which the respondent had received from the Insurance Company was not in his hands but was paid to his agents and that the amount was not paid to the Government agencies. The High Court held that the appellant was not authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf of the Insurance Company and that the appellant had no knowledge that the money received by the respondent was in the hand of the Union Agencies and that the respondent had no knowledge about the transactions. Held, that the appellant could not be said to have been authorised to purchase and sell securities on his behalf. The fact that the appellant did not know that the money in question was paid to him by the Insurance Company did not make him a person who was authorised to purchase the securities. The fact of the appellant having received the money from the Insurance company did not make the appellant a person who had no knowledge or knowledge of the transaction. The fact, however, that the money did not belong to the appellant was a relevant fact. The fact whether the money was received by the appellant or not was a relevant circumstance. The fact in the present case that the money belonged to the appellant did make no difference to the fact that the money could not be purchased by the appellant. The fact however that the money belonging to the appellant had been received by the Insurance company was not relevant. The fact was that the money of the respondent was received by him from the Insurance Companies and not by the Insurance Companies. The fact therefore that the money became the property of the Insurance Companies did not make any difference to the question whether the money belonged or was not the property of that company. The fact as to the amount received by the company was not a relevant circumstance to decide whether the money had belonged to the Insurance Companies or not. The fact is that the money is received by the Company and not by an Insurance Company. The fact remains that the money has been received by an Insurance company and not by a person who is authorised to purchase, and therefore, the fact that money was received in cash or purchase the a fore said securities does not make the person who is authorized to purchase or sale securities. The appellant could not therefore be said to be authorised to purchase securities on behalf the Insurance Companies, because, the money was not received by the Government agencies and the money had not been paid to them. The fact does not make any distinction between the money received and the money received. The fact must be taken to have been made in the name of the appellant.

The appellants were appointed to the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the State. The appellants challenged the validity of the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States Secretariat personnel to the State of Kutch. The High Court held that the transfer of these two officers was not open to objection. The High court also held that the transfers were not open to objections. The High. Court also held that there was no difference between the posts in the secretariats of the Secretariat and the posts in that of the Secretariat. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the transfer was not open. [522 B] (2) The transfer of the two officers was made in the interest of the administration of the State and was not violative of the fundamental rights of the appellants. [523 C] (3) The transfer was not a transfer of an officer in the Secretariat with the consent of the Public Service Commission. [524 D] (4) The transfer is not open to question on the ground that they were posted between 1956 and 1960 in the Districts. [525 D] (5) The transfer in the present case was not open, because the transfer was made in contravention of the provisions of the order of the Central Government. [526 D] (6) The transfer order was not open for objection. [527 D] (7) The transfer could not be challenged on the ground of violation of the fundamental right vested in the personnel of the former State.

The petitioners were dealers in goods sold to the respondent State. The respondent State issued a notification under section 5(1) of the , imposing a tax on the sale of goods manufactured or produced in the State. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that the tax was not at all leviable on the goods manufactured or manufactured in the State and that the tax could not be levied at more than one stage. The High Court held that the tax levied was not at more than two stage and that the levy was not at a single stage and that it was not necessary for the State to say that a person, who was not liable to pay tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund at a later stage. The petitioners contended that the tax had been levied on the first purchase in the State of any declared goods and that the State had no power to levy tax on the first sale. The High court held that the levy of tax was not a tax at more than the one in the case of imported goods and that it could not be said that a person who was not a liable to pay the tax must nevertheless be paid at more than another stage. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The Act itself did not indicate the stage at which the tax was to be levied and because under section 15(1) the stage was fixed and that the dealer could always claim exemption under section 5 (2)(a)(vi) or a refund under section 12 of the Act. [554 E] (ii) The Act was not intended to provide for the levy of sales tax on the last purchase in the case where the goods were sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The Act itself does not indicate the stages at which the levy was to be made and because under Section 15(1), the stage was the sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to pay sales tax and the tax is also levied at more one stage. [554 F G] (iii) The Act does not indicate that a person is liable to pay a tax on first purchase in respect of the declared goods. The tax is at the same rate and therefore the tax cannot be said to be higher in the case. [554 G] (iv) The Act is not intended to make a provision for the levy and collection of tax on the second purchase in the absence of any provision in the Act or the rules thereunder. [554 A] (v) The Act also does not indicate any stage at which tax is to be levied. [554 C] (vi) The Act has not indicated the stage at where the tax was levied and because the tax was at the same time a tax at the same point. [554 D] (vii) The Act clearly does not indicate a stage at which a tax can be levied and the tax cannot therefore be said to have been higher in the cases of imported goods. [554 H] (viii) The Act did not indicate that the tax can be collected only at one stage. It is not enough for the State Government to say that the tax cannot he collected at more than a single stage. [555 D] (ix) The Act, therefore, does not indicate either stage at which it can be collected or the tax can only be levied at a single point. [555 E] (x) The Act cannot be said that the tax is higher than two stage. The tax cannot be levied at less than two stage, and the tax can not be said to fall under the Act. The Act does no more than indicate the stage when the tax is to levied and the rate is to be fixed. [555 F] (xi) The tax is not at more. The tax can be said to include the first purchase. The tax has to be at the same stage.

The appellant was the defendant No. 1 in a mortgage suit and the respondent No. 2 was the defendant. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent No 1 for recovery of the mortgage debt. The respondent No. 1 filed a suit for recovery of a sum of Rs. 1,05,000 and odd. The appellant contended that the amount so deposited together with the payments already made out of the decree was to be settled at Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition under section 47 and 297 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, praying that the amount be paid to the respondent No 2 and that the amount should be paid to him. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the amount deposited together with interest was not a debt within the meaning of section 47 and that the suit was not barred by section 47. The High court also held that the suit could not be dismissed on the ground that the amount was not paid as a result of the scaling down of the decree. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the amount of Rs. 3215 was a debt within section 47 and not a debt. The decree holder was a agriculturist and hence entitled to have his debts scaled down under the Agriculturists ' Relief Act. The decree holders were agriculturists and hence entitled only to the benefit of the decree which had been scaled down by the High Court in favour of the original debtors. The decreeholders were agriculturists and therefore entitled to have their debts scaled up under the Agriculturists' Relief Act.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in question under the first defendant. The first defendant was a tenant of the premises. The first plaintiff was a tenant under the first plaintiff. The first appellant was a tenant. The first respondent was a tenant in the premises. In the suit filed by the appellants the City Civil Court held that the first plaintiff was not a tenant of a tenant of that premises. The City Civil Court, however, held that the second and third plaintiffs were lawful sub tenants of the first defendant and were entitled to protection under the Act and that the second defendant was not a sub tenant of the first plaintiff and that the first respondent was not a licensee of the first appellant. The City civil court held that the suit filed was not one between the landlord and the tenant and that the suit was not one for eviction of the first respondent. The City Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the ground that there had been no lawful subletting by the first appellant of the premises to the second and the third plaintiffs. The City High Court, on appeal, held that it was not a case of a sub tenant but a sub tenant. The City of Bombay, therefore, was not a "tenant" within the meaning of the Act. The City, Civil Court, therefore, had jurisdiction to try the suit. The City Revenue Court held that there had not been a lawful subletting by a landlord to the second respondent. The High Court, however held that the City Civil court had jurisdiction to decide the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The City Civil court could not have jurisdiction to try such a suit. The suit was one relating to possession of premises to which the provisions of Part 11 of the Act apply.

The appellant was a director of a company which was incorporated under the name of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd. The company was incorporated under a name of the Oriental Metal Pressings Works Ltd. and the appellant was appointed the managing director of the company by the will of Dadoba. The appellant was appointed as managing director of a private company by the company. The appellant challenged the appointment of the appellant as the managing director by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appointment of appellant was void. The High court took the view that the word "assignment" in the section included "appointment" and so the word "promotion" would include appointment. The High. Court also held that the word 'assignment ' in the section was intended to give a right to a director to be appointed to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the word "'assignment" used in section 312 of the new Act did not include appointment. It was not intended that the word was intended to include "appointment". The word "assign" in section 312 meant a transfer of office by a director for the old Act contained in section 83B of the new. The section was intended only to give a power to the directors to appoint their successor. The section did not indicate that it was intended that the words "assignment of his office" in section 83A of the new act would include "appointment". The section does not indicate that the word is intended to include appointment.

The appellants are the tenants of the respondent landlady. They carry on business there. The respondent filed eviction petition being H.R.C. No. 641 of 1975 in the Court of Small Causes at Madras against the appellants and one other partnership firm, M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart. The appellants filed an eviction petition being No. 641/75 in the Court. The respondent contested the eviction petition on the ground that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop let out to the said M/s Adeshwar Glass Item. The appellants also filed an application for eviction on the ground of subletting under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Trial Court held that the appellants were not liable to be evicted for contravening the provisions of section 10(1)(ii)(b) of the Act. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal. The appellants then preferred a revision petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision petition upholding the finding of the Trial Court that the appellants have unlawfully and without consent of the Respondent sublet the shop to the said respondent. The appellants thereafter preferred a revision application before the High court. The High court dismissed the revision application holding that the appellants could not be evicted under section 10 (2)(ii) (a) of Act. The appellants preferred a revision before the High. High Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have been consistently taking the view that the appellants cannot be evicted under the provisions of the Act either and hence the ratio laid down in the aforesaid decision is directly applicable to the case before us. [420C] 2. The provisions of section 13(3)(iv) of the Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Order, 1949, are not applicable to the proceedings under the said Rent Act either and the Act does not apply to the proceedings before the Rent Controller. [420D] 3. The provisions contained in section 10(3)(v) of the Rent Act are not applicable in the proceedings under that Act either and therefore, the ratio laid in Chhotelal Pyarelal 's case is directly applicable. [420E] 4. The provisions in section 10 (1)(ii) of the said Act are not attracted to the proceedings of the Rent Controller either and hence, the ratio of the said decision is directly applied to the case. [420F] 5. The provisions under section 10 of the Act are not in any way inconsistent with the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [420G] 6. The provisions are not inconsistent with the Act.

The Andhra Pradesh Act sought to impose ceiling on land situate in urban agglomeration and since the concept of agglomeration defined in section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Central Act was an inclusive definition, the Andhra Pradesh Act was amended by the Andhra Pradesh Amendment Act, 1976. The Andhra Pradesh Act came into force on 1st January 1975 and it was with reference to this date the surplus holding of land in excess of the ceiling area was required to be determined and if there was any surplus it was to be surrendered to the State Government. The Andhra Act was amended in 1976 and the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1976 was passed. The Andhra State Act was amended on 1st April, 1976 and the Act was amended with effect from 1st January, 1975. The Andhra area in the State of Andhra Pradesh was not included in the family unit. The Andhra Area (Abolition) Act, 1975 was passed on 1st May, 1976 and it was amended by Act 1st January 1976. The Act was amended and the Act came into effect on 1st February, 1976. In the writ petitions filed by the landholders, the High Court held that the Andhra Pradesh (Abolition) Amendment Act, 1975 had no retrospective effect and that the Andhra Area (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 was ultra vires and void as being beyond the legislative competence of the Andhra Pradesh Legislature. The High Court held the Andhra Area Act, 1975 to be ultra vires and invalid as being beyond legislative competence of Andhra Pradesh Legislature and therefore the Andhra Pradesh law was ultra vires. The State of Andhra Act, 1976 came into force with effect from January 1, 1975. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the landholders that the Andhra Act sought to be imposed ceiling on land in excess thereof and since the Act was not within the legislative competence, the Andhra Act was ultra vires, and void as it was beyond the legislative power of the Andhra State Legislature. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Andhra Pradesh (Ceiling on Land Holdings) Act 1975 was passed by the Andhra State legislature on 1st July, 1975 and it came into force from 1st April 1975. The Act came into existence on 1st November, 1975 and came into force in 1976. The State Legislature was competent to enact the Andhra Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1973. [1157B] 1.2 The Andhra Pradesh Land Ceiling Act, 1973 came into force only on 1st December, 1975 and the Andhra Area was not included within the ceiling area. The Andhra Areas (Ceiling on Holdings) Act 1973 was passed on January 1, 1976 and came into effect from 1.1.1975. The Andhra areas (Ceiling on Lands) Act, 1974 came into force w.e.f. 1st January. 1975.

The appellant company was a company which was carrying on business in the manufacture of iron and steel products. The company was charged with misconduct and misconduct. The company, however, did not take any action against the company. The company filed a complaint against the company and the company was directed to take back the workmen. The company did not take back the workman but the company was asked to take back his workmen. The appellant company did not give any notice to the company and did not give the workmen any opportunity to explain their position. The company also did not give notice to the workmen. It was contended on behalf of the company that the workmen had not been taken back in service and that the company had not taken back the workmen with effect from August 24, 1953, and the notice dated August 23, 1953, was not given to the workmen and that the workmen were not taken back in employment. Held, that the company having held a regular and proper enquiry in which Samar Sen had an opportunity of meeting the charges against him, it was for the company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial Tribunal should not have interfered with the decision of the company unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. The company having held that the decision of its management to terminate the services of Chattoraj was justified, the proper order would have been to give the company permission to dismiss Chattoraj. The company had not given any notice to its workmen before terminating the services of the workmen.

Mishra, Dr. Uja Kant and Dr. Upa Kant for appointment of Professor in the Department of Botacah. The Selection Commi sion Committee, after considering various aspects of the matter, prepared a list of candidates selected by it in order of merit and recommended the name to the State Government for appointment of the appellant Dr. LR. Mishra. The Selection Committees, after considering several aspects of the case, recommended the appellant Dr, Upa Kant and Dr, Uja Kant for appointment to the post of Professor in B.O. Mishra. [423C] 1.3 The Selection Committee in the present case was constituted for the Selection of a Professor, in the year 1983, and the Selection Committee in its meeting held on 3.12.1983 decided that the reserve list recommended by the Selection Board shall be valid upto six months from the date of approval of the Syndicate which was subsequently extended to one year instead of six months in a resolution passed on 3.2.1983.
