This recommendation was approved by the Selection Commi ssion Committee. [420C D] 1.4 The Selection Committee was constituted for selecting a professor in the University and the Selection Committe was constituted for Selection of a teacher. The Selection List was prepared by the duly elected Selection Committee. It was submitted by the appellant that the Selection Committee constituted for the select ment of a professor was proper and in accord ance with the provisions of Section Uma Kant was found suitable for the post of professor in the department and his name was recommended in the list of the candidates selected by the duly nominated Selection Committee. Therefore, the Selection Com mission was not justified in holding that the Committee constituted for selection the appellant was not selected for the concerned post of professor. [420D E] 1.5 The Selection Committee had approved and recommend ed the name of appellant Dr. D.P. Misra for appointment to this post. The Selection Panel was prepared by duly constituted Selection Commit ment. The Selection list was prepared by a duly constituted Selection Commi tee.

The petitioners, who were the owners of certain lands, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Act. The High Court held that the provisions of sections 4 and 11(3) of the Act were ultra vires the Constitution and that the provisions were ultra vires. The petitioners contended that the provisions in sections 4 and11(3) were ultra vires and that the Act was ultra vires the State Legislature. The High court held that the Act did not violate article 14 of the Constitution and the Act was not ultra vires. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of the impugned Act are ultra vires the provisions of article 14 of Constitution. The Act is a piece of legislation and is not a piece of law. The Act does not violate article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The provisions of sections 14, 15 and 16 are not ultra vires the Act. [284 E] (ii) The provisions in sections 14,15 and 16 are ultra vires. [284 G] (iii) The provisions are ultra vires and the Act is not ultra vires as the Act is a colourable piece of legislation. The Act was not a piece or legislation. The provisions in the Act are not ultra legislative. The Act has been passed with a view to giving effect to the policy of the State. The Act cannot be said to be a colourable piece. The Act, therefore, is not a colourable piece and is not one of the provisions in the impugned Act. [285 G H] (iv) The provisions contained in sections 4 to 16 are ultra virus. The Act contains a detailed procedure for the determination of the question whether the land is needed for public purpose or not. The procedure for the disposal of the land is laid down in section 11(3). The procedure for disposal of the objections is laid down by section 12(3) and the procedure for the hearing of objections is laid in section 13(4). The procedure prescribed by section 12 is not a mere formality. The procedure prescribed under section 12(4) is not a merely formal procedure. The procedure is a procedural one. The procedure under section 12 is a procedural provision. The procedure of the Act is to be followed in the case of the land.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the United States of Kutch, was the owner of a land in the State of Kutch. The land was acquired by the Government of India under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The appellant claimed that the land was a part of the territory of India and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions, that the land had been acquired by the State of Gujarat under the Land Acquisi tion Act, 1894, and that the appellant had never been in possession of the land. The Land Acquisition Officer rejected the claim and the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of article 31(1) (d) of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The claim of the appellant was accepted. The claim of Indian citizens to exercise fundamental rights in respect of the territory in that sector may be entertained only if it be established that the territory is found to be originally governed by the Maharao of Kutch. [289 E] (ii) The claim by Indian citizens to the effect that in the State the territory is not a part of India, the territory in this sector is Indian territory and deprivation of the rights of the citizens under article 19(1)(d) and (e) can only be achieved if the cession of what is now part of the State of Saurashtra is established. [289 F] (iii) The claim to the Government of the State to exercise fundamental right in respect of territory in that Sector may be entertained even if it is established that the territories are now in different states. [289 G] (iv) The claim made by the claimants that in absorbing the territory of the State, the territory which is Indian is now declared foreign territory, and it cannot be implemented without the authority of an amendment modifying the boundary of the State is within the competence of the Executive wing of the Government and no constitutional amendment is necessary. [289 A] (v) The claim for the Government of Indian citizens is not a matter of right. The claim is not a question of any fundamental right. [289 C] (vi) The claim is made by the claimant that in the territory of Indian State, the State of Bombay was a part and parcel of the territory. The claim was made by the State in the High Courts of Bombay and Bombay. The claim made in the High courts was the same as in the present case. [289 D] (vii) The claim was accepted. [289 B] (vii). The claim of India was accepted.

The appellant mortgaged the property to the mortgagee in the suit out of which this appeal arises. The mortgagee executed a mortgage deed in favour of the mortgagee in respect of the mortgaged property. The mortgagee 's right, title and interest in the mortgaged property was transferred to the auction purchaser on April 7, 1937. The appellant filed a suit on July 12, 1946, for a decree for the enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. The suit was decreed by the Subordinate Judge on April 7. 1937. The High Court held that the suit was barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, she could still maintain the suit relying upon the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 7 1937. The plaintiff 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The suit was barred under the law of Limitation. The suit to enforce the mortgage was barred by limitation. [675 B] (ii) The right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the mortgage security or where he is not secured in his possession of the mortgaged Property or where possession is not delivered to him as agreed, the claim maintainable by the mortgagee is one for compensation and the period of the limitation for a suit to recover the mortgage money is governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act from the date of destruction or deprivation of the mortgage. [676 D] (iii) The right of the mortgagee to sue where he is deprived of his mortgage security or when he is not obtained possession of the property or where possession was not delivered to the mortgagee as agreed, is one for the benefit of the mortgagee of the property. [678 D] (iv) The right, title, interest and interest of the mortgagee are governed by article120 of the Limitation act from the date when the mortgage money was paid. The right to recover the amount of principal and interest is governed by Article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act from date of destruction of the property and not from the date on which the mortgage money has been paid. [679 E] (v) The right is not a right to sue when the mortgage is extinguished or extinguished. The right is a right to recover money which is extinguished or relinquished. The right of a mortgagee to sue when extinguished or relinquished is one for a specific period. The right can be enforced only when the mortgage has been extinguished or relinquished or relinquished. [682 F] (vi) The right under article 120 of Limitation Act is governed by articles 120 and 120 of the [Limitation Act] from the date the mortgage money becomes due. [683 G] (vii) The right in the present case is governed by the covenant in the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922. The mortgagor 's right to sue for the recovery of royalty in respect of Mauza Bahaldih was transferred to extend the time for the suit. The suit filed on July 12. 1946, was, therefore, barred by limitation, because the mortgage was partly simple and partially usufructuary. [685 G] (viii) The right claimed by the mortgagee in his suit to enforce his mortgage was barred under article 120. [686 B] (ix) The right was not a right of the mortgagor to sue where there was a mortgage. The right was a right to enforce the claim to recover the mortgaged money. [687 C] (x) The right which the mortgagee is entitled to sue where his mortgage is extinguished is one for compensa tion. [690 G] (xi) The right given to the mortgagee under the mortgage deed is not a mere right to sue in respect of a mortgage. [643 D] (xii) The right conferred by the mortgage deed was not a mere personal right but a right to defend the mortgage.

The appellants were engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling motor vehicles. The appellants were charged with the tax under section 3 of the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958. The appellants contended that the tax was not leviable on the passengers and that the appellants were liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. The appellants also contended that the levy of penalty was not justified as the appellants were not liable to pay tax. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the challenge to the tax sought to be realised by the Revenue was not tenable and the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 3 which was the charging section. The High court held that the tax could be levied only on passengers who were carried by a stage carriage which was of the nature of a public service vehicle. The High, Court held that there was no justification for the appellants to pay the amount of tax as also penalty. The High. Court held that it was not possible to hold that the appellants had not levied any charge at all for the transport facilities granted to the employees. The High 'Court held that the levy was not justified. The appellants filed appeals to this Court. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The tax could be imposed only on passengers and not on passengers. The transport provided to the employees by the appellants could be a public service vehicles. The transport service in the present case was not a public service car within the meaning of the Bombay Act. [361 E] 2. The tax can be levied only if the passengers are carried on a public service motor vehicle. It cannot by any process of reasoning be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. The transport services in the present cases which were registered as private service vehicle fall squarely within the ambit of the definition of the Bombay and the Bombay Motor vehicles (Taxation on passengers) Act,1958. [361 F G] 3. The definition of 'stage carriage ' in section 2(7) of the Act defines 'stage ' thus: " 'stage' means a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which carries passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. " [361 F] 4. The definition in section 2 (7) of Act is wide enough to include a motor vehicle which could not be termed as a contract carriage. [361 A] 5. The definition is wide enough. The definition includes a motor vehicle. The definition does not create any difficulty, because having regard to the Preamble of the Act, the tax can be levy only on passengers. [361 C] 5. In the instant case, it is not disputed that the transport provided to employees by the appellant was reserved for them only and no other member of the public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. In these circumstances, it cannot be said that the transport vehicle provided to the employee by the appellants cannot be a public servant vehicle in any sense of the term. [361 D] 6. The definition makes it clear that the tax would be leviable only if the passenger is carried on a road service vehicle.

The appellants, who were the owners of a cinema house, filed a petition under section 795 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952, for a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to grant a licence for a quasi permanent cinema to the appellants. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not influenced by the fact that there was a mosque, and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence having been re opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a temporary licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Government on being satisfied that there was no impediment to the grant of a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and that the High court was not justified in granting a writ of certiorari. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the High Courts were not justified in interfering with the grant of the no objection certificate. [897G] 2. The High Courts have been invested with the power to grant a certificate of no objection to the location of the cinema at the site proposed by the applicant. The High courts have been invested by the State Government with the power of granting a certificate to the applicant that there is no objection to a location of the Cinema at the site. [898A] 3. The HighCourt was right in granting a certificate of a "no objection" certificate. [889C] 4. The High. Courts have been conferred with the power under section 5(3) of the Act to grant a "no objections" certificate. The Act does not confer any right of appeal on a person who might have raised objections before the licensing authority against the grant of such a certificate. [891D] 5. The High 'Court was right that the High 'Court should not have granted a writ of "no objection". [891E] 6. The High Curt was right in directing the State to grant a 'no objection certificate ' to the third respondent. [892F] 7.

The plaintiffs instituted a suit against the defendant claiming a declaration that they were entitled to remain in possession of the mining lease. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The plaint was not an acceptance of the offer, not was it intended to be an acceptance. The plaint was an acceptance and that the service of a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons was a communication of the acceptance. [584 E] The plaint was in the nature of an acceptance and the service of the copy of the suit along with the Writ of summons was the service of notice. [584 F] Bloxam 's case, referred to. Bloxam vs Biden, A.I.R. 1957 Cal. 142, referred to, distinguished. Bloxom vs Ayerst, , referred to. The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not an accepted form of acceptance. The plaintiffs had not agreed to purchase the mining lease, and the defendant was at liberty to revoke the offer at any time before its acceptance by the plaintiffs. [584 B C] Bloxom 's case was not an acceptation. The plaint did not contain any concluded contract. The plaintiffs were not entitled to the declaration that they had been entitled to remain as in possession of mining area. [584 C] Block vs Ayernd, , referred. Bloxem vs Ayerton, A. I.R.

The appellants were owners of agricultural land in the State of Bihar. They were charged with the offence of taking under sub section (3) of section 3 of the , read with section 7 of the , for the contravention of the provisions of the , and section 3 of that Act. The appellants contended that the investigation which was being carried on against them was not in accordance with law and the police had no jurisdiction to investigate the same. The High Court held that the investigation was not in conformity with the provisions of section 3 and the Act was not applicable to the facts of the case. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : The investigation was not carried on in accordance with the provisions Of the Act. The investigation was carried on in contravention of the provision of section 3. The investigation could not be carried on in a manner which would be contrary to the provisions of that Act and the Act. [676 B] The object of the Act was to bring under control the cultivation and sale of food crops. The Act was enacted by Parliament in exercise of the concurrent power of legislation under Entry 33 of List III. The Parliament was well within its powers in legislating in regard to sugarcane and the Central Government was also well within its power in issuing the Sugarcane Control Order, 1955 in the manner it did because all this was in exercise of concurrent power of the Parliament under Entry 33. [676 G] The power conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of Act cannot be questioned as invalid. The power conferred by the Act cannot be challenged as invalid.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain lands in the State of Mysore, filed writ petitions before the High Court of Karnataka challenging the validity of the orders dated 12th January, 1977 and 12th January 1977 issued under the said orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of Karnataka that the concessions granted by the earlier order dated 30th June, 1969 were being misused and undue advantage taken of the said concessions by the newly established industries. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The doctrine of Prom promissory Estoppel is not applicable in this case because it is found by the State Government that the concessions were granted by it to the new industries. The doctrine is not applicable to the present case since it is found that the concession granted by the said order dated 30. June, 1969 was being misused and unfair advantage taken of it by the newly created industries. [950C D] 2. The doctrine in the present cases is not applicable because it is not found by the High Court that any such misuse was being made or undue advantage taken by the newly existing industries. The High Courts have not been able to appreciate the effect of the doctrine of promissory estoppel. [951C D] 3. The doctrine has been applied in the present set of cases. The doctrine cannot be invoked in the present instance because it is well settled that the doctrine is not applied in the instant case because it has been found by the Court that the concession was granted by the Government. [952E] 4. The doctrine does not apply in the present situation because it is a well settled principle of law that the doctrine cannot be applied in the case of an exemption or reduction in the sales tax liability to the extent stated in the order. [954F] 5. The doctrine applies only to cases where the source of power under which it is issued is not stated in an order but can be found on the examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegation that they caused the death of the deceased and caused his death. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 to A 3 but convicted A 1 to 3 under Sections 148 and 302 I.P.,C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 1 to 4 under Sections 148, 302 read with section 149 I.p.C. and acquit them of all the charges. The High court confirmed the conviction of A 1 and A 2 under Sections 148 I.P,C. and sentence of imprisonment for life and acquitted A 1 and 2 under Section 302 read with 34 I.P..C. The High Curt also confirmed the conviction under Section 302 I.p.,C. The appellants were convicted under Sections 148/149 I.P./149 and sentenced to imprisonment for one year. The High. Court confirmed the convictions and sentences of A 1, 2 and 3 under Sections 147 and 302 readwith Section 34 I.p./s. 34 I. P.C. The conviction and sentence were set aside by the High Court and the appellants were convicted and sentenced under Sections 148 read with 149 I. P./s. 302 read with 149 and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life, and a fine of Rs. 500/ each. The appellants filed appeals to this Court. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in confirming the conviction and sentences of the appellants under Sections 148 & 302 read with Sections 149 I.PC. [804E] 2. The High courts fell into error in confirming the convictions and sentence of the appellants. [805E] 3. The High 'Court fell into error on the ground that the appellants were only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.P.'C. [806F] 4. The HighCourt fell into an error in confirming conviction and sentence. [808F] 5.

The assessee, a registered firm, was carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton yarn. The assessee was assessed to income tax on the ground that the transfer of the goods was effected by the assessee in the course of his business and that the transfer was effected by him in the course or in other words, that the transfer had been effected by him with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains. The assessee contended that the transfer by the assessee was effected by way of transfer of the capital asset and that the transaction was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Act and that the assessee was not liable to pay tax on the transfer of capital asset. The Income tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax on the basis that the transfer and sub section (2) applied only where the consideration for the transfer was shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal, on reference, held that the transfer did not amount to transfer of capital assets and that the value of the capital assets transferred was not the value of capital assets as on the date of the transfer. The High Court, on reference. held that the assessee had not been able to prove that the transfer took place by way of sale of the capital goods and that the sale was not a transfer of capital goods within the meaning Of section 2(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. On reference, the High Court held that the transaction did not amount either to transfer of the property as on the dates of the transfer or transfer of the asset. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the transfer in question was not a transaction of sale within the definition of section 2 (2) of Act, and that the High Court was in error in holding that the transfer could not be said to have been effected by way or in any way connected with the assessee and that the mere fact that the transfer is not shown or disclosed and in most of the cases, if not all, it would not be possible for the Income tax officer to determine precisely what is actual consideration received by the transferor and permit the Revenue to take the fair market value of the assets as the full value of the consideration declared by the assessee by not less than 15% of the value so declared, but it is furthermore necessary that the full value should be disclosed at a lesser rate than that actually paid by the assessee, and that it should be confined to cases where the actual consideration received for the transfer is under stated and the burden of proving such under statement or concealment is on the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The transfer of the shares by the assessee as on the relevant date is not a transfer within the meaning ofs.2(2) and the transfer of shares by the transferor as on the said date is not the transfer of any capital asset. [645B] 1.2 The transfer of shares is not a sale of capital asset within the meaning section 2(3) of the Indian Income tax Act. [646C] 1.3 The transfer of a capital asset is not a transaction in the sense that it is a transfer of a right to transfer of property. [647C] 1:4. The transfer of capital property is not a mere transfer of a transfer of the right to transfer the property. The transfer is not a pure transfer of the transfer of property but a transfer of property which is a transfer for consideration of the transfer and is not a gift of property. The mere fact that a transfer is not made in the course, or in other manner, of the transfer does not by itself make the transfer a transfer of title. [648C] 1 5. The transfer in question is not a "transfer of property" within the meaning o[648F] 1.6.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 7(i)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the appellant was selling adulterated food to the Food Inspector and that the appellant had only black Tils used for Pooja. The Food Inspector, who stated that the black Tils in his shop were only meant for Pooja, did not know that the Food Inspector had not used the same for Pooja. He stated that the Food inspector had not given any information to the Food inspector that the black tils were unfit for human consumption. The appellant was charged under section 7 (i)(f). The trial court acquitted the appellant. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the acquittal and convicted the appellant under section 7 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human consumption and thereby committed an offence under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution was not able to prove that the appellant sold the food to the food Inspector specifically for the purpose of Pooja after the accused had told him that they were not meant for human use. [330F] 2. The prosecution has not been able to prove the presence of the Food Inspector on the spot. The prosecution witnesses have not been able even to prove the actual purpose for which the articles of food were kept in the accused 's shop. [330G] 3. The evidence of the prosecuting Food Inspector who said that the black ly had not been used for human consumption, or that the food Inspector had written on the cash memo, was not more reliable. The evidence was not sufficient to prove that what was stored or sold in a shop was not really food meant for human food. [330H; 331A] 4. The evidence in the instant case shows that the appellant, who had a grain shop, must have known that the Food Inspectors could prosecute him if he kept adulterated foodstuffs for sale for human consumption.[330H; 330A] 5. The evidence shows that the Food Officer had not given the information about the sale of the Til seeds at his shop. The appellant, who was on bail need not surrender. [330B] 6. The evidence is not sufficient to show that the appellant has not been in possession of adulterated foodstuffs for the purpose for which he was kept in the shop. [334C] 7. The evidence does not show that the Food Commissioner had given the information that the black market was not for human consumption or that the appellant 's explanation was more reliable. [330D] 8. The evidence, of the prosecuting witnesses, who said that Tambe was there, cannot be implicitly relied upon in this case. The evidence has not been sufficient to prove the absence of the Food Commissioner 's refusal to give information about the appellant '. [330E] 9. The evidence on record shows that the food inspector had not been examined to corroborate the food inspector 's refusal. The appellant had a grain market. He had a grain Market. He had no knowledge of the sale of that market. He was not present at the time when the seeds were sold by the appellant to the Food Inspectors. He had not given information about the purchase of the Til seed from the Food Inspector. The appellant could not have been kept for the purpose. [330C D] 10. The evidence showed that the Food Analyst had not given him information about the use of the Til oil. The appellant 's evidence shows that he had not given such information to the Public Analyst. [330A] 11. The evidence that the appellant did not give information about his use of the oil was not sufficient. The evidence also shows that the prosecution witnesses had not been able enough to witness the occurrence. [330 D] 12.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th of January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the dismissal of his appeal on the ground of limitation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on 31st October, 1966. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of dismissal of the appeal was bad and he continued to be in service. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order of the higher authority where a statutory remedy is provided entertaining the appeal or representation is made and where no such order is made, though the remedy has been availed of, a six months ' period from the date the appeal was filed or representation was made and where the remedy has not been availed of the remedy, though the remedies have been availed of a six months period from the order of preferring of the appeal or making of the representation shall be taken into account. [55B C] 2. The cause for action shall be the date when cause of action has been instituted or representation has been made, the right to sue shall first accrue. The date when the right to the sue shall first accrued, and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from the date when such appeal was filed, or representation was received, the right shall first accrue unless the right to suit shall first accrue, and where the right to file a suit has been made and where such right is not made the suit shall first accrued. [55C D] 3. The cause is not the same as the cause of action. The cause must be the same as that of the plaintiff. The cause has to be the same. The cause does not mean that the cause of actions shall be the same, but the cause of the action shall be different. [55D] 4. The cause or action shall be deemed to have been taken to arise in the course of the proceedings. [55E] 5. The cause, of action shall not be taken to have first accrued. The cause shall be taken, to be the date on which cause of action may be taken to has first accrued. If the cause of a action shall be determined by the Court of first instance and not by the Court at which the suit is instituted or representation made, the cause of such action shall first accrue and where such action is not so determined, the Court shall proceed to decide the suit on the basis of the merits of the case. [55F G] 6. The cause in the present case is not the date on the date of filing of the suit. The cause was not the same. [55G] 7. The cause would be taken to be the last of the dates on which the order of his dismissal was passed. [55H] 8.

The respondent, a member of the family of the appellant, filed a suit for partition of his share in the suit property. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and held that the trial court had no jurisdiction to pass a decree for partition. The High court, however, held that the decree was not a decree of affirmance but variation in regard to the order as to costs. The High, Court, however, reversed the decree of the trial court and held that it was a decree of affirmation and not a decree for affirmance. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the decree passed by the trial court was not a judgment of affirmance and the decree was a decree for confirmation. The High Courts were not right in holding the decree of affirmation as a decree of affirmedance. The High courts were right in holding, that the decree of confirmation was not a confirmedance and the High Courts were right in interfering with the decree of reversal. The High. Courts were not correct in holding that a decree of confirmation is not a decree in affirmance but a decree of confirmance. The decree of confirmation of the trial Court was not a final decree and the High Court had no jurisdiction under article 133(1) of the Constitution to interfere with the decree. The High 'Court was right in interfering in the appeal. The HighCourt was right. The High Curt was right in setting aside the decree of confirming the trial Court.

The appellant, a Small Cause Court, was constituted under the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The District Judge, Lucknow, passed an order under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, disposing of a revision petition filed by the appellant. The appellant filed a revision petition before the High Court, which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a revision application before the High court, which was allowed. The High Court held that the High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, read with section 115, and that the High court had jurisdiction under section 25. The High court, however, held that the revisional power of the District Judge under section 25 Provincial Small Cause Court Act was not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under section 115. The High, Court, however, allowed the revision petition and set aside the order of the District Court. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts (Amendment) Act, 1976, which repealed the provisions of section 115, code of Civil Procedure and section 115, in so far as it related to the revisional powers of the High Courts, had the exclusive jurisdiction under Section 115, Code. [38C] 2. The High courts (Amendment) Acts, 1976, and 1976, which were in force at all material times, were not amenable to revisional jurisdiction of High Court under Section 115 Code of Civil procedure. [38D] 3. The High 'Court had jurisdiction under Section 25, Provincial Civil Courts Act, to make a clear cut division of jurisdiction between the High Court and the District Court, resulting in exclusive revisional jurisdiction to the High Court in cases arising out of original suits of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above, and exclusive jurisdiction under s. 115 to the District Court in other cases. [38E] 4. The High. Court had jurisdiction under s, 25, Provincial. Small Cause Courts (Amendment). Act, 1976. The High Curt had jurisdiction under that section in cases arising under the original suits of value of Rs, 20,000 and above, but in other cases the revisional jurisdiction was concurrently shared between the High Courts and the District Courts. [38F] 5.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands in Jaipur and wanted to construct a building thereon, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the service of notice under section 52 (2) of the Act served on the respondents at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road, Calcutta by the Special Officer Town Planning Department, Jaipur was an integral part of the cause of action and was sufficient to invest the Calcutta High Court with jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity and propriety of the notice issued by the Special officer Town Planning Department Jaipur. The High court held that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 was an integral parts of the cause and was sufficient for invest ing the Calcutta High court with jurisdiction to try a petition under Article 226 of the constitution. The High. Court also held that the writ petition was not maintainable. The respondents appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have jurisdiction to entertain the petition under article 227 of the Constitution. The High courts have jurisdiction to try the petition under Article 227 of the constitution and the High Courts have power to entertain the writ petition under article 32 of the Constitution against the notification issued under section 52 of the Act. [605F] 2. The High 'Court has jurisdiction to entertain any petition under article226 of the Constitution and the High Court has jurisdiction to try such petition. [606F] 3. The HighCourt has jurisdiction under article 226 to entertain a writ petition under Article 32 of the constitution against the notification dated February 8, 1984 issued by the Government of Rajasthan under section 52. [608F] 4. The High Curt has jurisdiction to hear a petition under articles 226 of the Consti tution. [609F] 5.

The appellant was the tenant of the premises in suit. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that the building in question was constructed in 1968 and that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, reversed the decree of the trial court and held that the building was constructed in 1969 and that it had been constructed in 1968. The High court also held that the appellant could get any protection of the new Rent. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the building had been constructed by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the trial court that the building is not ten years old on the date of the suit and was exempted from the operation of the new rent Act was manifestly erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts have taken the view that the building will be deemed to have been completed on the date on which the first assessment thereof comes into effect and where the said dates are different, the earliest of the said dates and in the absence of any such report, record or assessment, the date onwhich it is actually occupied (not including occupation merely for the purposes of supervising the construction or guarding, the building under construction) for the first time. [334E F] 2. The High courts have taken the same view in the case of a building in 1968 and the trial court has found that the building would be deemed to be completed on the dates of the first assessment. [335E] 3. The HighCourt has found that it is the date of first assessment which will be deemed not to be the date of completion of the construction in the circumstances of the case and in that view of the matter the building had not become more than ten years old. [337F] 4. The High. Courts have taken a view that the buildings will be deemed as completed on the first date of the first year of the assessment and if that be so, the appellant would be entitled to the benefit of section39 of the Act on the date when the revision came to be decided by the High Court. [338G] 5. The High 'Court has found on the basis of the evidence that the building has been constructed in 1969, and that the building on which the house was constructed was constructed by the respondent and, therefore the view taken in the High Court setting aside the decree for arrears of rent and remanding the case to the trial court remains intact and the case is sent back to the III Additional District Judge who will apply the new Rent Acts and give him an opportunity to deposit the dues contemplated by section 39 of the new Act after first determining whether any amount is due from the appellant towards rent as directed by the High court.

The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and its Managing Director, was appointed as the sole arbitrator. The appellant filed an application under section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, for the appointment of an arbitrator. The arbitrator made an award in terms of the agreement. The appellant contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills, and that the agreement had been duly executed. The arbitrator held that the agreement did not comply with the requirements of section 175(1) of the Act and that the award passed in proceedings instituted by the appellant was a nullity and that no decree could be passed in terms thereof. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the award was a nullity, that the award had been made in terms of an arbitration agreement and that the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to make the award in terms thereof, and that no suit could be filed in terms of section 175 (3) of Government of India act, 1935, and that therefore the award was not a nullity. Held, that the agreement to refer to arbitration was not one in respect of execution of works and that the arbitration clause was not one of the terms of the contract. The agreement was not a certified copy and was not a copy thereof. The award was not liable to be set aside on the ground that it was not a decree but a certified copy. The award did not comply within the meaning of section 175. The award in terms was not a final decree and the award was therefore not a nullity and the award could not be set aside. The award could not therefore be set aside in terms thereof and the award passed by the arbitrator was a nullity. The award passed by him was a nullity because it was not signed by the arbitrator. The award had been signed by the appellant and the arbitrator had been authorised to execute it. The award made by the arbitrator to the court was a nullity as the award was passed by the court which was a copy of the award. The award, therefore, was not a valid award. The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 175 of the Government Act. The award of the arbitrator was not a judgment in rem and was not binding on the appellant. The award under the Government of the India Act was a nullity in so far as it was not binding upon the appellant.

The appellant was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. He was working as Superintending Engineer in Public Health Department in the year 1980. He was prosecuted for offences under sections 120B, 420, 467, 468, 471 and 420 IPC. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been convicted for the offences under sections 420, 467 and 468 IPC. The High Court acquitted him on two grounds, namely, (i) that the first information report against Kailash Nath and the prosecution as against Kailash Nath was not lodged within four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said rule and the High Court committed an error of law in taking the said view. The High court, however, quashed the first information Report and directed the trial court to decide afresh the second report. The High Curt also quashed the second report and directed the Sessions Court to decide afresh. The State of Punjab filed an appeal against the High Court 's order. The High, Court, in appeal, quashed the second FIR and directed the Trial Court to decide the second report afresh. The High. Court also quashed the first FIR and the second FIR. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in taking the view that the second FIR was not lodged in the first information case and the second report was lodged after a lapse of more than four years of its institution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second FIR was lodged after the first information was lodged. The second FIR is lodged after a gap of four years of filing the first FIR. The second and third FIR are lodged after a delay of more than 4 years. The second proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2.2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume I, provides that the right of the Government servant to withhold or withdraw etc. of pension of such a Government servant is not coverable in the case of a Government servant referred to therein for prosecution in respect of a cause of action which arose or an event which took place more than four year before such institution the government will not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause (b). [919G H; 920A] 1.2.3 The third proviso to clause 2.2 is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the Rule has been framed. [921B] 1.4. The third proviso is in the form of a proviso to clause(b) of sub rule 2. The third Proviso to clause (a) of Rule 1.2 is, in the nature, a beneficent enactment and in case the omission to do so is not to be found in the main rule 2.2, but in the third proviso to the said rule. [922C] 1.5.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The company was floated by the respondent company as a public company under the provisions of the Indian Companies (Amendment) Act, 1955, and the respondent company was formed as a public Limited Company under the Indian Company Act, 1913. The respondent company was registered as a public Company under the Companies Act, 1956, to acquire, and carry on business of manufacture, sale and sale of 'Amrutanjan '. The respondent Company was formed as public limited company on the basis of a resolution passed by the shareholders of the company. The respondent was formed as the public limited company. The appellant company was formed on the basis that the public were substantially interested in the business of the company and the respondent was a subsidiary company of the appellant company. The company was formed in the name of "Amritanjan". The respondent company filed a petition under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1955 56, for the year 1955 56. The Income tax Officer rejected the petition holding that the respondent company had no right to the shares in question and on that footing he held that the respondent was one in which the public were directly interested. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the appellant was one in whom the public were not substantially interested, and that the respondent had no right in the balance of the profits. The Appellate Tribunal held that the company was one in whose favour the public were indirectly interested and there was no question of any right in the shares in the public company as the public were merely interested in the disposal of the shares. The High Court, on reference, held that there was no right in shares in the company and on that basis answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant company was one of the largest shareholders of the respondent company. The High court was right in its view that the respondent 's right to the public was one in Which the public were substantial interested. [714 B] (ii) The High court had rightly held that the shares in dispute were not entitled to a fixed dividend. The High Courts were right in holding the shares in favour of the respondent. [715 C] (iii) The High Courts have rightly held that there is no right in a public limited Company to the shares. [716 D] (iv) The High courts have rightly held the shares in a public company to be one in which public are substantially interested. The High courts were right in taking the view that the shares were not entitled in law to the shares as the public had not substantially interested in such accumulation. [717 E] (v) The High. Court was right. [718 G] (vi) The High 'Court was right in taking a view that the appellant could not be said to have any right in shares.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21 of the Constitution. He was a public officer within the meaning Of section 21 of that Act. He was prosecuted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code for committing an offence punishable under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted him under section 161 and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The High Court, however, acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the ninth clause of section 6 of the Act was not applicable to the case of the appellant because the ninth clause was not applicable because the ninth Clause was not applicable. HELD: (i) The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receivers one may accept money, that if offered or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion, in each case, lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public servant. [624 D E] (ii) The word 'obtains ' on which much emphasis was laid does no doubt include an element of efforts on the part or the receivers one who was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty. [625 D] (iii) The abuse of position as a Public servant is clearly implied. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. [626 D] (iv) The abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise, the abuse being either either by corrupt, illegal or illegal means, or by otherwise. For that section 405 of the Indian penal Code has to be looked at. [627 D] (v) The abuse is one which is punishable under section 161. The abuse being one of the essential ingredient of the offence, the abuse is clearly implied in what capacity he has committed the offence. [628 D] (vi) The abuse, being either by secret or illegal means and by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's(1) case, the abuse having been either by corrupt and illegal means or otherwise abusing his position, the abuse was clearly implied. [629 D] (vii) The abuse was either by corrupt. or illegal means. [630 D] (viii) The abuse having been made in the course of the performance of the duties of an examiner, one may accept or solicit payment or extort money, or extorts the bribe by threatening payment of a gratification or extort of the bribe by the threat or inducement. [631 D] (ix) The abuse in the present case was not of any kind. The abuse was neither by corrupt or unlawful means nor by other means. [732 G] (x) The abuse by corrupt or improper means or by other means or by any other means of a nature mentioned in the section, is clearly implied, and the abuse being one which is not punishable under section161 of the Indian Code, the abuse, being one of an essential ingredient of that offence, the misuse being either by illegal means or in otherwise. [733 G] (xi) The abuse must be either by corrupt motive or by other method of the nature specified in the section. [734 G] (xii) The abuse or abuse of position would be the necessary ingredient of the offences. [735 G] (xiii) The abuse and abuse of position are clearly implied. The abuse of the position would be a necessary ingredient of that offences.

The petitioners, who were casual labour, were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Northern Railway. The petitioners were engaged in the work of casual labour on terms of contract for periods varying from 10 140 to 16 years in different departments. The petitioners, who had put in continuous service for quite a long period, were absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Railway Board. The petitioners challenged the validity of the circulars issued on January 1, 1984 and January 1,1984, on the ground that they were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc. They also sought a direction to treat them as temporary servants and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent post. The Railway Board 's order was challenged by the petitioners in a Writ Petition filed in the High Court. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition and directed the Railway Board to treat the petitioners at par with the maintenance workers and to declare them as permanent servants and to treat them at par with maintenance workers and grant them the benefit of the circulars. The petitioners filed the present writ petitions challenging the validity of circulars issued on the basis of the Railway Board ' order dated January 1,84 and January 1.1984. The petitioners contended that the Railway Board had no power to issue circulars on the basis that the Railway Administration had no power or authority to issue circulars. They also contended that the circular dated January 1. 1984 was not given effect to. Dismissing the writ petitions, the Court, HELD: 1.1. The petitioners should be treated as temporary servants. They should be treated at par with regular employees. They should not be treated as permanent servants. They must be treated as regular employees. [144C] 1.2. The Railway Administration has not been able to show that the petitioners were appointed on terms of the circulars dated January 1 1, 1984. The petitioners have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. [144D] 1.3. The petitioners are entitled to the same pay as is 1) admissible to others either in the project or in the open line. The Railways have to take prompt steps to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet be tested for the purposes of regularising the service. [145E] 1.4. The Railway Boards order of 1st of June, 1984 has not been given effect to and the petitioners have been discriminated against. [145F] 1.5.

The Forward Markets Commission, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 12 of the Forward Markets Commission Act, 1954, framed bye laws in respect of the Forward Market. The Forward Markets Commission was constituted under the Act and the Forward Markets Act, 1954. The Forward Market Commission was constituted by the Central Government under section 3 of the Act. The Forward markets Commission was constituted in accordance with the provisions of the Act and was to function in accordance with its bye laws. The Forward market Commission was constituted for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of section 12 of that Act. The Central Government issued a notification under section 12 of this Act declaring the Forward Markets commission to be a proper recipient of the power conferred by the Act. By a notification issued under section 12(1) of the Act the Forward Markets Board was authorised to make bye laws for the conduct of the Forward markets. The Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1954 was passed by the Central Legislature. The Forward Marketing Board was constituted under section 3 and the Forward Market Board was constituted. The Forward Boards were constituted under section 18 of the Act, and the Forward Contracts (Regulations) Act, 1955, was passed by Parliament. The Forward Committees were constituted under the Forward Contracts Regulation Act, 1954 and the Forward Boards were appointed under section 18. The Forward Areas Commission was constituted and the Forward Committees were appointed under the Forward Markets Regulation Act, 1955. The Forward Area Commission was constituted on January 21, 1956, and the President of the Forward Areas Commission appointed the Forward Markets Committee under section 18, and the Central Government issued an order under section 12 on January 21. 1956, declaring the Forward Market Committee to be a valid entity. The Forward Produce Market Committee was constituted under s.3 of the Forward Contracts Regulations Act, 1955 and the Forward Marketing Board had power to make bye law with retrospective effect. The Forward Commodities (Regulation) (Amendment) Act, 1956, was passed on January 21 and the Forward Areas (Regulation) Amendment Act, 1956. The Forward Price Control (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956, which was passed by Act No. 1 of 1956, was repealed by the Forward Markets (Regulation) Ordinance, 1955, and the Act was repealed by Act No 1 of 1956. The Central Legislature passed the Forward Markets Control (Amendment ) Act, 1956 (Act No. 1 Of 1956) which was passed after the Act came into force. The Forward Control (Amendment Act) Act, 1957, was passed in exercise of powers conferred by the proviso to section 12 of Act No. I of 1956. By section 12 of these two Acts, the Forward Markets Regulations were repealed and the Forward markets (Regulation) Regulations were made in exercise of that power.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1357 B.S. Rs. 20,469/ for the years 1357 B and 1358 B.S., Rs. 21,822/ for the assessment year 1357 C. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire amount was income in the hands of the assessee and taxable as dividend income. The Appellate Tribunal held that the whole amount was income assessable as dividend income and the remaining amounts were not taxable. The High Court, however, held that the amount was income of the assessee from other sources. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to the salami was taxable. [732 B] (2) The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain. [733 C] (3) The High Courts have to decide on facts of each individual case whether any sum of salami is capital gain. The question of law raised in this group of cases is more extensive. to the effect that the High Court has not recorded final answers, the order is subject to another infirmity. [734 E] (4) The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the case is remanded to the High Court for disposal according to law. [735 G] (5) The High 'Court had to decide the facts of the case whether any money of salami had been capital gain. If the High Court had decided that the distribution was taxable, it was not open to the assessee to contend that the receipt from the capital gains was still income liable to tax. [736 G] (6) The High. Court had to decide whether any amount was capital gain and whether any part of the compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gain or not. [737 G] (7) The High, Court had to determine on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, whether any amount had been capital gains.

The Kerala Forest Act, 1963 was enacted to provide for the control and regulation of the forest produce and the regulation of the manner in which it is to be done. Section 2(f) of the Act defines 'wood oil ' to mean any article of food or drink which includes any article of animal origin. Section 2 (f) defines 'wood Oil ' to mean 'any article of food which includes any animal or drink which is capable of being used as a raw material or in any process or process or in any other manner whatsoever. Section 2 of the Act provides for the control of the forest and the regulation and control of the manner of its use. Section 2 provides for the regulation and regulation of forest and the control of forest and regulation of manner of its disposal. Section 2 empowers the State Government to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the purposes of the Act. Section 2 lays down the procedure for the disposal of the forest. Section 2 makes the provisions of the Act applicable to all forest produce except those which are included in the definition of 'land produce '. Section 2 further provides for the establishment of a new forest in the State of Kerala. Section 2 also provides for the constitution of a new Forest Produce Board. Section 2 provided for the establishment and regulation of a new State. Section 2, which is relevant for the purpose, provides for the levy of property tax on timber and other forest produce. Section 2 deals with the levy of the property tax on the timber and other produce. Section 3 provides for the imposition of the tax on timber. Section 4 provides for the payment of the tax. Section 5 provides for the collection of the tax from the forest produce. The appellant State of Kerala filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of tax on timber under the Kerala Forest Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the expression 'wood oil" in the definition in section 2(f)(i) must receive its colour from its context and meaning in which it was used and the purpose the Act sought to serve and the family to which sandalwood oil belonged being an essential oil would include wood oil. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'wood oil used in the Act will require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [164F] 2. The word "wood oil" used in the definition is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary, popular and natural sense when that word is being understood in trade, business or transaction known to the trade. [164G] 3. The word wood oil used in section 2 (f)(i), must receive its ordinary, scientific and natural sense. [164H] 4. The word `wood oil ' used in the context in section 2 of the Kerala Forest (Vidaran Oil) Act, 1963 is not static vehicle of ideas and concepts change, as they are bound to do in any country like ours with the establishment of an independent structure based on agalitarian values, the meaning and content of the statutory provision undergo a change. [164A B] 5. The word „wood oil" is used to indicate that the word is to be construed in the sense in which it has been used in trade, commerce or transaction known as agalitarian value. [164C] 6. The word is to include in its ambit cut pieces in the context and purposive approach of the word 'forest produce '. [164D] 7. The word forest produce is used in the sense of forest produce. It is a forest produce. [164E] 7. In the instant case, the word 'wood Oil" used in section 3(f)(1) must receive a colour from its significance and content. [164B] 8.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code but was acquitted. The High Court convicted him under section 302 and sentenced him to transportation for life. The High court convicted him under s.302 read with section34 and sentenced him under section 34 to transportation for a period of life. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High, Court held that there was no evidence against the appellants sufficient to warrant a conviction and that there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal. Held, that the High Court was in error in accepting the testimony of the doctor P. W. 1 and holding that the doctor was not a fit person for the purpose of holding the appellant guilty. The High. Court was in a position to find out whether the doctor was in a fit state of mind and whether he was asked to say that Bega was also present. The doctor was not asked to say whether Bega was present. The High 'Court was in error when the Sessions Judge was of the opinion that the doctor had not been asked to say what was the exact nature of the injuries. The HighCourt was in a better position to find whether the doctor had given any such reasons for his opinion. The High Courts were in error in holding that the evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt of the accused could properly be drawn. The High Curt was in error, in accepting the evidence of the doctor in support of the correctness of the two dying declarations.

The appellant company was an all India establishment having establishments in different parts of the country. The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Bihar. The appellant was incorporated in Bihar in the year 1948. The appellant 's factory was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. The appellant, a company incorporated in the year 1949, was incorporated in 1950. The appellant had two factories in different parts. The factory was an ally situated in the State. The appellant and its workmen were employed in the factory at Jamshedpur. The appellant claimed that the workmen of the factory at the other establishments were entitled to special leave to attend the meetings of the executive committee of the union. The Tribunal held that the constitution of the said union was duly amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963, the appellant was entitled to special Leave to attend the meeting of the executive Committee of the union, and that as there was no change in the constitution of that union, the appellant could not be said to have been a member of the executive committees of the union and that the appellant was not entitled to special special leave to the workmen of its other establishments. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant had not been given special leave to defend the proceedings and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for special leave. The Tribunal also held that the application for leave was not maintainable. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant company to grant special leave asked for by the union. [554C] The Tribunal, on the considerations aforesaid, was not justified, in obliging it to grant special Leave asked for by it. [554D] The Tribunal was, therefore, not justified in insisting on special leave asked by the union for the purpose of special leave asked in the present case. [554E] The Tribunal on the considerations of the matter, was not right in obliging its decision to grant special special leave asked to the union. It was not justified on the considerations that the appellant company was not entitled, to special leave asked under the Act, to attend the proceedings of the executive council of the union at Jamshedpur and the Tribunal 's extension of that award to workmen in the company 's other establishments was clearly without jurisdiction.

The appellant firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939, before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939, by the Income tax Amendment Act 7 of 1948, and the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax (Amend ment) Act 7 Of 1939, was passed by the Income Tax (Amendment) Ordinance 7 of 1939. The assessee contended that the firm was dissolved by the Income T. A. Act 7 of 1938, and that the assessee was not entitled to the benefit provided in section 25(3) or 25(4). The Income tax Officer rejected the contention and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the firm had been dissolved on March 1, 1939, and that it was not entitled, under section 25 (4) of that Act, to the benefit of section 25(5) of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee had not been carrying on business at the commencement of the Indian Incometax (Amendment)Act 7 of 1939 and that the business of Messrs Hakam Mal Tani Mal, was taken over by the assessee. The High Court, on reference, held that the appellant was carrying on business when Act 7 of 1940 was brought into operation and was on that account entitled to the benefits provided in section 2(4) and 25(4), and that the appellant could not claim the benefit provided by section 25(2) of the Income tax Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The assessee was carrying on the business immediately after the dissolution of the firm of Lala Hakam Mal, and the business at Abdullapur in the name of firm Hakam Mal. The business of Messrs. Hakam Mal was taken over on April 1, 1943, and the firm alone was entitled to the relief under section 2(5) Of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, in relation to the assessment in question. [675 B C] (ii) The assessee 's business was taken over in March 1943, and it could not be said that the assessee 's income was not carrying on business after March 31, 1943. [676 B] (iii) The assessee had not become a partner in the firm of the firm, and the income, profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of such succession, could not be deemed to have been the in come profits. [678 C] (iv) The assessee could not claim that the firm should be carrying on business in the year of dissolution of the partnership. [679 C] (v) The assessee, was constituted to carry on the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1, 1939. The business at Abdulapur in the year 1943 was taken over from April 1. 1939, and the partnership was taken over. The business was taken up by the assessee in March 1943. The business in timber was taken over only on April 1. The assessee was not carrying out any business after March 1, 1943. The assessee could claim the benefit of the provisions of section 25 (3) or section 25 (5) of that Indian Income tax (Second Amendment) Act, 1939. [682 C D] (vi) The assessee continued to carry on timber business till the midnight of March 31, 1938, and immediately thereafter the business of the assessee commenced. The business, therefore, came into being at the precise point of time at which the Indian Income. Tax (Amendment). Act 7 of 1942 came into force and it could never be said that it was carrying on any business after the dissolution. [683 G H] (vii) The assessee did not carry on business at commencement of the Act, and the Income tax Officer was right in holding that the assessee commenced doing business immediately after March 31. 1939.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority Shimoga. The permit was issued on the same day. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order of his permit. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was right in dismissing the writ petition of the appellant on the ground that the Secretary to the Regional Transport authority, Shimoga, had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore State Motor Vehicles Rules 1963. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was not right in dismissing a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [189B] (2) The High Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the order of Regional Transport Authority granting the permit which had already been affirmed in appeal by the State Transport Authority. [189C] (3) The High court was right in holding that no appeal lay under section 64 of the Act to the State Transport Tribunal against the issue of a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Transport Authorities granting the permit. [189D] (4) The High. Court was right. [189E] (5) The High 'Court was right in rejecting the writ petition filed by the appellant.

The appellant was the President of Parliament. He was a sitting member of Parliament. The respondent was a sitting Member of Parliament. On 7 February, 1967, the appellant filed an election petition against the respondent. The appellant alleged that at the meeting of the Republican Party, respondent was a Congress candidate. The appellant denied that he was the President. The respondent alleged that the appellant was the leader of the Congress Party. The appellant also alleged that the respondent was the leader in the Congress Party and that the respondent had been falsely implicated. The appellant further alleged that the Congress election meeting was held at the Town Hall Maidan at Hapur on 7 February,1967. The appellant was alleged to have been guilty of corrupt practice. The respondent denied that he had been falsely involved in the election. The appellant contended that the respondent could not be said to have been falsely implicated in the election petition. The High Court held that no meeting was held in the town Hall Maidyan at Hapur on the date 7 February, 1968 and there was no attack on the office of the Republic of India at Hapur on that date. The High court held that no notice was given to the appellant before the election petition was filed. The High. Court held that the appellant had not been able to prove that the respondent belonged to particular castes and sects. The High 'Court held that the respondent 's evidence was not sufficient to prove that respondent belonged to the particular castes and section sects. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant failed to prove that he belonged to particular caste and sects and section sect.s. 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, was not proved to be published with the consent of the respondent Prakash Vir Shastri. [895C] (2) The appellant was not able to prove the truth of the contents therein. The appellant failed not to prove that respondents were members of the Congress party. The appellant did not prove that respondent was the President or the election agent of the appellant. The appellant had failed to prove the fact that respondent was a member of the Congress. [896E] (3) The appellant did riot show that respondent was not a member of any particular caste. The appellant could not be convicted under section 123(1). [896F] (4) The appellant had not proved that respondent was member of the political party. The evidence on behalf of the respondent was that the respondent belongs to particular castes. The appellant 's case was that the appellant belonged to particular classes. The appellant, therefore, failed to prove his case. [897F] (5) The appellant could have been convicted only if he was a member. The appellant has not been able, to prove that his name was included in the Vir Arjun of 892 the Congress Party on 7 February 1967. The appellant cannot be convicted under the Act. [898F] (6) The appellant has failed to prove by evidence that respondent Prakash Vir was the leader. The appellant fails to prove that Respondent Prakash Vir Shastri was the leader, in the Congress party on 7 February. 1967.

The appellant, a judgment debtor, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property auctioned to him. The application was rejected by the District Judge on the ground that the application was barred by limitation. The District Judge dismissed the application. The High Court, in appeal, reversed the order of the District Judge and held that in view of Article 136 of the Limitation Act, the application for setting aside sale could not be filed within a period of 12 years from the date of the dismissal of the application for set aside the sale. The High court also held that the period of limitation under Article 134 of the Limitation act should be computed from the date when the application for execution was made and all questions relating to the delivery of possession were to be decided by the District Court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the period for setting aside the sale was not the period of Limitation as prescribed by Article 134 of Limitation Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 134 of The Limitation Act, 1963 is applicable to an application under order XXI Rule 95, CPC. The application for setting up a decree is maintainable only after the decree is put into execution within the period of the limitation as prescribed by article 136 of the . [361C] 2. Article 134 will apply to an application for setting it aside on the ground of fraud and not to the date of sale. [361D] 3. Article 134 is applicable to a proceeding under Order XXI, Rule 95 of Civil Procedure Code by the auction purchaser for delivery of the property sold in execution of a decree. It is submitted by the learned Counsel that on the disposal of that application on July 21, 1979, the sale became absolute and the decree holder respondent having filed the application for delivery of Possession on July 17, 1980, that is, within one year from July 21,1979, it should be held that the application for the delivery of posses sion having been made within one year of the dismissal, the application was within the period prescribed by Article 136 of that and that as held by the High Court, Article 134 stands impliedly repealed by section 47 read with Article 136 of The . [361D E] 4. Article 134 does not apply to an applications under Order XXI Rules 95, 90 or 91 of the Code.

The appellant was the owner of a house in which the respondent was residing. He had a shop in the house in which he had a shop. He had also a shop in which he was residing. The respondent was also a tenant of the appellant. The appellant filed a petition under section 116A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for setting aside the election of the appellant to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from the constituency. The appellant contended that the wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appellant and that the said wall poster was affixed prior to the election. The High Court dismissed the petition.
