In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the wall posters were pasted on a portion of the wall at the behest and with the permission of the appellant 's election agent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The contents of the wall poster clearly indicate that the wall was pasted on the wall at his instance and that the appellant had gone to the extent of saying that it was the appellant himself who along with his election agent and other workers had gone to his residence to deliver the copy. The appellant 's case that the wall hoarding was affixed prior prior to the date of election by the workers of the appellant with his knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition, was not established. [776G H] 2. The contents in the wall poster directly named the first respondent as the murderer of the four victims, and if it is proved that the said poster was affixed subsequent to the election by the worker of the appellant, nothing more has to be established to hold the appellant guilty of the corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Act. [775B C] 3. The contents and contents of the walls of the poster clearly indicate the fact that the appellant himself had not seen the wall poster together with exhibit P 1 being pasted on the said wall. [778C] 4. The contents thereof are not material. The contents are not material and the contents are not relevant. [777D] 5. The contents have been proved by the appellant himself. [785E] 6. The appellant has not been able to prove the wall poster either by himself or through his election agent as alleged in his petition. [786F] 7. The appellant had not been able either to prove the walls poster or exhibit P 1 or his election agent.

The respondent No. 5, a public limited company, was granted a licence to develop a hotel. The respondent No. 1, a society registered under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, was granted the licence to develop the hotel. The appellant No. 1 was granted the permission for development of the hotel. Respondent No. 1 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the grant of the permission. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal in this Court. The respondent filed a writ application in the High court challenging the grant. The High court dismissed the writ appeal. The appellant then filed a writ Petition in the High, Court challenging the rejection of the plan submitted by the respondent No. 2. The High, Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not justified in rejecting the application for approval of the plan. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The ground for rejecting the plan submitted to the Municipal Corporation was no longer tenable, regard being had to the fact that the draft revised development plan had since been published and the plan submitted was the plan submitted. The respondent no. 2 directed sanction of the plan out of 44,820.49 sq. yds. belonging to the respondent No 1. The respondent, therefore, directed sanction of a plan out of the residential zone and no proposal to exclude it therefrom in the draft revised plan had been published. [924C D] 2. The ground of rejection of the plans submitted by the Respondent No. 2 was no longer available to the Municipal Commissioner. The respondent had been granted the permission to develop the building on the said land. The respondent was not, in fact, concerned with the question as to the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by the Government to the respondent. [925C D] 3. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park or recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public is a matter of fact, which has to be decided by the High Court. [926C] 4. The question as to whether or not the sufficient quantity of the land has been properly considered and taken into account by the High court is not a question of fact. [927D] 5. The question of legality or otherwise is a matter which is to be decided in the light of the evidence adduced before the High Court and the High Court has to decide the legality or else of the exemption. [928F] 6. The question is whether or not enough quantity of land had been kept reserved. The question that the respondent No 2 directed sanction to the plan out from 44,820,49 sq. yards belonging to the appellant No. 2 has all been considered and taken to be the same. [929G] 7. The question regarding the legality or other wise of the exemption is no longer tenable. The question Whether or not sufficient material has been placed before the High court in the judgment disposing of the review applications. [930H] 8. The question, whether or not adequate quantity of land have been kept reserved is a matter to be decided on the basis of the evidence produced before the High Courts. [931H] 9. The question about the legality or any other wise of exemption granted by Government to the Respondent No 1 has all been examined by the High Courts in the light.

The appellant union, a trade union, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. The workmen were dismissed from service by the appellant union. The workmen filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the dismissal of the workmen. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant union filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High court held that the employers were guilty of unfair labour practice and directed the Industrial Court to appoint the workmen as a result of the closure of the industrial undertaking. The High Courts held that the employer was guilty of unfair Labour practice and directed that the workmen should be continued in service. The appellant Union filed a writ application in the High court challenging the validity of the closure order. The HighCourt dismissed the writ application. The appellant filed a writ Petition in this Court challenging the validity and validity of the order of the High Court. The appellant contended that the industrial undertakings of the employers had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Industrial Court before which the action of the employer is questioned must keep in view the relevant circumstances at the time of closure. [678C] 2. The intention of the employer at the time when it resorts to lock out or claims to have closed down the industrial undertaking is an unfair labour practice. [679D] 3. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer. The duration may be a substantial fact to determine whether the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer.[678E] 4. The duration is the significant fact to decide whether the closure is a device or camouflage to determine the employment of the workmen or whether the closure would be adjudged a device or pretext to determine the services of the workmen.[678F] 5. The duration for which the closure is sought to be closed is normally a substantial fact. The intention is to be gathered from the circumstances of each case. [671G] 6. The duration during which the closure may not be possible is a relevant factor. The duration can be a substantial factor to determine whether a closure is a result of imposing lock out or the owner employer has decided to close down the industrial activity. [672A] 7. The duration cannot be a substantial one to determine whether closure is a consequence of imposing lockout or the owner or employer has decided not to do so on the pain that the closure would not be adjudged a devices or pretence to determine the service of the workmen [678G] 8. The duration has to be necessarily a substantial fact, to determine whether it is a device, pretence or pretence to decide the services of workmen. [673B] 9. The duration will depend on the circumstances of the case. The duration must be a substantial question to determine whether there was a device, device or pretence. [674C] 10. The duration should be a substantial part of the process of the industry. The duration would depend on the facts of each case and the nature of the activity. [684D] 11. The duration, if any, of the closure can be a relevant factor to determine the nature of business. [685E] 12. The duration in the present case may be a material fact to determine that the closure was not a device or device to determine the activities of the workmen, [685F] 13. The duration could be a substantial piece of evidence to determine whether an employer has imposed a lockout or has closed the establishment. [686G] 14. The duration was not decisive of the matter.

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The assessee company was registered on July 29. 1924 as an Investment company. The Income Tax Officer, on a reference made to him under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, assessed the assessee company to income tax for the assessment year 1962 63. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee company was a dealer in shares, securities and properties and held that the company was a 'dealer ' and was not a dealer in investments and properties. The Tribunal held that in the case of the assessee company not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case of an investor was a mixed question of fact and law and that the question of law was misapplied by the Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee was a dealer and not an investor and that the case was not a case of pure fact but was a mixed one of fact and Law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question as to what are the characteristics of the business of dealing in shares or securities of the assessee is a mixed question and the legal effect of the facts found by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal is misapplied by it. [655 D] (2) The question of law as to what were the characteristics of a business of dealing with shares or securities and properties was a mixed questions of fact and legal effect. [656 D] (3) The question whether the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities or immovable properties of the assessee can be taxed as business profits. [657 D] (4) The question involved in this case was not one of pure fact and law. The question involved was not a pure question of law. [658 E] (5) The question was not a mixed question or a mixed question. The question of fact was a mixed issue of fact and the legal consequence of the facts proved by the Appellate Court and the Tribunal was not competent on the questions as framed at present.

The appellant was appointed to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the post of Subordinate Judge in 1935. On April 28, 1954, he was promoted to that post. On April 29, 1954, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954. The High Court held that the order of the High Court was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. The appellant contended that the order was void as the High Court had no jurisdiction to decide the question finally. Held, that the order passed by the High Court on January 28, 1955, was not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311 of Constitution. The order of suspension was not one passed by the Governor of the Province, and the order of dismissal was not one made by the Governor. The order was not one by the Governor, and the Government was bound to hold a fresh enquiry into the charges. The order passed by a High Court on the basis of the report of the High Commissioner was not one under article 311 of that Constitution. The Government was bound by the report of a High Court and the Government had no power to decide the matter finally. The order made by the High court on January 28. 1954, was not a one of dismissal, but of removal from service. The order dated January 28. 1955, was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government, and such an order was neither one of dismissal nor of removal from the service within article 310 of the Constitution, and was not one which was one of dismissal. The order in question was merely one and not one of suspension. The order could not be said to be one of dismissal and therefore, the order of suspended was not one in respect of any other. The order, therefore, was not an order of dismissal or of removal from Service within article 311. The order having been passed by the Government on January 28., 1954, the order was not a single order of dismissal.

The appellant was a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company a private limited company with its registered office in Bombay. The share capital of the company was Rs. 1,00,000. The share price of the share was Rs. 2,00,00, 000. The share value of the share of the company in the share was about Rs. 1.00,000 and the share price was about Rs, 2,00.000. The Income tax Officer, on a reference, held that the dividend was not taxable under section 2(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but the company was liable to pay tax on the dividend so deemed to be distributed. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal, on reference, held against the appellant. The High Court, on reference. held that the company was not liable to pay the tax on the dividends deemed to be received by the deceased person and that the company had not been assessed to income tax on the income of the company. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression "assessee" in section 2(1) of the Act means a person by whom income tax is payable. The expression "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" cannot be deemed to have supplied the machinery for taxation of income received by a legal representative to the estate after the expiry of the year in which such person died. [601 B C] (2) The expression 'assessee ' in section 2 (2) of that Act means a legal representative of a deceased person in respect of whom any proceeding and this Act has been taken for the assessment of his income or of the loss sustained by him or of the amount of refund due to him. The expression 'any tax which the would have been paid by him under the Act if he died, has a limited application. [602 C D] (3) The expression used in section 2 of the Act is "any tax" which would have to be paid if he had died. The expression is not defined in the Act. The expression has been used in the Act to include a person by whose death the estate of a deceased has been acquired. The expression includes a person by which the estate of the deceased has been received. The expression does not mean a person by who dies. The expression means a person who has died. The word 'assessee ' is defined in section 2. The expression in section 2 is used in the sense of a person by himself. The expression, therefore, in section 2, means a person, by whom income or other every person in respect o which any proceeding and the said Act has been take for the assessment or reassessment of his income, or of the losses sustained by him, or of any amount of refund, due to him, or any amount of refunds due to him or any amount or of refund due from him.

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. He was the Ruler in the State of Madhya Pradesh. He was a Ruler of the United State of Vindhya Pradesh. He had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages. He was also a maufidar. He was granted a lease of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of the petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The appellant contended that he was still a Ruler and that the provisions of the Act did not apply to him. The High Court held that the appellant was an ex Ruler and that he was not a maufaidar. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the appellant had given no evidence to establish that the villages in question were not assessed to land revenue. The appellant was an Ex Ruler and was not a person who by or under the provisions contained in the wajib ul arz, was recognised by the President as the Ruler of Vindhya Pradesh and was a Ruler as defined in article 366(22) of the Constitution, and therefore, the appellant was not an ex Ruler. The High court rightly held that the petitioner was an ex- Ruler and that article 366(23) did not make him a Ruler for the purposes of the Act. The High Courts rightly held that in the circumstances of the case it was for the appellant to establish that he was an ex successor to the State or a Ruler of a State. The High. Court rightly held that it was for him to establish that, the villages in dispute were not assessed or assessed to land Revenue.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. The order of transfer was challenged by the respondent in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court quashed the order of transfer on the following reasoning: (i) The transfer order was passed in violation of the statutory rules and the guidelines issued by the Government. (ii) The guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. (iii) The order of the Tribunal was not vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order. (iv) The order was passed by the Senior administrative officer in a former Judge of the High Court and was thus aware of the norms and constraints of the writ jurisdiction. (v) The order dated 3.3.1986 was passed in contravention of the administrative instructions issued by the Central Government. (vi) The order passed by the Tribunal was a non speaking one and was therefore not sustainable. (vii) The order is vitiated by mala fide. The Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order of the transfer. The order is therefore quashed. The appeal is allowed. The order dated 13.7.1991 passed by the High Court is set aside. The writ petition filed by the respondent is allowed. However, the order of promotion is set aside and the respondent is directed to be posted at Shillong. The respondent shall be posted at the same place.

The appellants were charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The Trial Court convicted A1 to A3 under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34 I.P.,C. and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 302 I.P,C. and reduced the sentence of imprisonment to one year. The appellants filed the present appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The conviction and sentence are set aside. The conviction of the appellants is set aside. [1033C] 2. The conviction is set aside and the sentence of the appellant under Section 304 part I read with section 34, I.p.C. is restored. [1034C] 3. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High court while confirming the conviction of A1 to six under Section 304, Part I readwith Section 34, I PC, and instead convict them under Section 325, I. P.C., read with Section34, I.Ps. and sentenced to undergo rigor ous imprisonment for five year. [1035C D] 4. The conviction under Section 304A read with Section 149, I.PC. read with Section 302, I.A.C. and instead convict A1 to 4 under Section 325 readwith Section 149, and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 7,000 each, in default to undergo rigorous Imprisonment for five years, is set aside, and the sentence is reduced to one year rigorous imprisonment.

The appellant Bank was constituted by the Indian Parliament under the Indian Parliament. The appellant Bank was formed by or under and not in pursuance of any `special Indian law '. The appellant bank was formed by and under and not with the aid of the Indian Parliament and the Banking Companies Act, 1949. The appellant was formed by the Indian Legislature and not by the Indian Parliamentary Legislature. The appellant 's name was not included in the list of companies. The appellant had been formed by or on behalf of the Indian Legislature. The Indian Parliament enacted the Indian Parliament Act, and the Indian Parliament was a 'special Indian law" and the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the appellant Bank. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant contended that the words `special Indian Law ' were placed after the words `any special Indian law ' and before the words `in pursuance of ' in section 4(e) of the Act. The appellant also contended that even assuming that the expression `special Indian ' was placed after the word `in pursuance ' in section4(e) the Legislature had not meant that the corporation in question should be formed by a third party in pursuance of the law and not by a law itself in order to come within the purview of section 4(a) of the . The High Court held that the words 'in pursuance of" in section 4 (e) of Act VIII of 1969 meant a law enacted by the Indian legislature and that the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1969 was a special Indian law and the provision of section 4 (a) was applicable to the respondent Bank. The High court held that the word `special Indian" was not placed after the expression `in pursuance to ' in section 2(e) and therefore, the words `by or under ' in section 3(27) of the Indian Act were not placed after 'the words `in pursuant to ' in Section 4(e). The High Court also held that the expression 'in pursuance to a law ' meant a law made by the Indian Legislatures and not by an Indian Legislature. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words `any other law ' refer to a law made in pursuance of or by or under the special Indian law. It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by and Under and not in pursuant to such a law and not in compliance with such a law, it will not come within the ambit of section 4.(e) of The Act.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of sugar, were allotted sugar to the State of Uttar Pradesh. The State of Uttar Prades. by a notification dated July 30, 1958, fixed the price of sugar in Punjab. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the impugned notification was illegal and invalid as it contravened article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the impugned notifications were illegal and invalid. The petitioners contended that the impugned orders were illegal and void as they contravened article 19 (1)(g), inasmuch as they contravened articles 19(1) (g) and (g) of Constitution. Held, that the impugned order was not illegal and invalid because it contravened article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore bad. The impugned notifications were not invalid because they contravened article 14. The impugned notification was not invalid because it was not issued by the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and the impugned notification did not authorise the Central Government to fix the price arbitrarily. The impugned orders were therefore bad. Held, further, that the notification was not illegal as it contravened articles 19 (1) (f) and (k) of the constitution. The impugned order was therefore bad as it contravened the provisions of article 19(6) of the Consti tution. The impugned Government order was therefore, bad. The petitioners were not entitled to the protection of article 19 (6) of Constitution because the impugned notification had been issued by the Government of the State of U.P. under section 3 Of the Act and not by the Central Govt. The impugned Notification was therefore bad in law. The impugned Notifications were therefore bad as they contravened the provisions Of article 19(5) of theConstitution. The impugned notices were therefore bad in the eye of law. The petitioners had not been able to show that the impugned notices were in any way invalid. The impugned notice was therefore bad because it contravened articles 14 and 19(1), (g) or (g) Of the Constitution.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948. Its factory was situated in Calcutta. The factory was situated at Calcutta. The appellant company was in Calcutta. Its factory consisted of four manufacturing units, one of which was a factory of the appellant company. The factory consisted of a factory of which the appellant company was a part. The factory of the company consisted of four factories. The factory consists of four factories, one of whom was a factory in Calcutta, and the other a factory of a factory in Bengal. The factory also consisted of four other factories. The appellant was a factory within the meaning of the Factories Act, 1948, and the factory consisted of five factories. The company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and the appellant was a company within the meaning Of section 2(1) of the Act. The appellant, a company incorporated in Calcutta, was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, and the company was incorporated on April 26, 1950, and the Company was incorporated in Calcutta. On April 26, 1951, the appellant company filed a petition before the Industrial Tribunal under section 19(6) of the , for the issue of a direction to the company to pay the workmen the wages of the workmen at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to the wages of Rs. 2,000 per year. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on the ground that the award was not terminated under section 19 (6) of Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant contended that the award did not terminate the agreement and that the award had not been terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(1) and therefore the reference was bad in law. Held, that the award of the Tribunal was not a nullity and without jurisdiction. The award was not a decree of a civil court and the award was binding between the parties and therefore the award was bad in Law. The award of the tribunal was not a judgment within the meaning ofs.19(6) and therefore it was not binding between the appellant company and the company. The award did not bind the company and the award did no bind the company. It was not a mere order of the Tribunal but was a judgment of the High Court. The award in the present case was not a simple order of the High court. The award made by the Tribunal was binding between parties and the award made by it was binding between them. The award had been made to prevail under the agreement, that is to say, that the appellant was not aware of any substantial increase in the cost of living index. The Tribunal wrongly relied upon the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal, for ascertaining the working class cost of living Index. The Tribunal erred in holding that the working class costs of living index were not payable to the appellant. The Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was a fall in the rate of working class cost. The Tribunal had the power to make a reference under section 19 of the Act to the Tribunal. The Tribunal could not have made a reference under the Act.

The appellant was the Matadhipati of Sri Gavi Mutt. He was appointed under the scheme made no difference to the actual administration of the Mutt. The scheme was framed under the Madras Act 11 of 1927. The appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the scheme having been framed under the provisions of the earlier Act, it must now be deemed to be a scheme which was not in existence before the 26th January, 1950, and that the appellant 's Writ Petition should not be entertained because he had a definite adequate alternative remedy under the latter Act. HELD: (i) The scheme was not a scheme which could be said to be inconsistent with the relevant provisions of the latter Act and was not warranted by the provisions of that Act. [264 G] (ii) The scheme framed under the Act was a scheme settled or modified by a Court under the earlier Act. The intention was not to examine the schemes once again by reference to the relevant provisions. [264 A] (iii) The scheme could not be said to have been framed after the 26th February, 1950, it was open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme on the ground that it contravened the fundamental right under article 19(1)(f). [264 B] (iv) The scheme in the present case was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive Officer could not take over the actual administration, it was wholly unnecessary to examine whether all the provisions of Chapter IV of the Act were necessarily justified by or consistent with the provisions of this latter Act. [265 B] (v) The scheme had been framed under section 63 of the Act and the Executive officer was appointed as soon as the Act came into force. The scheme had not been fully implemented till 1952. The scheme could be deemed to have been settled or modified under the provisions Of the latter Act without examining whether all the sections of the said Act were necessarily valid or not. [265 C] (vi) The scheme did not come with in the purview of and were not warranted by, the provisions of section 103(d) of the Act. [267 D] (vii) The scheme, therefore, was not a valid scheme. [267 E] (viii) The scheme having been prepared and published under the provisions, the Executive Officer appointed as early in 1952, was not competent to take over the possession of the actual administration. [267 G] (ix) The scheme is not a scheme settled by a Court of law. The scheme is a scheme settled and modified by a court under the earlier law. The effect of this decision is to make the scheme in question operative as if they were framed under the latter law. [267 A] (x) The scheme has been framed and the executive officer was appointed. If the executive officer could not take possession of the real administration of the estate, it was partly because the appellant has been obstructed the said implementation. But it is clear that when the scheme was framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law. his property rights had been taken away. [267 B] (xi) The scheme cannot be said to contravene the MatadNESHWAR 's fundamental rights under article 19. [267 C] (xii) The scheme must be deemed to continue to be settled or modified. If the authority is not satisfied with the scheme, the court cannot interfere with the validity of it. [267 F] (xiii) The scheme does not come with the purview of the Act, under which it was purported to have been issued. The scheme has not been fully executed till 1952. [267 H] (xiv) The scheme itself was not complete. The scheme itself is not complete. [267] (xv) The scheme which was framed and published under section 63 was a scheme which had been framed and published.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He continued to serve the school with repeated breaks of 89 days. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India claiming regularisation as Hindi Teacher with effect from July 12, 1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant preferred a writ petition in the High Court claiming regularisation as a Hindi Teacher with retrospective effect from July 13, 1982. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. The High Courts erred in denying such benefit to the appellant. [904C D] 2. The High Curt erred in denying relief to the appellant because his initial appointment was conditioned by stipulation that he will continue until replaced. The High courts erred in denying him the benefit of regularisation. [905D] 3. The HighCourt erred in denying to the benefit of Validation Act to a person who has completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December, 31, 1984. The High. Court erred in denying that benefit to the Appellant on the ground of the Validation act. [906E] 4. The High 'Court erred in allowing the prayer for regularisation. [9905F] 5.

The appellant was a member of a Panchayat Samiti and the Chairman of a Panchayat Samitis and the ground that he was disqualified from being a candidate was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965. The appellant was defeated by respondent No. 1 who was defeated by the respondent No. 2. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the rules on the ground that the rules were ultra vires the Punjab Panchayat Samiti Act, 1965. It was contended that the rules did not violate the fundamental rights of the appellant under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (i) the rules were invalid because they violated the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(6) of the constitution; (ii) the rules did violate the fundamental right guaranteed by article 14 of the Constitution; and (iii) the rules violated the fundamental right of the appellant guaranteed by article 31(1) of the Consti tution. HELD: (i) The rules did not infringe the fundamental right under article 19 (1)(g). The rules did violate article 19(5) of the Act. The rules did infringe the fundamental rights under article 19. [426 B] (ii) The rules violated the right of equality guaranteed by article 16 of the Constitution and the rules violated Article 14. [427 C] (iii) The rules were not invalid because they contravened the fundamental right to equality guaranteed by Article 14. The rules violated article 14. [427 C] (iv) The rules contravened article 14. The rule violated article 14 of Constitution. [428 E] (v) The rules infringed article 14. Article 14 is not violated. The rules infringed Article 14. Article 16 is not violated because the rules violated article 19(2). [428 G] (vi) The rules do not violate article 14. They violate article 14 because the rules infringed article 19(i). The rules violated Article 19(5). [429 G] (vii) The rules violate article 14 of our Constitution. [427 G] (viii) The rules are not invalid because the rules violate article 19. The rules do violate article 14 and are therefore invalid. [429 A] (ix) The rules cannot be struck down on the ground of violation of Article 14. It is not correct to say that the rules violated articles 14 and 16. [430 B] (x) The rules have been violated because the rule violated article 19. Therefore, the rules violated Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. [431 E] (x)(x) The rule violated Article 14 of the constitution because, in the present case, the rules did infringe article 14. Therefore, there was no question of any disqualification arising. [432 G] (xi) The rules failed to establish that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 7 were in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. [433 G] (xii) The rules also violated article 14 because, in any case, such a payment is clearly meant only to cover additional expenditure and out of pocket expenses of the Chairman and, while no evidence has been advanced to show that out of the amount received as daily allowance the Chairman will in fact invariably make a say, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office an office of profit. [434 G] (xiii) The rules, therefore, violated article 14 and the rules are invalid. [427 D] (ix)(a) The rules in question violated article 14, because, the rules failed to prove that the allowances payable under rules 3 and 7 were in addition to the payment of the consolidated monthly allowance under r. 3.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground of sub stantial construction. The appellant contended that the tin shed was not material alteration and that the tin sheds were constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin shed marked with letters CDGH on the Eastern side on the open land adjacent to the accommodation, was not a material alteration. The appellant also contended that the respondent landlord had no right to file suit for eviction of a tenant without obtaining permission of the District Magistrate. The trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate court affirmed the findings of the trial court. The High Court affirmed the findings. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the tin roof was permanent and temporary in nature and the tin shed put by the appellant was not affected at all by the disputed tin shed as it had been constructed by the respondent landlord with the consent and the tin sheds marked with letters D.H.C. on the Eastern Side of the accommodation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material alteration. [975C] 2. The High Courts have to consider whether the constructions have been made with the consent or not. The High courts have to consider the nature, character, character of the constructions and the extent to which they make changes in the front and structure of the accommodation, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out to the tenant. The HighCourt has to consider whether these constructions have been raised with the consent, and if so, whether those constructions are of such a nature and character as to materially alter the accommodation. [976D E] 3. The High Curt has to consider the question whether the constructions are permanent or temporary in nature. The High. Court has to consider all the aspects of the matter and decide whether the constructions materially alter the premises or not. [977E] 4. The High 'Court has to examine the nature, nature, character of constructions, whether they are permanent or Temporary, is a relevant consideration in determining the question of material alteration. If the constructions are temporary in nature, the question of the material alteration would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. [978F] 5.

The appellant company had filed a suit for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 29 7 1975 against the appellant. The respondent firm had filed a written statement on 29 71975. The appellant filed a written objection on 29 7 1976 against the said written statement. The Trial Court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 776. The Trial court held that summons was duly served on a company and it was not served on the appellant company. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the respondent firm. The High court held that since the summons was duly sent to the registered office of the company, unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on the company itself. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the respondent firm had no knowledge of the ex parte decree, even otherwise, before 29 7 1975, the summons will be deemed to have been duly served on it within the meaning of the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Code. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The words "Principal Officer" in clause (b), have got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons. [1032C] 1.2 The meaning of clause (a) has got to be interpreted in the background and context of the provisions in Order 5, Rule 13 C.P.C.

The respondent No. 1, a tenant of the appellant, filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the appellant on the ground that the appellant had committed breach of the peace. The appellant contended that the respondent No. 2, the tenant, had committed breach and that the respondent had committed breach. The Magistrate passed a final order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. The appellant filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a revision before the High court which was dismissed on the ground of limitation. The appellant thereafter filed a revision application before the High Curt which was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant thereupon filed a revision against the High Court 's order. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was absolutely essential for the Magistrate to give a finding that a breach of the said peace existed and that the apprehension of breach of peace was implicit in the final order passed by the Magistrate so it was not necessary that the breach of peace should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there was clear evidence to show that the dispute had ceased to exist. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the final order of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of the law was not necessary at the time when a final order was passed. [941C] Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors. ; , referred to. 2. Under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Magistrate is empowered to take cognizance of an offence and to pass a final order under sub section (1) and thereafter to make an enquiry under sub section(4) and pass a final orders under sub section It is not necessary that at the time of passing the final order the apprehension of the breach of the duty should continue or exist. The enquiry under section 145 is limited to the question to who was in actual possession on the date of the preliminary order irrespective of the rights of the parties. The High Courts in the exercise of their revisional jurisdiction would not go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the Magistrate is based. [942C D] Hari Ram vs Banwari Lal and Ors. ; ; Ramarao vs Shivram & Ors. , ; Ramarao & Ors. V. Shivram & Anr. ; ; Hari Ram & Anr. vs Banwari lal & Ors. [1969] 2 S.C.R. 813; Ramarao vs Ramarao & Anr.

The appellant was a nonresidents of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and was assessed to income tax on the income of the appellant. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information furnished by the appellant, determined the income of his business as a non resident. The appellant filed a petition under section 66(1) of the Act before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, Madras, for the assessment years 1941 42 and 1943 44, and the Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant was not liable as it had not been treated as profits by the assessee and that the decision of the Tribunal was final. The Tribunal held that it was not liable to be taxed under section 14(2)(c) of the Income tax Act. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 66 (1) of that Act, and that the Tribunal was not competent to entertain the applications under section 66. The appellant contended that the decision in Commissioner of Income tax and Excess Profits Pax vs section Sen(2) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 was not binding on the Tribunal, and that it was open to review under section 66, to review under that section, and that, therefore, the decision of that Court was final. Held, that the decision was not a pure question of fact, and was not open to attack on any of the grounds on which such a decision could be challenged in a reference under section 66 of the Act. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (I.L.R. , referred to.

The assessee was a company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. The assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager. The Income Tax Officer determined a sum of Rs. 70,465 as the commission paid to him by the General Manager, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount of Rs. 37,733 paid to the general Manager was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business. The Appellate Tribunal held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of the General Manager and that the commission paid was not really spent wholly or exclusively for the purpose for carrying on business, but was a part of the business of the assessee. The High Court, on reference, held that the assessee was entitled to a deduction of Rs 75,465 paid to theGeneral Manager, the assessee preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High court held that the allowance was not made out or expended wholly or exclusively, for the purpose, of carrying on the assessee 's business. The High, Court, however, held that it was not necessary to determine the remuneration which the assessee was required to pay to the General manager. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in taking the view that the allowance made to the General Manger was not really a laid out or expended for the purpose. [557B] (2) The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or expenditure was not really one of fact, but there was some collateral reason. But considering the practice in similar business concerns, the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner expressed the view that it was reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assessee. [558C D] (3) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the assessee the entire amount of Rs 75465 paid to him was an amount laid out or financed wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business. [559E] (4) The principle is that in the case of a person who worked in the mill at the initial stage and of the Managing Director is entitled to consider the extent of his business, the nature of the duties to be performed and the special aptitude of the employee, future prospects of extension by the business and a host of other related circumstances.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. He was a member of the union of which Bata Shoor was a member. The appellant filed a fresh petition for a writ of certiorari to quash the Tribunal 's order of dismissal on the ground that the Tribunal had wrongly rejected his application for separate representation. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting the appellant 's application for separate representations. The Tribunal committed an error in rejecting his application for a writ. [201 G] (ii) The Tribunal was in error in rejecting a claim for separate representation by a person of his own choice. The Tribunal was not justified in refusing to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 'S '. [201 D] (iii) The Tribunal had committed a serious mistake in rejecting the application of the appellant. The Tribunal had not committed any error in refusing to give him proper relief on the question of representation as well as regarding the award that had been made. [201 E] (iv) The Tribunal acted in error in refusing the appellant ' prayer for representation through representatives of his own option in preference to Fateh Singh. The Tribunal acted without jurisdiction in refusing to issue a writ of mandamus. [201 F] (v) The Tribunal 's decision was not correct. The Tribunal 'had not committed any mistake in rejecting his prayer for separate representation and the Tribunal had acted in error. [201 C] (vi) The Tribunal could not be said to have committed any error of law in refusing to grant separate representation. [201 B] (vii) The Tribunal has not committed any illegality in refusing to consider the appellant ' s prayer for separate representations and the Tribunal has acted in error of law. [201 H] (viii) The Tribunal did not commit any error in rejecting appellant 's prayer for representation. [202 C] (ix) The Tribunal failed to take note of the fact that when an individual workman becomes a party to a dispute under the Industrial Disputes Act he is a party, not independently of the Union which has espoused his cause. [202 D] (x) The Tribunal, in rejecting the claim for separate representations, has not committed a mistake in refusing to direct the appellant 'to be represented by representatives of his personal choice. The appellant 's refusal to be represented by representative of his own volition in preference to the representatives of his father was not justified. [202 E] (xi) The Tribunal erred in refusing to accept the appellant ' 's prayer to be represented through representatives of the appellant '. [202 F] (xii) The Tribunal should have taken note of the facts and circumstances of the case and should have given its decision on the appellant ' application for separate consideration. [202 G] (xiii) The Tribunal ought to have taken note Of the fact that the appellant 'did not have been represented by representatives. The Tribunal should not have taken note that the appellant was actually represented in the proceedings before the Tribunal by an officer of that Union. [202 H] (xiv) The Tribunal is not justified in rejecting the appeal of the appellant for a writ under article 226 of the Constitution. [202 B] (xv) The Tribunal cannot be said to be in error in not giving the appellant 'review of the order of the Tribunal.

The appellants were tenants in a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the respondents. The respondents filed a suit for eviction and recovery of arrears of rent against them. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the surviving appellants could not be ejected from the premises in view of the provisions of O. XLI, r. 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure. HELD : (i) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellants when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated as the Court could have passed a decree in favour of all or any of the respondents or parties. [556 E] (ii) The High court could not have dismissed the appeal of kedar Nath on the ground that the surviving appellant could have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in pursuance of the provisions Of O. XLI r. 33. [556 G] (iii) The High Courts could not have decided the appeal of Kedar Nath on merits. The appeal could not have been taken to be an appeal filed by some of the plaintiffs against the whole decree in pursuance to the provisions of r. 33, and could have been taken in the same manner as the Court had in the suit. [556 A] (iv) The HighCourt could not have disposed of the appeal of a dead person when the appeal was filed by all the plaintiffs. [556 C] (v) The High Curt could not have, therefore, heard the appeal in the absence of any appeal or objection. [556 D] (vi) The High. Court could not, therefore, have heard the appellant in the absence. of appeal or objection, and could not have passed a judgment in his absence. [556 F] (vii) The High 'Court could not, in the circumstances of the case, have heard an appeal of the deceased appellant when the appeal of Katarji was pending.

The appellant landlord sought to break through these defences by alleging that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The Rent Controller held that the lease was determined by forfeiture of the tenancy by forfeiture of a lease. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of the Rent Controller. The High Court, in appeal, held that the notice terminating the tenancy was not in terms of section 111(h) of the TP Act and that the forfeiture of the lease was not in accordance with the principles of justice, equity and good conscience. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the lease having expired by efflux, the lease could not be terminated by forfeiture of tenancy under section 111 (g) of TP Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The statutory law as it now stands, however, is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111(G) does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the lease by giving notice in that behalf. [920C D] 1.1 The statutory law, as it now stand, however, does not contemplate a notice to quit and the lessee is bound to accept the notice. The statutory provision is not based on any principle of justice, Equity and good conscience and would not govern the bases made prior to the coming into force of the TP. [921D] 1.2 The statutory law is that the event of the lessor 's termination of the tenancy in this case is good even without a notice as contemplated by section 111(k) of the Act. [922E] 1.3 The statutory law has been that the happening or the happening of a certain event or happening of a particular event or happening or happening of some event or happening which is not covered by the provisions of the TP ACT. [923F] 1.4 The statutory law does not contemplate any notice to quit. The statutory provisions are not intended to be exhaustive. The statutory rules are not exhaustive. The provisions of the Transfer Act are not exhaustive and the statutory law is not exhaustive. [924G] 1.5 The statutory law which is a statutory recognition of a principle of justice equity and good faith, or the mere institution of legal proceedings for ejectment would be tantamount to an act evidencing the intention of the lessor to avail himself of the forfeiture clause and sufficient to satisfy the justice, equity, and good conscience, and the question was clearly answered in the negative. [925H; 926A] 1.6 The statutory law in this case does not contemplate the notice to quit, but only expose a notice to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the ground that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux of period limited thereby in terms of the principle embodied in section 111 (h) of TP ACT. The statutory rule is that the existence of a written notice is not conclusive of the fact that the landlord has been given a notice of termination of the lease. [926C D] 2.1 The High Court erred in holding that the statutory law as such stands, though it does not deal with the question of notice, but only with the question whether the notice was valid or not. [927D] 1:2 The statutory provision of the TP act is that the notice must be given by the landlord to the tenant. The statutory presumption is that the landlord is not in possession of the property and the tenant is not entitled to the benefit of the Act, but of the Act itself. [928F] 1:3 The statutory provision has been made in the form of a statutory recognition by a principle of fairness and good conscience which is not based upon any principle of equity.

The Governor of Assam, by a notification dated June 10, 1966, issued under section 3(1) of the Assam Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1964, directed that the appellant who was a member of the Assam Service of Engineers in the Assam Service, shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order on the grounds (1) that the Governor had no power to give the appellant any opportunity of showing any cause against the proposed action; (2) that the appellant had been given a fair opportunity of showing causes against the action taken against him; and (3) that the order was not in accordance with the provisions of the Assam Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Act, 1965. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Governor is further satisfied under sub clause (c) of the proviso to clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution that in the interest of the security of the State it is not expedient to give that person such an opportunity. [488 B] (2) The Governor has to arrive at a conclusion that the Governor has to come to a conclusion that it is not reasonably practicable to give that he such an opportunity and that the Governor 's satisfaction under the unamended provision is that in the interests of the security, it is not desirable to give that man such an opportunity, and that the Government servant is not likely to be prejudiced by the proposed action. [488 C] (3) The Governor 's power to give a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the actions proposed to be initiated in regard to the appellant is not confined to the exercise of the power under the unamended provisions. [488 D] (4) The power to give an opportunity to show causes against the proposed actions is not confined only to the exercise by the Governor of the power to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank. The power to dismiss, or remove a public servant is not confined merely to the exercise or the exercise of that power but extends to the exercise and discharge of that power. [488 E] (5) The power of the Governor to dismiss or removal a person or reduce him in status is not confined either to the exercise, or discharge of that function. The power of dismissal or removal is not confined in its ambit to the exercise in the interest or the security of a State. [488 F] (6) The power under the amended provision is not confined by the unamended provision to the exercise which is to be done by the Governor in writing.

The petitioners, who were the members of the Shia community, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board. The High Court held that the notification dated 1st December, 1956 issued under section 4 of the 1936 Rules was of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of the Shias to perform their religious ceremonies and functions over the plots and structures thereon which had been listed as Shia Wakfs under the Notification dated 15th January, 1954. The High court held that the Notification dated 26th January, 1944 issued by the Sunni Boards was of no consequence and that the notification issued under section 6(1) was of no help to the Sunkhan and the Shia Community to perform their educational ceremonies and functions. The High, Court, however, held that the petitioners were not entitled to the customary rights in the customary rights to perform their customary ceremonies and functions as Shia Mutawalli under the 1936 Act. The High. Court, however held that the impugned notification dated 26.2.1944 issued under section 3 of the 1936 and published in the U.P. Gazette dated 15th February, 1954, were of no avail and that the petitioners could not be regarded as having been issued by the Shia sect. The High 'Court, however, allowed the writ petition and quashed the notification dated 7th January, 1955 issued under section 7(1) and published in U.P., Gazette dated 15.1. 1954. The petitioners have come to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the notification was of no legal consequence and that it was issued by the respondent No. 1 in exercise of its statutory powers under section 4(1) read with section 5(2) of the Act and that the impugned notifications were of no consequence. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The notification dated 26 th February, 1944, issued under section 2 of the 1936 Amendment Act, 1954, was of no assistance to the SunMOo 's community to perform their religion, practices, observances, ceremonies and functions minus the recitation and utterance of Tabarra (detailed in the writ petition) over the Plots and structures in question and respondents 5 and 6 and the Sunni community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi are permanently restrained by an injunction from interfering with the exercise of the said rights in any manner by the petitioners or members of Shia community and respondents 1 to 4, particularly the executive magistracy of Varanasi is directed, if action under section 144 Cr. P.C.

The assessee, a registered firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1965 66 corresponding to the previous year ending 31st December, 1961. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim of set off on the ground that the loss was claimed as a notional capital loss. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal, on reference, held that there was no genuine loss and set off of loss on the ground of set off. The High Court, on reference under Section 256(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, held that the claim of the set off was admissible in the computation of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital receipt and that it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim for set off was not admissible. The High court, on reference by the Tribunal, held that it was not a notional capital expenditure and that the assessee was entitled to set off on that basis. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee had filed its return showing the loss and the Income tax Officer had not computed the loss or passed an adverse order, the Income tax officer was not entitled to take advantage of his own failure and reject the assessee ' s claim of setoff. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The benefit conferred under Section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that the claim was admissible in its view '. [1166D] 2. The benefit of section 24 of 1922 is continued to be available to the assessee for more than eight years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed under the Act or as the case may be. The High Courts were not right in holding that it was entitled to take benefit of section24 of 1922 Act. [1167E] 3.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), which was later transferred to the Defence Science Services. He was promoted as Scientist 'E ' in the Defence Engineering Service. He joined the Defence Science service on October 12. 1966. He was transferred to the Directorate of Tech nical Development and Production, (Air) (D.S.A. in the grade of Scientist 'E) and he was posted in that grade for a period of three years. The respondent was posted in a post in the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) in the Defence Department. He was appointed in the Defence science Service on October 12 and was posted according to the exigency of the service. The respondent challenged the order of his reversion on the ground that he was not liable to be retired at the alleged superannuation age of 58 years. The Tribunal held that the respondent was not liable for the retired age of 58. The Tribunal also held that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members of the DRDS was increased, it could not be held that the Respondent who belonged to another unit, viz. DAQAS, was entitled to the said benefit. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the re spondent was not liable. The appellant Union of India filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that the respondent had a right of regular promotion to the post of Scientist 'F ' and that the respondent could not be retired at any time after the superannuation age. The Tribunal further held that the appellant was not liable as he was not entitled to the benefit of the power so exercised in the facts and circumstances of the case. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court.

The appellant was the President of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. He was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the election of the respondent was void under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the procedure adopted by the trial court was wrong in that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the learned Judge had in the exercise of jurisdiction vested in him refused to issue summonses to them when he was asked to do so on August 21, 1968. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The trial court was right in refusing to quash the order of the Judge based on the evidence of these two witnesses. [975 B] (2) The trial Judge was right in allowing the respondent to be called as court witnesses. [ 975 B] The trial Judge examined two witnesses as court witnesses and it is quite clear that but for the evidence of those two witnesses, it would have been very difficult. if not impossible for the Judge to have come to the conclusion he did and found the appellant guilty of corrupt practice. But it cannot be said that there was no evidence on which the Judge could have come to his conclusion. [976 C] (3) The trial judge examined two witnesses and it was quite clear that though the evidence about the distribution of the pamphlet was meagre and not beyond reproach it was not for the High Court to take the view that the order ought to be quashed on the ground of the evidence of the two witnesses. The trial Judge did not come to the finding that the distribution of pamphlet was accepted. The trial judge was right in not considering the evidence of two witnesses. It could not be said that the trial Judge was wrong in refusing to exercise jurisdiction under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution and for ourselves, the High Court was not right in refusing the petition to quash the impugned order. [977 C D] (4) The trial Court was right in rejecting the evidence with regard to the distribution of a pamphlet.

The petitioner company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, its registered office being at Kanpur in the State of Uttar Pradesh, and it is carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of U.P. imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the State Legislature. The High Court held that the Validation Act was not ultra vires. The petitioner contended that the Validation Acts were ultra vires the Legislature and that the Validation Ordinance was not saved by the new Act. Held, that the Validation act was not ultra legislative. The Validation Act was intra vires and the Validation Act could not be held to be ultra vires. Held, further, that the validation Act was not unconstitutional as it was not within the competence of the legislature. The Validation Acts were not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, and as there was no other entry in List II or List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, under which the Validation Act had been passed, the Validation Act must be held to have been intra vires. The Validation Ordinance was intra vires. Held further, that it was not ultra Legislative. The Validation act was ultra vires. It was not ultra legislation. The Validation was not ultra. The Validation acts were not ultra legislative, and the Validation Acts could not be said to be ultra legislative. Held, also, that the Validating Act was not intra vires.

The respondent, a limited company dealing in land, owned land and was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1956 57. The Income tax Officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assessee on the date of the award. The Income Tax Officer treated the amount as liable to tax under section 4(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The IncomeTax Officer treated the said sum as liable for income tax during the previous year ended March 31, 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1957 57. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the amount of compensation received by it related to the land and was, accordingly, a trading receipts of the business of the assessee. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the amount received by the respondent related to the acquiring of land which had been taken over by the Government and was, thus, a trading income of the business. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in the view taken by it and the Tribunal was right. [397B] The High Court is right in the further view taken by the Tribunal. [397C] The High court was right in holding that the compensation was received by the appellant related to the acquired land and was therefore a trading receipt. [397D] The High Courts were right in the conclusion that the compensation paid by the assessee was not a receipt of a revenue nature. [397E] The High courts were right in holding, that the compensation given by the Collector was not a trading receipt but a trading receipt and therefore, a receipt of revenue nature liable to tax. [397F] The High. Court was right. The High Court has rightly held that the payment received by the Revenue related to the purchase of land and was not a payment of revenue nature. The High Courts have rightly held that it was on the final determination of the amount of the compensation that the right to receive payment was an inchoate right until the question is set at rest finally. [397G] The High 'Court was right in its view that the compensation awarded by the Collector is merely an offer or tender of the compensation determined by the Collector to the onwer of the property on the acquisition, the High Court may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation. [397H] The HighCourt was right. It is sufficient to point out that there is a clear distinction between cases such as the present one, where the right to receiving payment is in dispute and it is not a question of merely quantifying the amount to be received, and cases where the right is admitted and the quantification only of the amount payable is left to be determined in accordance with settled or accepted principles.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for a decree for eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement of the premises. The respondents pleaded that the appellants had withdrawn all his defence to the application filed by the appellants and submitted to a decree for ejectment and other reliefs. The appellants contended that the compromise was lawful and was in accordance with the terms of the compromise. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court in second appeal reversed the decree. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the compromise in question was lawful and the decree was valid. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The compromise was lawful. The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for possession because the landlord, in the circumstances, is entitled to have such a decree under the law. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise. the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded, and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith. " The protection of section 12(1) is inherent in a language of Order 21, Rule 3, when it says that the Court shall pass a ' decree on the basis of the compromise, and if necessary, by considering them in the context of the pleadings and other materials in that case that the agreement is lawful, as in any other suit so in an eviction suit the Court is bound to record the compromise and pass a decree. [882 C D] 2. The protection under the tenant is implicit in the language used in Order 23, Rules 3 and 4, and the protection of the tenants is inherent in it. [883 C] 3. The protection given to the tenant is an inherent in the words of Order 23 Rule 3 when the Court is satisfied on consideration of the terms of compromise and, if necessary, on considering them in context of the pleading and other materials. [884 E] 4. The protection is inherent in an language of Order 22, Rule 3 which says that where it is proved that a ground for passing such a decree in according with the requirement of the Statute has been established, the Court shall, on the basis thereof, pass a decree, in accordance therewith, [886 G H] 5.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton and cotton textiles. The company was assessed to income tax on the total income of the company. The Income tax Officer, however, held that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The High Court, in reference, held that in view of the capital loss of Rs. 12,00,000, the company was not entitled to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of capital loss incurred and he therefore cancelled the orders of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the loss suffered by the company in the value of the shares in Elphinstone Mills Ltd. was a capital gain. [864C] (ii) The loss incurred by a company in the course of its business is a capital loss and the directors of a company would have done just what the Directors of the company would have doing. [865C] (iii) The loss in the value is a capital gain and the directors are justified in not declaring dividends in view of its capital loss incurred. [866D] (iv) The loss of the shares is a capital asset. The question is not whether the value of shares may not go up in future but whether the Directors are justified in refusing to declare dividends in view Of the capital loss incurred, and he therefore, cancelled the orders. [867E] (v) The question is whether the value is capital gain or not. If the Directors of a company had reasonable grounds for not declaring dividends, it is not open for the Income tax officer to constitute himself as a super director. [868E] (vi) The question of law is not whether a particular dividend should be declared or not is a matter primarily for the Directors of an company. If the directors of the company had reasonable ground for not declaring any dividend, it is open for the Incometax Officer to constitute himself, as a super Director. [869G] (vii) The statute by the words used while making sure that " losses and smallness of profit" are never lost sight of require all matters relevant to the question of unreasonableness to be considered capital loss, if established is one of them. [861A] (viii) The statute does not say 'having regard only ' to losses previously incurred by the Company and to the smallness of the profits made. their Lordships are of the opinion that the Statute by the words "having regard only" to losses previously suffered by the Company, and to the largeness of the profit made. their Lordship are of the view that the Statute does not say "having regard to losses previously instituted by the company and to the Smallness of the income made.
