The petitioner was a diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. The respondent Corporation issued a resolution on the basis of the resolution passed by the Corporation. The resolution was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the resolution was discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High court held that the petitioner was not entitled to the relief claimed. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have consistently held that the rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to the exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and16 of the Constitution and must be upheld. [717C] 2. The High courts have consistently held in the judgments that the rule of reservation is permissible and does not violate Article 14 and 16. [718C] 3. The rule providing that graduate engineers shall be eligible to such promotion to be exclusion of diploma holder does not violate articles 14 and 16 and must be struck down. [719D] 4. The rule provides that graduates shall not be eligible for promotion to the excluded post of Assistant Engineer. The rule provided that graduates shall have the same qualification as the diploma holder Junior Engineer 's out of the 50% quota for promotion a Assistant Engineer. [720E] 5. The rule provide that graduates shall also be eligible for the promotion to the exclude of diploma holders. The rule also provides that graduates will be eligible for appointment to the exclusion from the exclusion of Diploma holders. [721F] 6. The rule is not violative of Articles 16 and 16 of Constitution. [722F] 7.

The petitioner in the writ petition was appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court of India in the year 1973. He was appointed as an Additional Judge of the High Court of Delhi. He was confirmed in the post of Additional Judge of that Court. On the basis of the recommendation of the Chief Justice of India, the Chief Justice made a recommendation that the appointment of a person as a Judge should be made. The Chief Justice of the High Courts, however, recommended that the appointment should be made without any delay. The Chief Justices of the High courts, however, rejected the recommendation of Chief Justice of Delhi. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the recommendation. The High Court rejected the writ petition. The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the recommendations of the Chief Justices of India before this Court. The petitioner contended that the recommendations of Chief Justice were not binding on the Union of India and that the recommendation of Justice of the Chief justice of the High court was not binding on him. The petitioner also contended that the recommendation was not binding upon the Union of the States. The High court rejected the contention. The petitioner then filed a writ Petition in the High court challenging the constitutional validity. The High Courts rejected the contention of the petitioner. The petitioner thereupon filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The Chief justice of India is the Chief Justice and the Chief Justice is the Chief Minister of the State concerned. The Chief Minister of a State is the Chief Secretary of the State. The Chief Secretary of a State has a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Government. The Chief Judge of the State is the Chairman of the Commission. The Chief Judicial Magistrate is the Chief Judge of a High Court. The Chief Judges of the HighCourt are the Chief Justices and the Chief Justices are the Chief Ministers of the State and the Chief Minister is the Chief Ministers. The Chief Ministers are the Chief Minister and the Chief Ministers are both the Chief Ministers and the Chief Secretary. The Chief Secretaries are the Chief Secretaries of the State, and the Chief Secretaries are both the Ministers. The President of India is a constitutional functionary having a consultative function and the power to appoint a person as Judge has nothing personal either to the Chief Justice or the Chief Minister. The Chief Executive of the High Commission is the Chief Justices. The Chief Election Commissioner is the Chief Election Commissioner. The Chief Electoral Officer is the Chief Electoral Officer. The Chief Commissioner is the Chairman and the Chief Election Commission is the highest judicial authority in the country. The Chief President of India, therefore, is the Chief Executive of a High Commission. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered by a larger bench. [445C D] 2. The Chief Sequeler of the State of Delhi is the Chief Commissioner of the State in the case of the High Judges and the Chief justice is the Chief Sequer of the High. The Chief Commission has quite often both before the Parliament and outside has stated that it has, as matter of policy, not made any appointments to the superior judiciary without the name being cleared by the Chief Justice. The Chief Law Officer is the highest Judicial Officer in the country and the Chief Judicial Officer is the lowest Judicial Officer in that country. The matter was not, therefore. considered by a smaller bench. [441C D] 3. The Chief Information Commissioner, the Chief Secretary and the Chief Electoral officer are both constitutional functionaries having a consultatory role and the powers of appointment resides exclusively and exclusively in Central Government. [441D] 4. The Chief Administrative Officer is the Chairman, the Chief Election Officer, the Chief Electoral Officers and the Chief Executive Officers of the State are merely constitutional functionaries having the consultative role. The Chief Personnel Officer is the chief Secretary of the States concerned. The President is the Chief Information Commissioner.

The respondent was appointed as a Bank official on 20th December, 1978. He was appointed as an Enquiry Officer. He was given a show cause notice on 20th March, 1979. The respondent did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Enquiry Officer. The Enquiry Officer submitted his report on 20th November, 1979. He was informed that the enquiry was not conducted by a competent authority. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the enquiry. The High Court held that the enquiry officer was incompetent and without jurisdiction and, therefore, null and void. The High court held that the Enquiry Officer was incompetent and, therefore null and void, and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The High, Court, however, held that the respondent was estopped from raising such a contention for the first time in a writ petition, more so because he had submitted to the jurisdiction of the Enquiry Officer. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in quashing the impugned order of punishment. [199B] 2. The High Curt was right in quashing a show cause notices. [199C] 3. The High. The appellant, a Municipal Corporation, was carrying on the business of constructing buildings on a plot of land in the area of Delhi. The respondents, who were the owners of the plot of land, were granted a lease of the plot in question for a period of five years. The appellant, who was the owner of the plot, was granted a lease for a period exceeding five years. On the expiry of the lease period, the respondents filed a suit for a declaration that the appellant was entitled to the land in question. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the Commissioner refusing sanction was legal and was justified by the provisions of cl. (2) of section 336 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, and that the order was justified by section 14 of the Development Act. HELD: (i) The order of rejection of the appellant 's application was legal and is justified by the provision of cl. 3 of the Development Control Act. [167 E] (ii) The appellant 's lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of the proposed road, nor are they in any manner specified in the Master Plan. The appellant ' s land is not in any way covered by the Master Plan, and the only thing that is required is to be done by the Municipal Corporation. [167 G] (iii) The appellant was not in any case indicated as being taking up the land for the purpose of the road, nor was it in any manner stated that the land was taken up by the Municipal Commissioner. The appellant was therefore not in any respect indicated as being take up by any particular road. [167 D] (iv) The appellant had a right to use the land as asked for by them. The appellant had to establish that any land or part of a land or building in a zone has been dealt with in a particular manner by the Master plan and that it is proposed to be used in a different manner. [167 F] (v) The appellant has to establish that the proposed building or the use of the site for the building, by the respondents, would contravene the provisions of any other law. [167 H] (vi) The appellant is not entitled to the protection of section 14 of ' the Development Act, 1957. [167 A] (vii) The appellant cannot be permitted to use the site for a road or portion of a road. The appellant has no right to use it as asked for. [167 B] (viii) The appellant could not be permitted to utilise the land for a road, or portion of the road. [168 C] (ix) The appellant should establish that any building or work would be hit by section 14. [168 E] (x) The appellant would have to establish that a land or part thereof is covered by a road, and it is proposed that the proposed road should have, all use of land adjoining that road is prohibited for an indefinite period. [168 G] (xi) The appellant must establish that any road should have been dealt with as a different manner by the master plan and that the appellant is proposed to use the same for a different purpose. [168 D] (xii) The appellant, therefore, was not in a manner indicated as having been taken up by some part of the land of the proposed Road, mentioned in the Master plan. [168 F] (xiii) The appellant did not establish that any other road should have existed. [168 H] (xiv) The appellant having been granted a lease in respect of the plot for a period not exceeding five years, the appellant was not entitled to any protection under section 14 of. the Development Act and the Development Act as amended by the Development Act of 1957.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No. 2 was the Minister in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The appellant No. I was the Minister for Industries and the Minister of State for Industries and was the Minister at the time of the incident. The appellant was the Minister. The appellant. No. 1, the Minister of Industry and the Minister at Bhopal, was the Minister, and the Minister was the Minister when the raid was organised and was the instruments of the offence of taking of the bribe or illegal gratification by the appellant No 1. The appellant, therefore, was the Secretary of Industries and was responsible for the conduct of the raid. The appellant also was the Secretary to the Government of India. The appellant 's case was that the Minister of the Industries and the Government of Madhya Pradesh was the Minister and the Minister, who was the Minister on the one hand and the police authorities and the appellant, who was a Minister on the other, were responsible for the illegal raid. The evidence of the witnesses was that the appellant No, 1 was the Secretary and the Minister who was the Secretary, and the appellant was the Secretary. The appellant had no authority to do so. The appellant did not give any evidence to show that the Minister was responsible for any illegal raid. Held, that the evidence of the two witnesses was not reliable and could not be accepted. The evidence was not corroborated by any evidence. The evidence given by the appellant was not corroborated in material particulars. The evidence in regard to the statement made by the appellant to the Minister was not corroborated. The evidence relating to the statement of the appellant No., 1 to the Minister, was not corroborated and could not therefore be accepted.

The respondent was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971. He was dismissed from service on 20.4.1971. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. The trial court dismissed the suit on 20.1.1982. The respondent preferred an appeal against the decision of the trial court. The Senior Superintendent of Police, Patiala, thereafter dismissed the plaintiff on 20.2.1976. The plaintiff filed a regular second appeal before the High Court against the decision. The High Court dismissed the second appeal in limine. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [825F] 1.2 The question involved in this case should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Court in the manner it has done. [825G] 1.3 The question involved is whether the suit was barred by limitation and whether the order of dismissal was illegal on the ground that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. [825A] 1.4 The High Court erred in dismissing the second appeal. [825B] 1.5 The question involved was whether the suit is barred by limitation. The High court erred in dismissing a second appeal in the manner the High has been done. [826C] 1.6 The question involved herein is a question of law which is in volved in this case and the High Court erred. [825D] 1.7 The question involved relates to the question of limitation. The question involved does not arise in this case. [826E] 1.8 The question involved has been decided by the High court in the manner as it has been done, the case is distinguishable. [826F] 1:9. The question raised in this appeal should not have be ignored on the ground of limitation. [826H; 825A] 1:10. The question of limitation is a question which is in the nature of a question of fact. The High Courts should not interfere with the concurrent findings of the courts below. [826B] 1:11. The question is not one of law. The question involves a question of facts. The High courts should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High Court shall permit the plaintiff to file relevant rebutting evidence. The operation of the decree of the first appellate court shall remain stayed till the final disposal of the second appeal by the High Page 12 of 24 High Court.

The assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The assessee was a registered company carrying on the business of selling tea garden tools. The assessee had a business in tea gardens and requisites and was carrying on business of selling the tea garden tools, requisites and tools. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal by the assessee held that the transaction was not speculative transactions within Explanation 2 to section 2(2) of the Act. The Tribunal held that the assessee was not a speculative transaction within the meaning Of explanation 2 to Section 24(1). The High Court on reference answered the question referred to it in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the transactions in question were speculative transactions and the loss should be treated as business loss. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the transactions entered into by the assessee were mere sales of delivery orders or sales of goods so as to bring them to charge under section 24(l) of the Indian Income Tax Act. [183B] The High Court rightly held that the sales in question were not speculative transactions. [183C] The High Courts of Calcutta and Calcutta have taken the view that the transactions are speculative transactions within section 24(I) of the Incometax Act, 1922 and the assessee 's loss suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the assessee ' s income. [183D] The High. Court was right. The question referred to the High Court was correctly answered by the High Court. [183G] The High court was right in the view it took. [183H] The High, Court was right on the question referred.

The appellant, who was the candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, filed an election petition challenging the election of the respondent. The respondent contested the election. The appellant contended that the nomination paper was not signed by the proposer and that the Returning Officer had no power to reject the nomination paper on the ground of any technical defect which was not of a substantial character. The Election Tribunal rejected the nomination paper. The High Court held that the Returning officer had not properly considered the nomination paper and that the nomination papers were not signed by him. The High court, on appeal, held that the nomination was not signed and the Returning Officer was not competent to reject the same. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the Returning Officers had not properly examined the nomination paper, and that the appellant had not been properly examined. The Returning Officer had not properly counted the nomination paper but had merely made a mistake in the nomination paper which was not signed. The Returning officer had omitted to record the satisfaction of the Returning Officer, and the omission to record the signature was not of the nature of a stamped, or other mechanical error of a signature. The word "sign" in the section means "to sign" and not to "sign" and in the ordinary way; it means to sign. The word 'sign ' is not defined but it is equally clear, when the Act is read as a whole, that "sign" is not defined. The word is not defined in the Act. The word has been used in the Act itself, and it is clear that the word "sign " is not defined, but it is also clear, when, a " signature " is necessary, must be in strict accordance with the requirements of the Act and that where the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by the Rules.

The appellants were working as Chemical Workers in the Company in the year 1972. They were dismissed from service on the ground of misconduct. The Company filed a complaint against the appellants and the Company under section 33(A) of the . The Company filed its reply to the complaint. The Company did not refute the averment made by the appellants in their letter dated September 7, 1972 that the Company 's letter dated September 21, 1972 had reached them only on September 20, 1972. The Company sent separate communications to the appellants and 10 others informing them that their letter dated October 21, 1972 was received by them only on October 2, 1972. On September 20, 1973 the Company sent separate communication to the appellants stating that their letter of September 21,1972 had reached them at only on September 21, 1973. On September 21, the Company sent a separate communication to them stating that their letters dated September 21 and September 21, were not accepted by them. On September 26, 1972 the Company sent another communication to the Company stating that the letter dated September 20,1972 had been received by them on September 20. 1972. On October 2, 1973 the appellants sent a separate communications to them and the Company sent their reply to the Company 'reply on September 21. 1972. The appellants ' reply to the said communication was rejected by the Company on October 2. 1973. On October 3, 1973 the company sent a separate letter to the Company to send its letter dated September 26, 1973 to the Company and stating that its letter dated October 2,1972 had come to be replied by the Company. On October 4, 1973 the appellant sent a separate letters to the Company requesting them to send their letter dated August 20, 1972 to the Company. The Company replied to the said letter on September 21 and stated that the letter of September 7, 1973 had reached them on September 21 in response to the strike notice given by the Company to the Company on September 21/22, 1972. Thereafter the Company sent the letter to the appellants on September 21 to the Company informing them that the letter had reached them even on September 20 and that their letter had reached the Company on that day. On September 22, 1973 the respondent sent a separate notice to the appellants asking them to report for duty on or before September 21,1973. On September 23, 1973 the respondents sent a separate intimation to the Company that their letter was received by the Company and that their letters were received by them at the time of their joining the Company. In the meantime, the Company issued a notice to the Company calling upon it to show cause why the said letter should not be cancelled. The Company thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notice. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary and that the action was manifestly illegal and arbitrary. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the action taken by the Company was illegal and invalid. [629G] 1.1 The High Court was right in taking the view that the action on the part of the Company clearly amounted to a change in the condition of service of the appellants during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour Court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced.

The appellant was the trustee of a public trust. He had agreed to abandon the execution proceeding and to wait for six months for receiving payment of the mortgage dues from the trustees. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the mortgage debt. The suit was decreed and the appellant was directed to pay the mortgage debt within six months. The appellant 's appeal to the District Court was dismissed. The High Court in appeal held that the expression 'sale ' in section 36(a) includes a sale of the property of a public Trust. The High court held that the word 'sale ' includes a sale and that the expression "sale of property of a Public Trust" in section 36 (a) includes sale of the properties of a public trusts. The High. Court, however, held that the words 'sale ' and 'sale ' were not complied with and the Subordinate Judge had no power to set aside the sale held in execution of the decree. The High 'Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression 'sale of property ' in section 2(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, includes a sale in execution of a decree of a civil Court for recovery of a debt due by the trust. [462 E] (2) The expression "sale" in section 2 (a) means a sale of property of public trust in execution of decree of a Civil Court for recovery. The expression "transfer of property of any public trust in executing a decree of civil Court for the recovery of a debts due by the Trust" in the context in which it occurs, is not defined in the Act. [462 F] (3) The expression sale ' in section 24(a) means the sale of the whole or any part of the property. The expression 'transfer of property ' includes a transfer of the whole property. The word 'transfer ' includes a mortgage of the whole. The word "transfer" includes a mortgage. The word transfer includes a mortgage, but does not include a mortgage. [462 G] (4) The expression transfer of property of the public trust in section 24 (a) is not defined either in the Act or in the Act, and the expression 'transfer ' in section 17(1) of the Act includes a mortgage in execution of any decree of a court. [462 C] (5) The expression is not defined by the Act. The expression is defined in the context of the Act. It is not defined. It is defined in section 2 of the Act, as meaning a transfer of property made by a public trust in pursuance of a title to apply to a public trust for recovery of which the sale was ordered. [462 D] (6) The expression in section 24 is not defined as meaning a sale of immovable property of a private trust. The expression in the context is not defined, but is defined in a statute. The expression includes a mortgage and a mortgage. It is only a mortgage of immovable property in execution of an order of a Civil court for the recovery or recovery of a loan. [462 B] (7) The expression includes the sale of property in execution. of a decree. [462 A] (8) The expression has to be construed in the context and in the context. [462 H] (9) The expression does not mean merely a sale of a public or a trust. It is merely a transfer of a property of a trust. The word sale ' is not defined merely because it is a transfer of immovable property. The definition of 'sale ' is not exhaustive. The expression does include a mortgage of property of which the transfer is ordered. [463 D] (10) The expression, 'sale ' means a transfer of an interest in immovable property of the trust. The words 'sale of the property ' in the context are not defined in section 17 (1) of Act.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He was retired on June 4. 1935. The Government of India issued a circular dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which laid down that the retirement under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. The Government issued a circular on July 11, 1956 and February 8. 1956 which laiddown that the retirement of a Government servant in public interest after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service should be effected before he has attained the age of 55 years. The appellant challenged the said circular by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The appellant contended that the Government of India had issued instruc tions dated July 11 1956 and February8, 1956 which lay down that the retiring under Rule 2 (2) of Pension Rules should he effected when such retiring is necessary in Public interest. The High court held that Rule 2(1) of the Pension Rules was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The High Curt held that Rule 2046 having been framed under Article 309 of the Constitution and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover ned by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. Rule 2(3) of the Railway Pension Manual is ultra vires Articles14 and 16 of Constitution of India and as such cannot be statutory. [899B] 2. Rule 2 (1) of Pension Rule is ultra vires Article 14 and 16. The object of Rule 2( 2) of Pension rules may also be to weed out unsuitable employees. [898C] 3. Rule 2 of the Pension Manual is in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) and Article 77(2) respectively. The said para 620 is in the character of executive instructions but is similarly worded as Rule 2(a) of Pension Manual. [897C] 4. Rule 2 is in the form of executive instructions and is generally speaking. The said Rule is consistent with the provisions of Article 77(i) and (k) of the Constitution. [895C] 5. Rule 2. (2) is ultra vires articles 14 and 16 and is void and inoperative and inoperative. [896D] 6. Rule 2, (2) and (3) of Pensionary Rules are ultra vires Articles 19 and 16 of India. [894F] 7. Rule 2 has been framed under article 309 of the constitution and being aqueous rule, the Railway employees are onlygover by the said Rule and para 620 is void and ineffective. [893F] 8.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1944. The chargeable account ing period was 1.4.1943 to 31.3.1944. The assessee was assessed to tax under the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940. The assessee claimed that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable accounting periods from October, 1940 to 31st December, 1944 should be allowed a set off in computing the excess profits for the chargeable accounting period ending 31st March 1944. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The Appellate Tribunal held that the deficiency of profits pertaining to chargeable accounting periods ending 31st December 1944 to 31st of March, 1944 must be set off when computing the excess profit for the chargeable accounts ending 31st of 3rd March, 1943. The High Court, on reference, held that the loss in the chargeable accounting years ending 31st May, 1944 to 31.03.1944 must be set aside. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the revenue that as provided in the Act, the provisions of the Act would apply to every business of which any part of profits was made during the chargeable accountingperiod ending 31st day of March, 1943, and that the provisions of section 7 of the Act should have been allowed a setoff in computing the total profits for the relevant chargeable accounting period. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Income tax Act would apply only to every business carried on by which part of profits is made during the relevant chargeable accounts ending March 31, 1944. [605C] 1.2 The provisions of section 4 of the Act are applicable to every business where part of the profits is made in any charge able accounting period, and the deficiency of profit worked out on that basis in respect of the chargeable accounting year ending 31st. March, 1944, must be set at rest in computing the income of the chargeable accounts during the chargeable account ending 31st 3rd, 1943. [606D] 1.3 The method of computation under section 7 of Act must be on the basis of 'accounting period ' and after that the deficiency is not assessed to excess profits tax under the third proviso to section 5 of the Act. [607E] 1.4 The method of computing the excess of profits for the year ending 31.3, 1944 must, therefore, be on the principle of apportionment of profits to which it had adverted to, the profits earned upon sales effected during the chargeable accounts end 31st March 1943 must be setoff in computation of the excess profits. [608F] 1.5 The method of calculation under section 7 must be on a basis of ' accounting period ', and after that, the deficiency in profit for that period should be computed on that basis and after set off carried forward to be set off during the chargeable Accounting period. [609F] 1:6. The method of computed under section 7 is on the basis that the deficiency has been in the course of the chargeable account. [610G] 1.6. The accounting period was the period from 1st April 1943 to 31. March, 1943 and the deficiency in the profits for that period must be computed on the basis on that basis. [611A] 1.7. The method adopted by the Income Tax officer in computing the loss for the chargeable account of the chargeable business ending 31st August, 1944 must also be set off in computation of income of the assessee. [612B] 1.8. The method for computation under section 4 of Act must, therefore be on the principles of apportionment of the profits for the purpose of computing the total income for the chargeable business. [614C] 1:9.

The petitioner who was a Mechanical Engineering degree holder was one of the Special Leave Petitioners before this Court. The petitioner challenged the judgment and order of the Division Bench of the High Court dismissing his writ petitions. The petitioner contended that the respondents had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after they had been appointed. The petitioner also contended that the procedure for selection was not followed. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the special leave petitions filed by the petitioner, the petitioner contended that he had come high in the Common list prepared by the Public Service Commission and there after in an interview held by it. The High court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the respondents who had qualified in Civil Engineering question paper and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had qualified therein were not entitled to the post. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list prepared by Public Service Commission. [239B] 2. The petitioner would be entitled to a post, if he has exercised his option in terms of this Court 's order and he is high enough in the common List for claiming the post. The petitioner shall be entitled to the posts if he has exercise his option in accordance with the judgment and that he is high sufficient in the common merit list for claiming the posts. [239C] 3.

The respondent No. 1, a partnership firm, filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm. The plaintiff respondent No. 2, who was the partner of the firm, filed an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for appointment of a new partner. The trial court rejected the application on the ground that the suit was governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, and the plaintiff had not discovered any decision to the contrary. The trial Court rejected the application. The High Court, however, allowed the plaintiff 's application. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit is governed for the purposes of court fees and the plaintiff has the absolute right to put on the plaint any value he wishes to and the court has no jurisdiction to examine the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The valuation put by the plaintiff on the plaint is arbitrary and unreasonable. The court is bound to accept that the plaintiff has not discovered any such decision. The case of the plaintiff is governed by section 7 (iv)(f). The plaintiff cannot arbitrarily and deliberately under value the relief. [513C D] 1.2 The valuation put in by the plaintiff is arbitrary and unacceptable. The case is governed by a suit for accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. [514D] 1.3 The valuation put up by the plaintiff appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable and cannot be accepted. [515E] 1.4 The case of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be correctly decided. The case in hand is governed for Court fees by section7(iv)(b) of the court Fees Act and the plaintiff is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. [516F] 1.5 The case of one of the High Court which has taken a different stand must be held not to be correctly disposed of. The case has been decided by the trial court on the ground of some of its rights. The case was governed by section7 (iv)(b). The plaintiff has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under values the relief the court is entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation given by the plaintiff and to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. [517F G] 1.6 The case of any of the High courts which have taken the different view must also be held to have been correctly decided.

The respondent State Government exempted the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who have set up industries in any of the districts of Madhya Pradesh specified in the annexure to this notification and have commenced production after 1st April, 1981 from pay ment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in column(2) of the said Schedule. The respondent State Government issued a notification under section 12 of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, exempting the class of dealer specified in column 1 of the Schedule to the said notification. The respondent challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the notification. The State Government appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect of the industries mentioned in column (2) of that Schedule is based on the words which require that the Director of Industries should grant a certificate (a) that the dealer is entitled to claim the exemption and (b) that he has not opted for the scheme of deferring the payment of tax under that Act for the periods specified in column 2, and that he has failed to opt for the scheme. [608C D] 2. The exemption under column (1), with which we are concerned, is based on words which require the Director of the Industries to grant a certificate. [609D] 3. The word "exclusive" in the notification is not used in the sense of a word or expression. It is used in the context of the notification itself. [610E] 4. The word 'exclusive ' in the notification means that the dealer has to satisfy himself that those condi tions are fulfilled. The word `exclusive ' is used in a sense of the word 'excluded '. The word is used in its widest sense. The word has been used in the widest sense. It is not used as a word of a wider import. It is a word of wider import. The word in its widest connotation is used in wider sense. The expression "exclusively" is used in wide sense. It has a wider connotation. It is an inclusive one. It is intended to include all the elements of a particular kind of business. [611F G] 5. The word used in the notification includes the word "excluded" in the context. The word includes all the elements which are included in the notification. [612G] 6. The word, 'exclusively ' has been used with reference to the word 'in the notification itself and all that the Director has to do is to certify that the applicant is entitled to the exemption. [613H] 7. The wordings of the notification are wide enough to include all kinds of dealers. The word does not carry the State 's case further, for what the Director of industries has to do was to certify that he is entitled to exemption. [613H] 8. The word must be interpreted in the context in which it is used. [614H] 9. The word may be used in the wider sense of the term. The word cannot be used in a restricted sense. The words "in the nature of an altera tion" are used in the narrower sense of the expression.

The petitioners were appointed as Additional District and Sessions Judges in the Delhi Judicial Service in accordance with the provisions of the Delhi Judicial Services (Recruitment) Rules, 1954. The petitioners were appointed to temporary posts in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service in the year 1954. The Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1954, provided for recruitment to the Delhi Higher Service by promotion from amongst members of the Delhi Higher judicial Service. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Delhi High Court 's order dated December 18, 1954, on the ground that the Delhi Judicial service Rules, 1954 were ultra vires the Delhi Judicial services (Recruitment) Act, 1954, and that the Delhi Higher Administrative Service (Recruitment) Regulations, 1954 were violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Delhi High Courts had no power to make rules for recruitment to posts in the service, and that in view of the provisions of Rule 7(a) of the Delhi Subordinate Service Rules, the Delhi Higher Services (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1955 were not applicable to the Delhi Judicial Officers. The High Courts held that the rules were ultra vires and that the rules did not violate Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution and that the Rules did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution, and that there was no violation of Article 16(1) of the Constitution as the Delhi High court had no power under Article 226 to issue the writ of mandamus to the Delhi High courts to make rules in respect of the persons appointed to the service. The High court held that the Rules were ultra vires, and that, in any event, the Delhi HighCourt had no jurisdiction to issue the impugned rules. The HighCourt, however, held that the High Court had no jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue the rules. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Delhi Subordinate Judicial Service Rules were ultravires Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution inasmuch as they were not in any way inconsistent with the provisions contained in Articles 14 and 17 of the Constitution; that the Delhi high Court had no power or jurisdiction to issue a writ of mandamus against the Delhi High Judicial Service to make rules and that the High Courts had jurisdiction to issue such a writ; that the High court had jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition and that the impugned rules were ultraviations of Articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution of India; that the rules framed by the Delhi High Curt were ultra vires Articles 14 and 14 of the constitution; that the Rules framed by the High Court were ultra vires Article 14 of Constitution; that in any event the Delhi High. Court had no authority to issue the Rules; that the impugned Rules were ultra virus the Constitution; and that the appointments made by the Full Court were without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Delhi High Court had jurisdiction to frame rules in respect to the persons appointed by the Full court and the appointments were made on merit cum seniority basis so much so that persons found not fit for promotion were ignored as in the case of Shri C.D. Sharma, and that appointments were made in consultation with the High Court from amongst members, of Delhi Judicial Service as required under Rule 7(b) of the Rules. [395B C] 2. The Delhi Higher Judicial Services (Appointment and Conditions of service) Rules, 1956, were not ultra vires Articles14 and 15 of Constitution. The Delhi Subordinate Judicial Services ( Recruitment) Rules, 1953, were ultra vires. [395C] 3. The Delhi high Court has no jurisdiction to frame the rules in respect the persons appointed in the service. [395D] 4. The Delhi Superior Judicial Service (Recruitment and conditions of Service) Regulations, 1955, were not violative of Articles14 and 16 of Constitution. [395E] 5. The Delhi subordinate Judicial Service (Appointment and conditions of service) Regulations, 1956, are ultra vires Articles 15 and 16 of India. [395G] 6.

The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant company in the status of a Hindu undivided family. The Income tax Officer, on the finding that the business was carried on by an association of persons, held that the business of the company was carried on in the name of a Hindu Undivided Family. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income of the company could not be assessed in the hands of the family of the company. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was liable to be assessed in respect of the income of his family. The High Court, on reference, held that there was no evidence to show that the income from the business was liable to tax in the hands. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the income was liable to income tax. [392 B] (ii) The income of the assessee was assessed to tax as income of an association of individuals. The income from the said association was assessed to income tax as income. The Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had no jurisdiction to direct after setting aside the order of assessment that the income should be assessed in his hands. [392 C] (iii) The income from business was assessed to be income of an Association of persons. The income of a company could not therefore be assessed in its hands. [393 C] (iv) The income earned by the assessee was assessable to tax as the income of an associations of persons. [393 D] (v) The income was assessed to the income of a Hindu association of persons. It was not shown that the income had been assessed in the name or in the name. The income was not assessed in the names of the members of the association. [393 E] (vi) The income in the hands was assessed to sales tax as income from the association of persons and not from the association. The income in question was assessed to taxation as income of the association of individuals and not from its association. [394 E] (vii) The income tax officer was of the view that the income belonged to the association of the persons and not to the association. There was no evidence that the income in the name was assessed in the individual name. The Income Tax officer was of that view. [393 F] (viii) The income could not be taxed in the hands o the family of a Hindu joint family. The income could be assessed in a separate name. [393 G] (ix) The income received by the assessee in the name is assessed to tax. The income earned in the name cannot be assessed in any other name. [395 G] (x) The income is assessed to income of an individual. The income is assessable to tax.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share of the suit property and for partition of the same. The appellant contended that the value of the suit properties should be taken to be the value given by the appellant also for the purposes of court fees under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal reversed the decree and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in directing the appellant to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the memorandum of appeal. The High court was in error when it held that the plaint filed in the present suit did not attract the provisions of section 7(v) (b) of Act. [1037 B] (ii) The High court had no jurisdiction to direct the appellant to make the jurisdictional valuation. The court fee on his memorandum of appeal must be taken to have been paid either under section 7 (iv)(b). The court fee has to be paid either under s 7(iv) or under section 7A of the Act, and the court fee has been paid either by the appellant or his advisers. [1038 C] (iii) The court fee paid by the appellant in respect of the suit for partition for the payment of court fees is not a fee paid under section 7. The court fees has to be collected by the court in computing the court fees payable in respect of a relief sought by the plaintiff for the purpose of court fees. [1039 C] (iv) The court fees on the plaint is not a court fee. The court Fees on the plaint are not a court fees. The court Fee on the plaint has to be computed under section 7 of the Act and it is on this valuation alone that the appellant can be justly called upon to pay court fee. [1040 C] (v) The court Fees paid by the plaintiff in respect of his relief of partition for the amount of court fees are not a fee payable under section 7 A of the Act because the court fee on the plaint was not paid under section 6(iv)(a) or under s 7A of that Act.

The respondent No. 1, a company, sought to impugn the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2. Respondent No. 2, the Executive Engineer, Delhi Fire Service, under Section 14(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, on the ground that the construction of refuge areas in the ratio of one sq. metre per person on each floor was not permissible. The NDMC, however, sought to withdraw the said decision. The respondent No. 2 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the decision of respondent No.2, the Executive Fire Officer, Delhi Fire Services, and the Executive Engineer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the NDMC had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition, that the construction was not in conformity with the Bye law 16.4.8, and that the clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 17.1 was an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the NDMC to satisfy itself that the building plans provided for adequate fire safety measures were adequate and that the location and distribution of the refuge areas in each floor was a better and more reliable fire safety measure. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The approval of the Chief Fire officer envisaged by Byelaw 17.1 is an additional condition, and not a bar on the power to satisfy itself, that the building plan provided for adequate Fire safety measures which in judgment of the NDMC are considered to provide for the safety in a measure better than those envisaged by the Bye laws 16.4, 8.1.8 and 16.4.(1). The construction of the refuge area in each floor is a better and very reliable fire safety measures than those envisaged in the Bye laws. The construction of refuge area is a better, and more reliable Fire safety measures than the envisaged by the bye laws. [608C D] 1.2 The construction of a refuge area is not an additional condition. The construction is not an "external" wall for purposes of the said bye laws. The only way in which, perhaps, the zonal developmental requirements in this behalf and the difficulties and probity inherent in the insistence upon construction of such pedestrian walk way in an isolated particular case could be reconciled is to direct the NDMC, in the event of its success, to keep the requirement of the pedestrian walk course and the podium in abeyance for the present, subject to a written undertaking to be lodged with it by the respondent 1 and 2 to the effect that whenever the policy to implement the Zonal Developmental requirements in this respect is finally decided upon, the respondent 1and 2 would undertake to put up such a pedestrian walkway and Podium. [609C D] 2.1 The construction of small portion of the refuge zones in each floor separately provided that it could be shown to the satisfaction of the NDMC that such a measure would better promote fire safety in the building and, pro vided further, that they are located on external walls "by cantilever projection or in any other manner" abutting a vacant space from which rescue operations are rendered possible. [610E F] 2.2 The clearance from the chief fire officer envisaged by bye law 17.2.1, the wall abutting such vacant space would not be an "ex external" wall for the purposes of the aforesaid bye laws. It is not a bar to the power of NDMC to satisfy themselves that such a measures would better promote the fire safety in a measures better than those contemplated by the Bye Laws 16.4 and 16.5.1. The construction would be at the risk of the respon dent 1 and 2.

The appellant, who was the owner of a motor business, was the owner and the respondent was the owner. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the business and for accounts of the motor business. The appellant contended that the compromise was made after due deliberation and that the compromise had been made after due deliberations and that the parties agreed by way of compromise that account of all the businesses should be taken up to March 31, 1946, and that the suit was barred by res judicata or by Order II, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the compromise did not amount to a compromise and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the principle of res judicata. The High court also held that the suit had been barred by resjudicata or by Order I, rule 2, of the Code. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit was not barred under Order II, Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code. [104 F] (ii) The cause for action in the first suit was the desire and intention of the family to separate from his brothers and to divide the joint family property. The intention of the parties was to separate the joint family properties from the joint family. The intention was to separate from the joint families. The intention to separate from each other was to separate all the properties from the family. [104 G] (iii) The cause was different from the cause of action, in the first case, and the suit was therefore barred under Order I, Rule 2, of Code of Civil procedure. [104 C] (iv) The cause is not the same as the cause of the action in the second suit. The cause of actions in the two cases being the same the suit is barred under Order 1, rule 2. [104 E] (v) The cause Of action in the subsequent suit was the intention of the joint family to separate the family property from the joint Hindu family. The cause was not the same. [104 H] (vi) The cause in the first two suits was the same, and the cause of actions was the same. The cause for the action in both the suits being the one, the suit is not barred under O. II, r. 2 of the C.P.C. [104 D] (vii) The cause, in the second suits, was the same as that of the cause of suit in the first suits. The cause, therefore, in the two appeals being the same. the suit is therefore barred under O I, r. 1, r. 3 of the Code, and the plaintiff is bound by the terms of the compromise decree.

The appellant was carrying on the business of manufacturing salt. The salt works were carried on in the Salt Works and the salt works were constructed in the Salt works. The salt work was carried on in a building. The salt was then taken out of the salt works. The appellant was charged with the offence of working the salt works in the Salt Work. The appellant pleaded that the salt works did not come within the definition of the word " factory " in el. (k) of section 2 of the Act. The trial Court held that the salt work did not come under the definition of " factory " and that the salt Works did not come in the definition of factory " in cl. (k). The High Court, on appeal, held that the Salt Works did come within the meaning of the expression " factory " within the definition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression " factory" in el. 3 of the definition of ' factory ' in el. 4(k) of the Act means " building and its appurtenances". The expression "factory" in els. 4(m) of the definition is not restricted in scope to buildings alone. The expression " premises " in els 4(m), therefore, is not restricted to buildings alone and the salt Works cannot be said to be a factory. [606 D E] (ii) The expression ' premises ' in els.(k) of s. 2 of the , is used in the sense of premises used for the manufacture of salt. The expression 'factory ' in el.(k) is used in a sense of the same thing as a factory. The expression includes a factory. Therefore, the salt works carried on in an Salt Works, that it is just the force of gravity and the solar energy which (1) (2) do the necessary work for the occupier of the Salt Works to convert sea water into salt and that no human agency is employed in such conversion. [607 D E] The definition of the term " factory" is wide enough to include a factory where the process of converting sea water into water is carried on. The expression is used in el. 5(k) to mean " buildings and its appurtenance" and not in el. 6(k). The expression " building and the appurtenance" in el, 5(k), therefore, means " buildings and the appurtains of any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal is carried on". [607 G H] (iii) The expression in el. 7(k) is not restricted by el. (p) to buildings and its accessory. The expression in cl. 7(p) is not confined to buildings and the accessory. The word "factory" is used in cl. 5(p) to mean a factory which is meant building and its adjuncts. The expression does not mean a factory. It is used in relation to buildings and it is used in connection with the word "factory". The expression 'premises ' in el, 4(k), is used in its widest sense to include buildings and its appurtenants. The word 'factory ' is used in cls. 4(p) and 4(k). [607 B C] (iv) The expression includes buildings and its accessories. The expression has to be construed in the context of the definition. The expression must be construed in its popular sense and not in the sense in which it is used. The expression means a building and its accessory and not a part of the building. The expression used in els 5(k). is not restricted or restricted to buildings and their appurtenances. The expression, therefore, is wide enough.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor of Tailoring in the Department of Public Instructions. He was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangere. He joined the new post on November 28, 1949. He joined duty in the Polytechnics at Devangare and he joined the new Post on November 28. The respondent was sent on transfer to Devangere as Instructor in the Poly Technics. He joined service in the Poly Clinic at Devangotte as Instructor in that Department. He was reverted at this distance of time for no fault of his. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the respondent in the Department should be given effect from November 28, 1950 when he initially came on deputation. The High court held that the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in the service of the Department of Technical Education from a particular anterior date or to be given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in the service. The High. Court also held that the case of the respondent did not stand on the same footing as that of Narayanaswamy Chetty because the order of the appellant 's absorption was passed in 1951 and that of the respondent 's absorption in 1964. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was fully justified in granting the relief, and that the case was identical in all respects as that of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the State Government had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department of technical Education from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date on which he was initially sent. [261C] (2) The High court was right in granting the reliefs, and issuing a direction that it did, to the respondent to give effect to the order of his absorption in 1964 and there was a break in the service between the respondent and the appellant. [261D] (3) The High.Court was right in directing the State Government to give effect from November 1, 1949 when he initially resumed duty on deputation to the Polytechnic. [261E] (4) The High Courts were right in holding, that the State Govern ment had evolved a rule "that if the person was deputed in the Department to the Department, of Technical Education, from another department, he stayed on the same other department for the reasonable long time and his absorption in the Department was made to relate to that anterior date or the date onwhich he was initially brought on deputation.

The foreign parent who has taken a child, study report as also the home study study report together, would normally have been the child study Report with them before they select the child for adoption and in case they do not have the child Study Report, the same should be supplied to them by the recognised social or child welfare agency processing the application for guardianship and from the child study. [804F G] 2. The foreign child who has taken the child on adoption will normally have the son study report with them before he select the child. If the biological parents have taken a son in adoption, they will be able, to get warmth and affection of family life as also moral and material stability and security and whether it will serve a useful purpose. [805F G] 3. The foreign father who has taken child in adoption will normally be entitled for the child 'Some care and care of the child and will be able not only to get wrowth and affection but also to get wight and affection of the family life as well as moral and material progress and security and if the biological parent is known, he will get warm th and affection of his family life as and when the adoption is effected so that the child will get wrowst and affection of her family life. [806F G] 4. The foreign mother who has taken care of the minor child will be entitled to get wormth and affection for the child. [807F G] 5. The foreign guardian who has taken charge of the child will also be able to take care of the children available with him for adoption. [808F G] 6. The foreign children who have taken care of their child will be given the child 'sever and the child study ' report of such child to the foreign parent. [809F G] 7.
