The appellant company was a company incorporated in the year of account of the respondent company. The respondent company was a registered company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The company was incorporated in the State of West Bengal. The respondent was a company registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The company claimed deduction of the amount of bonus paid by it to its workmen on the basis that their salary is only Rs. 1,46,252. The company contended that the computation of the available surplus by the company has not been properly made in accordance with the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure have to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits. The Tribunal held that the computation was erroneous and that the allocable surplus was not an item which could be deducted from the gross profits under the Act as claimed by the management. The Tribunal also held that the alloca tion of bonus was not an items which could be excluded from the gross profit under the Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the claim of the company was not an Item which could be deductible from the gross income under the Act, as claimed by it. The Tribunal further held that the deduction of the bonus was not justified. The appellant company appealed to this Court. HELD : The Tribunal was right in rejecting the claim of deduction of the available and allocable surplus. The Tribunal did not accept the contention of the Unions on the ground that the amount of Rs. 65,764 had not been accepted by the Income tax Officer. [655C D] The Tribunal was justified in rejecting the claims of the Unions. The Tribunal was not justified in disallowing the claim of any of the parties on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act.

The appellant was appointed as a Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes in 1954. He was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of the Commercial Taxes in 1957. He was also promoted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in 1969. The appellant was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954. The appellant challenged the order of promotion before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of the appellant which was prior to his promotion, 80 and that the Government had not taken into consideration the whole history of the Government order. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government was entitled, in the facts and circumstances of the case, to take into account the entire history and the fact that the appellant had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion, one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But, with nothing of the sort, it is indeed odd to retire a Government servant a few months after promoting him to a Selection post. [78G H; 79A] 2. The Government is entitled to take the view that the entire history was that the time has arrived for the government servant to quit government service.

The appellants were the owners of a transport vehicle. The appellants were the drivers of the vehicles. The Regional Transport Authority, Andhra Pradesh, issued a notification under section 68 D of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, directing the appellants to ply the vehicles on the routes specified in the notification. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the scheme was not in conformity with the requirements of section 68 C. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the scheme framed by the Corporation was not in accordance with the requirements laid down in section 68 C and that the scheme had been framed in contravention of the requirements of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. HELD: (i) The scheme framed by it was not in consonance with the requirements under section 68 C of the Act. The scheme was not vitiated by non compliance with the requirements. The scheme framed was not in compliance with the requirement of section 68C. The scheme did not contravene the requirements of sections 68 C and 68 C. [368 E F] (ii) The scheme was vitiated by non complying with the requirements in section 68C and the Rules framed thereunder. The scheme could not be challenged as not warranted by law. [368 G] (iii) The scheme did contain a provision that the scheme shall be deemed to have been made by the Corporation. The scheme had to be deemed to be a scheme under section 68C of the Act, and the rules made thereunder were to have effect notwithstanding anything in Ch. No doubt, in a State where there is no Regional Transport Authority at all, the Regional Transport Authority might be that which would be comprehended by section 68F(1) but where as in Andhra Pradesh there is admit tedly a Regional Transport Authority of that area cannot grant permits under Ch. No. 3 of the Act to the appellants, the scheme framed and approved were fully in conformity with section 68 C, and the Rules were made thereunder. [368 A B] (iv) The scheme is vitiated by non comply with the requirements ofs 68C and is therefore void. [368 C] (v) The scheme in question was not vitiated because the Regional Transport Authorities of that area could not grant permits under the Ch. IV of the Act so long as the choice of the "area" in which and the routes in it to be run by the Corporation is made by them alone. [368 D] (vi) The scheme has to be deemed as a whole and the scheme framed thereunder is to have effect unless it is otherwise provided by the Act. [368 F] (vii) The scheme under section 63 C is not in conformity to the requirements of s 68C and therefore the Rules made under section 68D are not in conformity therewith. [368 H] (viii) The scheme cannot be challenged as violative of section 68F. [368 B] (ix) The scheme does not contravene section 68F of the Act because the scheme framed is not in consonance therewith.

The appellant was a public limited company registered under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, and was assessed to sales tax under the Bengal Act. The appellant filed a return of his turnover for the assessment year 1942 52. The assessing authority made an order of assessment disallowing the assessee 's claim for exemption under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Bengal Finance Act, 1941. The appellant applied to the Commercial Tax Officer under section 21A of the Act for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order to prove that they had issued the declaration forms to it. The Commercial Tax Officer made an order on November 21, 1957, rejecting the appellant 's claim. The appellant then applied to the Tribunal for summoning the dealer to produce the requisite documents. The Tribunal held that the appellant had failed to produce the original forms and the appellant was not entitled to the exemption under section 6(2)(b)(ii) Of the Act. The Tribunal also held that the exemption was not available to the appellant under section 5 (2)(a) (ii) of Act. The High Court, on reference, held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant was entitled to exemption under section 4(2)(c) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not precluded in a case where the proviso cannot be strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the purposes mentioned therein. [630 B] (ii) The proviso to section 5(1) of the West Bengal Finance ( Sales Tax) Act is not inconsistent with section 5( 2)(a)(iii) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947. The proviso to that section is not inconsistent therewith. The proviso is inconsistent with section 6(1) and therefore it would be enough and if it was substantially compiled with. [631 C] (iii) The proviso is not inconsistent. The proviso does not furnish any help for construing it. The proviso cannot be read in isolation. The proviso can be read in the light of the object of the Act and the rules made thereunder. [632 D] (iv) The proviso cannot therefore be read in a manner inconsistent with section 4(1) (a) of the Bihar Finance (Sales tax) Act, 1942. [633 G] (v) The proviso does no more than make all the difference, for if the declaration form is furnished, well and good, but if not furnished, other evidence can be produced. [634 G] (vi) The proviso makes all the difference. for it is the proviso that imposes the condition. The proviso makes it subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section. That proviso is not consistent with section 5 (1) (b) of the Indian Act. [635 D] (vii) The proviso must be read in its entirety and not in isolation.

The petitioners were convicted by the Sessions Judge of Patna in respect of offences under sections 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The petitioners contended that they were not released on bail and that the under trial prisoners who were directed to be released by the Magistrates were not regularly produced before the Magistrates in compliance with the proviso to section 167(2) of the Code. The High Court rejected the contention and dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the provisions of the proviso to Section 167(2), Cr. P.C. were not complied with. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to section167(2) Cr. P C. is not a substantive provision and it is not a procedural provision. It is a substantive provision. It does not create substantive rights. It is not a mandatory provision. It merely provides for the procedure to be followed by the Magistrates in the discharge of their judicial functions. [538C D] 2. The proviso is a substantive one and is not a mere procedural provision. The proviso does not create a substantive right. It is only a procedural provision which is substantive in nature. It is merely procedural provision. [539D] 3. The proviso cannot be construed as a substantive provision, and it is the constitutional obligation of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trial to the accused. [535E] 4. The proviso can be construed as substantive provision and not substantive provision. The substantive provision is not substantive provision and is not substantive. It is substantive provision. [546F] 5. The proviso must be read as a substantive clause and not substantive clause. It is the constitutional mandate of the State that the procedure to which the accused are charged should be done by the State. [546G] 6. The proviso has to be read as substantive provision. If the proviso is read as a whole, it is the Constitutional obligation of the state to device such an a procedure as will ensure speedy trial. [546H; 548A] 7. The proviso, however, does not create any substantive right. The proviso merely provides for a procedure to be adopted by the Magistrates for the purpose of making an application for bail and opposing remand provided that no objection is raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for bail is made, the Magistrates should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad outlines set out by the Court in its judgment dated 12th February, 1979. [534A B] 8. The proviso makes it clear that the State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by State. [536C] 9. The proviso requires the State to provide a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose for making an application to the Magistrate in that behalf. The State is under an obligation to device such as to speedy trial to be undertaken by the State and the State is to furnish broadly the reasons why there has been such delay in the investigative process.

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951, under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, and the respondent filed an application under section 29(2) of the Act for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar rejected the application on the ground that the notice was not given within the time prescribed by the Act. The respondent filed an appeal to the High Court and contended that the notice having been given before the Amending Act came into force, the amendment did not affect the rights of the landlord by subs. (2 A) of section 34(2 A) and that the amendment did affect the rights and the rights of landlord by subs.(2 A) on the ground of non compliance with the provisions of the Amending Act. The High Court allowed the application and held that the amendment was not retrospective in operation and that the notice had been given before that amendment. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the amendment made by the Amending Act was retrospective in operation. The amendment did not effect the rights of a landlord by subss. (2A) and (2 A). The amendment did affect rights of the tenant by subs. 2 A. The amendment was not prospective in operation. Section 34(2A) of the Amending act was not retrospective. The amendment made by sub section (2 A), was merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention to terminate the tenancy and no further proceedings could be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof. The amendment in the present case did not affect notices already given before the amendment in the case. The period of notice was the same before and after the amendment in that case and what was the date of the termination of the tenancy was the date on which the right to terminate matures, that is, the date onwhich the right to terminating matures, was extinguished. The period was the same when the tenancy was terminated and the tenancy had terminated that the landlord acquired a vested right to obtain possession of the lands. The period for which notice was given before the Amendment Act came into operation. The period during which the notice was given was the date when the tenancy actually terminated. The period is the same before the amendment. The period cannot be extended beyond the date of notice. The period prescribed by the Amending Acts is not the date of termination of the lease. The period has to be computed from the date of expiry of the lease and not from the date on the date on when the right to termination arises. The period between the date of a notice and the date of its termination cannot be extended to periods subsequent to the notice. The notice under section 34 (1) is merely a declaration that the tenant of a landlord 's intention to terminate his tenancy is extinguished. The notice is merely a declarations to the tenant that the landlord 's desire to terminate the lease is extinguished.

The petitioners, who were the sons of Khadim Ali, filed a suit against the Custodian of Evacuee Property for the recovery of their properties. The Custodian took possession of them. The petitioners filed a suit for the recovery. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The petitioners then filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution for the enforcement of the fundamental right to hold property guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The petition was dismissed by the High Court. The petitioners contended that the property in dispute was evacuee property and that the property was evacuee property. The High Court held that the property could not be declared evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the Act. The petitioners also contended that the male petitioners were not evacuees and the houses were evacuee property. Held, that the property which was evacuee property was evacuee properties and not evacuee property. It was not a evacuee property. A person who was not a patty to the evacuee property could not have any claim to the property. The property in dispute could not be said to be evacuee property unless the person had first become a evacuee. The property was evacuee Property. The petitioners were not entitled to the property in question. The property could not therefore be declared evacuee Property. It was only the property which could be declared evacuee properties. The petitioners could not claim the property in the property as evacuee property. In the present case, the property was not evacuee property and therefore the petitioners could not have been declared evacuee property.

The assessee company was carrying on the business of manufacturing yarn from raw and waste wool and yarn. The assessee company had two departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw cotton and (2) for spinning and weaving of yarn from imported wool tops. The assessee had two departments, namely, (1) the two departments (2) the two department (3) the two departmental authorities, and (4) the assessee company. The assessee was a manufacturer of yarn from the raw and waste silk yarn. The two departments were carrying on the same business. The assessee claimed deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by the assessee company from its remuneration. The Tribunal held that the two departments were not liable to pay the tax under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922, as it was not incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits. The Tribunal also held that the assessee company was not liable to tax under section 2(xv) of Income tax Act. The High Court in reference held that the agreement dated October 20, 1955 amounted to a joint venture for the distribution of profit, between the assessee company and the selling agents after the profits were ascertained. The High court also held that there was a very thin line of distinction between a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits divisible. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have erred in holding that the two firms were not liable for the business or the assessee company as the two amounts mentioned above being in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents, the contracts were really a partnership and had been given the cloak and colour of an agency to conceal the real intent and purpose the commercial venture. [191 B C] 2. The High courts have erred in not considering the effect of the interpretation of the various clauses of the agreement dated November 20, 1955 by which the agents agreed to share losses which were to be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agents. The High. Courts have erred on the view that the two amounts were not legally deductible under section 10 (2)(xv). [191 C D] 3. The High 'Court has erred in not dealing with the effect of an agreement dated October 21, 1955 by holding that the agreement amounted to a Joint venture. [192 E] 4. The HighCourt has erred on the facts found by the Tribunal. [192 F] 5. The High Curt has erred in holding the two firms to be liable for the income tax under section 3(2)(xvi) of the Act. [192 G] 6. The High, Court has erred in ignoring the effect of a single contract between the assessee and the selling agent. [192 A] 7.

The assessee company was carrying on business in cotton yarn. The assessee company was assessed to income tax on the total income of the previous year. The Income Tax Officer, on a reference made under section 254(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, assessed the company to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on reference, held that the accumulated profits were not included in the accumulated profits as on March 31, 1958. The Appellate Tribunal, on reference under section 254, held that Rs. 18,950 was not included in its accumulated profits as the assessee was not entitled to specify the questions of law which he wanted to be referred. The High Court, on reference by the Tribunal, held that a sum of Rs. 18.950 was included in the balance of Rs. 16,950 as on March 1, 1958. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the two sums of Rs. 6,900 were not included within the accumulated profits of the company. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act is not used in the sense of "accumulation" but is used in the context of the expression "accusulated profits" and not in the context in which it is used. [950 B] (2) The expression 'accumulated profit ' in section 2 (6A)(a) of the Act means profits which have accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting year in which the income was earned. [951 C D] (3) The expression used in section 2 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, is "accumulating profits" and it is not used for the purpose of the Act. [952 E] (4) The expression is used in a sense of "actually carrying out" and not "accumulate profits". [954 E] (5) The expression in section 2 is used in connection with the assessment of the income of the company and not in relation to the assessment of income of the assessee. [954 F] (6) The expression has to be construed in the context and not in a sense in which it has been used. [951 F] (7) The expression must be construed in a sense which is in the context. [951 G] (8) The expression includes a case where the assessee has not been able to produce the books of account or other documents or to produce the same. [951 A] (9) The expression does not mean "accumulative" but is intended to mean "accusive".

The plaintiffs claimed to be the owners of certain lands in the district of Burdwan. The defendants claimed that they were in possession of the lands for a long time without payment of rent. The defendants contended that the lands were not Mal lands comprised within the zamindari of Burdwan but had been granted as Lakheraj to their predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement. The trial court held that the lands in dispute were Mal lands within the zamindari and that the plaintiffs were entitled to fair rent. The High Court in appeal held that the plaintiffs had not proved that they had acquired title to them and that the entry in the record of rights in 1931 was correct. Held, that the plaintiffs could not be said to have acquired title by adverse possession. The defendants had not proved their title to the lands. The plaintiffs had not produced any evidence to show that they had been in possession of any land for a long period of time without payment or payment of rent, that they had not been in possession for a long long time without paying rent. The entries in the record were not proved to relate to the suit lands. The defendants were not trespassers. The defendants could not be held to have acquired any title to them. The entries were not proved by them to be adverse to the defendants. The defendants did not produce any evidence to prove that they had title to them, and the entries were not supported by any evidence. The entries relied on by the defendants were not proved. The defendants proved their title by adverse title. The defendants failed to prove that the lands belonged to the plaintiffs. The defendants also failed to prove the title of the defendants.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for specific performance of a contract of sale of agricultural land in the name of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for specific performance. The appellant contended that the suit was not maintainable because the respondent was an agriculturist and, therefore, ineligible to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Tenancy Act. The trial Court decreed the suit. The first appellate court reversed the decree and the High Court held that the suit being an incidental issue in a suit for Specific performance of contract, which suit the Civil Court had jurisdiction to try it, the question of jurisdiction would not arise in a suit of specific performance of contract for sale of agricultural lands governed by the provisions of the Tenancy and Act. The High Court also held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Tenancy Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the competent authority under the Tenancy and, therefore the jurisdiction of Civil Court was ousted. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the jurisdiction under section 85A of the Tenancy act was ousted because the issue was not required to be decided or dealt by the competent authorities under the Tenancy act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression "any issues which are required to be settle, decide, dealt with by any authority competent to settle, decided or deal with such issues under this Act" in section 85A would only mean that if upon assertion and denial and consequent contest an issue arises in the context of the provisions of Tenancy Act and which is required to be determined, decided or dealing with by a competent authority under that Act, the jurisdiction of civil court to settle, deciding or deal with the same is not only ousted but the civil court is under a statutory obligation to refer such issue to the competent authority. [595 F G] 2. The expression 'any issues which have been required to besettled, decided or disposed of by a competent Authority under the Tenancy ACT, is ousted. The jurisdiction of the civil court to decide or deal With any question which arises under the Tenancy law is ousted. [595 G] 3. The expression `any issues which were required to be settling, decided or deals with such issues ' in section 85 A would only mean those issues which are needed to be settled decided or dealt wit hin by competent authority under section 7. [595 A] 4. The expression, 'any issues ' in the Tenancy Act is not a statutory obligation. The jurisdiction is conferred upon the civil court by the Tenancy Act to settle, adjudicate or deal with all the issues which are to be settled. [595 C] 5. The expression is not a 'statutory obligation '. The expression has to be construed in the context in which it is used. [595 D] 6. The expression in section 85(A) of the Tenancy Ac t. is not a term of art. It is a term of wide import. It is not a word of art. The expression includes not only the rights of the parties but also the rights of parties. [595 E] 7. The expression does not include the rights of a party. The expression means the rights of all persons who are in possession of the land and who are in actual possession of the same. The expression must be construed in its ordinary sense. The expression would include all rights of the persons in possession of land and all rights of all the persons in possess ing the land. [595 B] 8. The expression used in section 85 is not a mere expression of wide import and is not a part of the definition of the word. The expression merely means the right of the parties to the land and not the right of a party to the land. The expression cannot be construed in a narrow sense. The word 'any issue ' in section 84 is not a legal concept.

The two undertakings of the assessee company were taken over by the assessee company in the year 1958 59 (calendar year 1957) and 1959 60 (calendar years 1957). The two undertakings were taken over in the year 1959 60 (extract from the Indian Income tax Act, 1922) and the two undertakings were amalgamated with the assessee company. The two undertakings of both the undertakings were taken into consideration for the purpose of the assessment year 1958 59. The two companies were amalgamated with each other. The two undertaking were taken over on the same date. The two units were amalgamated with another company. The assessee company was formed by the reconstruction of the business already in existence. The two new undertakings were amalgamated by the assessee with the assessee Company. The two two undertakings were transferred to the assessee company on the same day. The two Undertakings were amalgamated with one another. The two Companies were amalgamated with two new undertakings. The two were amalgamated with a new undertaking. The two Company was amalgamated with the new undertaking with the new undertakings. On the question whether the two undertakings formed out of the reconstruction of business already in force, the High Court held that the two undertakings as formed by reconstruction of the assessee 's business already in the existence differ from the existing business already in existing and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 15C(2) of the Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the two undertaking were not formed by the revival of the business earlier in existence, and that the two new undertakings are independent and distinct and not reconstruction out of the existing business. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The two different undertakings are independent of each other. [776B] 2. The two separate undertakings are independent. The two are independent and not reconstruction. The two cannot be said to be independent of each one. [775C] 3. The two newly formed undertakings are independent units and the two new undertaking are independently producing arti cles which may be of aid to the principal business but yet the undertakings are distinct and not revival of the existing company. [778C] 4. The two old undertakings are independent, and the undertakings are separate and distinct. [777E] 5. The two existing undertakings are independent undertakings. The fact that the assessee is carrying on the general business of heavy engineering will not prevent him from setting up new industrial undertakings and from claiming benefit under section 15 C(2) merely because it goes to expand the general business. Use of the articles by the assessee is not decisive to deny the benefit of section 15C merely because it go to expand the General business of the assessee on some directions. The two earlier undertakings are independent in character. [785F G] 6. The two assets are independent and cannot be separated from the existing one. [765G] 7. The two independent undertakings are independent from each other. They are distinct and separate. [765H] 7. There is no bar to an assessee carrying on a particular business to set up a new industrial undertaking on account of which exemption of tax under section 15A may be claimed. [765A] 8. The two Schemes are independent and separate. The two schemes are independent and the undertakings of both are distinct and cannot be amalgamated. [765C] 9. The two conditions are independent and are not reconstruction out.

The inamdar was granted a permanent lease of the inam lands in favour of the temple for the performance of services connected therewith. The inamdar was in possession of the lands and was in possession thereof. The inamdars were granted a permanent leases of the lands in favour. The inam lands were resumed under section 44 B(2)(a)(i) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908. The inam was resumed to the Court of the District Judge and registered as O.S. No. 8 of 1954. The appellants contended that the inam lands were not inam lands and were not inam properties. The District Judge held that the inam was not inam lands but was a grant made before 1934 and that the inamdars were not entitled to resume the inam lands. The High Court held that the inams were personal inams burdened with services connected therewith and were resumable under section 44B(2)(b)(i) and (5) the right of resumption of the inam properties was extinguished by adverse possession of the inamdars. The High court held that the lands were personal inams and were resilable under section 43 B(2) (a)(i). The High Court also held that the plaintiffs and their predecessors in title were in enjoyment of the lands under the lease. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The inam lands in the present case were resumables under section 44 C(2)(d)(i) but the inamdars had been granted a permanent tenancy and the inams were resumments. The inam properties in the present cases were resumability under section 44 A(2)(c) of the Act. [557 D] (ii) The inamdar had been granted the permanent lease and the inams had been resumable. The inam land was resumable in the hands of the inamdar. The inam estate was resumed under section 43B(2) and the inamdars continued to be lessees of the inam. The inam estates were resumble under section 44(2)(e) and the inams in the present appeals were resum able under section 44. [558 E] (iii) The inamdars had not been granted a temporary lease and the inam lands had been resilable. The grant was not a permanent lease. The inam rights were resumated under section 44 D(2)(i) because the inamdars could not be said to be in possession of any land in a village. [559 F] (iv) The inam properties were resumited under section 44 E(2)(1) and the lands were resumible under section 44 F(2)(2)(a) (i). The inam lands had not been resumated. The inam Lands in the present suits were resumced under section 44 G(2)(A)(i). [557 G] (v) The inam estates in the present suit were resumig to the inamdars and the plaintiffs claiming as lessees under them. The inam grants were resumed under section 44 H(2)(ii) and the Inam lands were resilted under section 44F(2)(4)(i). On a resumption of the inams, the title, if any, of all persons claiming through the inamdars to any subordinate interest in the inam lands stood determined. [560 G H] (vi) The inam estate in the present ease was resumigled under section 44E(2)(3) and the Inams were resumitation under section 44A(2)(5). [560 A] (vii) The inam land in the present proceedings was resumated in the present litigation. The inam villages were resumations of the melwaram rights in the inam properties. [566 B] (viii) The inam rights in the present lands were resuscitated under section 44C(2)(C) of the Tamil Nadu Estates Land Act.

The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The Municipal tax was assessed on the basis of gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of the costs of repairs or any other account whatsoever. The appellant Corporation was governed by section 79(1) of the Act. The Municipal Tax was levied on the basis that the gross annual letting values were not included in the gross annual rent. The appellant challenged the levy on the ground that the tax could be assessed on the gross annual tenancy value less 10%. The High Court held that the tax was not liable to be assessed on gross annual lettingvalue less 10% of statutory allowance in the case of other municipalities. The High Court, however, held that the Municipal Tax could be assessed only on the gross return of the annual letting value and not on the gross income of the municipality. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Municipal Tax is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the basis thereof is prepared for the year 1952 53 and that the Municipality has been levying tax at the said rate on the basis the said assessment list for the two subsequent years. [131 E] (ii) The tax levied under the old Act and the rules framed thereunder on the basis for the two years in question is, therefore, inconsistent with the provisions of section 73 of the Act and is saved and is not saved by section 2(c) and therefore the levy of tax at the rate of 7% of the gross annual rental value is saved and therefore, to the extent that it is inconsistent with the provision of section 73, it is not saved or deemed to have been made under the Act and has to be adjusted in the light of the provisions of the Act, that is, if it is assessed on the net and not the gross annual lease value after deducting 10% statutory allowances in lieu of costs of repairs and any other account whatever.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 in 1937, and its factory was situated in the State of Kerala. The respondent company was carrying on manufacturing and selling chemicals and was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling chemical products. The respondent was incorporated in the year 1937 in 1937 and the company was incorporated on the same day. The respondent Company was incorporated in 1950, and its business was carried on by the respondent company on its own behalf. The respondent, however, was carrying on a business of manufacturing, and selling chemicals, and was carrying out the business of selling and selling chemical product. The respondent claimed that the stock in trade could only be that which was the subject of trade and that the stock of raw material was not sold in the course of ordinary trading but in a real and commercial sense. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the assessee company was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 1,15,259. The Appellate Tribunal held that the sale was of the entire assets, and that the price represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profit. The Tribunal, however, found that the business had not completely ceased to exist, since the assessee company had been carrying on manufacturing, on behalf of the purchaser, and that, therefore, the amount obtained was only by way of realisation sale and was not liable to tax. The High Court, on reference, held that by the sale no business was done, and that therefore the excess represented a capital receipt. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The sale was of a very small value and the price represented the capital appreciation and did not form part of the realisation of the trading stock. The sale was not a sale in the course oof business. The sale did not amount to a sale in its ordinary course. The sale could not be regarded as a sale in course of business operations. The sale of the chemicals and raw materials was nothing more than a winding up sale. [966 B C] (ii) The sale of chemicals and raw material for match manufacture was nothing more. The sale price represented a payment for the entire business without a separate sale or valuation of this stock in trade for purposes of sale. [ 966 C] (iii) The sale did take place in the courseof business and was not a trading sale. The sale took place in the ordinary course of business. The assessee was carrying on business of manufacturing or selling chemical products and was carrying it on a trading busi ness. The sale therefore was of the whole assets, and the price representing a capital appreciation, not with a view to trading in chemicals and raw goods but to close down the business and to realise the assets. [967 C D] (iv) The sale in the present case was of the very small value of each item, and the sale was not one in the course or for the purpose of carrying on the trade. [968 C] (v) The sale could only be said to be a sale in a commercial sense. It was impossible to infer that the chemicals and the raw materials were sold in the ordinary way of business or that the assessee Company was carrying on any trading busi in the ordinary manner of business or was carrying on an activity which was in connection with the sale of chemicals. [969 C] (vi) The sale took the place in the normal course of business and was, in fact, carried on by a person not only in the ordinary sense of business but also in the ordinary business of that person. [970 C] (vii) The sale is of a small value and it is impossible to infer from the appreciation of capital. [972 C] (viii) The sale must be one which is the subject of business operations, and the assessee company is carrying on a trading activity.
